Public Warning from the Hashimoto Family | 2026

A Warning Against Unsupported Claims of Fujiwara Descent
Before Using Genealogy for Advertising, Elections, or Credibility(intangible assets)

When a company, candidate, organisation, or public figure publishes a genealogy linking itself to an old and prestigious family, readers may assume that it has a long history, elevated status, or special credibility.
That impression can produce advertising and public-relations benefits unavailable to an ordinary business. It may strengthen a brand, attract customers, and reduce part of the advertising expenditure otherwise needed to create the same image.
Anyone who uses genealogy in business, elections, fundraising, religious activity, or organisational promotion should therefore provide verifiable historical evidence supporting that genealogy.

For readers seeking the detailed examination
This page is a simplified introduction. Images of the records, source details, and the full historical analysis appear in the specialist section later on the site.

⚠ Warning: When a company, politician, religious organisation, business, or other body presents an unverified genealogy as “descent from a prestigious family” or “legitimate descent,” and uses it to promote products, services, elections, fundraising, or social credibility, this is not merely the private sharing of a family memory.
Such a statement can create advertising value, brand value, customer appeal, and differentiation from competitors. When the evidence cannot be shown, the claim should either be withdrawn or displayed prominently as an unverified tradition or hypothesis that has not been confirmed by primary historical records.

The Site in Four Points

Read these four points before moving on to the more difficult historical records.

1

An 1874 administrative document records Hashimoto Heisaku as a member of the shizoku class

A document dated 1874 and entitled Karoku Hōkan Negai (Petition for the Surrender of a Hereditary Stipend) records the name of Hashimoto Heisaku, his status as shizoku, and information about his hereditary stipend. Seals belonging to administrative officials can also be seen on the document.

The term shizoku was a status classification used by the Meiji government mainly for former members of the warrior class. It did not by itself rank a person as “upper” or “middle” class.

Among the records concerning Hasshiin Village that have so far been examined, the Hashimoto family appears to have occupied an important position among the village’s shizoku. Any statement that it was the only such family is limited to the surviving records currently confirmed.

2

Records connected with the name “Hashimoto” and the Hasshiin area survive from the Muromachi period

The 1496 Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki (Diary of Daijō-in Temple and Shrine Affairs) contains “Hashimoto” as a separately indexed name. The 1582 Tamon-in Nikki also mentions a man called Hashimoto Yaroku in connection with Hasshin-in.

These records show that the name Hashimoto appeared in diaries and accounts written at the time, rather than only in genealogies compiled centuries later. Whether each person was a direct ancestor of the present Hashimoto family must be examined using additional evidence.

3

A genealogy is not sufficient evidence merely because it has been written down

A family tree may preserve an important tradition. However, genealogies edited in later centuries may lack contemporary records supporting their earliest generations.

This site therefore asks the following questions:

  • Is there a document from the lifetime of the alleged ancestor?
  • Do the dates and places match?
  • Can relationships of parentage, adoption, inheritance, or office be traced?
  • Is there evidence written by an independent third party rather than only by the family itself?
4

Publishing a prestigious genealogy can produce advertising and economic benefits

Descriptions such as “a descendant of the Fujiwara clan” or “heir to a distinguished family” can make readers associate a person or organisation with history, status, and trust. When a business publishes such a claim on its official website, it can distinguish itself from ordinary competitors, strengthen its brand, attract customers, and reduce part of the advertising cost otherwise required to create that image.

A person who uses genealogy in business, elections, or fundraising cannot avoid responsibility simply by saying that the information was only a private family tradition. If an unsupported claim is presented in a way that makes it appear historically established, consumers, voters, business partners, and competing businesses may be disadvantaged. Furthermore, with respect to the terms "shizoku" (士族), "buke" (武家), "samurai" (侍), and other similar expressions: where these are used — not as mere figures of speech, but on the basis of the status or lineage (由緒) of the Hasshiin Hashimoto family or its ancestors — to establish credibility in business or social contexts, the historical documentary grounds for such use will likewise be subject to verification.

⑤

Publicizing a Genealogy Can Create Advertising and Economic Benefits by Enhancing Credibility

Descriptions such as “descendant of a distinguished family” or “descendant of the Fujiwara clan” may give readers an impression of history, prestige, and credibility. When a company or business publishes such claims on its official website or in similar materials, they may differentiate it from other businesses and potentially produce economic benefits through branding, customer acquisition, advertising, and promotion.

Likewise, when genealogy, family background, or historical authority is used in business activities, elections, fundraising, organizational activities, or similar contexts, it is no longer merely a matter of private family tradition. It becomes information capable of influencing the judgment and trust of third parties.

For this reason, when genealogy is used as a basis for social or economic credibility, this website examines whether historical sources exist to support the claim and whether confirmed facts are properly distinguished from inference, tradition, or unverified assertions.

Respecting the Historical Traditions of Former Shizoku and Warrior Families

The concern addressed by this website is not limited to the historical background of the Hashimoto family of Hasshiin. When terms such as “shizoku,” “warrior family,” “samurai,” or other historical statuses and traditions are used by a particular family, company, or organization as a source of historical authority, credibility, branding, or business value without sufficient documentary support, the issue is not unrelated to other former shizoku or warrior families whose own histories can be verified through historical records.

This website does not claim to represent all former shizoku families or their descendants. However, each family has its own history, ancestors, status, and traditions, and we believe that both the wishes of the family itself and the historical facts established by documentary evidence should be respected in the treatment of that history.

This website does not support the use, as established fact, of claims such as “shizoku,” “warrior family,” or “samurai” that may be confused with the historical status or traditions of another family, or that lack sufficient documentary support, when such claims are used for authority, credibility, corporate history, advertising, branding, or other forms of benefit.

This is not an attempt to restrict the use of the words “shizoku,” “warrior family,” or “samurai” themselves. Rather, it is a request that each family's history be respected as its own, and that unverified traditions not be presented in the same manner as historically confirmed facts.

Retrospective Claims of Participation in Another Family's History

The issue addressed by this website is not the relative social status or prestige of a person's ancestry. The issue is the attempt by a third party, without sufficient documentary evidence, to place itself within, or present itself as equivalent to or continuous with, the genealogy, historical status, or traditions of another family that are independently documented by primary sources, on the basis of later traditions, genealogies, family accounts, or similar materials.

Later social or economic success, subsequent fame, or the creation of a large company or organization does not, by itself, provide a basis for retrospectively becoming part of the ancestors, historical status, genealogy, or traditions of another family that existed before that success.

The historically verifiable traditions of a family belong to the history of that family. If a connection is claimed with the ancient or medieval Imperial House, court nobility, warrior families, temples, shrines, or other historical lineages, the claim should be supported by evidence proportionate to its strength, and family tradition, oral tradition, and later genealogies should be clearly distinguished from facts confirmed by independent primary sources.

Where supporting evidence cannot be confirmed, we believe that such matters should not be stated categorically as historical fact. Instead, labels such as “tradition,” “inference,” or “unverified” should be used in a manner appropriate to the strength of the available evidence.

[Source Criticism] How Far Can Shogunate-Compiled Genealogies Be Trusted? — Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Clan Name and the Kansei Chōshū Shokafu

In examining the genealogy of the Hashimoto family of Hasshiin, this website does not treat a later genealogy as sufficient proof by itself. Instead, it gives particular weight to contemporary records and compares genealogical claims with diaries, documentary records, landholding evidence, residential continuity, and other independent sources.

This approach is applied not only to the Hashimoto family, but also to officially compiled genealogies and to the genealogical traditions of historically prominent families.

1. Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Clan Name — From “Fujiwara Ieyasu” to “Minamoto Ieyasu”

When Matsudaira Ieyasu adopted the surname Tokugawa and received the court title of Mikawa-no-kami in 1566, a genealogical precedent was sought that would permit the Tokugawa name to be associated with the Fujiwara clan. Contemporary documentary evidence confirms that Ieyasu was formally styled “Fujiwara Ieyasu” in connection with his court advancement.

Ieyasu later came to use the Minamoto clan name. This change illustrates an important distinction: a historical person’s officially used clan designation does not necessarily constitute proof of biological descent from the remote ancestor associated with that clan name.

Research by historian Fujii Jōji has also examined the surviving documents relating to Ieyasu’s court ranks and appointments. Fujii points out that, in 1645, during the reign of the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu, documents concerning Ieyasu’s earlier appointments were revised or reconstructed.

In particular, Ieyasu’s appointment in 1587 as Sakon'e no Taishō (Captain-General of the Left Division of the Inner Palace Guards) has been examined as a case in which the documentary record was retrospectively reorganized during the early Edo period.

This does not mean that Tokugawa Ieyasu’s biological ancestry itself was literally “rewritten.” Rather, it demonstrates that documents relating to court rank, clan designation, hereditary tradition, and official genealogy must be examined according to when they were created, copied, revised, or reconstructed.

Sources: Fujii Jōji, “Tokugawa Ieyasu no Joi Ninkan” (“Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Appointments to Court Rank and Office”), Shirin, Vol. 101, No. 4, 2018. National Diet Library Search . See also the National Diet Library Collaborative Reference Database discussion concerning Ieyasu’s change from Matsudaira to Tokugawa: NDL Collaborative Reference Database .

2. The Kansei Chōshū Shokafu Is an Essential Historical Source, but Not Automatic Proof of Remote Ancestry

The Kansei Chōshū Shokafu, compiled by the Edo shogunate in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, is one of the most important genealogical collections for the study of daimyō, hatamoto, and other warrior families.

Its historical value is extremely high. However, the compilation relied in substantial part on genealogies, records of service, family traditions, and other materials submitted by the individual warrior houses themselves.

The shogunate did carry out editorial examination and comparison of materials, so the work should not be dismissed as a mere collection of unverified claims. At the same time, the fact that a lineage appears in an officially compiled genealogy does not by itself prove every statement concerning its remote ancestry.

Individual genealogical claims should therefore be compared, wherever possible, with contemporary diaries, court records, temple and shrine documents, administrative records, land records, inscriptions, and other independent evidence.

Sources: The Imperial Household Agency discusses the compilation of major Edo-period genealogical works, including the Kansei Chōshū Shokafu, and the use of information submitted by individual warrior houses: Imperial Household Agency . See also the description of the Kansei Chōshū Shokafu in Cultural Heritage Online: Cultural Heritage Online .

3. Genealogical Fabrication Was Also a Recognized Problem in Early Modern Japan

Genealogical fabrication and retrospective embellishment were not unknown in early modern Japan. Sawada Gennai (1619–1688), for example, became famous in later genealogical criticism for works regarded as fabricated or unreliable.

Later scholars explicitly examined and criticized genealogical works attributed to Sawada. The existence of such criticism is itself significant: early modern genealogies were not necessarily accepted uncritically merely because they appeared old or authoritative.

This does not mean that every genealogy associated with Sawada, or every Edo-period genealogy more generally, should automatically be treated as false. Rather, it demonstrates why the provenance and supporting evidence of each genealogical claim must be examined individually.

Source: Daikeizu Hyōban Shachūshō, a work preserved in the National Diet Library, criticizes genealogical material associated with Sawada Gennai and examines problems in the genealogy of the Rokkaku-Sasaki lineage. National Diet Library Search .

4. Applying the Same Standard to Hasshiin, the Daianji Mukai Lineage, and the Hashimoto Name

The same standard of source criticism must also be applied to the present study of the Hashimoto family.

Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century sources record several persons, family names, and residences relevant to the Hasshiin area. Among them are Chōjitsu (Zenkan-bō / Inaba-kō), who is associated with the Daianji Mukai lineage, a “Hashimoto residence” recorded in 1481, the name “Hashimoto” appearing independently in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki in 1496, and Hashimoto Yairoku and Hashimoto Sama in records from the Tenshō era.

Chōjitsu is not known only from a later genealogy. He appears repeatedly in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, and the General Index to the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki provides numerous references to him across multiple volumes.

The index also connects the designation Inaba-kō with Daianji Mukai Chōjitsu, providing further evidence for the identification of the historical person.

Modern scholarship likewise identifies Chōjitsu in connection with the Daianji Mukai lineage. Katsuramoto Takamasa’s study of the Daianji Mukai group and Koshinji provides an independent modern scholarly discussion based on medieval sources.

Source: Katsuramoto Takamasa, “Ritsu Monks and Local Lords in Late Medieval Yamato: Koshinji and the Daianji Mukai Lineage,” Rakuhoku Shigaku, No. 15. J-STAGE .

5. What Has Not Yet Been Proven

The existence of Chōjitsu as a historical person and his association with the Daianji Mukai lineage are separate questions from whether the later Hashimoto family of Hasshiin descended from him.

At present, no documentary source has yet been identified that demonstrates an uninterrupted parent-child lineage from Chōjitsu to the early modern and modern Hashimoto family of Hasshiin.

Likewise, the “Hashimoto” recorded in 1496 cannot presently be identified with certainty as a direct ancestor of the family of Hashimoto Heisaku.

The same caution applies to the “Hashimoto residence” recorded in 1481 and to Hashimoto Yairoku and Hashimoto Sama in the Tenshō period. These records are important evidence for the historical presence of the Hashimoto name and related residences, but continuity between those records and the modern Hashimoto family must still be demonstrated separately.

Conclusion — Authority Does Not Replace Source Criticism

An officially compiled genealogy may be an extremely valuable historical source, but official compilation alone does not automatically prove remote ancestry. Conversely, the appearance of a person in a contemporary record does not by itself establish a blood relationship with a later family.

This website therefore applies the same evidentiary standard to both prominent historical families and the Hashimoto family.

Wherever possible, the investigation distinguishes between:

  • whether a person is documented in sources produced during his or her lifetime;
  • whether parent-child, adoptive, marital, or other family relationships can be independently confirmed;
  • whether residence, landholding, office, or estate continuity can be demonstrated;
  • whether a family can be traced continuously from the medieval or early modern period into the modern period; and
  • which connections remain hypotheses rather than established facts.

Accordingly, this website does not treat either “official recognition by the Edo shogunate” or “frequent appearance in medieval sources” as sufficient by itself to establish biological descent. Each generational connection must be examined on its own evidence.

HOW TO READ THE RECORDS

Separate What a Record States from How It Is Interpreted

This site broadly classifies the strength of evidence as shown below. The discovery of the same surname does not make every genealogical link “proven.”

Category Meaning Example Proper conclusion
A: Recorded fact A name, date, office, or other fact is actually written in the document A 1582 diary contains the name “Hashimoto Yaroku” The existence of that name at that time can be confirmed
B: Supported by multiple records Separate documents connect the date, location, office, or other details A late-Edo village document and a Meiji administrative document The likelihood of the same individual or family becomes stronger
C: Strong inference Records exist, but identifying the person or relationship requires interpretation Identifying “Hashimoto Chūnagon” with a particular court noble Both the supporting grounds and competing interpretations should be shown
D: Hypothesis or tradition A genealogy or tradition exists, but independent contemporary evidence is insufficient Connecting a gap of several centuries using only a later family tree It should remain a research question rather than be stated as fact
The basic approach of this page
A name appearing in a document, a person being connected with the same locality, and a continuous line of direct descent to the present family are three different questions. This site states what can be confirmed and identifies what remains unknown.
On the Claim that "If You Trace Back to the Medieval Period, Even Ordinary Commoners Connect to the Fujiwara Clan"
Conclusion:
The fact that many people in the distant past could share a common ancestor, and that the same ancestor appears repeatedly across genealogical charts, does not establish that that common ancestor was the Fujiwara clan.

Even if demographic and mathematical models show that many people in the distant past could share a common ancestor, this does not identify any specific individual or clan as that common ancestor.

Therefore, the claim that "if one traces back to the medieval period, most Japanese people — ordinary commoners included — connect to the Fujiwara clan" cannot be derived solely from common-ancestor theory or from the mathematical "collapse" of pedigree charts.

"A common ancestor exists" and
"that common ancestor was the Fujiwara clan" are two separate propositions.

If one claims that a specific individual or family connects to the Fujiwara clan, a concrete genealogical link — through parent-child descent, marriage, adoption (養子), adoptive kinship (猶子), entry into a temple (入室), or other means — connecting that individual or family to the Fujiwara clan must be separately demonstrated.

Regarding Hosshin-in and the Hashimoto Family

This site does not assert a relationship between Hosshin-in / the Hashimoto family and the Fujiwara clan on the basis of the generic argument that "anyone, traced back far enough, connects to the Fujiwara."

Rather, drawing on the Sonpi Bunmyaku, the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, the Tamon-in Nikki, and other historical sources, this site individually verifies actual historical figures, dates, kinship relations, adoptions (養子/猶子), temple entries (入室), and temple-shrine affiliations, and examines, on the basis of primary sources, whether a concrete connection exists between Hosshin-in / the Hashimoto family and the Fujiwara lineage.

Accordingly, this site does not permit
the use of the unsubstantiated generalization that "even ordinary commoners are Fujiwara descendants if traced back far enough" to lend authority to, build credibility for, or promote Hosshin-in / the Hashimoto family, their ancestors, family name, or lineage.

This Site's Basic Position on the Continuity of Other Families

This site holds that publicly discussing an institution is distinct from a third party intervening in the continuity or discontinuation of a specific family, lineage, or individual.

As for the author's own family, there is a genealogical connection to the Imperial Household, reached through several marital relations and originating from a marriage confirmed by koseki (family register) records. However, the author does not believe that such a distant relation gives rise to any special right of intervention concerning individual members of the Imperial Family, or the Imperial House itself.

Likewise, when a third party makes a strong public claim regarding the continuity or discontinuation of a specific family, it is desirable that they clearly identify who is speaking, state their grounds and sources, and take responsibility for their own statements.

PUBLIC WARNING

To Those Who Use Genealogy to Promote a Business, Election Campaign, or Organisation etc.

A small disclaimer saying “there is no conclusive proof” does not give unlimited freedom to advertise prestigious ancestry. A prominent statement such as “descendant of the Fujiwara clan” or “heir to a distinguished lineage” may create an immediate impression of trust, status, and security. A smaller statement added later saying that the claim is unconfirmed may not be sufficient if the overall presentation continues to create a misleading impression.

1. Publishing genealogy can function as advertising and public relations

When genealogy is placed on an official website, company profile, candidate biography, product description, lecture announcement, or fundraising page, it can create the impression that the person or organisation is different from an ordinary business, has a long history, and deserves special trust. This is an intangible brand benefit and can substitute for part of the effect that would otherwise require paid advertising.

How genealogy can be used commercially
Publish a prestigious genealogy
↓
Create an impression of history, status, and credibility
↓
Differentiate the business, attract customers, and increase name recognition
↓
Reduce part of the advertising and public-relations expenditure needed to obtain the same effect

Prestige attached to a family can influence the people around it

The authority or prestige created by a family history does not affect only the person or organisation that directly presents that history. It can also influence how relatives, in-laws, business associates, supporters, and other people connected with the family are viewed.

Even today, parents may tell their children, “That family used to be the village headman,” “That is an old and distinguished family,” or “That family came from the former samurai class.”

When children repeatedly hear such statements, they may naturally grow up with the impression that a particular family has special historical status, social authority, or greater credibility than an ordinary family. In this way, prestige attached to a family can be passed from one generation to the next through the surrounding community.

This means that the effect of genealogy or family status is not limited to direct advertising by the family itself. Once a reputation has become established in the local community, other people may continue to repeat and reinforce it without being asked to do so.

The benefit can also spread to people connected with that family. A relative, an in-law, a business partner, a supporter, or another associated person may be trusted more easily, introduced to influential people, receive greater attention, or obtain business and social opportunities simply because of that connection.

In everyday terms, such a person may simply think, “I was lucky to be connected with that family.” However, if the prestige behind that advantage is based on an inaccurate, exaggerated, or insufficiently verified genealogy, the effect is no longer limited to the person who originally made the claim.

The relevant question is therefore not only who claimed the prestigious ancestry, but also how far the resulting authority and credibility spread, and who benefited from that reputation.

If a claim about an old family, former samurai status, village leadership, or another form of historical prestige continues to produce social or economic advantages in the present day, it is reasonable to ask what evidence supports that claim and how widely its benefits have been distributed.

2. Those who receive the benefit should provide supporting evidence

A genealogy discussed privately within a family is not the same as a genealogy published to society and used to support the credibility of a business or election campaign. A person who obtains a public or commercial benefit from the claim should at least disclose the following:

Matter to be verified Explanation required
Contemporary records Documents produced during the lifetime of the alleged ancestor
Continuity between generations Parentage, adoption, and inheritance should be explained for each generation
Independent third-party records Independent evidence other than a family tree compiled later by the family itself
Gaps in the record Any gap of several centuries should be disclosed rather than concealed

3. Action requested when the evidence cannot be shown

Please take one of the following actions:
  • Remove statements such as “descendant of the Fujiwara clan” or “legitimate heir” when they are presented as established fact.
  • State as prominently as the main claim that the genealogy is an unverified tradition not confirmed by primary records.
  • Separate the genealogy from the promotion of products, services, elections, fundraising, or organisational authority.
  • When evidence is requested, provide verifiable sources rather than only a family tree.

4. Possible legal and social consequences

Publishing a genealogy is not automatically unlawful in every case. However, if it is connected with products, services, or the credibility of a business and gives consumers a materially better impression than the facts justify, rules against misleading representations may become relevant under Japanese law. A representation concerning the quality or content of goods or services may also raise issues under Japan’s Unfair Competition Prevention Act when it is likely to cause misunderstanding.

Unsupported genealogy may also distort competition when it is used to obtain trust or customers that businesses making accurate representations must earn through performance, quality, and paid promotion. It may affect the decisions of consumers, voters, and business partners. This site calls for the disclosure of verifiable evidence, the correction of misleading statements, and the discontinuation of misleading uses.

Legal conclusions depend on the wording, context, purpose, supporting materials, relationship to goods or services, and overall impression created for the audience.

References: Consumer Affairs Agency: Misleading Representations / Japan Patent Office: What Is a Trademark? / Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry: Misleading Indications and the Unfair Competition Prevention Act

TIMELINE

A Timeline of Records Connected with Hasshiin and the Hashimoto Family

This timeline places records spanning approximately six centuries in chronological order. The existence of the records does not automatically prove one continuous line of direct descent. The timeline is a framework for examining how the records may relate to one another.

1415–1427 (Ōei era)
Sanehiro Sōzu and Hasshiin

Record: Sanehiro Sōzu is associated with land and temple administration in Hasshiin.
Significance: This is local historical evidence showing that Hasshiin was connected with central temple and court-aristocratic society.

📚 Local historical source
1456 (Kōshō 2)
Chōjitsu (Zenkambō) signs a written pledge

Record: Chōjitsu’s signature appears on a written pledge signed by people connected with Daijō-in.
Significance: This document helps identify members of the temple organisation at that time. A direct relationship with the Hashimoto family requires separate examination.

📄 Signed document
1491 (Entoku 3)
A record of “Hashimoto Chūnagon”

Record: “Hashimoto Chūnagon” appears as a person associated with a festival at Kasuga Taisha.
Significance: This site is examining whether the name refers to Hashimoto Sanenori, but that identification remains an interpretation requiring further evidence.

🔎 Identification under review
1496 (Meiō 5)
“Hashimoto” in the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki

Record: The diary contains an entry concerning “the Kirino brothers, Saionji, and Hashimoto.”
Significance: The name Hashimoto can be confirmed in a contemporary late-fifteenth-century source. A blood relationship with the present family requires additional evidence.

✅ Recorded in a contemporary source
1582 (Tenshō 10)
Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Sama as people connected with Hasshin-in

Record: The Tamon-in Nikki mentions Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Sama.
Significance: The entries indicate that people bearing the Hashimoto surname performed temple- or shrine-related work around Hasshin-in.

✅ Recorded in a contemporary source
1692 (Genroku 5)
“Hashi-no-in” and “Hashi-no-bō” in an inspection register

Record: Names of temple-related facilities appear in an official inspection register.
Significance: The register is evidence for the local temple organisation, but similarity of names alone cannot establish a connection with the Hashimoto surname.

📚 Related local source
1850 (Kaei 3)
Hashimoto Hyōsaku in a village document

Record: A village petition seeking relief after a poor harvest contains the name Hashimoto Hyōsaku together with wording connected with a village office.
Significance: It indicates that Hashimoto Hyōsaku held a public role in the locality before the 1874 administrative document.

✅ Village document
1874 (Meiji 7)
Hashimoto Hyōsaku in the Karoku Hōkan Negai

Record: An administrative document records Hashimoto Hyōsaku’s shizoku status and hereditary stipend.
Significance: This is one of the most important official sources for identifying the Hashimoto family from the closing years of the Edo period into the early Meiji period.

WARNING

Do Not Use Unsupported Genealogy as Authority, Advertising, or Electoral Promotion

Public Warning from the Hashimoto Family Do not use claims such as “descendant of the Fujiwara clan” or “legitimate descendant of a prestigious family,” when unsupported by primary historical records, to promote a business, product, service, election campaign, fundraising activity, religious activity, or organisational credibility.
Publishing such a genealogy can produce advertising value, brand value, customer appeal, competitive differentiation, and savings in advertising expenditure. Once those benefits are sought or obtained, it is not sufficient to describe the claim as merely a private family tradition.
📣

Publishing genealogy can operate as advertising

A prestigious genealogy on an official website or in a company profile can make an organisation appear older, more distinguished, and more trustworthy than an ordinary business. That impression can attract customers and reduce part of the cost of paid promotion.

👥

Consumers, voters, and business partners may be misled

Readers may transfer the prestige of the alleged genealogy to the person, company, product, policy, or organisation itself. Unsupported authority can interfere with rational decision-making.

🏪

It can distort competition with businesses making accurate representations

An ordinary business must build trust through performance, quality, and advertising expenditure. Obtaining trust through unsupported genealogy can create unfair competitive conditions.

⚖️

Provide the evidence or correct the representation

Anyone using genealogy for social or economic benefit should provide verifiable primary records. When those records cannot be produced, remove the claim or state clearly that it is an unverified tradition or hypothesis.

Response policy of this site
When this site identifies unsupported genealogy being used for advertising, elections, fundraising, or the acquisition of social credibility, it may consider preserving the public representation, requesting the supporting evidence, seeking correction or discontinuation of the claim, and publishing counter-evidence where appropriate.
The Ongoing Significance of This Public Verification Record
The verification content published on this site is not limited to claims made at any single point in time. Should the same or a related genealogy be used again in the future in advertising, public relations, election campaigns, or other efforts to build credibility, this record may be referenced as a prior verification. Because claims regarding genealogy can be inherited and reused across generations, each generation's claims require independent confirmation based on primary sources.

📌 Purpose and Position of This Site

This site publishes a record of historical-source verification regarding the genealogy of the Hashimoto family.

The views presented on this site are academic considerations based on primary historical sources and independent third-party documents, and are not intended to criticize or deny any specific individual or organization.

Regarding the authenticity of this genealogy, there are aspects that cannot be definitively confirmed due to the limitations of the available historical sources. Readers are encouraged to independently evaluate the evidence and reasoning presented on this site.

We welcome academic dialogue from anyone who has opinions or counter-evidence regarding the content of this site.

Introduction

In recent years, there have been cases in which certain individuals, including public figures, have claimed to be "descendants of the Fujiwara clan" without presenting clear historical evidence (genealogical claims for which historical verification is difficult to confirm are occasionally observed).

What this site takes issue with is not mere self-proclamation, but the act of using genealogical claims that lack historical evidence to gain authority, economic benefit, or social benefit. Such cases call for verification from a historiographical standpoint, while also constituting real harm from which specific beneficiaries exist.
Such unfounded claims are occasionally used for a variety of purposes, including the legitimization of authority(intangible assets), the enhancement of social reputation, the exercise of influence, and business promotion or the improvement of corporate image.

There are cases in which unfounded genealogical claims are spread by third parties, forming a structure of beneficiaries.

Under civil law, "inheritance" is not limited to property. For public figures and others, intangible assets such as "lineage," "family standing," and "bloodline" are passed down across generations (comprehensive succession, issues of money laundering, and illegitimate capital origins), forming the basis of social credibility, electoral strength, and influence.

In the 1970s, through the research of Toyoda Takeshi and Ōta Ryō, as well as the spread of the "Comprehensive Dictionary of Surnames and Family Lineages" (Seishi Kakei Daijiten), the recognition that "90% of genealogies compiled during the Edo period are fabricated" became an established consensus among specialists.

As the Hashimoto family, connected to the historical genealogy of the Fujiwara clan (not necessarily limited to the Kan'in line — a mixed lineage is also possible, and descent from the Nagazane line is also possible, though the work carried out by Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Heisaku is consistent with one another), we would like to present our views on this situation and share our basic approach to discussing genealogy.

📌 On the Degree of Certainty of Evidence for the Claims on This Site

The historical sources and claims presented on this site are classified into the following three tiers according to the degree of certainty of the evidence.
The same classification is also indicated at the beginning of each section. Readers are asked to refer to this classification and independently judge the reliability of each claim.

✅ Confirmed FactIndependently confirmed by primary historical sources and administrative documents

  • ✅【Added May 2026 – Confirmation of Status through Comparison】Status Comparison with Ochi Taibei — The Fact That Even a Prominent Villager Was a Commoner

    The contents of the "Biography of Ochi Taibei" (Ochi Taibei-den), which describes village officials of Hosshi-in and its surrounding area, are not inconsistent with the Hashimoto family's standing within the village. The rank of village headman (shōya) recorded in the Biography of Ochi Taibei is lower than that of Hashimoto Heisaku, and Ochi Taibei himself was classified not as shizoku (former samurai class) but as heimin (commoner) during the Meiji period. This fact is confirmed by the absence of Ochi Taibei's name in the same shizoku records held at the Nara Prefectural Library and Information Center that also hold Hashimoto Heisaku's petition for the return of his hereditary stipend.

    Ochi was the family name of a powerful medieval warrior band in Yamato Province (a distinguished lineage that appears frequently in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki as a rival of the Tsutsui clan), and even a prominent villager bearing this name and having a surviving biography was classified as a commoner in the Meiji period. In contrast, Hashimoto Heisaku is the only person in Hosshi-in village recognized as shizoku. This contrast — that a prominent villager bearing the name of a distinguished lineage was a commoner, while only the Hashimoto family held shizoku status — is corroborated through parallel verification by third-party administrative records, confirming that the Hashimoto family's standing was exceptional, clearly surpassing the ordinary class of village notables.

    This contrast reinforces the proof of absence — that "the Hashimoto family was the only shizoku in Hosshi-in village" — with a concrete comparative example, namely that "even a prominent villager with a specific name and biography was a commoner." It concretely substantiates the fact that the high-ranking stipend of 19% of the Ichijō-in territory's hereditary income, as shown in the petition for return of hereditary stipend, stood out prominently within the village.

    📚 Source: Biography of Ochi Taibei; Shizoku Records of the Nara Prefectural Library and Information Center (same holding institution as Hashimoto Heisaku's petition for return of hereditary stipend; related to Film ID 811013157)
    Certainty: ✅ Confirmed Fact (status comparison confirmed by third-party administrative records)

  • ✅【Most Important Additional Confirmation from "Botan to Fuji" (Peony and Wisteria): A History of Kōfuku-ji as Seen from the Sekke Monzeki Families, Vol. 3】

    🔴 【Most Important New Discovery】The 7th Abbot of Daijō-in, Jisshin, "Styled Himself Hosshi-in"

    This document states explicitly on page 103: "The seventh [abbot], Jisshin, was the son of Konoe Motomichi... In the first year of Kōgen (1256), he passed away. He styled himself Hosshi-in (per the 'Order of Succession')."

    The fact that an abbot of Daijō-in, a direct descendant of the Fujiwara Hokke regental family (Konoe line), personally adopted "Hosshi-in" as his own name demonstrates that the name Hosshi-in was not merely a place name or facility name, but a title personally identified with the abbots of Daijō-in who were sons of the regental family.
    This stands alongside the case, previously presented on this site, of "Ryōshin's title of 'Go-Hosshin-in,' the 15th abbot of Ichijō-in," as the highest-level evidence of the personal bond between Hosshi-in and the regental family.

    Jisshin had been abbot of Ichijō-in, but on the 23rd day of the 6th month of the 4th year of Kenchō (1252), he assumed the position at Daijō-in concurrently. In the 6th year of Kenchō (1254), he built the Jizō Hall of Fukuchi-in.

    The fact that a son of the regental family directly descended from the Konoe house (Fujiwara Hokke) used "Hosshi-in" as his personal title conclusively demonstrates that, by the mid-13th century, Hosshi-in was a central institution identified personally with the abbot of Daijō-in.     📌 【The Evidentiary Significance of "Styled Himself Hosshi-in"】

    Combining the evidence previously presented on this site with this new discovery shows that the name "Hosshi-in" was integrated with the regental family and Daijō-in at the following three levels:

    ① Institutional level: Hosshi-in functioned as the azukaridokoro (deputy administrator) of Yokota-shō, a Daijō-in territory (Sanka-inge shō, 1463, etc.)
    ② Systemic level: Grant fields (kyūden) and institutional service (inji) from Hosshi-in to the Daijō-in residence (Zenjō-in) (Kōza Nihon Shōen, Vol. 7)
    ③ Personal level: Jisshin, the 7th abbot of Daijō-in (son of Konoe Motomichi, Fujiwara Hokke), "styled himself Hosshi-in" (this document, 1256)

    Furthermore, combined with the title "Go-Hosshin-in" held by Ryōshin (15th abbot of Ichijō-in, previously presented on this site), it is confirmed that the names "Hosshi-in" and "Hosshin-in" were both used as personal titles by abbots of both Daijō-in and Ichijō-in, corroborating through multiple independent pieces of evidence that Hosshi-in was an institution personally connected to the very center of the Kōfuku-ji monzeki (princely abbot) system.

    📚 Source: Botan to Fuji: A History of Kōfuku-ji as Seen from the Sekke Monzeki Families, Vol. 3, p. 103

  • ✅【Added May 2026 – Most Important Confirmation】Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho, Vol. 124, "Kōfuku-ji Inge-den" (p. 78, entry on Tōhoku-in) — Independent Confirmation of "Keien. Hōin. Resided at Tōhoku-in. Styled Hosshi-in."

    In the entry on Tōhoku-in in the "Kōfuku-ji Inge-den" in Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho, Vol. 124, it is recorded: "Keien. Hōin [Dharma Seal rank]. [Per the] Order of the Hossō Sect Dharma Lineage. Resided at Tōhoku-in. Son of Ise Ason. Styled Hosshi-in. In the 3rd year of Kenryaku, age 20, [performed] the Yuima-e ryūgi [debate]. In the 2nd year of Jōkyū, age 22, [served as] lecturer of the same assembly." This independently confirms, through an official Kōfuku-ji record (Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho), that Keien, a Hōin who held the title "Hosshi-in," resided at Tōhoku-in.

    In the same text, it is recorded: "Jissu. Hōin Gon-Daisōzu [Provisional Great Archbishop rank]. Son of Grand Minister Kinsuke (Saionji). In the 7th year of Kenchō, age 18, [performed] the kengaku ryūgi [study debate]." This corroborates, through the independent primary source of the Kōfuku-ji Inge-den, the previously confirmed fact on this site that "Jissu, [recorded in] Sonpi Bunmyaku Vol. 6, [held the position of] Hōin at Tōhoku-in of Kōfuku-ji." The institutional connection whereby Jissu, son of Saionji Kinsuke (the base point of Hashimoto Sanetoshi's lineage), belonged to Tōhoku-in as the successor to Keien (who styled himself Hosshi-in) is confirmed through the Order of the Hossō Sect Dharma Lineage.

    The place name/title "Hosshi-in" was used by Keien at Tōhoku-in during the Kenryaku era (around 1213), which is later than the oldest record from the 2nd year of Jōtoku (1098). This can be interpreted as meaning that Hosshi-in (the place) existed first, and that Keien, having resided there, adopted it as his personal title. This independently confirms, through a primary source, that the institutional origin of the estate house known as Hosshi-in traces back to the Hossō sect Dharma lineage of Tōhoku-in at Kōfuku-ji in the early Kamakura period.

    📚 Source: Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho, Vol. 124, "Kōfuku-ji Inge-den" (National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. 353-10), pp. 78–79

    📌【Supplementary Confirmation】In the same text (image 1000032308.jpg), it is recorded: "Zōchō-in-den Kakuyo, Shūnan-in Kōson. [These are] those entrusted with sealed matters." This records that Shūnan-in Kōson (teacher of Ichijō-in Kakukei and Daijō-in Jinken, during the Tenbun era) was appointed as manager of the sacred texts, diaries, and other materials at Tōhoku-in, where Keien (who styled himself Hosshi-in), confirmed on the previous page, had resided. It is also recorded that "Tōrin-in. Passed down through several generations. A follower temple of Daijō-in... having no adopted successor, its temple estate was attached to Shōrin-in, [with its] hall combined into a single building [under] Daijō-in," recording that after the line of Tōrin-in (a Daijō-in follower temple) died out, its estate was attached to Shōrin-in. This independently confirms, through the Kōfuku-ji Inge-den, the institutional chain linking Daijō-in, Tōrin-in, and Shōrin-in.

  • Hashimoto Heisaku's shizoku status as established by the 1874 (Meiji 7) "Petition for Return of Hereditary Stipend" (held at the Nara Prefectural Library and Information Center; bears the registered seals of two deputy village heads)

    ✅【Confirmed Fact】Continued Confirmation of Family Standing through the Marriage Network from the Meiji Period Onward

    Family register documents (koseki tōhon) confirm the following marriages in the children's generation of Hashimoto Heisaku (the sole shizoku of Hosshi-in village, per the 1874 petition for return of hereditary stipend):

    • Hashimoto Heisaku's eldest son × Baba Gihei's eldest daughter
    • Hashimoto Heisaku's second son × Baba Gihei's second daughter

    The fact that the Hashimoto and Baba families formed a double marriage alliance — eldest son to eldest daughter, and second son to second daughter — indicates not a personal match but an institutional alliance between families that mutually recognized one another as of equal standing.

    Furthermore, the second son of Baba Yoshioki (Gihei's second son) married the president of Momotani Juntendō, and the Momotani family (children of Baba Yoshioki) intermarried with the Kanbe-Honda family, holders of the viscount (shishaku) rank. The fact that the Momotani family, an emerging merchant house, sought connections both to the Hashimoto family's marriage network (shizoku of the Fujiwara lineage) and to a viscount family functions as indirect evidence that the Hashimoto family's standing as "shizoku of the Fujiwara lineage" was actually recognized externally even during the Meiji and Taishō periods.

    The fact that this recognition of status remained effective during the Meiji and Taishō periods reinforces the substantiveness of the high-ranking Edo-period stipend of 19% of the Ichijō-in territory's hereditary income that formed the basis of that status. In combination with the medieval records confirmed in the index of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki — "Baba (resident of Heguri, under the control of the Mitsune [party], father of En'kanbō)" and "Baba Kaison (Lord of Harima)" — this suggests the possibility that the relationship between the Hashimoto and Baba families continued from the early modern into the modern period.

    📚 Source: Family register documents; Meiji–Taishō period marriage records (held by the Hashimoto family)
    Certainty: ✅ Confirmed Fact (directly confirmed by family register documents)

    • 📌【Corroborating Record – Retrospective Confirmation of Judicial Authority – Added May 2026】In the "Petition Concerning the Repair of the Hosshi-in Pond Sluice Gate between Nakajō and Hosshi-in" (Naka-jō, Hosshi-in ike-ban-hi fushin kōjō, c. 1670, 10th year of Kanbun), contained in the Yamatokōriyama City Historical Materials Collection, p. 483 (National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. 216.5-Y539y), it is recorded that Hosshi-in village (referred to in the text as "Hashinoin village") brought a water-dispute lawsuit against Nakajō village before the "Ojimon" (the Temple Gate, i.e., Ichijō-in or Daijō-in), and that Hōshō-in-dono and Sankaku-in-dono traveled to Yokota village to render a direct ruling. The addressee was "the magistrates of Nakabō" (the Nakabō bugyō of Kōfuku-ji), and this independently confirms, through a village-held document, that the judicial and administrative authority of the estate house (inge) over Hosshi-in village continued to function institutionally even in the latter half of the 17th century. Combined with the administrative documents addressed to "Ichijō-in Miya-sama" from the 18th year of Kyōhō (1733) and the 9th year of Meiwa (1772) (pp. 460 and 463), the final adjudicatory authority of the estate house over Hosshi-in village is continuously corroborated by five independent documents spanning at least from the latter half of the 17th century to the latter half of the 18th century.     This is recorded, and the official report from the Nakajō village side records that a "tax-exempt tract" (muneigu-chi) existed within Hosshi-in village. The existence of tax-exempt land can be interpreted institutionally as the early-modern continuation of an institutional relationship of subordination to the estate house (i.e., exempted fields and grant fields).   • ✅ Confirmed Fact 1590

    Tamon-in Diary — Named Record of Hashimoto no Sama, a Shrine Priest (Negi)

    The entry for the 11th day of the 5th month of the 18th year of Tenshō (1590) records: "The shrine priest (negi) known as Hashimoto no Sama was also a relatively young man; he suddenly fell ill with a strange sickness and died. He was a man who had mastered Shinto, and this too is a great loss for the jinin [shrine attendants]." In the personal diary of the Kōfuku-ji monk Eishun — who had no relation to the Hashimoto family — a Kasuga Shrine negi (a ranked Shinto priest) bearing the Hashimoto surname is independently recorded as a person of jinin (shrine-attendant) status. The same entry also records, immediately before this, the death of the jinin Magozaemon (aged 66), placing the two side by side, which indicates that Hashimoto no Sama held a jinin-level position within the organization associated with the Dainagon-dono (the abbot of Ichijō-in). This is a continuous piece of local evidence appearing just eight years after the 1582 (Tenshō 10) record of Hashimoto Yaroku.

    Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 4, Book 36 (entry for the 11th day of the 5th month, Tenshō 18)
    National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. 640-324 / pp. 223–226

  • ✅ Confirmed Fact 1590

    Tamon-in Diary — Record of Goods Sent from Hosshin-in (Hosshi-in)

    The same volume (entry for the 25th day of the 5th month, Tenshō 18) records: "Bean-and-walnut mochi came to us from Hosshin-in." This records that Hosshin-in (Hosshi-in) sent bean and walnut mochi to Tamon-in, providing evidence that it continued into the Tenshō era not merely as an administrative name but as a functioning institution capable of exchanging material goods. Combined with the 1567 (Eiroku 10) record of a loan from the treasury office (nandokoro), noted below, two independent primary sources corroborate the continued existence of Hosshi-in from 1567 to 1590.

    Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 4, Book 36 (entry for the 25th day of the 5th month, Tenshō 18)
    National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. 640-324

  • ✅ Confirmed Fact 1590

    Tamon-in Diary — Record of Ichijō-in Directly Overseeing Treasury Office Personnel

    The entry for the 14th day of the 5th month in the same volume states explicitly: "This is not a nandokoro [treasury office post] by agreement of the temple as a whole, but a nandokoro appointed directly by Ichijō-in." Through the handling of a specific personnel matter, the source confirms that the nandokoro post in question belonged not to a post established by consensus of Kōfuku-ji as a whole, but to Ichijō-in's own independent chain of command. Furthermore, the entry for the last day of the month also records: "The nandokoro of the former Jōkō-in, at Yayada-hon, was assigned to Konzō-in by order of the Dainagon-dono," an actual instance of the Dainagon-dono (the abbot of Ichijō-in) exercising the authority to appoint nandokoro officials. This is an independent source that institutionally corroborates that the nandokoro of Hosshi-in, to which the Hashimoto family belonged, was likewise positioned within this direct chain of command under Ichijō-in.

    Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 4, Book 36 (entries for the 14th day of the 5th month and the last day of the month, Tenshō 18)
    National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. 640-324

  • Tenshō 18 (1590)

    Hashimoto no Sama and Hosshin-in — Multiple Independent Records in the Tamon-in Diary

    The entry for the 5th month, 11th day records by name a shrine priest (negi) called "Hashimoto no Sama" as a Kasuga Shrine jinin-status figure (described as a ranked Shinto priest who had mastered Shinto). The entry for the 25th day of the same month records that Hosshin-in (Hosshi-in) sent goods to Tamon-in. The entries for the 14th day and the last day of the month record a concrete instance of Ichijō-in directly overseeing nandokoro personnel appointments. Eight years after the Yaroku record (1582), this corroborates from multiple angles both the continued local presence of the Hashimoto family centered on Hosshi-in and its institutional bond with Ichijō-in.

This coincides with the period during which Kōjin, also known as Senken-bō (1516–1580), resided at Nishi-Hosshi-in, corroborating the institutional continuity of Hosshi-in in the late medieval period.

    ✅ Confirmed Fact Added May 2026 – Original text of primary source confirmed

    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11, p. 26 (entry for the 1st day of the 3rd month, 5th year of Meiō, 1496)
    ——Record of the 25th Memorial Service for Nishinotōin Zenni; Direct Confirmation of the Original Text Regarding the "Hashimoto" Yūshi

    ◆ Original Text (p. 26, relevant passage on the left-hand page)

    This is the twenty-fifth memorial for Nishinotōin Zenni. Born in the 2nd year of Kōryaku, kanoe-saru [1380], she passed away on the first day of the third month of the fourth year of Bunmei [1472], at the age of ninety-three. She was the mother of Ryōjū, Abbot of Takenouchi Monzeki, Tendai Zasu, and Jusangō. The Great Archbishop of San-Okazaki and Myōtō-shū, Abbot of Kenpuku-ji, were also her sons by the same mother, three in all. The Kirino brothers, Nishi-sonoji, and Hashimoto became her yūshi and paid respects to Go-Kōzei-in-dono; I personally took full charge of their upbringing to adulthood. She had the Lotus Sutra recited in its entirety by Kyōmyō, and various memorial rites, including a relic (shari) service, were performed on her behalf.

    📚 Source: Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11, pp. 26–27 (entry for the 1st day of the 3rd month, Meiō 5)

    ◆ Evidentiary Significance

    • The original text confirms that the yūshi relationship was established before 1472, and the primary source directly proves that identification with Hashimoto Kinnatsu (who became Sangi in 1482) is chronologically impossible.

    • The editorial judgment of the General Index, Personal Names, in listing entry ⑪26 "Hashimoto" as an independent entry distinct from both Hashimoto Kinnatsu and Hashimoto Junsei, is supported at the primary-source level by this confirmation of the original text.
    • Combined with the fact that neither Shimizudani Sanehisa (index Vols. 1, 4, 8) nor Hashimoto Kinnatsu (index Vols. 8, 9, 10) appears in Vol. 11, it is established from the structure of the index that "Hashimoto" in entry ⑪26 is unrelated to the Shimizudani line as well.

In the context of the continuous record "Vol. 7 p. 124 (1480), Jōjin-in Myōshun-bō Junmori → Vol. 11 p. 96 (1497), Hashimoto Junmori (Tsutsui retainer)," the same index — together with the Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei ("Jōjin-in Kōsen held the position of guardian to the Tsutsui clan") — independently confirms the historical background of Jōjin-in functioning as the Tsutsui clan's guardianship institution.

✅ [Original Text Confirmed — Confirmed Fact] Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 6 (8th month, 22nd–25th days, Bunmei 7) — Confirmation of the Original Text of "Jōsei Sōzu Nari, Hosshin-in Jū Nari" and the Source-Critical Significance of the Surrounding Entries

From the entry for the 8th month of Bunmei 7 (1475) in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 6, held in the National Diet Library Digital Collections (call number 210.46-D18-T), the statement "Jōsei sōzu nari, Hosshin-in jū nari" ("Jōsei is a sōzu and resides at Hosshin-in"), cited on this site as a confirmed fact, has been directly verified against the original text. The full text of the relevant passage and related entries is given below, together with an analysis of its source-critical significance.

◆ Original Text (Entries for the 22nd–25th Days of the 8th Month, Bunmei 7)
English rendering:

22nd day. Rain.
Item: I personally conducted a rehearsal for the kōmon [lecture-and-debate] session.
Item: Regarding the arrival and provisioning of the lecture-masters for the Yuima-e [Vimalakīrti Assembly], detailed instructions were sent to Kenshū, that the matter be duly calculated and considered; the messenger was Senshin. In particular, regarding the disbursement records for the examiner from another temple, orders were given to Shōrin-in, which summoned him.
23rd day.
Item: Kakuin (Zenjō-bō, 15 years old) entered the discipleship. Jitsugyō Hosshi accompanied him, and through the Dainagon Sōzu it was reported that he is the son of Asahi, a close attendant, and the yūshi [adopted heir] of Furuichi Taneie. On the recommendation of his teacher Jōsei — a sōzu, who resides at Hosshin-in — [he was admitted].
Item: I paid a visit to Jōjū-in.
Item: Regarding the Saho-ta myō, various instructions were given by Kun'ei; it was first decided that the annual tribute should be delivered to the myōshu of the Ichijōin side. This is most fortunate; the particulars arrived last evening. In particular, regarding the dispute between myself and Ichijōin, since it arose among the ranks of heavenly demons, I have reported the details in a letter to His Excellency the Udaijin.
24th day.
Item: I personally conducted a rehearsal for the kōmon session, [and performed] the Jizō dharma-offering.
Item: A letter arrived from Ichijōin; the dispute is said to be an inconceivable matter.
Item: Regarding the annual tribute of the Uda-Taguchi side, since Keiei had unlawfully seized last year's portion, various exchanges took place and a document of release was issued and collected. Regarding the annual tribute of Uda-Kuroiwa and the Seki-shin matter, the Tanibō side is pressing for it; it should not be accepted, and I have accordingly requested that this be duly reported. With trepidation and respect.
 8th month, 24th day. Sealed by Keiei.
 To the Reverend Gyōzen.
Item: It is said that Shungen, a junior lecturer-candidate, has passed away.
25th day.

* "Kadō" [價都] is a variant orthography of "sōzu" [僧都]. Reproduced as in the original. Source: Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 6 (National Diet Library Digital Collections, call number 210.46-D18-T)

◆ Contribution to Confidence Level and Overall Assessment

Through this confirmation of the original text, item ① of the description of Jōsei (Hosshin-in, Kusuba Nyūdō) — presented on this site as "confirmed by three independent sources" — namely the main text of Vol. 6, "Jōsei sōzu nari, Hosshin-in jū nari," has been independently verified against the original held in the National Diet Library Digital Collections. The accuracy of the citation ("kadō" as a variant orthography of "sōzu") has also been confirmed, and this third-party examination corroborates that this site's descriptions are faithful to the primary sources.

In addition, the operational example of the yūshi institution, the tribute-management structure with Ichijōin at its apex, and the kōmon network, all recorded in this same Bunmei 7 (1475) entry, serve as circumstantial evidence reinforcing this site's overall institutional argument — functioning as medieval precedents for the 1496 "Hashimoto" yūshi record (Vol. 11) and for the early-modern administrative structure of Hosshi-in Village shown in the History of Yamato Kōriyama City.

That is, named residents and associated figures of Nishi-Hosshi-in other than Kōjin are recorded in multiple independent documents, reinforcing the conclusion that the in-ke was not a temporary base of activity for a single individual, but an institutional entity whose personnel activity was continuously recorded.

Furthermore, the continuous record of Gyōkō (Nishi-in Bōzu) across 9 entries, paralleling the "political contest over the Nishi-Hosshi-in goshi office" in Daiei 2 (1522) (Shiryō Sōran, Vol. 9), shows that the office of bōzu at Nishi-in (Nishi-Hosshi-in) was continuously registered as an institutional post even in the Daijōin diary catalog. This is consistent with the office system of the in-ke continuing to function under the institutional definition of "appointed from the ryōke" (Meiō 8 / 1499).

14th day.
Item: Hirashimizu Mikawa is said to have passed away the day before yesterday. During this time, Niiki-no-shō and other monzeki territories had fallen into disorder from afar, and so, on behalf of the temple, [his] name was confined at the Five Shrines and Seven Halls; this is [regarded as] divine punishment.

15th day.
Item: Kakuin came to report, offering congratulations. He further reported that, regarding the matter of Hirashimizu's name, it should now be withdrawn; I gave my consent to this. Tomorrow it is to be conveyed to Ritsushi Keiei; this is truly a fortunate matter through the divine authority and sincerity [of the shrine].

17th day.
Item: Sōsei of Gyōjō-bō submitted a petition sealed by the Shōjisshi [Ten Minor Masters]; five sheets of dove-gray [silk], conveyed through the mediation of Keishun-hō.

    ✅ [Confirmation of Institutional Background from History of Medieval Garden Culture (Nara National Cultural Properties Research Institute Bulletin, No. 6)]

    This document details the founding history of Daijōin monzeki and Zenjō-in, and reinforces the historical basis for the institutional chain already cited on the site: "Hosshin-in → Daijōin → Zenjō-in."

    Date Confirmed Content Source Confidence
    Before Kōhei 1 (1058) Zenjō-in was founded by Jōgen, Junior Sōzu of the Rank of Gon (Asuka Sōzu, d. December 1058), "son of Ōkurakyō Fujiwara no Kanesada."
    Jōgen subsequently transferred the administration of Zenjō-in to his disciple Daijōin Raijitsu, after which the administration of Zenjō-in was held concurrently by successive heads of Daijōin monzeki.
    This confirms that Zenjō-in was a facility founded by a monk of Fujiwara descent (Jōgen) and subsequently inherited by Daijōin.
    The record already cited on the site — "a two-tan stipend field from Hosshin-in to the officiants of Zenjō-in (the Gosho)" (Kōza Nihon Shōen 7) — can thus be understood as institutional service to this Fujiwara-founded Zenjō-in.     		History of Medieval Garden Culture (Nara National Cultural Properties Research Institute Bulletin, No. 6)
    Section 2, "The Position and Architectural Overview of Daijōin Monzeki"     		✅ Established
    Kanji 2 (1088) Ryūzen, the first head of Daijōin monzeki, founded Daijōin at the site of Ryūge-in (present-day Nara Prefectural Government Office).
    Ryūzen is recorded as "said to be the son of either Fujiwara no Masakane, Junior General of the Left, or Fujiwara no Masakane, Assistant Captain of the Left Palace Guards — a member of a distinguished family."
    This confirms, via an academic report from the Nara National Cultural Properties Research Institute, that Daijōin monzeki was administered from its very founding by a member of a distinguished Fujiwara family.

    Jishō 4 (1180) Daijōin was damaged in Taira no Shigehira's attack on Nara.

    The record already cited on the site — "a two-tan stipend field for the officiants of the Zenjō-in Gosho (provided from Hosshin-in-shō)" — presupposes this system, established after 1180, whereby Zenjō-in functioned as Daijōin's Gosho, confirming the institutional basis for Hosshin-in's role as a facility in service to Daijōin's direct residence.     Sanehiro (field contractor, early 15th century onward) → Giin (head administrator, until his death in 1466) → Sadakiyo petitions for restoration (1469) → rejected as a "borrowed residency"

    This suggests that after Giin's death (1466), the position of head administrator became vacant, and that Furuichi Inei recommended Sadakiyo as successor to his uncle Giin, a recommendation that Daijō-in rejected — a structure that can be derived from the index.

    [Most Important] Scholarly Confirmation that the Establishment of Hosshin-in's Yokota-shō Estate Rested on the Authority of Daijōin Abbot Jinzen (Son of Fujiwara no Morozane)

    Independent third-party scholarship confirms that the basis on which Hosshin-in's territory (Yokota-shō) was established as in-ke (院家) land was the authority of Daijōin Abbot Jinzen (尋禅) — son of Regent Fujiwara no Morozane, a direct-line descendant of the Fujiwara Hokke regental house.
    This provides, for the first time, a specific named individual (Jinzen = son of Fujiwara no Morozane) behind the previously cited thesis by Yasuda Jirō (already referenced on this site) that Hosshin-in's territory was "granted as in-ke land through the founder's (hongan) initiative at the time of Hosshin-in's establishment."

    This is the same genealogical context already noted on this site in "Botan to Fuji" (牡丹と藤, Vol. 3) — "Jinpan was the son of Regent Fujiwara no Morozane" — and confirms, through multiple independent scholarly sources, that Hosshin-in's territory was established through the father–son relationship between the Daijōin abbot and Fujiwara no Morozane.     		"For example, in the case of Hosshin-in's Yokota-shō, briefly mentioned earlier, the Daijōin abbot later came to concurrently hold the position of in-ke abbot, thereby forming part of the broader Daijōin domain — but the very establishment of the estate as Hosshin-in's territory in the first place rested on the authority of Jinzen (son of Fujiwara no Morozane), the Daijōin abbot, suggesting that the systematization of in-ke institutions was already underway behind the establishment of in-ke landholdings." p. 568 ✅ Confirmed

    Scholarly Confirmation that Yokota-shō Was "Hereditarily Transmitted" Within Hosshin-in

    Independent third-party scholarship confirms that Yokota-shō (Hosshin-in's territory) was land transmitted hereditarily from master to disciple within Hosshin-in. This is consistent with the "Record of Successive Transmission" (代々相承目六) already cited on this site (from the Fukui Prefecture Local History Series, "Hosshin-in's successive transmission").     		"Ein's Yokota-shō was land hereditarily transmitted within Hosshin-in." p. 564 ✅ Confirmed
    Scholarly Confirmation that "Hosshin-in as Landholder" and "Ein (the Individual) as Landholder" Were Institutionally Interchangeable

    Confirms an institutional structure in which the landholding rights of Hosshin-in as an in-ke institution and the landholding rights of its individual abbot (Ein) were "interchangeable in expression." This provides institutional grounding for the previously cited fusion of abbot and institution — "Jisshin styled himself Hosshin-in" (7th Daijōin abbot, from "Botan to Fuji," already cited on this site).     		"Regarding Hosshin-in's Yokota-shō estate, the lord Ein stated on one occasion, 'the landholder is Hosshin-in,' and on another, 'the landholder is Ein' — showing that the landholding (jinushi) rights of a temple monk as lord were interchangeable in expression with those of the in-ke institution." p. 564 ✅ Confirmed
    Scholarly Confirmation that In-ke Landholdings Generally Originated from "Grants by a Founding Patron (Hongan)"

    Kawabata's thesis independently supports Yasuda Jirō's argument (already cited on this site) that Hosshin-in's territory was "granted as in-ke land through the founder's initiative at the time of its establishment." Kawabata cites Yasuda's point approvingly as "an important observation."     		"Based on this case and on his reconstruction of Daijōin's core founding estates, Yasuda makes the important observation that the general origin of in-ke landholdings lies in grants entrusted by a founding patron (hongan)." p. 563 ✅ Confirmed

    📌 [Significance of the Earliest-Confirmed Human Link Between Hosshin-in and the Fujiwara Hokke Line]

    Kawabata's thesis (p. 568) establishes that the founding of Hosshin-in's Yokota-shō territory rested on "the authority of Daijōin Abbot Jinzen (son of Fujiwara no Morozane)", reinforcing the site's overall argument for a human link between Hosshin-in and the Fujiwara clan, as follows:

    Late 11th to early 12th century: Establishment of Hosshin-in's Yokota-shō territory ← by the authority of Daijōin Abbot Jinzen (son of Fujiwara no Morozane, Fujiwara Hokke line) (Kawabata thesis, p. 568, primary source)
    Mid-12th century: The seal of the "Western Hosshin-in" institution is affixed to a work authored by Kakuken (覚憲, son of Fujiwara no Michinori) (Catalog of Calligraphy by Eminent Monks of Nanto — already cited on this site)
    Mid-13th century (1256): The 7th Daijōin abbot, Jisshin (実信, son of Konoe Motomichi), "styles himself Hosshin-in" (Botan to Fuji — already cited on this site)
    Early 15th century (1415–1427): Sanehiro (実弘, of the Fujiwara Hokke Kanin line, Muromachi house) resides at Hosshin-in (Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names, etc. — already cited on this site)

    The institutional and personal link between Hosshin-in and the Fujiwara Hokke line is thereby confirmed across more than 400 years, from the late 11th century to the 15th century, through multiple independent scholarly sources.

    📌 [Kawabata Thesis, p. 560 — Additional Confirmation] Identity of Mita-shō and Yokota-shō, and Ein's Strategy for Expanding Landholding Rights

    Kawabata's thesis (p. 560) states: "According to a dispute record from Kaō 1 (1169) concerning Mita (Yokota) Estate, the issue at hand was that the temple-monk lord Ein was not fulfilling his temple duties. Both Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji had assigned tribute fields (fusho-den) there, but Ein skillfully exploited this arrangement to expand his lordly rights. Tōdai-ji, as the tribute-recipient lord, was entirely powerless against Ein's activities on the ground, stating merely, 'owing to the lord's dispute, the temple has been unable to intervene either way.'"

    The parenthetical notation "Mita (Yokota)" independently confirms, via third-party scholarship, the identity of Mita-shō and Yokota-shō (Hosshin-in).
    The analysis that "Tōdai-ji was entirely powerless" also shows that Ein (of Hosshin-in) skillfully exploited the institutional frameworks of both Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji to expand and consolidate his lordly rights, providing scholarly grounding for the institutional background behind the previously cited statement "the landholder is Hosshin-in."

    Jōsei's Dates (1399–1477) and His Death Record as "Abbot of Hosshin-in"

    Scholarly sources confirm Jōsei's (定清, of Hosshin-in) dates as 1399–1477. His death in the 12th month of Bunmei 9 (1477), recorded as "Abbot of Hosshin-in," is confirmed from the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki (12th month entry, Bunmei 9).

    [Notable Contrast]

    • Bunmei 9 (1477): the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki records his death as "Abbot of Hosshin-in, Gon-daisōzu, Master Jōsei, age 79, deceased"

    The Tamon-in Diary (Tenbun 13, 1544) records: "Senkei of Western Hosshin-in [is] a scholar-monk as solid as a piled stone storehouse."

    This work records Jōsei's sub-temple title (bōgō) as "Ken'ya-bō," whereas the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki General Index of Personal Names lists "Kenshun(-bō) → see: Jōsei."

    Item Confirmed Original Text Confidence Level
    Hideyoshi's vermilion seal document dated the 21st day of the 9th month of Bunroku 4 (1595) explicitly records Hosshi-in's holding as 563 koku, 9 to, 2 shō.

    Of the roughly 15,033 koku total in Kōfuku-ji temple-gate holdings across Sōkami District, Hosshi-in is registered in Hideyoshi's document as an independent holding of 563 koku, 9 to, 2 shō.

    The same document records Hosshi-in (approx. 563 koku) and Yokota (approx. 2,177 koku) side by side, confirming at the primary-source level that the institutional unity between the Daijō-in-held Yokota estate and Hosshi-in was maintained even in the official documentation following the Taikō land survey.     🔵 High ProbabilityMultiple independent sources converge, but direct proof has not yet been established

    • The possibility that the Hashimoto family belonged to a lineage of court-noble relatives or illegitimate-branch descendants connected to the Kōfukuji monzeki institutions as a whole (Ichijōin, Hosshin-in, etc.)
    • A probable kinship relationship between Hashimoto Hyōsaku and Hashimoto Masakata, a yoriki (constable) of the Nara Magistrate's Office and the adoptive father of Fujiichi
    • The fact that Chōjitsu (Zenkan-bō) is distinguished from the Tsuji family (the asymmetry of the "Tsuji" annotation)
    • The convergence of the record in Volume 1 of the Tamon-in Diary noting Zenkan's (Chōjitsu's) absence with the absence of the "Tsuji" annotation (§2-E), reinforcing the possibility of monzeki-lineage origin (Evidence Block 124)
    • 🔵【Added May 2026】Confirmation of the name-succession pattern within the resident Hosshi-in family
      ――Emonkurō (1497) → Emonsaburō (1542) → Kurobei (1647) / Shichirō (1497) → Magoshichi (1542)
    • The probability that the Hashimoto family's assumption of the post of kobettō (sub-administrator) at the Hosshi-in estate (Hashi-in estate) is connected to the institutional definition in the Meiō 8 (1499) entry of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki ("to be conferred upon a ryōke [noble house]," "the sub-administrator's portion beneath the administrator"), placing the Hashimoto family within the category of "ryōke" (noble house) under the Kōfukuji institutional system (based on a composite assessment together with Sources 7, 47, and 57)
    • Compendium of Japanese Festival Rites, Vol. 6 (Kashima Shrine festival rites): the title "Hashimoto Negi" is recorded as a festival office alongside "Ōgami Kobettō." Kashima Shrine, paired with Kasuga Taisha, is a clan shrine of the Fujiwara, and the appearance of the Hashimoto surname among its negi (priest) offices offers circumstantial evidence of a broad institutional connection between the name "Hashimoto" and the Fujiwara ritual system (a direct connection to the Hashimoto family of Hosshi-in is still under investigation).

    The Yokota-shō Kōshō-shō Nōchō (Tenbun 11 / 1542) from the Daijōin Documents has been confirmed to record "Emonsaburō of Wo-Hashi-no-in" and "Magoshichi." Cross-referencing this with entry 123 of Volume 11 of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki (1497) and the village-headman records in the Yamatokōriyama City History (1647) reveals the following name-succession pattern.

    DatePersonSourceSuccession element
    1497Hashi-no-in EmonkurōDaijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11, entry 123Emon, Kurō
    1497Hashi-no-in ShichirōSame as aboveShichi
    1542Hashi-no-in EmonsaburōDaijōin Documents, Yokota-shō NōchōEmon (succession)
    1542MagoshichiSame as aboveShichi (grandson of Shichirō)
    1582Hashimoto YarokuTamon-in DiaryHosshin-in / Hosshi-in
    c. 1620Hashimoto Tajima (150 koku, Tsutsui village)Koizumi Domain Register (Genna 6 revision; Yamatokōriyama City History, p. 274)Warrior status; continuation into the early modern period of a Tsutsui retainer
    1647Kurōbei (village headman)Yamatokōriyama City HistoryKurō (succession)

    In particular, "Magoshichi" literally means "grandson of Shichirō," and the appearance of a grandson 45 years after Shichirō of Hosshi-in in 1497 is naturally consistent as a generational interval. Likewise, the name element "Emon," borne in 1497 (Emonkurō) and again in 1542 (Emonsaburō), is passed down within the same lineage, while "Kurō" is carried from 1497 (Emonkurō) to 1647 (Kurōbei), a span of roughly 150 years and five to six generations. This name-succession pattern functions as circumstantial evidence that the resident family of Hosshi-in continued without interruption from 1497 to 1647. Combined with this site's account that the village headman "Kurōbei" (Shōhō 4 / 1647), recorded as an established fact in the Yamatokōriyama City History, corresponds to an institutional ancestor of Hashimoto Hyōsaku, the continuity of the Hosshi-in resident family is corroborated by name succession across multiple independent sources.
    📚 Sources: Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11, entry 123; Daijōin Documents, Yokota-shō Kōshō-shō Nōchō (Tenbun 11); Yamatokōriyama City History
    Certainty: 🔵 High Probability (based on convergence of the name-succession pattern)

    The Kan'ei 17 (1640) document also states, "In Hashi-in village, within the temple lands (bōryō) of Tōin (Daian-ji), a fixed 1 koku 2 to of paddy land," confirming through a 17th-century third-party document that Daian-ji held temple-land paddies within Hosshi-in village. Daian-ji is located roughly midway (5.4 km) between Hosshi-in and Kōfukuji, and this further reinforces, through early-modern documentation, the geographic and institutional consistency with the repeated references in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki to "Chōjitsu of Daian-ji-mukai (Inaba-kō)."
