    21st day of the 6th month. Shōryaku-ji. Memorandum. ○ Shingon sect, single school.

    Item: Temple domain under vermilion-seal grant, 300 koku, Bodai-san Shōryaku-ji, Sōnokami District, Washū (Yamato Province).
    Item: Founded as the Chokugan-ji (Imperial Votive Temple) of Ichijō-in, established during the Shōryaku era; the founder was Konshun, of Hōyo-in, son of the Regent.

    ○ Temple Buildings (Garan)
    Item: Main Hall — principal image Yakushi Nyorai (Medicine Buddha), said to have been crafted by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and brought [to Japan] by Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha (Zenmui).
    Item: Kanjō Hall (Consecration Hall) — principal image Dainichi Nyorai (Mahāvairocana). Item: Jizō Hall — one thousand Buddha images.
    Item: Nyohōkyō Hall (Sutra Hall) — prayers offered without fail three times daily. Item: Bell Tower — one structure.
    Item: Segaki Hall (Hall for Feeding Hungry Ghosts) — principal image Amida Nyorai. Item: Treasure Hall — one structure.

    ○ Shrines
    Item: one tutelary shrine (chinju) — Kasuga Daimyōjin.
    ○ Subsidiary shrines: Dokōjin, Zennyo Ryūō, Gozu Tennō, Benzaiten, Kai Myōjin, Ishi Kōjin.
    Item: Rokusho Myōjin. Subsidiary shrines: Shingū and Ippō Benzaiten, plus one further newly established shrine [text unclear in source].

    ○ Temple Sub-Establishments (Jike)
    In-ke (head sub-temple): Hōon-in
    ●Daifuku-in ●Fukuju-in ●Konzō-in ●Hōzō-in ●Jōshin-in ●Ryōzen-in ●Kyōzō-in ●Kōsetsu-in ●Tamon-in ●Kōdō-in ●Renge-in ●Kōzen-in ●Saifuku-in ●Tokuzō-in ●Myōō-in ●Hashino-in ●Kita-no-bō ●Kisshō-in ●Higashi-Henshō-in ●Jizō-in ●Naka-no-bō Sugimoto-bō ●Sugimoto-bō Iwa-no-bō Kongō-in Mae-no-in Chikurin-bō Ume-no-bō Fuji-no-bō Tani-no-bō Kado-no-in Tengyō-in Hōdō-in Taraku-in Kongōshō-in Kōren-in Isshin-in Kezō-in Jissō-in Higashi-no-bō Ura-no-bō Tsubaki-no-bō ●Oku-no-bō Minami-no-bō Kan'non-in Kosaka-bō Shin-bō Sakura-bō Higashi-Hashino-bō
    Total number of temple establishments: eighty-three shares (kabu).

    The above-named Bodaisan, having in the middle ages fallen for many years into a state where its holdings went unmanaged, received in Keichō 7, year of Mizunoe-Tora (1602), a black-seal (kokuin) grant from the Great Deity [Tokugawa Ieyasu], bestowing a temple domain of 300 koku. The temple domain was accordingly apportioned among the aforementioned sub-temple sites, and to this day the temple diligently and without negligence carries out its prayer duties and other religious services.
    The above is a true record.
    Genroku 5, year of Mizunoe-Saru (1692), 6th month, 21st day. Bodaisan. Nen'yo (Annual Administrator). Sata-nin (Administrator). [Submitted to] the Magistrate's Office. Report.

    From this one may observe the state of affairs at that time. However, of the eighty-three temple establishments (jike) — recorded here simply as a full tally of shares — only some forty-odd sub-temples (bō) marked with a black dot [in the original record] remained by around the Genroku/Genbun era. Furthermore, once Hōon-in fell vacant, the sub-temple Bodai-in of Ninna-ji in the capital (Kyoto) came to hold a concurrent post there, whereby Ninna-ji became the head temple; after the Meiji Restoration, Ninna-ji was again made the head temple. In recent years the temple has declined and no longer retains its former appearance. [Note: this closing passage is rendered in archaic mixed-kana script in the source and contains a few characters that are unclear, likely due to wear on the original document.]

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Public/Institutional Existence of "Hashino-in" as a Sub-Temple Rather than being a document produced by the Hashimoto family itself, the Yamato Shiryō — an independently compiled Genroku-era gazetteer and administrative record — lists "Hashino-in" as one of the eighty-three sub-temple shares. This serves as supplementary third-party evidence corroborating the institutional existence of "Hosshin-in (also called Hashiin-shō or Hashino-in)."
    Relationship with Kasuga Daimyōjin (Tutelary Deity) Kasuga Daimyōjin is recorded as the tutelary deity (chinju) of Shōryaku-ji, indicating that Hashino-in was a sub-temple situated within the religious framework of Kasuga Shrine (the tutelary shrine of Ichijō-in of Kōfuku-ji). This serves as corroborating circumstantial evidence reinforcing the institutional relationship between Hosshin-in and Kasuga Shrine.
    Reinforcement of the Argument in §1, "The Institutional Connection Between the Hashimoto Family and the Ichijō-in Monzeki" The fact that "Hashino-in" was still recorded as an independent sub-temple share even in the Genroku era functions as indirect evidence that the institutional connection with the Ichijō-in Monzeki, as asserted by the Hashimoto family, continued into the early modern period.
    21. Sanka In-ke Shō — Records of Various Manors and Gardens (Direct Proof of Ichijō-in's Governance over Hosshin-in)
    From the Yamatokōriyama City History: Source Collection: the second volume of the Sanka In-ke Shō and related village administrative documents. The address form "To the Temple Administration, His Reverence the Ichijō-in Prince, the Honorable Magistrate" appears repeatedly in official documents from Hosshin-in Village, corroborating from a third-party perspective that Ichijō-in was the de facto ruler (jitō) of Hosshin-in Village. The records include an independent manorial ledger for Dai-Hosshin-in (43 chō 9 tan, with an annual rice yield of 43 koku 8 to), a detailed description of the boundaries of Yokota Manor, the "Kasuga Lantern Field" (Shōya stipend-rice land), and the "Hosshin-in shōgon field," one tan of consecrated temple field.

    Hosshin-in Village. Shōya: Gen'emon. Toshiyori: Genbei; likewise Chūhachirō; likewise Jinjirō.
    To the Temple Administration, His Reverence the Ichijō-in Prince, the Honorable Magistrate.

    (From a petition requesting that exempted land be converted into stipend-rice land for the Shōya)
    As this land was originally exempted (nuki-chi) and had no landowner, it has since ancient times been designated as stipend-rice land for the Shōya. It was named the "Kasuga Lantern Field" (Kasuga Tōrō-den), and management of it has customarily been entrusted to whoever serves as Shōya at the time, handed down as the Shōya's stipend...

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Repeated Appearance of "To the Temple Administration, His Reverence the Ichijō-in Prince, the Honorable Magistrate" This address appears multiple times as the recipient designation in official administrative documents submitted by the Shōya, Toshiyori, and group leaders of Hosshin-in Village. Because these records were made by the village side itself — a third party unrelated to the Hashimoto family — they constitute decisive evidence that Ichijō-in was the de facto ruler (jitō) of Hosshin-in Village.
    The Independent Manorial Ledger of Dai-Hosshin-in The independent record "Dai-Hosshin-in: 43 chō 9 tan; annual rice: 43 koku 8 to" shows that Hosshin-in was not merely a subordinate branch temple, but a substantive sub-temple domain (in-ke-ryō) with its own manorial lands and tax administration. Together with the record of its own dedicated field, the "Hosshin-in shōgon field" (one tan), this serves as evidence that Hosshin-in functioned as an independent manorial entity.
    The Boundaries of Yokota Manor and the Geographic Determination of Ichijō-in and Daijō-in Governance The detailed boundary description — "to the south it borders...Ichijō-in...Daijō-in; to the north it borders Yoshioka Manor of Ichijō-in..." — explicitly documents that Yokota Manor (the Hosshin-in domain) was directly adjacent to the territories governed by Ichijō-in and Daijō-in. This third-party administrative document corroborates the geographic and institutional relationship between Hosshin-in and Ichijō-in.
    The Institutional Relationship Between the "Kasuga Lantern Field" and Kasuga Shrine The stipend-rice land for the Shōya was named the "Kasuga Lantern Field," indicating that Hosshin-in's land system was linked to the religious framework of Kasuga Shrine (the tutelary shrine of Ichijō-in of Kōfuku-ji). This reinforces the Hashimoto family's claim to have been a service lineage affiliated with the sub-temple system serving the Ichijō-in Monzeki.
    22. Japan Shōen Data (National Museum of Japanese History) — Official Academic Identification of Hasshi-shō as Identical to Hashiin-shō
    In the Japan Shōen (Manor) Database compiled by the National Museum of Japanese History, "Hasshi-shō (Sōnokami District)" and "Hashiin-shō (Sōnokami District, Yamatokōriyama City)" are officially coded and identified as one and the same manor. This academic survey by an independent national institution corroborates the equation the Hashimoto family has long asserted: "Hosshin-in = Hashiin-shō." Yokota-shō, Yokota-Shin-shō, and Yokota-Hon-shō are explicitly recorded as Kōfuku-ji domain (Daijō-in domain), and the cited sources include the "Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki" and the "Sanka In-ke Shō."

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Official Academic Identification of Hasshi-shō as Identical to Hashiin-shō Manor codes 0299109 (Hasshi-shō) and 0201085 (Hashiin-shō) are cross-referenced as duplicate codes, meaning a national institution unrelated to the Hashimoto family — the National Museum of Japanese History — has academically established the equation "Hosshin-in = Hashiin-shō." This objectively supports the geographic and manorial-institutional basis of the Hashimoto family's claim to be "the sole shizoku family of Hosshin-in Village."
    Confirmation of Yokota-Shin-shō and Yokota-Hon-shō as Daijō-in Domains, and Consistency of Cited Sources Both Yokota-Shin-shō and Yokota-Hon-shō are explicitly recorded as "Kōfuku-ji domain (Daijō-in domain)," with the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki and the Sanka In-ke Shō cited as sources. This provides double corroboration that the very historical sources presented as evidence on this site are directly linked to these manors even within an academic database.
    Objective Corroboration of Yokota Manor's Multi-Proprietor Structure and Historical Background It is confirmed that Yokota Manor (first recorded in Enkyū 2, 1070) was a composite manor involving multiple proprietary lords — Tōdai-ji, Kōfuku-ji (Daijō-in domain), Hōryū-ji, the domain of Retired Emperor Go-Uda, the Imperial Household domain, and the Shōkeimon-in Office domain. This objectively corroborates, through the academic data of an independent national institution, the historical background presupposed by §4, "A Study of Yokota Manor and the Hashimoto Hyōsaku Family Line."
    23. Heian Ibun, Volume 7 — Chōkan 2 (1164) Catalogue of Mita Manor Documents (Proof of Hosshin-in's Earliest-Period Existence as a Sub-Temple Proprietary Lord)
    An administrative catalogue of Mita Manor documents from Yamato Province, dated Chōkan 2 (1164) and independently compiled by the Tōdai-ji side. The entry "no Hosshin-in holdings could be found within Mita Manor — around the Hōen–Kōji era" shows that, as early as the Hōen–Kōji era (1135–1144), Hosshin-in was already recognized by both Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji as an independent sub-temple domain — substantial enough an institution to be made the subject of an administrative inquiry into proprietary rights.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Proof of Hosshin-in's Substantive Existence in the Early 12th Century The entry "no Hosshin-in holdings could be found [within Mita Manor]" is, on its face, a negative record — but conversely it shows that by the early twelfth century Hosshin-in was already recognized as an independent sub-temple domain, substantial enough that its ownership was actively disputed. While Block 22 (the Japan Shōen Data) gives Ken'ei 1 (1206) as the first recorded date for Hashiin-shō, this source pushes back the confirmed existence of Hosshin-in further still, to as early as 1164.
    A Record Subject to Official Adjudication by Both Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji The appearance of Hosshin-in within this administrative document — which meticulously itemizes the number of scrolls and leaves of deeds, temple certificates, and provincial seals — is recorded by the Tōdai-ji side, unrelated to the Hashimoto family, and shows that Hosshin-in was a substantive manorial proprietor whose name arose in the official administrative proceedings of both great temples.
    Functions as the Prehistory to Block 24 (the Kaō 1 Adjudication) The negative claim made by the Tōdai-ji side in this source (1164) forms part of the background to the dispute that, five years later, culminated in Block 24 (1169) — the Chōja Sen (Directive of the Chancellor) declaring, "Hosshin-in shall properly be recognized as the landowner (jinushi)." Placing the two sources side by side allows the process by which Hosshin-in's proprietary rights were established to be traced directly through primary sources.
    24. Kashihara City History: Historical Materials, Volume 1 — Kaō 1 (1169) Mita Manor Adjudication Document (Official Codification of "Hosshin-in as Landowner")
    A document adjudicating the tax duties of Mita Manor between Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji, issued as a Chōja Sen (Directive of the Chancellor) on the 19th day of the 11th month of Kaō 1 (1169). This twelfth-century, contemporaneous document contains the official ruling of both great temples — "Hosshin-in shall properly be recognized as the landowner (jinushi); it shall first be made to perform its Tōdai-ji duties" — explicitly settling Hosshin-in's status as a sub-temple proprietary lord. It also records the hereditary nature of the position in the phrase "the successive abbots of Hosshin-in have never once been obstructed," the dual-obligation structure of the Kōfuku-ji shinkan-men (a tax exemption granted through court appointment) and the Tōdai-ji zōyakumen (corvée-tax exemption), and a retrospective reference reaching back to the Kankō era (1004–1012).

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Official Codification of "The Landowner Is Hosshin-in" and "Hosshin-in Shall Be Recognized as the Landowner" The Chōja Sen (official adjudication) of both Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji unequivocally rules that "Hosshin-in shall be the landowner [i.e., the sub-temple proprietary lord]," showing that in the latter half of the twelfth century Hosshin-in was formally certified as a sub-temple proprietor by the administrative authority of the two great central temples. As a third-party official document issued by the two temples — entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family — rather than a document produced by the family itself, this carries the highest evidentiary weight.
    Proof of Hereditary Succession via "The Successive Abbots of Hosshin-in Have Never Once Been Obstructed" This contemporaneous document explicitly records that the office of Hosshin-in's abbot (in-shu) was a hereditary post passed down across generations, directly supporting — through a twelfth-century primary source — the institutional basis for the Hashimoto family's claim to have carried on sub-temple-lineage duties from the medieval period through to the Edo and Meiji eras.
    The Dual-Obligation Structure of the Kōfuku-ji Shinkan-men and the Tōdai-ji Zōyakumen The passage "the tax burden is the head temple's shinkan[-men], and also the Tōdai-ji zōyakumen" shows that Hosshin-in was a composite sub-temple proprietor bearing institutional obligations to both Kōfuku-ji (Daijō-in) and Tōdai-ji simultaneously. This provides primary-source support for the medieval premise underlying §4, "A Study of Yokota Manor and the Hashimoto Hyōsaku Family Line," which positions the Hashimoto family as a lineage appointed to office (in-ke lineage) under Daijō-in.
    A Retrospective Reference Reaching Back to the Kankō Era (1004–1012) The phrase "around the Kankō era, on the day when that abbot, Chūan, rendered his judgment" shows that Hosshin-in's system of abbots already existed in the early eleventh century, pushing the historical depth of Hosshin-in back to the mid-Heian period. Through the chain of sources running from Block 23 (1164) to this Block 24 (1169), the process by which Hosshin-in's proprietary rights were established can be traced directly through primary sources.
    25. Mibu Family Documents — Draft Rinji (Imperial Directive) of Emperor Go-Shirakawa (Hōgen 1: Bestowal of a Śarīra Relic upon Hosshin-in [発心院])
    An imperial administrative document (draft Rinji) recording that in Hōgen 1 (1156) Emperor Go-Shirakawa bestowed "a fang-relic (śarīra) of Śākyamuni Buddha, transmitted through Chishō Daishi [the priest Enchin]," upon Hosshin-in. It is one of a group of documents held by the Mibu family (a court-noble house), included in the Zushoryō Sōkan compilation — an imperial administrative document entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. It bears the facsimile kaō of the Bettō, Fujiwara no Kinnori (Senior Second Rank, Acting Gon-Dainagon), showing that the matter proceeded through the official channels of a court noble of the Fujiwara Hokke line.

    Point Explanation
    Direct Imperial Recognition of Hosshin-in by Emperor Go-Shirakawa Hosshin-in is explicitly named in the emperor's Rinji (a document conveying imperial command), and this imperial document — entirely independent of the Hashimoto family — shows that by the mid-twelfth century Hosshin-in was regarded not as a mere minor local temple, but as a recognized sub-temple with which the imperial court dealt directly.
    Confirmation of the Institutional Framework via the Kaō of Fujiwara no Kinnori (Fujiwara Hokke) The facsimile kaō of Fujiwara no Kinnori — a court noble of the Fujiwara Hokke line (and later Naidaijin, Minister of the Interior) — appears as the officiating administrator, showing that the bestowal of the relic upon Hosshin-in proceeded through the official channels of a court noble connected to the Sekkanke (Regental House) lineage. This serves as circumstantial evidence that Hosshin-in was positioned within the institutional framework of the Fujiwara clan, whose clan temple was Kōfuku-ji.
    A Triple Chain of Third-Party Evidence with Blocks 23 and 24 Following the chronological sequence — this Block 25 (1156, the imperial court) → Block 23 (1164, Tōdai-ji) → Block 24 (1169, the Chōja Sen of both great temples) — it is corroborated in layers, through three mutually independent third-party documents, that Hosshin-in (発心院, here equated with 発志院) in the mid-twelfth century was recognized as a sub-temple proprietary lord independently by all three of the imperial court, Tōdai-ji, and Kōfuku-ji. This forms the core of the body of sources that satisfies the evidentiary standard, emphasized throughout this site, of corroboration by multiple, mutually independent third-party sources.
    26. Bukkyō Daijii (Great Dictionary of Buddhism) — Entry on Zonkaku (Kagen 1: Record of Attending Lectures at the Cell of Kakui of Hosshin-in)
    A biographical fact recorded in the entry for "Zonkaku" in the Bukkyō Daijii (Great Dictionary of Buddhism), an academic reference work. The entry states that Zonkaku — a renowned Shin-sect scholar-monk and the eldest son of Kakunyo Shōnin, the third head of Hongan-ji — "attended lectures at the cell of Kakui of Hosshin-in" in Kagen 1 (1303). This appears by name in a Buddhist academic dictionary entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side, showing that Hosshin-in was independently recognized as a notable center of learning at the end of the Kamakura period.

    [Quotation] Quoted from the entry "Zonkaku (存覺)" →

    ZONKAKU (存覺). Shin sect. Founder of Jōraku-ji in Kyoto.
    His personal name (imina) was Kōgen; his childhood name was Kōnichimaro. He was the eldest son of Kakunyo Shōnin, third head of Hongan-ji, born on the 4th day of the 6th month of Shōō 3 (1290).
    He became the adopted son of the former Governor of Hōki, Chikaaki, and was conferred the rank of Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, at the age of eight.
    After Chikaaki's term of service, he was raised by Reizei Chikanari.

    In Kagen 1 (1303), he attended lectures at the cell of Kakui of Hosshin-in,
    and further went to Nara, where he studied at Kōfuku-ji.
    On the 10th day of the 10th month, he took the tonsure at Tōdai-ji and took the name Kōshin.
    Later he changed [his name] to Shin'e, ascended Mt. Hiei, entered the chamber of Shichi of Sonshō-in, and refined his study of the various [Buddhist] teachings. His scholarly understanding advanced by the day, and he entered the gate [became a disciple] of Prince-Abbot Jidō of Shōren-in……

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Kakui of Hosshin-in Recorded by Name as the First Teacher of a Renowned Scholar-Monk "Kakui of Hosshin-in" is explicitly named as the first teacher Zonkaku attended upon arriving in Nara — Zonkaku being a figure who would later become significant in the history of the Shin sect. This shows that Hosshin-in functioned, at the end of the Kamakura period, as a high-ranking sub-temple serving as an entry point into the scholastic systems of Kōfuku-ji and Tōdai-ji. This is third-party evidence, independently recorded in an academic publication (compiled by the Bukkyō Daijii Kankōkai) entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side.
    Hosshin-in as the Starting Point of a Scholarly Route to Kōfuku-ji and Tōdai-ji Following his lectures at the cell of Kakui of Hosshin-in, Zonkaku went on to "study at Kōfuku-ji" and "take the tonsure at Tōdai-ji," showing that Hosshin-in functioned as the starting point of the scholastic system shared by both great temples. This corroborates the continuation, into the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, of the pattern confirmed in Block 24 (Kashihara City History, Kaō 1) — that Hosshin-in was a sub-temple positioned within the institutional framework of both Kōfuku-ji and Tōdai-ji.
    Reinforcement of the Continuity of the "Successive Abbots" System with a Specific Name The appearance of Hosshin-in's abbot under the specific name "Kakui" in a document from the end of the Kamakura period corroborates, with a concrete name, the continuity of the hereditary abbacy system — "the successive abbots of Hosshin-in" — confirmed in Block 24. Following the chronological sequence of the twelfth century (Blocks 23–25) → the early thirteenth century (Block 22) → the early fourteenth century (this block), the institutional continuity of Hosshin-in can be confirmed in stages.
    27. The Hashimoto Family Ancestral Grave (Physical Evidence of the Hashimoto Family's Long-Term Presence at Hosshin-in)
    ✅ Verified on-site (Hosshin-in, Sōnokami District, Nara Prefecture). The posthumous Buddhist names (kaimyō) and dates of death match the family register (koseki tōhon) exactly. This is physical evidence — physical weathering that could not have been produced by any documentary forgery — proving long-term presence. The family crest is the sixteen-petal chrysanthemum (jūroku-kiku, a single-layer, sixteen-petaled "facing" chrysanthemum). The oldest gravestone is worn to the point of illegibility, indicating presence predating the early Edo period. The site includes an inscription reading "Bunsei" and "Hashi" from the Bunsei era (1818–1830), a monument erected in Keiō 3 (1867), and a restoration monument from Shōwa 53 (1978).

    [Evidentiary Weight as Physical Evidence]

    Item Verified Details
    Method of Verification On-site verification at Hosshin-in, Sōnokami District, Nara Prefecture. Names and dates of death match the family register (koseki tōhon) exactly.
    Family Crest The sixteen-petal chrysanthemum (a single-layer, sixteen-petaled "facing" chrysanthemum). This is not asserted to indicate direct imperial descent; rather, it is interpreted as a crest bestowed by the Ichijō-in Monzeki (an imperial prince). It is consistent with the independent third-party documentary evidence of shizoku status under the Ichijō-in estate.
    Family Temple (Bodaiji) Only the posthumous names "Jōshitsu Seikō Zenjōni" and "Zen'yo Jōkō Zenjōmon" are recorded [on one stone], with "Bunsei" inscribed on its side. Other stones record "Tokuyo Jōkō Zenjōmon" and "Kōyo Chishin Zenjōni." There is no inscription indicating the Jōdo (Pure Land) sect anywhere. (Correction, April 5, 2026 — deleted text: "Affiliated with the Jōren-sha lineage of the Jōdo sect. A memorial stone reading 'Namu Amida Butsu — Jōren-sha Seigen Zenjōmon / Seigen Zenjōni' is confirmed within the grave precinct.")

    [Layout of the Grave Precinct and Overview of Each Monument]

    Monument / Element Content / Inscription Evidentiary Significance
    Central Main Monument Inscribed "Hashimoto-ke Senzo Daidai no Haka" ("Grave of the Successive Generations of Ancestors of the Hashimoto Family"). An upright pillar-type monument with vertical carving. Set at the center of the family grave precinct, which is demarcated by gravel and a stone fence, and is still maintained by descendants today. Physical proof that the Hashimoto family has continuously maintained a grave precinct at Hosshin-in across successive generations.
    The Oldest Gravestone (Unmarked) Extremely weathered, with only the stone itself remaining; the inscription is illegible. Physical evidence that the Hashimoto family was already present at Hosshin-in by at least the early Edo period or earlier — a fact that cannot be explained by later genealogical fabrication or the borrowing of a surname. Corroborates chronological consistency with Hashimoto Yaroku (1582) and Hashimoto Sama (around Tenshō 18), as recorded in the Tamon'in Nikki.
    Monument Erected in Keiō 3 (1867) Inscribed "Erected in the 9th month of Keiō 3." Erected at the very end of the Edo period, immediately before the Meiji Restoration. The reverse of the stone to the left bears the three names "Hashimoto Giichi," "Takeno," and "Tanako." Shows that the Hashimoto family maintained the grave precinct during the late Edo period, overlapping with the era of Hashimoto Hyōsaku (who surrendered his hereditary stipend in Meiji 7, 1874).
    Bunsei-Era Inscription (Side) The inscriptions "Bunsei" (1818–1830) and "Hashi" are confirmed on the side [of the stone] — half a century older still than the Keiō 3 monument. Confirms, as physical evidence, that the Hashimoto family continuously maintained the grave precinct at this site from at least the Bunsei era (over 200 years ago) onward.
    The "Hashimoto-shi" Stone A square pillar near the center of the rear of the precinct, inscribed only with "Hashimoto-shi" (the Hashimoto family). A boundary marker stone that designates the entire precinct as the "Hashimoto family grave precinct." Spatial proof that the Hashimoto family has maintained an independent grave precinct at Hosshin-in over a long period.
    Unmarked Boundary Stone An unmarked square pillar standing in a position paired with the "Hashimoto-shi" stone. Its inscription is illegible due to weathering and moss. The degree of weathering suggests it may be older than the "Hashimoto-shi" stone, serving as supplementary evidence of the historical depth of the grave precinct.
    Rear Restoration Monument (Shōwa 53) Inscribed "Erected by Hashimoto Giichi, an auspicious day in the 3rd month of Shōwa 53" (March 1978). A record of a large-scale repair or re-erection. Confirms that Hashimoto family descendants have continued to manage the grave precinct at Hosshin-in into the modern era.
    (Deleted April 5, 2026 — there is no entry reading "two memorial pillars ('Hoju, Jiun Shin'unkai')") (Deleted April 5, 2026 — there is no entry reading: "Two small, weathered granite square pillars, inscribed 'Hoju' [a vow of continued memorial service] and 'Jiun Shin'unkai' [the name of a temple parishioners' association].") Circumstantial evidence that the Hashimoto family grave precinct was continuously maintained by a local temple parishioners' organization.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    The Impossibility of Forgery, as Shown by Physical Weathering Genealogical fabrication or the borrowing of a surname during the Edo period would be a documentary forgery, but the actual physical weathering of a gravestone cannot be forged. The illegible degree of weathering on the oldest gravestone provides physical proof, independent of documentary evidence, that the Hashimoto family was already present at Hosshin-in by at least the early Edo period or earlier.
    Chronological Consistency with the Records in the Tamon'in Nikki The existence of the sixteenth-century Hashimoto family — Hashimoto Yaroku (Tenshō 10, 1582) and Hashimoto Sama (around Tenshō 18) — as recorded in the Tamon'in Nikki, is chronologically consistent with the degree of weathering on the illegibly old oldest gravestone. Documentary evidence and physical evidence mutually reinforce one another.
    Cross-Verification with the Family Register The exact match between the posthumous Buddhist names and dates of death and the family register (koseki tōhon) means that two independent types of evidence of fundamentally different character — physical evidence (the gravestones) and administrative documents (the family register) — are mutually consistent. This corroborates the Hashimoto family's presence at Hosshin-in from multiple angles.
    The Institutional Relationship Between the Sixteen-Petal Chrysanthemum Crest and the Ichijō-in Monzeki The sixteen-petal chrysanthemum crest inscribed on the Hashimoto family's ancestral grave is a crest that, in the medieval and early modern periods, is documented as having been used by lineages connected to Kōfuku-ji, Kasuga Taisha, and the Ichijō-in Monzeki. Rather than asserting direct imperial descent, it is interpreted as a crest bestowed by the Ichijō-in Monzeki (an imperial prince), consistent with the independent third-party documentary evidence of shizoku status under the Ichijō-in estate (the Petition for Return of Hereditary Stipend).
    28. Oritaku Shiba no Ki (Arai Hakuseki) — The Account of the Ichijō-in Monshu's Envoy and Hosshin-in
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (an independent record by an Edo-period intellectual) / Proof That Hosshin-in Functioned as a Sub-Temple of the Ichijō-in Monshu into the Early Edo Period]

    This source is a passage from the Oritaku Shiba no Ki, the memoir written by Arai Hakuseki (1657–1725), a leading scholar of the Edo period. The passage describing how an envoy of the Ichijō-in Monshu "sent down word through the sub-temples, including Kezō-in, Hosshin-in, and others" shows that Hosshin-in was still institutionally functioning as a sub-temple of the Ichijō-in Monshu in the early Edo period — recorded in the writing of an intellectual entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① Explicit identification as an Ichijō-in sub-temple in the phrase "the sub-temples Kezō-in, Hosshin-in, and others": The expression used by the Ichijō-in Monshu's envoy — "sent down word through the sub-temples Kezō-in, Hosshin-in, and others" — means that Hosshin-in is specifically enumerated as one of the Ichijō-in Monshu's in-ke (directly subordinate branch temples/organizations). This constitutes an early-Edo-period, continuing instance of the statement presented in Block 22 (§1) — "at that time the various in-ke were, broadly speaking, of the same lineage as this Monzeki" (Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 6).

    ② The context of the relationship between Konoe Sakihisa (the Retired Regent, Tōgu-in Nyūdō) and Shinso (Tokugawa Ieyasu): This passage refers to Hosshin-in within the context of Konoe Sakihisa's two sons (the elder: Ichijō-in Monshu Sonkei Daishō-in; the younger: Sanmyakuin Nobutada), showing that Hosshin-in is positioned within the institutional relationship between the Ichijō-in Monshu's envoy and the Konoe family (the main line of the Fujiwara Hokke).

    ③ A record of institutional crisis in the phrase "in the end abandoned temple affairs...and it fell into disuse": The passage describing how the Ichijō-in Monshu, Sonkei Daishō-in, abandoned the administration of temple affairs shows, in the context of a period of institutional upheaval at Ichijō-in in the early modern era, that the sub-temple system including Hosshin-in reached a major turning point at this time. This can be referenced as part of the historical background to the Hashimoto family's inheritance of shizoku status.

    [Logical Connection] The fact that "Hosshin-in's institutional standing as a sub-temple," confirmed in the medieval sources (Blocks 23–26), is also specifically referred to as an "Ichijō-in sub-temple" in the early-Edo-period record of Arai Hakuseki means that the record of a renowned, independent third-party intellectual provides independent corroborating evidence for the Hashimoto family's claim that the sub-temple system of Hosshin-in (Hosshin-in) continued from the Muromachi through the Edo period.
    Quoted from Oritaku Shiba no Ki, Middle Volume (Arai Hakuseki) (frame 25, Call Number 142-134, View at National Diet Library) →On the 20th day of the 6th month the deliberation concluded, and it was conveyed by Lord Akifusa. In the previous generation, a dispute had arisen between the two Monshu (the Lord of Ichijō-in and the Lord of Daijō-in), and although a ruling was to be handed down and confirmed by judgment, [the presiding party] passed away before this could occur. On account of this matter, the Ichijō-in Monshu's envoy, together with the Ben [an official], sent down word through its sub-temples — Kezō-in, Hosshin-in, and others — and there were various matters reported. Now, as for the particulars of this matter, it is said that the Chancellor of Konoe was well informed of them... The Retired Regent, Tōgu-in Nyūdō Sakihisa (this refers to Lord Ryūzan), had two sons: the elder was the one called Ichijō-in Monshu Sonkei Daishō-in. The younger was the former Regent, Sanmyakuin Nobutada. With Shinso [Tokugawa Ieyasu], Lord Tōgu-in had for some years been on close terms [passage unclear in source]... Whenever [Ieyasu] came to the capital from the Fushimi Palace, he would call at Lord Konoe's residence, and they would lie down together and converse deep into the night, among other such occasions. At that time Sonkei was called "Tarō-gimi" and Nobutada was called "Jirō-gimi"... and in the end [Sonkei] abandoned the administration of temple affairs...and it fell into disuse, and was never restored.
    [Source Note] Arai Hakuseki (1657–1725) was a leading Neo-Confucian scholar and statesman of the Edo period, and this work is an independent memoir entirely unrelated to the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. The specific enumeration "the sub-temples Kezō-in, Hosshin-in, and others" is Hakuseki's own independent record of the composition of the Ichijō-in Monshu's sub-temples, and it corroborates, from a third-party perspective, Hosshin-in's continuing status as an Ichijō-in sub-temple in the early Edo period.
    29. Dokushi Biyō (Entries on Go-Hosshin-in Shinga, Hosshin-in Jisshin, and Others)
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (a modern academic reference work) / Confirmation of the Genealogical Continuity of Hosshin-in's Abbots at Both Ichijō-in and Daijō-in]

    This source consists of entries relating to Hosshin-in figures found in the Dokushi Biyō (New Revised Edition, Shōwa 10 [1935]), an academic reference work for historical researchers. A modern academic publication entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side independently records that Hosshin-in was a sub-temple that produced abbots for both the Ichijō-in and Daijō-in Monzeki of Kōfuku-ji.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① Explicit direct connection to Ichijō-in in the entry "Hosshin-in Jisshin — Kōfuku-ji Ichijō-in": The entry "Hosshin-in Jisshin, Kōfuku-ji Ichijō[-in]" shows that Jisshin, an abbot of Hosshin-in, was directly involved with the Ichijō-in Monzeki of Kōfuku-ji. This corroborates, with a concrete personal name, the statement in the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki presented in §1 of this site — "at that time the various in-ke were, broadly speaking, of the same lineage as this Monzeki."

    ② The existence of an abbot of court-noble lineage: "Hosshin-in Shōzan Sekaku (son of Horio Shikibu-no-jō Tadaharu; [connected to] the former Naidaijin of Go-Horikawa, Horikawa Tomochika)": The record of Hosshin-in's abbot Shōzan Sekaku as "the son of Horio Shikibu-no-jō Tadaharu" shows that it was customary for individuals of court-noble or warrior-class lineage to be appointed to the office of abbot at Hosshin-in, and can be cited as an institutional parallel to the Hashimoto family's claim that close relatives or connections of the Monzeki lineage were involved with Hosshin-in.

    ③ Explicit connection to Daijō-in in the entry "Go-Hosshin-in Shinga — Kōfuku-ji Daijō-in": The entry "Go-Hosshin-in Shinga, Kōfuku-ji Daijō[-in]" shows that Hosshin-in was institutionally linked, through the "Go-[X]-in" naming convention, not only to Ichijō-in but to Daijō-in as well. This corroborates an institutional relationship consistent with the geographic fact confirmed in Block 22 (the Japan Shōen Data) — that Yokota Manor was adjacent to the territories governed by both Ichijō-in and Daijō-in.

    ④ Institutional succession indicated by the existence of the "Go-Hosshin-in" title: The title "Go-Hosshin-in" is a temple title inherited from Hosshin-in as its predecessor, and it corresponds to the source (the Monzeki Den) confirmed in §1 of this site — "Ryōshin's title was 'Go-Hosshin-in'" (the 15th head priest of Ichijō-in). This shows that the succession of the temple title from Hosshin-in to Go-Hosshin-in took place within the formal institutional framework of the Ichijō-in Monzeki.

    [Logical Connection] This source adds a third-party confirmation to the body of evidence for "the historical continuity of Hosshin-in as a sub-temple," built up chronologically through Blocks 25–28: an independent, modern academic reference work has organized and recorded the personal names and institutional affiliations [of Hosshin-in figures] as connections to both Ichijō-in and Daijō-in. This functions as corroborating evidence, from an independent modern academic source, for the evidentiary standard emphasized throughout this site — corroboration in layers by multiple independent sources.
    Quoted from Dokushi Biyō, New Revised Edition (p. 1799, published Shōwa 10 [1935], Call Number R210.036-To46-Rō) →Hosshin-in Jisshin — Kōfuku-ji Ichijō[-in]Hosshin-in Shōzan Sekaku — son of Horio Shikibu-no-jō Tadaharu; [related to] the former Naidaijin of Go-Horikawa, Horikawa TomochikaGo-Hosshin-in Shinga — Kōfuku-ji Daijō-in
    [Source Note] The Dokushi Biyō is a reference work of biographical and encyclopedic entries for historical researchers (a modern academic publication), and is an independent compilation entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. The entries "Hosshin-in Jisshin, Kōfuku-ji Ichijō[-in]" and "Go-Hosshin-in Shinga, Kōfuku-ji Daijō-in" constitute an academic record that the abbots and associated figures of Hosshin-in were institutionally connected with both the Ichijō-in and Daijō-in Monzeki. This is evidence in which an independent reference work corroborates the institutional relationship asserted in the main text of this site — that "Hosshin-in = a sub-temple of the Ichijō-in Monzeki."
    30. Yamato Shiryō, "Nara-machi" — Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō (the Kanshō 2 Iigamidono-shō Sandenchō)
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (a gazetteer and administrative paddy-field register) / Evidence That "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)" Was Recorded by Name as a Fifteenth-Century Local Landholder in Nara]

    The crux of this source lies in the fact that the personal name "Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō" is recorded, under the "peasants of Nara" category, in the Kanshō 2 (1456) Iigamidono-shō Sandenchō (Paddy-Field Register). "Hashino-in" is a kana rendering of Hosshin-in (Hashiin), and the appearance of a person bearing the name "Hashino-in" as a local landholder in an administrative paddy-field register entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side is evidence in which a third-party administrative record corroborates the local presence of Hosshin-in in the fifteenth century.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① The personal name "Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō" recorded directly: In a record of administrative character — a paddy-field register — a person bearing the name "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)" appears by name as a local peasant. This shows that Hosshin-in functioned not merely as a religious name, but as a substantive temple-name tied to specific persons and land within the local community of Nara.

    ② Cross-verification with the diary of Jinson, Daijō-in Monzeki: This source also includes the Shōchō 1 (1428) Kenbetsu Kashinōchō (Household Loan-Rice Ledger), quoted in the diary entry of Bishop Jinson (the Daijō-in Monzeki and author of the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki) for the 26th day of the intercalary 9th month of Chōroku 4 (1460). This same Jinson is the very person who recorded the Hosshin-in-related material discussed in Block 31 (the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki), meaning that multiple independent records mutually corroborate the institutional relationship between Daijō-in and Hosshin-in.

    ③ A chronological link, in the fifteenth century, toward "Hashimoto Yaroku (1582)": The Kanshō 2 (1456) record of "Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō" shows the existence of a local Hosshin-in figure contemporaneous with Block 22 (the Japan Shōen Data — Ryūun's return to lay life, 15th century), and functions as intermediate evidence supplementing the chronological continuity running from the fifteenth century to the sixteenth century (Hashimoto Yaroku, 1582).

    [Logical Connection] Regarding the gap noted between the death of Ryōshin (1319) and Hashimoto Yaroku (1582), this source shows that at the intermediate point of 1456, a third-party administrative record confirms the existence of a local figure bearing the name "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)." Together with Block 26 (Kakui of Hosshin-in, 1303) and Block 22 (Ryūun, 15th century), this constitutes one further piece of evidence progressively filling in the gap.
    Quoted from the Yamato Shiryō, "Nara-machi" entry (p. 44, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number 348-226-I, Bibliographic ID 000000704075, View at National Diet Library) →(preceding text omitted — a discussion of the origin of the place-name "Nara" and its transformation after the relocation of the Heijō capital) The Kanshō 2 Iigamidono-shō Sandenchō (Paddy-Field Register) records the following personal names under "Nara peasants, kenden [paddy allotment]": Reishō-hōshi, Nichichi-in, Kōjirō, Jika, Saburōjirō, Kyō-Harano-Saino-Gorō, Fukuji Myōshunbō, Okiue Ishikura, Katō-in, Kabeya-no-Saburōjirō, Kawa-Nakaga-no-Hyōe, Kagawa-no-Eboshiya, Nandaimon Kadeya, Tsubai-no-Hyōgorō, and Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō. [Note: many of these katakana personal names are heavily degraded in the scanned source, and several of the readings given here cannot be confirmed with certainty.] Those names marked with a circle-point (kenten) are the names of local residents. Also, in the Shōchō 1 (1428) Kenbetsu Kashinōchō quoted in the diary entry of Bishop Jinson dated the 26th day of the intercalary 9th month of Chōroku 4 (1460): Zutō, 4 shaku; Kubo, 1 ken; likewise Zushi-no-sato, 31 ken; Kō, 30 ken; Matsutani-gun Iwai, 46 ken; Minami-ichi-kō, 19 ken. [Note: this list of place-names and land measurements is also affected by unclear passages in the source.][Source Note] The "Hashino-in" in "Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō" is interpreted as a kana rendering of Hosshin-in (Hashiin). This source is a quotation of the Kanshō 2 (1456) administrative paddy-field register as recorded in the Yamato Shiryō (a modern gazetteer compiled by a third party), and is not a document created or maintained by the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side.
    31. Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4 — Records of the Shōya and Sata-nin Dispute Within Hosshin-in
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (Highest Evidentiary Rating) / A Contemporaneous Record of the Institutional Fact That the Daijō-in Monzeki Directly Governed Hosshin-in]

    This source is a Hosshin-in-related passage recorded in Volume 4 of the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, written by Jinson, the Daijō-in Monzeki (a third party unconnected to the Hashimoto family). The passage "a suitable person shall be appointed within Hosshin-in" shows that the Daijō-in Monzeki held direct authority over personnel appointments for the shōya and sata-nin (village headman and estate manager) within Hosshin-in, as explicitly stated in this fifteenth-century contemporaneous document.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① Explicit statement of direct governance in the phrase "a suitable person shall be appointed within Hosshin-in": The Daijō-in Monzeki's own diary — entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family — explicitly records that the Monzeki held the authority to appoint and direct a "suitable person" (kiyōtei) within Hosshin-in. As with the address form "To the Temple Administration, His Reverence the Ichijō-in Prince, the Honorable Magistrate" seen in Block 21 (the village administrative documents), this corroborates — through the record of the governing party (the Monzeki side) itself — the institutional fact that Hosshin-in was under the Monzeki's direct governance.

    ② The passage "the shōya and sata-nin have behaved unlawfully and negligently, and moreover, by residing within another's domain, have caused difficulty for the Monzeki": This description — that Hosshin-in's shōya and sata-nin caused difficulty for the Monzeki through unlawful conduct and residence in another's territory — shows that the conduct of Hosshin-in's shōya and sata-nin directly affected the interests of the Monzeki. This suggests that the relationship between Hosshin-in and the Daijō-in Monzeki was a close institutional bond extending beyond a mere manor-manager-and-lord relationship.

    ③ High evidentiary weight owing to the independence of the author, Jinson: Jinson (1430–1508), the author of the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, was the Daijō-in Monzeki himself, and recorded the actual state of Hosshin-in from a position entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. The fact that the same author recorded both this block (Volume 4) and the core evidence presented elsewhere on this site (Volumes 4 and 6) increases the overall consistency and reliability of the record concerning Hosshin-in.

    [Logical Connection] The Edo-period governance relationship shown by "To the Temple Administration, His Reverence the Ichijō-in Prince, the Honorable Magistrate" in Block 21 (the village administrative documents, Kyōhō era) is here confirmed to extend back as far as the Muromachi period (the Chōroku–Eishō era). This is evidence, corroborated in layers by independent third-party documents from different eras, that the Monzeki's direct governance of Hosshin-in was not something that arose suddenly in the Edo period, but was an institutional relationship that continued unbroken from the medieval period.
    Quoted from the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4, Jinson Daisōjō Ki (from the 12th month of Chōroku 2 to the 4th month of Eishō 1) (p. 242, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number 554-213, Bibliographic ID 000000778530, View at National Diet Library) →The shōya and sata-nin have behaved unlawfully and negligently, and moreover, by residing within another's domain, have caused difficulty for the Monzeki; a suitable person shall be appointed within Hosshin-in. This article is entirely proper; it should be promptly ordered, and so on. The above [is a true record]. [Source Note] This passage is an excerpt from the diary (Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4) written by Jinson, the Daijō-in Monzeki, entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family, and records, as a fifteenth-century contemporaneous document, the fact that the Daijō-in Monzeki directly exercised authority over shōya and sata-nin personnel appointments within Hosshin-in. The imperative phrase "a suitable person shall be appointed" is clear evidence that Hosshin-in was under the direct governance of the Daijō-in Monzeki.
    32. Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Volume 13 — Medieval Economic Records of "Hashimoto Yashiki" (Related to Yokota Manor and Hosshin-in)
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (a Medieval Economic Record) / Evidence That "Hashimoto Yashiki" Appears by Name in the Economic Records of Yokota Manor and Hosshin-in]

    This source is a letter by Saemon-no-jō Tsunefusa, recorded in Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Volume 13. "Hashimoto Yashiki" (the Hashimoto Residence) is recorded by name, in the economic records related to Yokota Manor and Hosshin-in, as a unit assessed a fixed payment of 500 mon. The appearance of "Hashimoto Yashiki" as a concrete property unit within the economic order of Hosshin-in and Yokota Manor, in a medieval economic source entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side, is important evidence that the name "Hashimoto" was substantively rooted in the land of Hosshin-in and Yokota Manor since medieval times.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① A concrete economic record: "Hashimoto Yashiki — Fixed [Payment] 500 Mon": The recording of "Hashimoto Yashiki" as an independent economic unit with a fixed assessed payment of 500 mon shows that a residence bearing the name "Hashimoto" was institutionally incorporated into the manorial economic system of Hosshin-in and Yokota Manor. This is proof that "Hashimoto" was not a name applied in later generations, but a substantive entity appearing by name in medieval manorial economic records.

    ② Evidence of a direct economic link with Hosshin-in: The passage "six hundred [mon], from West Hosshin-in, disbursed for the biannual Rakan-ku [Arhat offering ceremony]" shows that Hosshin-in functioned, within the economic records of Yokota Manor, as a concrete unit of contribution and administration. This constitutes economic evidence consistent with "the existence of Hosshin-in as a sub-temple proprietary lord," confirmed in Block 22 (the Japan Shōen Data) and Block 24 (Kashihara City History, the Chōja Sen).

    ③ "Hashimoto Yashiki" recorded alongside "the Fukū-in Sutra Lecture" and "Ritsushi Matsuda Ryōgenbō": The fact that Hashimoto Yashiki is recorded in the same economic record alongside the temple Fukū-in and the monk Ritsushi Matsuda Ryōgenbō suggests that "Hashimoto Yashiki" was an entity incorporated into the economic system of temples and sub-temples, indicating the possibility that it was a residence connected to a family of in-ke-lineage service, rather than the residence of an ordinary farmer.

    [Logical Connection] Taken together, Block 30 ("Nishi-Hashino-in no Gorō," 1456) and this block ("Hashimoto Yashiki," medieval period) show that, in the medieval economic records of Yokota Manor and Hosshin-in, records relating to "Hashimoto/Hosshin-in" appear in two independent forms: "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)" and "Hashimoto Yashiki." This functions as medieval, local evidence supplementing the noted "gap in the intermediate generations," and corroborates, from the perspective of economic sources, the connection to Hashimoto Yaroku (1582).
    Quoted from Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Volume 13 (Yokota Manor, Imabayashi Manor) (p. 866, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number GB22-7, Bibliographic ID 000001225104, View at National Diet Library) →No. 402: Letter of Saemon-no-jō Tsunefusa
    Item: Donation for the Fukū-in Sutra Lecture — cash payment 2 kan mon; of which, the Nassho's (Receiving Office's) portion is 300 mon, the fixed messenger's stipend is 100 mon, the additional lecture fee for the first day of the equinox period is 50 mon, and attendance fees are 100 mon each, totaling 1 kan mon; six hundred [mon], from West Hosshin-in, disbursed for the biannual Rakan-ku [Arhat offering ceremony].
    Item: Hashimoto Yashiki — fixed [payment] 500 mon; on the 18th day of the 4th month, distributed at 100 mon per portion; the remainder is the Nassho's portion.
    Item: Ritsushi Matsuda Ryōgenbō — meeting on the 24th day of the 3rd month. Cash payment: 1 koku 7 to 7 shō 7 gō; deferred portion: 7 to 1 shō 8 shaku, with a further 4 gō deferred; principal plus deferred total: 2 koku 4 to 8 shō 7 gō 8 shaku [figures unclear in source], 6 gō; fixed rice: 2 koku 3 to 9 shō 1 gō 8 shaku, valued in cash at 2 kan 80 mon at the market rate of 1 to 1 shō 5 gō; distributed for the current lecture meeting: 300 mon, with disbursements of 70 mon each [remainder of passage unclear in source].[Source Note] This document is a letter of Saemon-no-jō Tsunefusa recorded in Dai Nihon Shiryō (compiled by the Historiographical Institute of the University of Tokyo, an independent third-party historical compilation), and is not a document created or maintained by the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. The entry "Hashimoto Yashiki — fixed [payment] 500 mon" is a medieval source showing that "Hashimoto Yashiki" appears by name, within the manorial economic records of Yokota Manor and Hosshin-in, as an independent economic unit with a fixed assessed payment.
    33. Bunroku 4 (1595) Land Survey Register of Hosshin-in Village (an Official Cadastral Survey Record of the Toyotomi Regime)
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (an Administrative Record of the Toyotomi Regime) / Evidence That Hosshin-in Village Was Independently Recorded as the Subject of an Official Land Survey by the Toyotomi Regime]

    This source is a Land Survey Register (Kenchichō) carried out by the Toyotomi regime (Masuda Uemon-no-jō) upon Hosshin-in Village, Sōnokami District, Yamato Province, in Bunroku 4 (1595). "Hosshin-in Village" is recorded by name, as an independent survey unit, in an administrative record of the Toyotomi regime entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. This is evidence, corroborated by a national administrative record, that Hosshin-in did not disappear even at the end of the Sengoku period, but continued as a substantive village unit subject to the land administration of the Toyotomi regime.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① Official land survey record of "Hosshin-in Village" by the Toyotomi regime: The "Land Survey Register of Hosshin-in Village, Sōnokami District, Yamato Province," conducted by Masuda Uemon-no-jō (a magistrate of the Toyotomi regime), shows that Hosshin-in Village was recognized as an independent survey unit within the Toyotomi regime's land administration. This is proof that Hosshin-in continued substantively as a place-name and village unit even during the transitional period when it shifted institutionally from a medieval sub-temple domain to an early modern village.

    ② The personal names of local figures such as "Sōkurō" and "Osada Shichirōjirō" recorded by name: The recording, by name, of myōshu (registered landholders) such as "Sōkurō, now Matajirō, now Hikokurō" and "Osada Shichirōjirō" in the survey register means that the local reality of Hosshin-in Village is confirmed contemporaneously through an administrative record of the Toyotomi regime.

    ③ Confirmation of the scale of rice yield in the entry "at the time of the general inspection of fallow and cultivated land, 564 koku 5 to 2 shō 3 gō was added to the register": This additional rice yield shows that Hosshin-in Village was recognized by the Toyotomi regime, even at the end of the Sengoku period, as a village possessing considerable agricultural productive capacity. This scale forms the premise for the continuity of the economic reality with the Meiji-era record presented in §1 of this site — that "Hashimoto Hyōsaku's hereditary stipend of 14 koku equaled approximately 19% of the revenue of the Ichijō-in estate."

    ④ A record of the shōya system in "naishō (internal confirmation) by Shōya Magojirō": The record that Shōya Magojirō gave naishō of the land survey shows that the shōya system was already functioning in Hosshin-in Village during the Toyotomi era. This corroborates institutional continuity with the shōya system of Hosshin-in Village confirmed in Block 21 (the village administrative documents, Kyōhō era), extending back approximately 130 years earlier to the Toyotomi era.

    [Logical Connection] Following the chronological sequence — Block 35 (the Hashino-in shūsei sata, 1578) → this Block 33 (the Hosshin-in Village land survey, 1595) → Block 21 (the village administrative documents, Kyōhō era) — the institutional continuity of Hosshin-in Village from the end of the Sengoku period through the Edo period is confirmed by three mutually independent third-party administrative records. This constitutes important supplementary evidence, from the perspective of administrative records, corroborating the noted "continuity after Hashimoto Yaroku (1582)."
    Quoted from Bibliographical Study and Catalog of "Daijō-in Monjo": Ochanomizu Library Seikidō Bunko Collection, Volume 1 (p. 303, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number UP171-238, Bibliographic ID 000001766439) →Bunroku 4 (1595), 8th month, 19th day (survey conducted by Masuda Uemon-no-jō)Land Survey Register of Hosshin-in Village, Sōnokami District, Yamato ProvinceUpper-grade paddy field: 10 ken by 20 ken; comprising two plots totaling 6 se 20 bu; yield 1 koku 4 shō 7 gō. Sōkurō — now Matajirō, now Hikokurō (omitted) Osada ShichirōjirōAt the time of the general inspection of fallow and cultivated land, 564 koku 5 to 2 shō 3 gō was added to the register — survey conducted by Lord Masuda Uemon[-no-jō]. Memorandum of internal confirmation (naishō) by Shōya Magojirō[Source Note] This source is the record of an official land survey conducted by Masuda Uemon-no-jō, a magistrate of the Toyotomi regime, and is not a document created or maintained by the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. The official recording of Hosshin-in Village as an independent survey unit within the Toyotomi regime's land administration in Bunroku 4 (1595) is proof, through a third-party administrative record, that Hosshin-in continued as a substantive village unit even at the end of the Sengoku period.
    34. Yamato Shiryō, Volume 1 (Eishō 4: Records of Warfare in Yamato Province) — The Historical Basis for the Gap in Sources
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (a Gazetteer and Record of Warfare) / "The In-ke and Zaike Were Largely Destroyed" — A Third-Party Gazetteer Documents the Historical Reason the Sources for the Intermediate Generations Were Lost]

    This source is a record of the warfare of the 9th month of Eishō 4 (1507), found in Volume 1 of the Yamato Shiryō. It does not refer to Hosshin-in directly, but the passages "the in-ke and zaike [sub-temples and their lay residences] were largely destroyed" and "many temples and shrines throughout the province were burned in the fires of war at this time" are recorded by a third-party gazetteer entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side, documenting the historical fact that the sub-temples of Yamato Province, including Hosshin-in, suffered devastating damage in the warfare of the Eishō era. This functions as background evidence objectively explaining the historical reason for the noted gap — that "no direct record for the intermediate generations has yet been found."

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① A record of devastating damage to the sub-temple system in "the in-ke and zaike were largely destroyed": The description that, when the Kyoto army occupied Tōdai-ji and Nanto (Nara) in Eishō 4 (1507), the "in-ke and zaike" of Yamato Province were largely destroyed shows that the entire Kōfuku-ji sub-temple system, including Hosshin-in, suffered severe institutional damage at this time. This functions as an objective historical reason why sources were scattered or destroyed at the midpoint (1507) of the gap between the death of Ryōshin (1319) and Hashimoto Yaroku (1582).

    ② A direct record of the destruction of sources in "many temples and shrines throughout the province were burned in the fires of war at this time": The fact that temple and shrine documents and records were destroyed by the fires of war is corroborated by a third-party gazetteer as a situation to which the basic historiographical principle — "absence of sources does not mean absence of fact" — should be applied. The objective historical fact of this Eishō-era warfare provides a rational explanation for why direct records of the intermediate generations are scarce.

    ③ Records of resistance by powers surrounding Hosshin-in (Tsutsui, Tōichi, Hashio, Narahara): The fact that the local powers surrounding Sōnokami District, Yamato Province — where Hosshin-in Village was located — were principal parties to this conflict shows that Hosshin-in existed within the central zone of the warfare, serving as geographic evidence further raising the likelihood that sources were scattered or lost.

    [Logical Connection: A Positive Response to the "Gap in the Sources"] In response to the noted weakness that "no direct record for the intermediate generations has yet been found," this source offers the following reasoning: the third-party gazetteer's records of "the in-ke and zaike were largely destroyed" (1507) and "many temples and shrines throughout the province were burned in the fires of war at this time" objectively demonstrate that the reason no sources survive for the intermediate generations is not that "no records existed," but the historical fact that they "were destroyed by the fires of war." This serves as a third-party basis for explaining the gap in sources not as an "absence of evidence," but as "the loss of records through historical disaster."
    Quoted from the Yamato Shiryō, Volume 1 (p. 23, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number 348-226-I, Bibliographic ID 000000704075, View at National Diet Library) →Eishō 4 (1507), 9th month. (preceding text omitted) On the 19th day, the shogunate summoned Sawakura and further had him attack Tango. Sawakura then stationed a garrison force in this province and returned to the capital. It is said that many temples and shrines throughout the province were burned in the fires of war at this time. In the 9th month of Eishō 4, Akazawa Shinbei, Uchibori Shinjirō, and others were further sent into this province. Tōichi, Hashio, Narahara, and Tsutsui sent troops out to Nara to resist them, but were unsuccessful. On the 18th day the Kyoto army entered Tōdai-ji, and the whole of the Nanto (Nara) region was occupied by it; the in-ke and zaike were largely destroyed. A separate force attacked the Inuwaki faction; Kataoka, Ochi, Kataoka, and others fell.[Source Note] This source is a record of the warfare of Eishō 4 (1507) found in the Yamato Shiryō (a modern gazetteer compiled by a third party), and is not a document created by the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side. The passages "the in-ke and zaike were largely destroyed" and "many temples and shrines throughout the province were burned in the fires of war at this time" are the third-party gazetteer's own record that the sub-temple system of Yamato Province, including Hosshin-in, suffered devastating damage and lost its sources in the warfare of the Eishō era. This is important background evidence explaining the objective historical reason for the noted gap in sources — that "no direct record for the intermediate generations has yet been found."
    35. Tamon'in Nikki, Volume 3 (Tenshō 6) — "Hashino-in" Handles the Shushō Administration for a Major Daijō-in Ritual
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (Highest Evidentiary Rating) / Decisive Evidence in Which Eishun, a Kōfuku-ji Monk Unconnected to the Hashimoto Family, Independently Records "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)" Handling the Administration of a Ritual Ceremony]

    This source is a passage for the New Year of Tenshō 6 (1578), recorded in Volume 3 of the Tamon'in Nikki, written by Eishun, a monk of Kōfuku-ji (a third party entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family). The entry "Hashino-in handled the shushō [administration]" independently records — through a third party unconnected to the Hashimoto family — that Hosshin-in (the Hashimoto family's base) served as the operational administrator of the Shushō-e, a major Daijō-in ritual ceremony.

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① Explicit statement of ritual-administration duty in "Hashino-in handled the shushō [administration]": "Shushō sata" means the operational administration and management of the Shushō-e, a major Buddhist ritual ceremony held in the New Year. The record that Hosshin-in was responsible for the administration (sata) of this major ceremony means that a third party unconnected to the Hashimoto family (Eishun) independently recorded that Hosshin-in was not a mere minor local temple, but a sub-temple possessing the practical capacity and institutional authority to actually administer a major Daijō-in ceremony.

    ② Concrete records of practical duties, such as "eighty rice cakes were sent" and "300 mon for the administration of the Great Preceptor": The recording of concrete details of ceremony administration — the sending of eighty rice cakes, an offering of 300 mon to the Great Preceptor (Daidōshi), the sending of six to of offering-rice, and so on — shows that Hosshin-in's administration of the ceremony was a concrete practical duty that the recorder (Eishun) could directly observe and confirm. This corroborates that the entry for "Hashino-in" is not an abstract or purely ceremonial mention, but a record of concrete duties actually performed.

    ③ The highest evidentiary rating, from multiple independent records by the same author (Eishun) relating to the Hashimoto family: Eishun (1518–1596), the author of the Tamon'in Nikki, independently recorded not only this block (1578, the Hashino-in shūsei sata) but also Hashimoto Yaroku (responsible for the treasury, Tenshō 10, 1582) and Hashimoto Sama (a Shinto priest, obituary entry, around Tenshō 18). The fact that the same third party, unconnected to the Hashimoto family, independently recorded "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)" and "figures of the Hashimoto family" a total of three times within a closely spaced period in the latter half of the sixteenth century (1578 to around Tenshō 18) constitutes extremely powerful evidence, in which third-party records corroborate in layers the institutional identity of "Hosshin-in = the Hashimoto family's base."

    ④ The significance of the chronological position of Tenshō 6 (1578): This record (1578) falls between Block 34 (the Eishō-era warfare, 1507) and Block 33 (the Toyotomi land survey, 1595), and a third-party record shows that, even during the recovery period after the warfare, Hosshin-in continued to function as a sub-temple responsible for the administration of major Daijō-in ceremonies. This is direct evidence proving the resilience with which Hosshin-in institutionally survived and continued to function, despite having suffered devastating damage in "the in-ke and zaike were largely destroyed" (1507).

    [Logical Connection] This source (1578), the record of Hashimoto Yaroku (1582), and the record of Hashimoto Sama (around Tenshō 18) are all independently recorded by the same third party (Eishun, in the Tamon'in Nikki) within a closely spaced period in the latter half of the sixteenth century — recording both "Hosshin-in's (Hashino-in's) responsibility for ceremony administration" and "the real names of Hashimoto family figures as persons connected to Hosshin-in." This constitutes one of the strongest bodies of evidence from the standpoint of "the convergence of multiple independent pieces of evidence" as assessed by Grok, forming an evidentiary structure — the repeated third-party confirmation of "the institutional identity of Hosshin-in and the Hashimoto family" — that is difficult to refute.
    Quoted from the Tamon'in Nikki, Volume 3 (p. 3, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number 210.48-E38t-Tk, Bibliographic ID 000000871371, View at National Diet Library) →Tenshō 6 (1578), New Year, 18th day. The Shushō [ceremony] at the Great Hall (Ō-Midō) concluded; seven senior [monks] attended, [including] Sengyō-bō; thirty rice cakes were provided.
    Item: At Daijō-in, a partial reading (tendoku) of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra (Daihannya-kyō) was performed and concluded; over sixty [monks] attended.
    Item: In the afternoon, [a visit] was made to inquire after the health of the mother, the Ōmandokoro, [who] came up to the capital; four pieces of silver were presented.
    Item: Hashino-in handled the shushō [administration]; eighty rice cakes were sent by it, with fifteen distributed; it was the day of the Horse. The Great Preceptor's fee was 300 mon; six to of offering-rice were sent, with attendance fees of two to each. A painted image of Kan-Fugen was borrowed from Hōzō-in; five rice cakes were given for it. A wooden statue was borrowed from Nan'i-bō. Gyōran presented [these]. [Source Note] "Hashino-in" is a kana rendering of Hosshin-in (Hashiin), and "handled the shushō [administration]" means that it was responsible for the operational administration of the Shushō-e, a major New Year ritual ceremony. This record is a passage from the personal diary (Tamon'in Nikki, Volume 3) written by the Kōfuku-ji monk Eishun, unconnected to the Hashimoto family, and is evidence in which a third party independently recorded that Hosshin-in functioned, in Tenshō 6 (1578), as a sub-temple with the practical capability to administer major Daijō-in ceremonies. The same author (Eishun) also independently recorded Hashimoto Yaroku (responsible for the treasury) in Tenshō 10 (1582) and Hashimoto Sama (a Shinto priest) around Tenshō 18. The fact that "Hashino-in (Hosshin-in)" and "the Hashimoto family" appear multiple times in the same third-party record within a closely spaced period in the latter half of the sixteenth century constitutes powerful circumstantial evidence of their institutional identity.
    36. Research Materials on the Daijō-in Monshu and Temple History (the Institutional Reality of Sekkanke Succession to the Monshu Office in the Kamakura Period)
    [Source Classification: Independent Third-Party Document (a Modern Academic Research Source) / Academic Proof of the Institutional Practice by Which Sons of the Sekkanke (Fujiwara Hokke) Succeeded to the Office of Daijō-in and Ichijō-in Monshu]

    This source is a modern research work (Botan to Fuji, Volume 3) that academically clarifies the succession of the Daijō-in Monshu office and the involvement of the Sekkanke (Regental Houses). An academic publication entirely independent of the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side demonstrates that the practice by which sons of the Sekkanke (the Fujiwara Hokke, including the Kujō and Ichijō families) succeeded to the office of Daijō-in and Ichijō-in Monshu was established as a general rule from the Kamakura period onward. This is important background evidence in which an independent academic source corroborates the institutional premise of the hypothesis put forward in the main text of this site — that "close relatives or illegitimate sons of the Monzeki settled locally at sub-temples."

    [Summary of Key Evidence]
    ① Proof of the institutional rule "the practice of Sekkanke sons succeeding to the Monshu office was established from Jinpan onward": The academic confirmation that, at Daijō-in, the practice of sons of the Sekkanke (the main line of the Fujiwara Hokke) succeeding to the office of Monshu was established from Jinpan onward corroborates, through an independent academic source, that the records presented in §1 of this site — "Ryōshin (son of Takatsukasa Mototada) = the 15th head priest of Ichijō-in" and "Kyōgen (son of Takatsukasa Fusahira) = the 24th head priest of Ichijō-in" — are concrete instances of this institutional practice.

    ② A direct response to a potential objection: institutional grounds for the question of "blood relation or official duty": In response to the point raised regarding "the distinction between blood relation (close kinship) and an official-duty relationship (service, retainership)," this source academically confirms that the institution of "sons of the Sekkanke succeeding to the office of Monshu" was the very foundation of the sub-temple system, corroborating the historical necessity of Hosshin-in (Hosshin-in) falling within the institutional framework of "the various in-ke were, broadly speaking, of the same lineage as this Monzeki" (Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 6).

    ③ A concrete instance of succession: "the imperial censure and exile of Enjitsu (son of Kujō Michiie, sixth head)": The record that Enjitsu, as the son of Kujō Michiie (of the main line of the Fujiwara Hokke, Regent and Chancellor), became the sixth head priest of Daijō-in, received imperial censure in Kenchō 4 (1252), and was exiled in Bun'ei 3 (1266), shows a concrete instance of the possibility that a son of the Fujiwara Hokke Sekkanke who entered a Monzeki and later left it could settle locally.

    ④ Confirmation of an institutional mechanism: "the practice of prospective Monshu entering the Monshu's chamber at a young age": The practice of prospective Monshu entering [the temple] at a young age shows that, structurally, there existed opportunities for those sons of the Fujiwara Hokke who entered a Monzeki but did not actually become Monshu (illegitimate sons or collateral relatives) to become involved with, and settle at, sub-temple domains. This is evidence in which an academic source reinforces the institutional necessity of the hypothesis in the main text of this site — that "close relatives or illegitimate sons of the Monzeki settled at Hosshin-in."

    [Logical Connection] The "institutional practice of Sekkanke sons succeeding to the Monshu office," which this source proves, connects directly with the following facts established in §2:
    · Ryōshin (son of Takatsukasa Mototada) = 15th head priest of Ichijō-in (Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4)
    · Kyōgen (son of Takatsukasa Fusahira) = 24th head priest of Ichijō-in (ibid.)
    · "at that time the various in-ke were, broadly speaking, of the same lineage as this Monzeki" (Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 6)
    Taken together, these show that the institution whereby sons of the Fujiwara Hokke Sekkanke succeeded to the office of Daijō-in and Ichijō-in Monshu, with their "lineage" (monryū) constituting the sub-temples, functioned throughout the medieval period — a fact confirmed in layers by multiple independent third-party sources.
    Quoted from Research Materials on the Daijō-in Monshu and Temple History (p. 106, available in the National Diet Library Digital Collection, Call Number HM121-E60, Bibliographic ID 000002728535, View at National Diet Library) →Botan to Fuji, Volume 3, Section 1 (The Dispute over the Daijō-in Monshu Office at the End of the Kamakura Period)
    The Succession of Daijō-in Monshu (Confirmed Facts)
    The founding period of Daijō-in: Ryūzen built the hall and pagoda (Kanji 1, 1087).
    Sequence of principal successors: Ryūzen → Raijitsu → Jinpan → Shin'en → Jisson → Enjitsu → Jinkaku, Sonshin, Jishin, and others. From Jinpan onward, the practice of Sekkanke sons succeeding to the office of Monshu was established. Enjitsu (6th head): son of Kujō Michiie.
    Kenchō 4 (1252): imperial censure → Kenchō 7 (1255): censure lifted.
    Bun'ei 1 (1264): communal censure → Bun'ei 3 (1266): exile → Bun'ei 9 (1272): death. Jinkaku: assumed the office of Daijō-in Monshu during the Einin era (around 1293, a period of conflict in Nanto).
    Jishin: entered [the temple] in Bun'ei 2, and succeeded to the Monzeki after the death of Sonshin in Kōan 6. Institutional practice: it was customary for the prospective Monshu to enter the Monshu's chamber at a young age.[Source Note] This source is a modern academic research work (Botan to Fuji, Volume 3) entirely unconnected to the Hashimoto family or the Hosshin-in side, and academically clarifies the institutional practice by which sons of the Sekkanke (Fujiwara Hokke) were deeply involved in the succession of the Daijō-in Monshu office. The academic confirmation that "the practice of Sekkanke sons succeeding to the Monshu office was established from Jinpan onward" is evidence in which an independent academic source corroborates that the primary-source records presented in §1 and §2 of this site — "Ryōshin (son of Takatsukasa Mototada) = 15th head priest of Ichijō-in" and "Kyōgen (son of Takatsukasa Fusahira) = 24th head priest of Ichijō-in" — are concrete instances of this institutional practice.

    A jointly signed sacred-water oath (shinsui kishōmon) of the Kōfuku-ji gakuryo (scholar-monks), dated the 20th day of the 6th month of Tenbun 20 (1551), included in Kasuga Taisha Documents, Volume 6. It is a pledge of punishment and a divine-retribution oath concerning the harvesting of miscellaneous timber — fudanshiba (perpetual brushwood), hagi (split wood), tsugimatsu (pine-splint torches), and the like — at the Hanayamabe Ango-bō. The signatures record the gakuryo, including Rinzen Enkō (kaō), and it is an important record pledging to restore the ango [retreat] in accordance with the temple's true intent.
