    [Key Points of the Oath]

    Item Details
    Date 20th day of the 6th month, Tenbun 20 (1551)
    Type A jointly signed sacred-water oath of the Kōfuku-ji gakuryo (written on the reverse of a Miroku-kō [Maitreya assembly] goō [talismanic] paper)
    Nature of the Dispute A pledge of punishment concerning the case in which kushi-hōshi (lower-ranking temple servants) and others harvested — in an act of encroachment — miscellaneous timber (perpetual brushwood, split wood, pine-splint torches, and the like) at the Hanayamabe Ango-bō
    Provenance of the Ango A prestigious ango [retreat], connected to the secret rites and sacred offerings performed day and night before the deity, dating back to the votive founding by His Excellency the Regent (Hakuriku-denka)
    Content of the Pledge The gakuryo, the Roppō, and the Shimoman — the three ranks — unite in solidarity, with severe punishment pledged against violators. In case of violation, the doors of the five shrines and seven halls are to be opened and the religious rites and ceremonies suspended, leaving the matter to the will of the deity

    [Quotation] No. 127, Jointly Signed Sacred-Water Oath of the Kōfuku-ji Gakuryo

    Respectfully declared: concerning the jointly signed sacred-water oath invoking heavenly punishment, [written on] the reverse of the Miroku-kō goō [paper].

    The particulars of the above are as follows: the members of the assembly have this time resolved on the spot to punish the kushi-hōshi and others who harvested miscellaneous timber — perpetual brushwood, split wood, pine-splint torches, and the like — at the Hanayamabe Ango-bō; this is a matter beyond words. Now, this ango has, since its votive founding by His Excellency the Regent, been especially connected with the secret rites and sacred offerings performed day and night before the deity, and for this reason the cutting and use of the mountain's timber has long been forbidden of old. The whole patrol of that mountain had been entrusted to the assembly on behalf of the gakuryo; that some, on the strength of this very provenance, should instead act in encroachment, and commit such a violation against the temple, is utterly outrageous.

    Because of this, the daily necessities of the ango have already fallen into shortage, and it has repeatedly been said that the service of both clergy and laity has become difficult to sustain; should the matter of punishment drag on in time, the summer retreat (ketsuge) would swiftly collapse. How lamentable — that the rebuilding of this shrine should, against all expectation, be thus delayed, that the hidden sacred authority of the deity should be obscured, and that in these times both the ordained and the laity should lose their way; this is an age in which the realm of demons finds its opportunity, and flatterers work great evil against temple and shrine — a matter of more than sufficient grief and reproach.

    Accordingly, we shall promptly repel this evil and treachery, pursue the temple and shrine's true intent, and devise a plan for the restoration of the ango. The gakuryo, the Roppō, and the Shimoman — the three ranks — shall unite in solidarity, thinking of one another as fish to water, and without delay shall impose severe punishment upon that group. Should the present custom still fail to accord with the temple's true intent, the doors of the five shrines and seven halls shall be opened, the religious rites and ceremonies suspended, and the matter of restoration entrusted to the will of the deity. This resolution, agreed upon by the great majority, is to be firmly upheld, and no part of it is to be secretly leaked or omitted.

    Should anyone violate the articles above, may they incur the punishment of the great and small deities of the land of Japan, and especially of the Daimyōjin of this shrine. Accordingly, this sacred-water oath [is sworn].

    Tenbun 20 (1551), 6th month, 20th day.

    Source Bibliographic Details Link

    [Quotation] Bunmei 15, Year of Mizunoto-U — Record of Eishun of Chōjitsu-bō, Tamon'in

    New Year's Day. [Prayers offered for:] the prosperity of temples and shrines, the flourishing of the Buddhist Law, the revival of scholarly practice, the peace of the realm, the tranquility of the precincts, the increase of long life and fortune, and the fulfillment of all wishes — a thousand joys and ten thousand blessings, most auspicious. As in customary years, we made the shrine visit and entered the hall, presented offerings, and the precinct proceeded together as is the fine custom.

    On the 6th day, the shōya of Koma no Shō brought three bundles of nanakusa vine, as usual. In recent years, owing to the general disorder of the realm, the governance of that place has been in name only, without substance, and I was at first unfamiliar with the proper protocol. That person stated: "Each time, without fail, one offering of rice cakes on a single tray, one sheet, and one [further item] are given; and further, when bringing vine, three rice cakes are given to the bearer." As Zen'ei-bō had for many years been familiar with the Kyō Goshi office, I made inquiry [of him], whereupon —

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    The Author of the Tamon'in Nikki and Hosshin-in The Goshi office associated with Hosshin-in is mentioned in the day-to-day record kept in Bunmei 15 (1483) by Eishun of Chōjitsu-bō, Tamon'in (the author of the Tamon'in Nikki), allowing the relationship between Hosshin-in and temple administration to be confirmed from the perspective of a contemporaneous practitioner.
    Zen'ei-bō's Goshi Office The statement that "Zen'ei-bō had for many years been familiar with the Kyō Goshi office" shows that a specific individual connected to Hosshin-in held this office over many years, reinforcing the organizational continuity of Hosshin-in.
    Relationship with Koma no Shō Annual customary offerings from Koma no Shō (nanakusa vine, rice cakes, and so on) are recorded, showing that Hosshin-in maintained institutional relationships with multiple manors.
    41. Nihon Chūsei Yuishiki Bukkyō-shi (History of Yogācāra Buddhism in Medieval Japan) — The Scholarly Lineage of Hosshin-in
    Monks associated with Hosshin-in as recorded in the Nihon Chūsei Yuishiki Bukkyō-shi (History of Yogācāra Buddhism in Medieval Japan). It lists Kenshun-bō Jōsei (1399–1477), Zenjō-bō Kakuin (1423–1492), and Zengyō-bō, showing the scholarly lineage of residents of Hosshin-in within the history of medieval Yogācāra Buddhism.

    42. Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho — Tōhoku-in Dharma Lineage (Kyōen and the Name "Hosshi-in")
    The Tōhoku-in dharma-lineage record contained in Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho, Vol. 124. It sets out the Hossō-school line of succession — Engen (deputy abbot [Betto]; son of Major Counselor Fujiwara no Takasue; disputant at the Yuima-e assembly in 1190, among other roles), Kyōen (resided at Tōhoku-in; bore the name Hosshi-in), and Enken (served at the East Gate) — and gives a detailed account of Kyōen's appointment as deputy abbot and his lecturing career under the name Hosshi-in.

    The position of Hosshi-in within the Hossō-school lineage Kyōen is placed within the formal line of succession running Jōkei → Engen → Kyōen → Enken, showing that the name Hosshi-in was conferred upon a formally recognized successor within the Hossō school's line of transmission.

    43. Yamatokōriyama City History Sourcebook — List of Hosshi-in Village Headmen and Elders (Edo Period)
    A list of village headmen (shōya) and elders (toshiyori) of Hosshi-in Village during the Edo period, contained in the Yamatokōriyama City History Sourcebook. It includes Gen'emon (headman in Kyōhō 12 and 18, and Hōreki 14), Genbei (elder in Kyōhō 18, headman in Bunsei 3), Kihei (elder in Hōreki 14), Kurōbei (headman around Shōhō 4 and the Keian–Jōō period), and others. A petition for relief from crop failure dated Kaei 3 (1850) bears the signatures of headman Tahei and elder Hyōsaku (fief portion). The document also records the co-signatures of headmen and elders from neighboring villages (Nukatabe Village, Ichimoto Village, and others), showing the succession of village officials in Hosshi-in Village over time.

    44. Yamatokōriyama City History Sourcebook — Draft Retirement Petition of Headman Tahei (Bunsei 7)
    A draft of the retirement petition submitted by Tahei, headman of Hosshi-in Village, in Bunsei 7 (1824), contained in the Yamatokōriyama City History Sourcebook. It details his petition to retire due to old age and illness, the selection of his successor through village balloting, the handover to Nakayoshi Saburō, and the process of submission through the Lord Magistrate's Council of Five Masters (Gojichū) and the Annual Deputies (Nen'yo). This village-administration record notes the special treatment accorded to the headman for his many years of service.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Yamatokōriyama City History Sourcebook (p. 468 and others) Call no. 216.5-Y539y National Diet Library

    [Citation] Concerning matters from the second month through the twentieth day of the fifth month, Bunsei 7 (kōshin, Year of the Wood Monkey) — a copy of the draft headman's retirement petition is included

    Tahei, age sixty-one.

    The draft of Tahei's petition for retirement from the headman's office was submitted to the Lord Magistrate's Council of Five Masters, the deputy administrator (azukari-daikan), and the Annual Deputies. As this followed precedent from previous years, the petition was submitted. On the sixth day of the second month of this Year of the Monkey, a document was submitted to the Annual Deputies, as follows:
    Annual Deputies: Tomematsu Bunji-sama; likewise, Nakanishi Sakon-sama

    With all due respect, I humbly submit this petition:
    Item: Some years ago I was gratefully appointed to the office of headman, an honor I have humbly served in for many years since. However, in recent years I have grown infirm with age, and being particularly afflicted with illness, I am now unable even to walk; I have therefore been serving through a substitute, a state of affairs I find deeply regrettable. I therefore humbly and with much hesitation submit this petition requesting to be relieved of my duties as headman. (passage omitted) I earnestly request that I be permitted to retire from the office of headman, and would consider this an act of the greatest mercy, for which I would be endlessly grateful. Respectfully submitted.
    Sixth day, second month, Bunsei 7, Year of the Wood Monkey (1824)
    Hosshi-in Village. Petitioner: Tahei [seal]. Elder: Tajūrō [seal]. Likewise: Sōgorō [seal]. Group-head representative: Gonpei [seal]. Likewise sealed: Jinsuke [seal].
    To: The Lord Magistrate; The Council of Five Masters; The Annual Deputies

    (Ruling of the Annual Deputies) Thereafter, repeated inquiries were made, and instructions were gradually given. On the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month, it was declared: since Tahei had long served in the office of headman, his retirement from that office was hereby granted. It was further instructed that the matter be reported to the Temple Administration (Oteramu-sama), and that succession to the headman's office be provisionally assigned to Nakayoshi Saburō. As the family, across generations, had long served in the office of headman, it was stated that special consideration was warranted.

    (Draft petition to the Temple Administration)
    With all due respect, I humbly submit this petition. Hosshi-in Village, Headman Tahei.
    Item: In the matter above — I was, in years past, gratefully appointed to the office of headman, an honor I have humbly served in for many years since. However, I have gradually grown infirm with age, and, being particularly afflicted with much illness in recent years, I am unable to fulfill the duties of the office. Although I have until now carried out the duties through a substitute, there is naturally the concern of resulting improprieties, which I find deeply regrettable. I therefore humbly wish to retire from the headman's office and... [the draft breaks off here in the source]

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    The channel of submission through the Council of Five Masters and the Temple Administration The retirement petition was processed through a temple-administrative channel — the Lord Magistrate's Council of Five Masters, the Annual Deputies, and the Temple Administration — showing that even in the Bunsei era, Hosshi-in Village remained under the ecclesiastical governance of the Ichijō-in lineage.
    "Special" treatment accorded for the headman's long service The record explicitly states that Tahei received special treatment on account of his long service as headman, showing that the Hashimoto family occupied a central role in Hosshi-in Village governance across generations and was specially regarded by the governing authorities above it.
    Link to Hyōsaku's tenure as elder The elder "Sōgorō," who co-signed the retirement petition of Bunsei 7 (1824), matches exactly with the list of names in Document 43, confirming the consistency between the two sources. This document reinforces the continuity of the record as a village-governance document from the generation preceding Hashimoto Hyōsaku (elder, Kaei 3).
    45. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 — Record of Misconduct and Dereliction by the Hosshi-in Headman-Administrator
    A record concerning the headman-administrator (shōya sata-nin) contained in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4. This temple-administration record states that the headman-administrator's misconduct and dereliction of duty — residing in another domain — caused difficulty for the Monzeki (temple head), and orders that a capable person from within Hosshi-in be appointed at once. It shows that Hosshi-in was under the direct administration of the Daijōin Monzeki.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 — Jinson Daisōjō-ki (p. 254) Call no. 554-213 National Diet Library

    [Citation] Quoted from Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4

    The headman-administrator (shōya sata-nin) is a person of unlawful conduct and dereliction of duty. Moreover, he resides within another domain, which causes difficulty for the Monzeki. As for appointing a capable person from within Hosshi-in without delay — this matter is entirely reasonable, and such an appointment should be ordered at once, so it is said. The above. (Note: "shōya" and "sata-nin" are used synonymously here.)

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Direct administration of Hosshi-in by the Monzeki The record shows the Monzeki himself objecting to the headman-administrator's unlawful conduct as causing him "difficulty," and ordering that a capable person be appointed from within Hosshi-in without delay. This third-party source directly demonstrates that Hosshi-in was institutionally administered as territory under the control of the Daijōin Monzeki.
    The actual functioning of the headman-administrator system The phrase "residing within another domain" indicates that the headman-administrator was originally obligated to reside within Hosshi-in itself in order to carry out his duties, corroborating the fact that Hosshi-in's village governance and estate management functioned in tandem with temple administration.
    The evidentiary weight of Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki The author, Jinson, was the Daijōin Monzeki himself and an entirely independent third party with no connection to the Hashimoto family. The fact that this independent diary records the governance relationship of Hosshi-in gives it the highest evidentiary weight as contemporaneous evidence, wholly independent of any claim made by the Hashimoto family itself.

    47 (Ryōshin). Daijō-in Documents — Ryōshin (Go-Hosshin-in)
    An entry concerning Ryōshin found in the annotated study and catalog of the "Daijō-in Documents" (Daijō-in Monjo). It records that, as the Hosshin-in Sōjō Gobō, Ryōshin was the son of En'kōin-dono — Takatsukasa Mototada — descended to Nara at age four, and after a career in temple administration returned as Go-Hosshin-in Gobō, passing away at age forty-two. It notes that in the seventh year of Kenchō (1255) a three-story pagoda was erected, with a protective charm of Fugen-ji-dono and a single relic grain from Shōdai-ji enshrined within the body of the principal Śākyamuni image for the protection of the monzeki lineage, and it identifies Sōjō Shinken (honzan founder of Shuzen-in) and Sōjō Ryōshin (honzan founder of Hosshin-in) as honored founder-title holders — a monzeki genealogical source.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Details Link
    Annotated Study and Catalog of the "Daijō-in Documents": Ochanomizu Library, Seikidō Bunko Collection, Vol. 1 (item 105) Call number UP171-238, Bibliographic ID 000001766439 View at the National Diet Library

    [Biographical Details of Ryōshin]

    Item Details
    Origin Son of En'kōin-dono — Takatsukasa Mototada (of the Takatsukasa line of the Northern House of the Fujiwara)
    Entry into the temple Descended to Nara at age four. First resided at Tōmon-in, and thereafter entered [Kōfuku-ji]
    Career in temple administration Having passed through the offices of Gokōkō and various temple construction projects without incident, he held the post of temple administrator (jimu) two or three times. After the miscellaneous affairs of the two Nanto monzeki were entrusted to senior clergy, he returned as Go-Hosshin-in Gobō by imperial edict
    Cloister title (in-gō) Go-Hosshin-in Gobō (indicating a direct connection with Hosshin-in / Hosshi-in)
    Death Passed away at the age of forty-two
    Achievements in Kenchō 7 (1255) Erected a single three-story pagoda. Enshrined a protective charm of Fugen-ji-dono and a single relic grain of Shōdai-ji within the body of the principal Śākyamuni image, recording the protection of the monzeki lineage before and after

    [Source Passage — English rendering]

    Ryōshin, styled Hosshin-in Sōjō Gobō, was the son of En'kōin-dono, [that is,] Takatsukasa Mototada; he descended [to Nara], first arriving at Tōmon-in, and thereafter entered [the temple].

    Ryōshin descended [to Nara] at the age of four; having passed without incident through the offices of Gokōkō and various temple-building projects, and having served as temple administrator two or three times, an imperial edict was solemnly issued directing that, with the miscellaneous affairs of the two Nanto monzeki entrusted to senior clergy, he should return; accordingly he returned as Go-Hosshin-in Gobō, and this Sōjō passed away at the age of forty-two.

    (passage omitted)

    The Jizō Hall was restored; the founder of this cloister was styled Hosshin-in, and religious services were begun accordingly. For the sake of future repairs, a cypress grove was planted. In the second month of the seventh year of Kenchō (1255), a single three-story pagoda was erected; accordingly, a protective charm of Fugen-ji-dono together with a single relic grain of Shōdai-ji were enshrined within the body of the principal image of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, so that it might protect the monzeki lineage before and after.

    Accordingly, Sōjō Shinken Gobō was styled the honzan (founder) of Shuzen-in, and Sōjō Ryōshin Gobō was likewise the honzan of Hosshin-in; those specially styled and revered as founders of this mountain [temple complex] pertain to the lineage of Hosshin-in-dono. As for Sugawa, the estate name — Shuzen-in was the in-gō (cloister name) of the Hosshin-in residence.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Direct link between the Takatsukasa lineage and Hosshin-in The Daijō-in Documents — a primary source from the monzeki side — directly record that Ryōshin (son of Takatsukasa Mototada) held the cloister title "Go-Hosshin-in Gobō." This independently corroborates the entry found in the Son'pi Bunmyaku genealogy (Block 3)
    Succession of the "Hosshin-in honzan (founder)" title That Ryōshin was styled as the "Hosshin-in honzan" shows that Hosshin-in (Hosshi-in) was formally positioned within the monzeki lineage as an in-ke (cloister-house) holding founder status
    Contribution to the probability assessment This is one of the most important sources in which a monzeki-side document confirms both the historical existence and the cloister title of Ryōshin — the figure who forms the starting point for the hypothesis that a close relative of the Takatsukasa-lineage monzeki settled at Hosshi-in during the Muromachi period
    48. Daijō-in Documents — Tenshō 5 Yanagimoto-shō Hassaku Expenditure Record
    An economic record from the annotated study and catalog of the "Daijō-in Documents," concerning the Hassaku-season expenditure of Yanagimoto-shō (楊本庄), dated the sixth day of the ninth month of Tenshō 5 (1577). It records a manor-head's allotment of one koku, five shō, together with Bon-season offering rice and the administrative portion for the summer observances at Uchiyama, as belonging to Hosshi-in territory. It shows that even in the latter half of the sixteenth century, Hosshi-in continued to function as a territorial unit of Daijō-in.

    49. Hashimoto Yaroku
    An entry for the second month of Tenshō 10 (1582) found in Volume 5 of the Tamon-in Diary (Tamon-in Nikki). It records a consultation called from Jōshin-in regarding Junkei's journey to the capital (covering the shrine relocation ceremony, the province-wide land tax, additional repair assessments, temple-gate construction, and the treasury offices), together with the appointment of magistrates for the Kawara-ya, the newly built hall, and the thirteen-story pagoda's treasury office. It is an economic record that includes a note of a gift of twenty hiki given to Hashimoto Yaroku-dono among courtesy gifts to the surrounding mountain community. The entry for the third month records routine temple affairs — the newly built hall's first reading-master retreat and the preparation of the midday meal.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon-in Diary, Volume 5 (fascicles 41–46, appendix fascicles 1–5) (item 254) Published Shōwa 10–14 (1935–1939), call number 210.48-E38t-Tk, Bibliographic ID 000000871371 View at the National Diet Library

    [Source Passage] Tenshō 10, Second Month

    On the 20th, around the hour of the Horse (noon), a messenger named Shinshirō came from Jōshin-in [to say] that since Junkei was to go up to the capital that day, there were matters requiring consultation among the office-holders; accordingly, around noon the office-holders were each to gather near Jōshin-in, and so each attended. The particulars, conveyed through the two envoys Shōgon and Hōshū, were discussed as five articles based on private notes:
    — Item: the shrine relocation ceremony
    — Item: how the province-wide land tax is to be concluded
    — Item: additions to be made to the repair assessment
    — Item: the temple-gate construction
    — Item: the treasury/administrative offices
    The three treasury offices for the Kawara-ya, the newly built hall, and the thirteen-story [pagoda] are to have Kanzen-in, Shakain, and Hōju-in appointed as their magistrates.

    On the 21st, [he] made a retreat at Nishi-ya, this being the first appointment of the reading-master (dokushi), and there was a gathering to mark his entry into duty. On the 24th, as it was the reading-master's first appointment at Nishi-ya, a midday meal was prepared as a celebratory gift: two soups and six side dishes, along with accompanying dishes — chilled noodles and nikumi — and five kinds of sweets, with ten hiki given to each; including the attendants from other halls, ten people in all took part, and the celebration was duly held.

    On the same 24th, at the hour of the Horse, a meeting was convened at Higashi-muro to determine the treasury-office appointments. Regarding the Kawara-ya treasury office, it was ordered, in accordance with precedent, that it be settled by the Gakudō (the scholarly assembly), and the deputy in attendance was so instructed; thereupon, with Hōju-in's assent duly obtained, the matter was settled.

    As for the treasury office of the newly built hall, without need for further assent, it was decided outright that Shakain would hold it, and a document arrived stating that the Gakudō would also have oversight.

    As for the treasury office of the thirteen-story [pagoda], since it falls under the charge of the Roppō (six offices), it does not require adjudication by the Gakuryo (scholar-monks); it was settled by the Roppō that Kanzen-in would hold it.

    As for these treasury-office matters, for several days there had been no single agreed course, which all considered improper; from the 20th, two official envoys were dispatched, and through consultation the matter was unified.

    On the 28th, from early morning, [he] went down to Gunzan to pay courtesy calls.

    [List of Courtesy Gifts to Gunzan] (28th day)

    Shōnui 100 hiki —

    Genkichi 20 hiki —
    Yashirō 20 hiki —

    Hashimoto Yaroku-dono 20 hiki *Related to the Hashimoto family

    Third Month
    From the 1st, the newly built hall's chief reading-master began his first-appointment retreat.
    On the 2nd, the midday meal was prepared: seven attendants from other halls, ten in all; two soups, six side dishes, and accompanying dishes were provided — chilled noodles and accompanying konjac — and five kinds of sweets, and the celebration was duly observed in proper form.
    On the 3rd, for the seasonal-festival (sekku) provisions overseen by the Sentō, one to of rice valued at fifty mon each was distributed to the treasurer, the hall officiant, and three attendants.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Existence of a person surnamed Hashimoto In the Tamon-in Diary entry for Tenshō 10 (1582), "Hashimoto Yaroku-dono" appears by name as a recipient of a courtesy gift. This third-party record proves that a person surnamed Hashimoto existed with social connections in the Nara area at the end of the sixteenth century
    Social standing The gift amount (twenty hiki) was lower than that given to Shōnui, Nakai, and Morii (one hundred hiki each), but equal to that given to Hyōbu, Genkichi, and Yashirō, indicating that he was included in the social circle around the temple as a person of middling standing
    Chronological position In sequence — the 1577 record of Hosshi-in territory (Block 48) → this 1582 record of Hashimoto Yaroku → the 1598 stone lantern dedication (Block 14) — this source reinforces the continuity of Hashimoto-related records through the latter half of the sixteenth century


    50. Tamon-in Diary, Volume 1 — Eleventh Month, Tenshō 10 (Matter of the Road near Hashimoto Bridge)
    An entry for the eleventh month of Tenshō 10 (1582) found in Volume 1 of the Tamon-in Diary. It records that, regarding the matter of the road near Hashimoto Bridge, laborers from the seven villages were ordered to carry out repairs, alongside records of labor-levy and festival disputes in the surrounding areas of Tatsuichi, East and West Kujō, and Nima-de Bridge. This source shows the Hashimoto area appearing in a contemporary third-party diary as an object of practical administration within Kōfuku-ji's temple governance.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon-in Diary, Volume 1 (item 62) Call number 210.48-E38t-Tk, Bibliographic ID 000000871371 View at the National Diet Library

    [Source Passage] Tenshō 10, Eleventh Month

    On the 15th, regarding the matter that laborers from Tatsuichi and East Kujō were to be pressed into service for work at Takayama-kutsu, Ochi's deputy, Tsutsumi no Kageyu-zaemon, made this request; a joint document from the Goshi (five masters) was sent in reply stating that this could not be permitted. (passage omitted) ... as this is within the temple's own domain, and since it was represented that there was no precedent for such a labor levy, in the case of West Kujō — where the holding does not fall under Goshi jurisdiction — since it is temple/shrine land, a document to that effect was likewise sent to Kageyu-zaemon's office.

    On the same day, regarding the Daian-ji festival, because the dispute between East Kujō and Hachijō over seating had not been resolved, the festival itself was suspended for the time being. (passage omitted) ... the attendance of both villages was halted for now; although it was decided that only Daian-ji village should attend and the festival be carried out, since Hachijō would not consent, this arrangement likewise could not be carried out.

    On the same day, since the road near Hashimoto Bridge was in disorderly condition, the officials in charge summoned the scholar-monks of Tōin to the assembly hall, and ordered that laborers from the seven villages, carrying stone, earth, and the like, should carry out repairs promptly. The same laborers from the seven villages were also instructed to clear tree roots from around the third marker at Baba. Likewise, the matter of the Hashiri-i water channel was ordered at the same time. Next, regarding Nima-de Bridge, the order was again given to Ikoma-shō; the villagers of that estate came forward requesting permission regarding the repair matter, but this was refused — [it being decided that] repairs should proceed according to precedent, whether or not [the villagers] consented.

    On the same day, Shirōgorō of Tatsuichi came and reported that, among the fields subject to the labor-fee assessment, some were assessed at two hundred mon and others at one hundred mon. (passage omitted) ... fields assessed at one hundred mon; in total, if there are twenty-four tan, [the assessment] should not be reduced. There was some suspicion regarding irregularities in the amount of that levy.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Named record of "Hashimoto Bridge" In 1582, the diary's author, Eishun, independently recorded "Hashimoto Bridge" as a place name under Kōfuku-ji's administrative jurisdiction, providing contemporary third-party evidence that the Hashimoto area definitely existed as an object of practical temple administration at the end of the sixteenth century
    Repair order issued to laborers from the seven villages Laborers from the seven villages were mobilized to repair Hashimoto Bridge, showing that the Hashimoto area fell under the jurisdiction of a wide-ranging temple administration spanning multiple villages. This entry is consistent, as corroborating evidence within the same diary and the same year, with the record of Hashimoto Yaroku (Volume 5 of the Tamon-in Diary, same year)
    Relationship between Goshi jurisdiction and the Hashimoto area The same day's entry concerning East and West Kujō includes the phrase "a holding under Goshi jurisdiction"; that Hashimoto Bridge is recorded in the same context serves as corroborating evidence that the Hashimoto area was positioned close to the institutional framework of Goshi jurisdiction
    51. Appendix to the Jige Kahaku — Table of Contents of Family Records, Ansei 1 (1854): Multiple Appearances of the Hashimoto Family
    A family-records table of contents dated the tenth day of the twelfth month of Ansei 1 (1854), contained in the appendix to the Jige Kahaku. The Hashimoto family appears across multiple family-record categories — Uchitoneri (Kanbara, formerly Hamazaki, alternately Hashimoto or Nakagawa), Mondo-no-tsukasa (Hashimoto), Bancho (Hashimoto), the Kamikita house (Hashimoto), and the Ōimikado house (Hashimoto). It also records a Hashimoto serving as bōkan (temple steward) and taifu (senior officer) under the monzeki lineage of Omuro, making this a genealogical source documenting the household affiliations of attendants and ritual officiants serving the monzeki sōhōke — Ichijōin and Daijōin.

    The Hashimoto Family as Omuro Bōkan Hashimoto is recorded as a bōkan of Omuro (Ninna-ji), showing that the family's institutional connections extended beyond the Ichijōin estate and that Hashimoto held a position among the bōkan and attendant class of multiple monzeki temples. This serves as evidence that Hashimoto was recognized as a distinct family name within the jige official class.
    52. Index to the Tamon-in Diary — Hasshin-in (also "Hashino-in") and Hashimoto-Related Name Index
    Entries from the index to the Tamon-in Diary relating to Hasshin-in (also written Hasshi-in / Hashino-in / Hashinokin / Hashinowin). It lists Hasshin-in figures Zengyō-bō, Zenken, Zenshun-bō, Zenshō-bō, Magoemon, Chōin, and Yūsan, and indexes Hashimoto (Hashimoto-no-Sama, Hashimoto Yaroku) and Hashi-bō (Hashino-bō, etc.) as both personal and place names.

    Confirming the Identity of Hasshin-in and Hasshi-in The index organizes Hasshin-in, Hasshi-in, Hashino-in, Hashinokin, and related forms under a single entry, with the compilers explicitly indicating that these all refer to the same institution/locale throughout the Tamon-in Diary. This provides the basis for identifying Hasshi-in — the seat of the Hashimoto family — with "Hashino-in" as it appears throughout the body of the diary.
    The Inclusion of Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Sama in the Index Hashimoto Yaroku (Tenshō 10 [1582], responsible for treasury duties) and Hashimoto Sama (Tenshō 18 [1590], a Shinto priest) are recorded as independent index entries, indicating that both individuals had enough of a presence in the Tamon-in Diary to be repeatedly referenced there by name.
    The Organizational Diversity of Hasshin-in Personnel Multiple individuals associated with Hasshin-in — Zengyō-bō, Zenken, Zenshun-bō, Zenshō-bō, Magoemon, Chōin, and Yūsan — are recorded in the index, showing that Hasshin-in functioned as an institution with an organized personnel structure rather than being tied to a single individual.
    53. Tamon-in Diary (多聞院日記), Vol. 4 — Fifth Month of Tenshō 18 (Death Record of Hashimoto Sama, Shrine Priest)
    An entry from the fifth month of Tenshō 18 (c. 1590), found in Volume 4 of the Tamon-in Diary. It records the death of Hashimoto Sama as a negi (shrine priest), describing him as a young man who had mastered the way of Shinto and who died of a mysterious illness — a temple/shrine record concerning the jinin (shrine attendants). The Hashimoto family appears under its actual name in this independent, third-party record compiled by the author, Eishun.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 4 (Books 32–40) (235 items) Call number 640-324, Bibliographic ID 000000723487, Author: Eishun [et al.] National Diet Library

    [Quotation] Fifth Month, Tenshō 18

    On the 11th day: [I] visited the shrine. Around midday, [someone] came for a meal. Regarding the fifty koku to be received at Hayama, [he] said this was a troubling matter; but for the most part it was said that it would be handed over at Aimoto, which was a great relief.

    Item: The jinin (shrine attendant) Magozaemon has died, at sixty-six years of age. In recent years he had won the favor of the Major Counselor, and had fully carried out his duties, including the offering of sacred food to the kami. As the saying goes, "once such a talent is seen, it soon departs" — he was a skilled player of Go and excelled in the art of utai (chanted verse); truly a man whose loss as a shrine priest is much to be regretted. The priest known as Hashimoto Sama was likewise a young man of standing; he fell ill with a mysterious sickness and died. This shows that even one who has mastered the way of Shinto and possesses great talent cannot escape the workings of fortune — for all living things must surely perish. This much is beyond doubt.

    Item: Regarding the reading of sutras for the prayer rites at the great gate, Kiama came and reported on the matter; [I] said this was indeed proper, and that it should be arranged accordingly.

    Item: Jin'en has returned from Yamada.

    [Translator's note: This is an interpretive translation of an archaic, cursive-script diary entry; the readings of the place names "Hayama" (吐山) and "Aimoto" (爱元) in particular remain provisional pending further paleographic confirmation.]

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Record of Hashimoto Sama's name as a shrine priest The diary explicitly records "the negi called Hashimoto Sama" (橋本左馬卜云祢宜), providing a primary source of the highest evidentiary value: an independent record — compiled by a third party unconnected to the Hashimoto family (the author, Eishun) — confirming that a member of the Hashimoto family was actually active as a Kasuga-affiliated shrine priest (negi) in the vicinity of Hosshi-in during the Tenshō era
    Recognition as a master of Shinto practice The author praises him as having "mastered the way of Shinto and possessed talent," indicating that Hashimoto Sama was not merely a nominal shrine official but a substantive religious practitioner deeply versed in Shinto. This serves as corroborating evidence that the Hashimoto family was practically and deeply involved with the religious organization of the in-ke (院家, cloistered sub-temple) system
    Listed alongside the jinin Magozaemon In the same day's entry, Hashimoto Sama is recorded alongside the death notice of the jinin (shrine attendant) Magozaemon (age sixty-six), showing that Hashimoto Sama was positioned within the organizational context of the jinin/negi class. This serves as circumstantial evidence that the Hashimoto family was a member of the jinin organization affiliated with Hosshin-in and Hosshi-in
    54. Provisional Genealogy: The Local Family of the Hosshi-in (発志院／"Hashi-no-in") Lineage → Hashimoto Hyōsaku
    A provisional genealogy based on currently available sources. This represents the best current estimate of a lineage descending from the local retainer / jinin (negi) class attached to Hosshi-in (an in-ke, or cloistered sub-temple, of the Daijō-in monzeki), through Hashimoto Yaroku (Tenshō 10) and Hashimoto Sama (Tenshō 18), down to Hashimoto Hyōsaku (Meiji 7, the sole shizoku/samurai-class family of Hosshi-in village). It can be further confirmed through primary sources such as gravestones, the original hereditary stipend return petition, and family registers (koseki).

    [Provisional Genealogy] The Local Family of the Hosshi-in ("Hashi-no-in") Lineage → Hashimoto Hyōsaku

    G0 (Institutional Origin)
    Hosshi-in (発志院／Hosshin-in／"Hashi-no-in") ─── (an in-ke attached to the Daijō-in monzeki)
    Basis: Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki; studies of the Daijō-in temple estates (institutional succession of the monzeki)

    G1 (Medieval to Muromachi-period local retainer class)
    Local retainers / sata-nin (unnamed generation) ─── (function) on-site management of shōen estates / administration of offering rice and law-assembly provisions
    Basis: records concerning Yokota-shō and Hosshi-in (Daijō-in documents, history of Kōriyama)

    G2 (Sengoku period: first appearance of individual names)
    · Hashimoto Yaroku (橋本弥六) — Tenshō 10 (1582): named in the Tamon-in Diary in a list of nōsho (offering-rice) assignments ("Hashimoto Yaroku-dono" of Hatsu[no])
    Role: local administrator handling nōsho / recorded among those assigned to donation duties
    Basis: Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 5 (primary source)

    · Hashimoto Sama (橋本左馬) — Tenshō 18 (c. 1590): recorded in the Tamon-in Diary as a negi (shrine priest / jinin) in a death notice
    Role: negi = Shinto priest (in charge of Kasuga-related rites)
    Basis: Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 4 (primary source)

    (Note) Yaroku and Sama both appear in the same region within the same diary system. The coexistence of a shrine-priest (negi) role and a nōsho-administrator role within a single family is a typical pattern among local families under the in-ke system.

    G3 (Early Modern period)
    · Hashimoto Kikuemon (Edo period) — involved in kuji-kata (公事方, judicial/administrative affairs) and other practical matters related to Hosshi-in and its treasury
    Basis: Kokushi Ronsan and other temple/shrine records (early-modern secondary sources plus family tradition)

    G4 (Bakumatsu period)
    · Hashimoto Masakata (yoriki) — held the post of yoriki (a samurai administrative post), a household-head-equivalent role
    Basis: modern genealogical records, modern biographical works (Ruijū Denki, Yamato Jinbutsu-shi)

    G5 (Adoption)
    · Hashimoto Tōichi (Masataka) — eldest son of Nakajō Hijitsugu of the Nikaidō-ryū Fujiwara line, adopted into the Hashimoto family and succeeded as head of household (born Bunsei 5, died Meiji 19)
    Basis: Yamato Jinbutsu-shi, Ruijū Denki

    G6 (Bakumatsu to Meiji period)
    · Hashimoto Hyōsaku — shizoku (samurai class), resident of Hosshi-in (died March, Meiji 9)
    Perpetual hereditary stipend: Petition for Return of Hereditary Stipend, former Kōriyama Prefecture section, from February Meiji 7 to July Meiji 8

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Internal consistency of the genealogy across multiple independent third-party documents Each stage from G0 to G6 is supported by an independent, third-party source (Daijō-in documents, the Tamon-in Diary, Yamato Jinbutsu-shi, the hereditary stipend petition), meaning the genealogy as a whole is constructed from an accumulation of external records rather than from the Hashimoto family's own self-reported claims
    Institutional significance of the adopted line (Hashimoto Tōichi) In G5, Hashimoto Tōichi entered the Hashimoto family as an adopted son from the Nikaidō-ryū (Nakajō clan). This shows that, through the end of the early modern period, the Hashimoto family held a household status befitting the adoption of members of Fujiwara-descended lineages, and not only blood relations
    Confirmation of the genealogy's endpoint through Meiji-era administrative certification Hashimoto Hyōsaku in G6 is confirmed by a third party as the sole shizoku of Hosshi-in village, through the hereditary stipend return petition held at the Nara Prefectural Library and Information Center (bearing the official seals of two deputy village heads as administrative certification). Thus, the endpoint of this provisional genealogy is established by independent evidence from an administrative body
    55. Kashihara City History (橿原市史), Historical Materials Vol. 1 — Karyō 1 (1169) Adjudication Document on the Corvée Duties of Mita-shō (Naming Hosshi-in as Landlord)
    An adjudication document dated the 19th day of the 11th month of Karyō 1 (1169), concerning a dispute between Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji over the corvée duties (所役) of the Mita-shō estate, found in Volume 1 of the Historical Materials of the Kashihara City History. It designates Hosshi-in as the landlord (地主), states that successive generations of its abbots (院主) had gone unobstructed in their rights, and records the accusation of encroachment against Ein along with his statement of defense — establishing that Hosshi-in was landlord, that the estate was subject (負処) to Kōfuku-ji's authority to appoint officials, and that it was exempt from Tōdai-ji's miscellaneous labor duties (雑役免) — while nonetheless ordering that Tōdai-ji's corvée service be performed. It is a temple-estate dispute record bearing the seals (kaō) of officials including the chi-in-ji (administrator of temple affairs) and the bettō / shuri-sakyōshiki-shi / sachūben and concurrently Monjō Hakase, Fujiwara no Ason, among others.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Kashihara City History, Historical Materials, Vol. 1 (686 items) Call number GC176-E6, Bibliographic ID 000001902133 National Diet Library

    [Quotation] From the Mita-shō corvée-duty adjudication document, 19th day, 11th month, Karyō 1 →

    Item: The assigned kōsai (vegetable-offering) service duty of Mita-shō is to be promptly performed.
    Attached herewith: one copy of the Tōdai-ji directive (下文案) dated the 23rd day of the 6th month of last year.

    Regarding the above: according to that temple's [Tōdai-ji's] petition (解状) dated the 8th month of last year — this estate, since the founding of the temple, has provided sacred rice offerings to the Great Buddha, allotted by successive sage emperors from ancient times; and as for the sacred vegetable offerings, 360 chō of public land were assigned, from which offerings have been made daily over many years. Accordingly, successive provincial governors exempted the estate from assigned public duties and extraordinary miscellaneous labor, and, this having become established precedent from ancient times, imperial edicts to this effect were issued in the Kankō [1004–1012] and Manju [1024–1028] eras. However, because this exemption was of an unfixed nature, difficulties repeatedly arose; therefore in Jōhō 3 [1076] an edict fixing the land boundaries was issued, title deeds were established, and the land was made permanent temple estate, the duties of which have been performed to the present. Accordingly, in the time of the late Regent, when this province underwent a land survey, the estate was again exempted in line with the old precedent, as already recorded. That this is temple land is a ruling unchanged from ancient times to the present; this estate is included therein, there being a certain number of supporting documents, and its provenance is well established. Accordingly, successive generations of abbots of Hosshi-in have gone entirely unobstructed in their rights. However, in recent years Ein has begun to seize the cultivation rights (作手) of the estate's peasants, and in pursuing this dispute has suspended the customary temple service duties. Nevertheless, out of deference to keeping the landlord's affairs undisturbed, the temple did not forcibly intervene; and although it did not separately submit a formal petition, [Ein] has repeatedly resisted the assigned service duties. Hereupon Ein's statement of petition asserts that, as for the temple service, since the estate is exempt under Kōfuku-ji's authority to appoint officials (進官免), and there being grounds for prohibition, the service cannot be performed. On this point, upon comparing the documents of that temple [Kōfuku-ji], it was earlier adjudicated, in accordance with reason, that the estate should remain, as originally, Tōdai-ji land. Furthermore, as for the matter of the landlord: around the Kankō era, when the abbot Chūan issued a ruling, the Tōdai-ji official Kōsuke, having stated the particulars in his defense, and following the issuance of a Chōja Sen (長者宣, directive of the temple's presiding officer), it was decreed that the estate be treated as exempt for kōsai purposes; and since that decree, there has to this day been no dispute whatsoever. Yet Ein has contrived a new pretext, speaking now of cultivation rights, now of the subject party (負処), committing arbitrary encroachment as he pleases. In particular, in the course of this ruling, Ein has repeatedly submitted documents asserting that the land is temple land; therefore, first, as for the temple service duty, it should promptly be performed in accordance with precedent; as for the dispute over landlordship, the rights and wrongs are to be examined from the petitions of both parties, and moreover the parties are to be summoned so that the matter between them may be resolved.

    The Great Master (大法師) Ein's statement of defense, dated the 22nd day of the 5th month of this year, states: as for the paddy and dry fields in question, the landlord is Hosshi-in; the subject party is under this temple's [Kōfuku-ji's] authority to appoint officials, and the land is also exempt from Tōdai-ji's miscellaneous labor duties. Since, as the subject party, the matter should be left to the disposition of both temples, and this is not a matter to be decided at the landlord's discretion — accordingly, while awaiting the joint ruling of both temples, the Tōdai-ji officials brought suit demanding that the Tōdai-ji service be performed; the demand for accountability being especially severe, [Ein] stated that the Tōdai-ji service would be performed accordingly, and to this day that service has been carried out without negligence. However, according to a directive sent from that temple [Kōfuku-ji], it states that should a demand for service arise under Kōfuku-ji's authority to appoint officials, that matter is to be dealt with accordingly, and that directive is noted separately. Accordingly, since there has been no prohibition from the administrative office of Kōfuku-ji, [Ein] understood that the Tōdai-ji service should be performed, and has performed it entirely without negligence; and yet is now accused of not performing it — the purport of this suit is nothing other than an attempt to hold the landlord Ein to account. If that is indeed so, this is an unreasonable suit, utterly without justification.

    According to Ein's statement of defense: the landlord is Hosshi-in; the subject party is under Kōfuku-ji's authority to appoint officials, and the land is also exempt from Tōdai-ji's miscellaneous labor duties. Accordingly, since there has been no prohibition from Kōfuku-ji, the Tōdai-ji service is to be performed, and so forth. It is hereby decreed that Hosshi-in shall be treated as the landlord, and that the Tōdai-ji service shall first be performed accordingly; as for Kōfuku-ji's authority to appoint officials, should that temple bring suit in the matter, a determination shall be made at that time [a term appears to be missing in the source text here]. The above two matters are decreed as stated, in accordance with the Chōja Sen; they are not to be violated or neglected. Accordingly issued.

    19th day, 11th month, Karyō 1 [1169]
    Chi-in-ji (Administrator of Temple Affairs), Ōkura no Sakan, Takahashi (seal)
    Bettō (Superintendent), Shuri-sakyōshiki-shi, Sachūben, and concurrently Monjō Hakase, Fujiwara no Ason (seal); Minbu no Jō, Fujiwara (seal)
    Onshi, Fujiwara (seal)
    Chi-in-ji, Gyōbu no Sakan, Koremune
    Ōkura no Sakan, Abe
    Kunai no Sakan, Ōe
    Ushi no Shishō, Takahashi (seal)
    Takahashi

    [Translator's note: This is an interpretive translation of dense Heian-period administrative kanbun. Several court/temple office titles (e.g., chi-in-ji, bettō, shuri-sakyōshiki-shi, sachūben, Monjō Hakase, Minbu no Jō, Onshi, Gyōbu no Sakan, Kunai no Sakan, Ushi no Shishō) are retained in romanized form, as precise one-word English equivalents do not exist; readers seeking exact administrative definitions should consult a specialist glossary of Heian court and temple offices.]

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Official ruling naming Hosshi-in as landlord The Chōja Sen issued between Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji explicitly states that "Hosshi-in shall be treated as the landlord" (宜以発志院為地主), directly demonstrating — through an official temple document wholly unconnected to the Hashimoto family — that in the latter half of the 12th century Hosshi-in was formally recognized by both major temples as the landlord within the Mita-shō estate
    Proof of continuity in "successive abbots going unobstructed" The phrase "successive generations of abbots of Hosshi-in have gone entirely unobstructed" (発志院代代院主全無致妨) is recorded in this contemporaneous adjudication document, establishing that Hosshi-in's rights as landlord were recognized not as a one-time matter but continuously across successive generations. This constitutes primary-source evidence that Hosshi-in possessed a long-term, organized institutional presence as an in-ke
    Official certification through the seals of Fujiwara no Ason and others This is an official adjudication document bearing the seals (kaō) of multiple Fujiwara no Ason officials, including the chi-in-ji, bettō, and onshi, demonstrating that Hosshi-in's landlord rights were formally recognized within the central temple administration of the period. As an independent administrative document with no involvement whatsoever from the Hashimoto family, it carries the highest evidentiary weight
    56. Heian Ibun, Documents Edition, Vol. 7 — Chōkan 2 (1164) Catalogue of Mita-shō Documents (Record Noting the Absence of Hosshi-in Landholding)
    A catalogue of documents concerning the Mita-shō estate in Yamato Province, dated the 25th day of the 8th month of Chōkan 2 (1164), found in Volume 7 of the Documents Edition of Heian Ibun. It records the number and contents of scrolls of supporting documents (証文) concerning the Great Buddha's vegetable-offering exemption (香菜免) for Mita-shō and related matters, and lists a scroll stating that "no Hosshi-in landholding is to be found within Mita-shō" — a Tōdai-ji document indicating the non-existence of Hosshi-in landholding. It shows the course of the dispute between the two temples over Hosshi-in's rights as landlord.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Concerning the Supporting Documents for the Great Buddha's Vegetable-Offering Exemption, Mita-shō, and Related Matters

    25th day, 8th month, Chōkan 2 [1164] (seal)

    [Translator's note: the era name transcribed here as "濂和" is rendered as Chōwa (長和, 1012–1017) based on chronological context, as no era named "Renwa" exists; readers cross-checking against the original manuscript should verify this reading.]

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Evidence of the course of the dispute over Hosshi-in landholding As of Chōkan 2 (1164), Tōdai-ji had compiled and submitted a scroll of supporting documents asserting that "no Hosshi-in landholding is to be found within Mita-shō," showing that Hosshi-in's rights as landlord had already become a matter of formal dispute between the two great temples from the mid-12th century. This source supplements the earlier history leading up to the adjudication in Entry 55 (Karyō 1, 1169)
    Contrast between Tōdai-ji's claims and the final ruling In this document (1164), Tōdai-ji asserted the non-existence of Hosshi-in landholding; yet five years later, the Chōja Sen in Entry 55 (1169) conversely and formally recognized Hosshi-in's rights as landlord, stating that "Hosshi-in shall be treated as the landlord." Comparing the two documents allows the process by which Hosshi-in was ultimately confirmed as landlord, following the dispute, to be verified through primary sources
    Traceable back to the Hōen–Kōji era (early 12th century) The document is catalogued as supporting evidence "from around the Hōen and Kōji eras" (c. 1135–1144), showing that the dispute over land control involving Hosshi-in traces back to the early 12th century. This serves as circumstantial evidence that Hosshi-in, as an in-ke, was involved in regional land control from an early period
    57. History of the Development of the Shin Buddhist Order (Unebi Historical Studies Series) — The Betto/Ko-betto (Chief Administrator / Deputy Administrator) System and Branch-Temple Management (Records Concerning Daijō-in's Branch Temple Fukuji and Hosshi-in)
    A passage from page 75 of History of the Development of the Shin Buddhist Order (Unebi Historical Studies Series) discussing the betto/ko-betto system. It examines the case of Daijō-in's branch temple Fukuji, where the monzeki (temple head) held the betto post himself and dispatched a ko-betto — recorded as held by Oku-Hosshi-in — to maintain the temple's affairs. The passage also cites the case of Yokobō Zenkyūbō, appointed with the approval of the Tōrin-in high priest (Daijō-in jisha zōjiki, Bunmei 10 [1478]), and discusses in detail how the head temple's control over the right to appoint branch-temple administrators functioned to prevent encroachment by rival schools — an important source on temple governance.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    History of the Development of the Shin Buddhist Order (Unebi Historical Studies Series), p. 75 Call No. 188.7-Ka494s2, Bibliographic ID 000000906885 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Summary of the Passage] The following is a summary of the relevant content from page 75, rather than a word-for-word translation of the original text.

    An entry in the Daijō-in jisha zōjiki for the 23rd day of the 12th month of Bunmei 10 (1478) records that Yokobō Zenkyūbō became resident priest of the Fukuchi-in Jizō Hall, entering the temple that day with the approval of the Tōrin-in high priest. The same source notes that the head priests (kannushi) of the Shingū Sansha shrine attached to Hase-dera — itself a branch temple of Kōfuku-ji — were appointed directly by Hase-dera's own betto, who held that authority.

    At Fukuji, a branch temple of Daijō-in, the record states that "this temple's betto is the monzeki himself" — meaning the head temple's monzeki personally held the post of betto over this branch temple. In such cases, a ko-betto was dispatched to actually run the temple day to day, and the text specifies that this role was "held by Oku-Hosshi-in." Branch temples where the monzeki himself held the betto post, the author notes, tended to have substantial income and a prestigious history.

    Yakushi-ji, another Daijō-in branch temple, likewise had its betto post held by the monzeki, and the income attached to that post was very large — a matter the author says will be taken up further in a later section on the character of branch temples. Fukuji itself was known as one of "the three clan temples of the Fujiwara," a temple of distinguished lineage.

    Because of this system, branch temples were bound by strict rules: they could not change sectarian affiliation or hand the temple down to another lineage, and any oversight — whether by a lord or by a deputy — had to go through the head temple, leaving no room for independent action. Whenever a temple or its estate was donated, it was likewise stipulated that the choice of abbot always had to go through the head temple.

    As a result of the head temple holding the right to appoint branch-temple bettos, the appointee was necessarily either the head temple's own monzeki, a monk from the head temple, or a resident monk of the branch temple whose sectarian affiliation matched the head temple's — this alignment being a precondition for appointment.

    In this way, branch temples retained the same sectarian character as their head temple. Had a monk from a rival school ever been appointed through carelessness, there was a real danger that the branch temple would be lost to that rival school. (Abbreviated in the original.)

    Written pledges (ukebumi) were required from branch-temple abbots, stating that any violation of the above conditions would result in immediate removal from office, "with no grounds for complaint to be raised." The passage then repeats the same account of the 1478 Yokobō Zenkyūbō appointment and the Fukuji/Oku-Hosshi-in ko-betto arrangement described above.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Discussion
    Confirmation that "Oku-Hosshi-in" Was Dispatched as Ko-betto At Fukuji, the branch temple where the Daijō-in monzeki personally held the betto post, the record explicitly states that the ko-betto role was "held by Oku-Hosshi-in." This academic work thus documents that Hosshi-in (Oku-Hosshi-in) was dispatched to and stationed at the site as ko-betto — important corroborating evidence that Hosshi-in was not merely a subordinate temple (in-ke), but functioned as a practical administrative body responsible for managing branch temples.
    Clarifying How Control Over Betto Appointments Prevented Encroachment by Rival Schools This source details how the head temple (the monzeki) prevented rival schools and powerful lineages from encroaching on its branch temples by retaining control over betto appointments. It also cites the cautionary case of Hase-dera, which lost a branch temple to Ninna-ji in Shōryaku 1 as a result of a failed betto appointment — illustrating the institutional background and necessity behind Hosshi-in's dispatch as ko-betto.
    The Description "One of the Three Fujiwara Clan Temples" and Hosshi-in's Prestigious History Fukuji is identified as a prestigious temple, described as "one of the three Fujiwara clan temples." That Hosshi-in was involved as ko-betto at a branch temple of such standing — one where the monzeki himself held the betto post — corroborates the prestige and importance of Hosshi-in itself.
    Comparison with the Case of Yokobō Zenkyūbō and the Tōrin-in High Priest's Approval (Bunmei 10) The source also cites the entry for the 23rd day of the 12th month of Bunmei 10 (1478), recording that Yokobō Zenkyūbō's appointment as resident priest of the Fukuchi-in Jizō Hall required the Tōrin-in high priest's approval. This confirms that betto appointments required authorization from the head temple or a higher authority(intangible assets), and should be read as background evidence for the institutional legitimacy of Hosshi-in's role as ko-betto.
    58. History of the Development of the Shin Buddhist Order (Unebi Historical Studies Series) — The Ko-betto Oku-Hosshi-in and the Branch-Temple Betto Appointment System (Records Concerning Daijō-in's Branch Temple Fukuji and Hosshi-in)
    A passage from page 75 of History of the Development of the Shin Buddhist Order (Unebi Historical Studies Series) concerning the betto/ko-betto system. It details the case of Daijō-in's branch temple Fukuji, where the monzeki held the betto post himself and dispatched a ko-betto — recorded as held by Oku-Hosshi-in. The passage also notes the case of Yokobō Zenkyūbō's appointment with the Tōrin-in high priest's approval (Bunmei 10), and discusses how the head temple's control over branch-temple betto appointments functioned to prevent encroachment by rival schools.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    History of the Development of the Shin Buddhist Order (Unebi Historical Studies Series), p. 75 Call No. 188.72-Ka71u, Bibliographic ID 000000665088 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Summary of the Passage] As with Block 57, this is a summary of the relevant content rather than a word-for-word translation.

    The passage repeats that a written pledge bound abbots to immediate removal, "with no grounds for complaint to be raised," for any violation of the head-temple's conditions. It restates the 1478 entry recording Yokobō Zenkyūbō's appointment as resident priest of the Fukuchi-in Jizō Hall with the Tōrin-in high priest's approval, and the parallel case of the Shingū Sansha shrine head priests at Hase-dera, appointed directly by Hase-dera's own betto.

    It restates that at Fukuji, "this temple's betto is the monzeki himself," so the head temple's monzeki personally held the betto post; a ko-betto was dispatched to run the temple, and this role is recorded as "held by Oku-Hosshi-in." Temples where the monzeki himself held the betto post, the text again notes, tended to have substantial income and a prestigious history. It adds that Yakushi-ji's betto post was likewise held by the monzeki, with very large associated income — a point reserved for fuller discussion elsewhere in the book.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Discussion
    Institutional Basis for Oku-Hosshi-in's Function as Ko-betto The phrase "held by Oku-Hosshi-in" documents, at the level of academic scholarship, that at Fukuji — the branch temple where the Daijō-in monzeki held the betto post — Oku-Hosshi-in was dispatched to the site and took charge of its management as ko-betto. This is direct corroborating evidence that Hosshi-in, as an in-ke (subordinate temple), institutionally performed the practical function of managing branch temples.
    The Institutional Significance of Controlling Betto Appointments to Exclude Rival Schools This passage details the mechanism by which the head temple institutionally prevented rival schools or temples from infiltrating its branch temples, by keeping control over betto appointments in its own hands — backed by the enforceable requirement that abbots sign pledges accepting immediate removal without objection for any violation. This shows that Hosshi-in's involvement as ko-betto took place within the context of this strict head-temple/branch-temple governance system.
    Comparison with the Yokobō Zenkyūbō / Tōrin-in High Priest Approval Case (Bunmei 10) The entry for the 23rd day of the 12th month of Bunmei 10 (1478) likewise records that Yokobō Zenkyūbō's appointment required the Tōrin-in high priest's approval, confirming that formal authorization(intangible assets) from a higher authority was indispensable for betto appointments. A similar approval process likely applied when Hosshi-in was appointed as ko-betto, making this an important case that reinforces the institutional legitimacy of that appointment.
    Relationship to Block 57: Contrast and Complementarity Whereas Block 57 (an earlier passage in the same book) focuses on the character of the branch temple and its prestigious status as a Fujiwara clan temple, Block 58 focuses on the binding force of the abbot's written pledge and the concrete operation of the appointment-approval system. Reading both blocks together gives a fuller, three-dimensional picture of the institutional and historical role Hosshi-in played as ko-betto.
    59. Tamon-in Index, General Index to the Daijō-in jisha zōjiki, and the Genealogical Compendium to the Son'i Bunmyaku (Shinpen Sanzu Honchō Son'i Bunmyaku Keifu Zatsurui Yōshū) — Identifying Hosshin-in's Zengyōbō (Ryōjō, Hōgen) as Descended from the Suematsu Branch of the Nikaidō Lineage, and Its Genealogical Continuity with the Hashimoto Family
    A genealogical study cross-referencing three sources: the Tamon-in Index, the General Index to the Daijō-in jisha zōjiki (Biographical Volume), and Volume 5 of the Shinpen Sanzu Honchō Son'i Bunmyaku Keifu Zatsurui Yōshū. It identifies Hosshin-in's Zengyōbō (also known as Ryōjō, holding the rank of Hōgen) as belonging to the Suematsu branch of the Nikaidō lineage, and confirms him as the younger brother of Enge — Great Archbishop, betto of Kōfuku-ji, and head of Tōhoku-in. Linking this with the early-modern genealogical fact established in Blocks 74–75 — that Hashimoto Masataka (Kikuemon)'s biological father was Nikaidō Chūjō Hiyuki — three independent groups of sources together support a continuous genealogical line running from the Nikaidō lineage, through the abbots of Hosshin-in, to the Hashimoto family's adopted heirs.

    General Index to the Daijō-in jisha zōjiki, Vol. 1 (image 198) Records Ryōjō as identical to "Hōgen [rank] / Zengyōbō." The index confirms that the high clerical rank of Hōgen and the religious name Zengyōbō belong to one and the same person.

    Early Modern Period (Bakumatsu Era) Hashimoto Masataka (Kikuemon)'s biological father is recorded as Nikaidō Chūjō Hiyuki.     [Significance of the Source]

    Point Discussion
    Independent Cross-Referencing of Three Sources Establishes "Nikaidō Lineage = Hosshin-in" Three mutually independent sources — the Tamon-in Index, the General Index to the Daijō-in jisha zōjiki, and the Son'i Bunmyaku — together establish the chain "Hosshin-in's Zengyōbō = Ryōjō (Hōgen) = Suematsu branch of the Nikaidō lineage." Rather than resting on a single source, the fact that three sources compiled by different editors at different times all agree strengthens the reliability of the evidence.
    The Medieval "Nikaidō Lineage / Hosshin-in" and Early Modern "Nikaidō Chūjō / Hashimoto Adoption" Are Both Confirmed by Independent Source Groups This Block 59 (medieval: the Nikaidō origins of Hosshin-in's abbot, confirmed via the Son'i Bunmyaku and related sources) and Blocks 74–75 (early modern: Hashimoto Masataka's biological father as Nikaidō Chūjō Hiyuki) are two independent groups of sources that support the same underlying fact — an institutional and blood connection between the Nikaidō lineage and the Hashimoto family — from different periods and different source bases. This agreement is not easily explained by coincidence, and stands as strong corroborating evidence that the Hashimoto family continues the Nikaidō in-ke lineage.
    The Relationship with Elder Brother Enge (Betto of Kōfuku-ji, Tōhoku-in) Connects Directly to Block 116 The fact confirmed in this block — that Ryōjō's elder brother Enge headed Tōhoku-in — corresponds structurally to the fact discussed in Block 116, that Jisshu, younger brother of Jikken (who used the Hashimoto name), was Hōin of Tōhoku-in. This reveals a pattern in which the same Kōfuku-ji sub-temple, Tōhoku-in, functioned as a genealogical hinge point for the Hashimoto family in its relationships with different lineages (the Nikaidō line and the Kan'in line).
    Grounds This Block Provides for Raising the Prior Probability [of the Hashimoto Lineage Claim] It would be inappropriate to apply the same prior probability to the Hashimoto family's genealogical background as one would to a randomly chosen early-modern family. As this block shows, the Hashimoto family is a conditioned case: (1) a samurai family of the Ichijō-in domain based at Hosshi-in Manor (confirmed by primary administrative sources); (2) successors to the Nikaidō lineage through the abbots of Hosshin-in (confirmed by three medieval sources); and (3) a family for which an adoption tie to the Nikaidō line (via the Chūjō branch) is recorded even in the early modern period (confirmed by two early-modern sources). The prior probability should therefore be set considerably higher than for an ordinary early-modern family.
    60. Dai Nihonshi, Volume 128 — The Genealogy of the Tōin Family (Recording Sanetoshi, Younger Brother of Sanekane, as Founder of the Hashimoto Family)
    A genealogical record of the Tōin family from Dai Nihonshi, Volume 128 (image 11). It names Councillor (Sangi) Sanetoshi — younger brother of Chancellor (Daijō Daijin) Sanekane — as the founder of the Hashimoto family, and records the succession of ministerial posts among various Tōin lines (Kinhira, Kinmune, Sanetoshi, Kinshige, and others), along with Kinmune's execution for treason during the Kenmu era and Sanetoshi's subsequent service to the Northern Court as Minister of the Right. This is an important genealogical source tracing the Hashimoto family's ancestry to the Tōin lineage.

    [Bibliographic Information]
