    [Quotation] Quoted from Dai Nihonshi, Volume 128 (image 11):

    [...the] great-great-grandson [of the preceding figure] was Sane-yo (實世), a renowned minister under Emperor Go-Daigo, known as the Tōin Left Captain of the Gate Guards (左衛門督). Sanefuji (實藤), Provisional Major Counselor, became progenitor of several noble houses. Saneuji (實氏) begot Kinsuke (公相); Kinsuke begot Sanekane (實兼), who rose to Chancellor (太政大臣). Sanekane's younger brother, Councillor Sanetoshi (實俊), became the founder of the Hashimoto family. Sanekane begot Kinhira (公衡) and Kanesue (兼季). Kinhira became Minister of the Left; his grandson Kinmune (公宗) was executed for treason during the Kenmu era, while Kinmune's son — also named Sanetoshi (實俊) — served the Northern Court and rose to Minister of the Right. Kinmune's younger brother Kinshige (公重) served the Yoshino temporary palace (the Southern Court) and became Minister of the Interior; Kanesue became Minister of the Right and founder of the Imadegawa family, while [a further descendant] became founder of the Ogura family. Kinmori (公守) became Chancellor; his son, Provisional Major Counselor... [text continues]

    Translator's note: This is a dense genealogical excerpt beginning mid-passage, and a few name fragments are ambiguous in the original (e.g., the figure who founded the Ogura family is named only by a truncated fragment, "…言"). Note also that the name Sanetoshi (實俊) appears twice, referring to two different people one generation apart — the Hashimoto family's founder, and (separately) Kinmune's son who served the Northern Court. Readers working from this passage for genealogical purposes may wish to verify individual names against the attached source image.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Discussion
    Grounds for Tracing the Hashimoto Family's Ancestry to the Tōin Lineage Councillor Sanetoshi, younger brother of Chancellor Sanekane, is explicitly named as the founder of the Hashimoto family. Dai Nihonshi, a nationally compiled official history, thus records that the Hashimoto family, as a collateral line of the Tōin family, descends from the bloodline of the regental (sekkanke) house. This serves as a foundational source for discussing the Hashimoto family's rank and lineage.
    The Kenmu-Era Treason (Execution of Kinmune) and the Split Between the Northern and Southern Courts While Kinmune rose in rebellion during the Kenmu Restoration and was executed, his son (also named Sanetoshi) served the Northern Court and rose to Minister of the Right, and Kinmune's younger brother Kinshige served the Southern Court (at the Yoshino temporary palace) and became Minister of the Interior — the passage lays out how the Tōin family split during the turmoil of the Northern and Southern Courts period. It also confirms that Sanetoshi, founder of the Hashimoto family, lived through this turbulent era.
    Genealogical Position Relative to Other Branch Lines Such as the Imadegawa and Ogura Families Several court noble lines, including the Imadegawa and Ogura families, branched off from the same Tōin lineage, and the Hashimoto family is likewise situated within this genealogical network. This confirms that the Tōin family produced multiple branch lines within medieval court society, offering a broader genealogical context for understanding the Hashimoto family's standing.
    Connection with Block 59 (the Hosshin-in Genealogical Hypothesis) Whereas Block 59 situates the Hashimoto family as continuing an in-ke lineage through Ryōjō (Zengyōbō) of the Suematsu branch of the Nikaidō line, this Block 60 presents the existence of Sanetoshi, founder of the Hashimoto family, within the court noble (Tōin) lineage. Comparing the two allows for a multi-angled examination of the possibility that the Hashimoto family carries multiple genealogical strands — warrior, temple-affiliated (in-ke), and court noble.
    61. Kama Hōzōin Sōjutsu (鎌宝蔵院槍術) — Hōzōin's Financial Crisis and Hashimoto Kikuemon's Role as Intermediary with the Nara Magistrate's Office (Transfer of Management Rights after Infū's Sudden Death and the Public Martial Arts Review under Shogunate Administration)
    A record contained in the Kama Hōzōin Sōjutsu. It describes how, following the financial crisis brought on by the sudden death of Infū (胤風), the guardian Chōshōbō Gyōei (長性房行英) transferred the temple's management rights, residence, and weaponry to the Mitsuta (満田) family, and how in 1756 (Hōreki 6) Inken (胤憲) succeeded to the position, bringing to an end the long period during which the temple had no resident abbot. The record also shows that Hashimoto Kikuemon served as an intermediary with the Nara Magistrate's Office and was involved in a public demonstration of Hōzōin-ryū spear technique — historical evidence confirming the Hashimoto family's exchanges with both the local community and the shogunate.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Kama Hōzōin Sōjutsu (鎌宝蔵院槍術) Call number FS37-243　Bibliographic ID 000001537101 View at National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Citation / Summary]

    Quoted from the Kama Hōzōin Sōjutsu →

    Hōzōin fell into serious financial difficulty following the sudden death of Infū (胤風). Chōshōbō Gyōei (長性房行英), who had become guardian under the terms of Infū's will, sought assistance from his own family, the Mitsuta (満田) family, in order to resolve the crisis. He transferred the temple's management rights, residence, and weaponry to the Mitsuta family, and the Mitsuta family took over the hereditary name of Nakamikado Inbu (中御門胤武). However, no suitable successor could be found within the Mitsuta family for some time. In 1756 (Hōreki 6), Inken (胤憲), the third son of Mitsuta Gon'emon Inshō (満田権右衛門胤勝), entered the priesthood at the age of eleven and succeeded to the position, bringing to an end the long period during which the temple had no resident abbot. It is said that many old documents and treasured objects were lost during this interval.

    As Inken grew to adulthood he became the head priest (院主) of Hōzōin, and worked to rebuild the temple's shrine buildings on its grounds and to unite its disciples. In its relations with the Nara Magistrate's Office, Hashimoto Kikuemon (橋本喜久右衛門) served as an intermediary, and exchanges between the local community and shogunate officials deepened — including through a demonstration of Hōzōin-ryū spear technique presented before officials during a public martial-arts review held under shogunate administration.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    Confirmation of Hashimoto Kikuemon's role as intermediary with the Nara Magistrate's Office A member of the Hashimoto family (Kikuemon) appears in the historical record as the intermediary connecting the Nara Magistrate's Office with Hōzōin-ryū spear technique. This shows that the Hashimoto family held influence in early modern Nara with both local martial-arts and religious institutions and shogunate administrative offices.
    The course of Hōzōin's financial crisis and the transfer of management rights The sequence of events — financial difficulty following Infū's sudden death, the transfer of management rights to the Mitsuta family, and the period without a resident abbot lasting until 1756 (Hōreki 6) — concretely illustrates how the operational foundations of an early modern temple could be seriously destabilized by the death of a single individual. That the Hashimoto family took on the role of intermediary with the Magistrate's Office during this unstable period reflects the high degree of trust and standing the family held within the local community.
    Records of the martial-arts review and exchanges between the shogunate and the local community The record of the Hashimoto family's involvement in the public demonstration of Hōzōin-ryū spear technique stands as early modern evidence that the family was not merely a long-established local household, but also played a certain role in official events and occasions promoting the martial arts under shogunate administration.
    The continuity of the Hashimoto family from medieval in-ke lineage into early modern local society The Hashimoto family is presumed to have descended from a lineage of bōkan (temple administrators) and sata-nin (managers) attached to the in-ke (cloister-residence) Hosshi-in during the medieval period. The fact that the family's name continued to appear in connection with Nara's temples, shrines, and the Magistrate's Office into the early modern period serves as corroborating evidence of the family's continuity and sustained influence within the region across historical periods.
    62. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4 (Sixth Month, Bunshō 1 / 1466) — Record of Yokota-shō Laborers and the Presentation of Yamato Melons (Mobilization of Hosshi-in-Related Estate Laborers for Monzeki Official Duties)
    A record found on page 73 of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4 (sixth month of Bunshō 1, 1466). It shows that, on the occasion of presenting Yamato melons to Imadegawa-dono and Tanomura Hōgen, laborers from Yokota-shō (an estate associated with Hosshi-in) were mobilized for monzeki (cloister-head) official duties together with laborers from Wakatsuki-shō and Ōichi-shō. This is a record of monzeki official duties demonstrating that Yokota-shō, the base of the Hashimoto family, was directly connected to the administration of the monzeki's official affairs.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link

    [Citation]

    Quoted from the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Volume 4 (sixth month, Bunshō 1), p. 73 →

    Thirteenth day of the sixth month, Bunshō 1 (1466)

    Item: Recitation [of sutras] at the Five-Story Gate as an offering of gratitude to Jion (the founder of the Hossō sect).
    Item: Ten containers of melons sent up to the capital — [for] Imadegawa-dono (今出川殿); five containers under the management of Keiriki (慶力), assistant to Tanomura Hōgen (田能村法眼) — [borne by] laborers of Yokota-shō, Wakatsuki-shō, and Ōichi-shō. We humbly submit that it is proper to present ten containers of Yamato melons, and respectfully request that this be so reported. With reverence and humility, [signed] Jinson (尋尊).

    Sixth month, thirteenth day.
    To the assembled officials.

    Ten containers of Yamato melons, [packed] in four crates, are to be presented and duly delivered. Accordingly, although the route is inconvenient, it has been ordered that two additional baskets be sent as well. With reverence and humility.

    Sixth month, thirteenth day. Son'yo (尊譽)
    To the Reverend Tanomura Hōgen

    Item: Eighty melons arrived with the day's delivery; together with the earlier consignment, this makes three containers of twenty each.
    Item: In the evening, His Lordship of An'i-ji (安位寺殿) entered [the residence], accompanied by the Furuichi (古市) party; Takada (高田) brought melons and well-side plantings.

    Translator's note: this passage is written in the abbreviated diary style (kanbun-kundoku) typical of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, and the rendering above is an interpretive translation of a terse, elliptical original.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Explanation
    The actual mobilization of Yokota-shō laborers for monzeki official duties This primary source confirms that laborers from Yokota-shō — regarded as the Hashimoto family's base — were organizationally mobilized, together with laborers from Wakatsuki-shō and Ōichi-shō, for the official duties of the Daijōin monzeki (the presentation of Yamato melons to the capital). This demonstrates that Yokota-shō functioned as a subordinate temple estate incorporated into the monzeki's network for administering official duties.
    The political context of the presentation to Imadegawa-dono and Tanomura Hōgen The melons were presented both to Imadegawa-dono (a high-ranking court noble) and to Tanomura Hōgen (a practical administrator of religious affairs). This shows that the mobilization of Yokota-shō laborers was not simply an agricultural duty, but formed part of the practical network supporting the monzeki's political negotiations with Kyoto and the gift-giving rituals conducted with the court nobility.
    The position of Yokota-shō within the Hosshi-in / Daijōin branch-temple system As detailed in Block 63 (Kōza Nihon Shōensha), Yokota-shō was an estate that transferred from Hosshi-in holdings to Daijōin holdings, and the mobilization of "Yokota-shō laborers" recorded here is a practical expression of that head-temple/branch-temple system of control. This can be understood as reflecting the structural background in which the in-ke lineage connected through Hosshi-in linked the region that was the Hashimoto family's base to the official duties of the Daijōin monzeki.
    Consistency with the kintō-myō system and corvée labor duties This record corresponds directly to the point made in the explanation of Block 63, that "the primary purpose of the kintō-myō (equal-holding) system was the smooth requisition of corvée labor." It thus serves as empirical evidence that the corvée labor system, established since the Kagen 4 (1306) land survey, was still functioning as of Bunshō 1 (1466).
    63. Lectures on the History of Japanese Shōen, Vol. 7 (Kinki Region) — The Structure and Transformation of Yamato Province's Yokota Shōen (The Transition from Hosshi-in Territory to Daijō-in Territory and the Formation of Hosshi-in Village)
    A study of Yokota Shōen in Yamato Province, included in Lectures on the History of Japanese Shōen, Vol. 7 (Shōen of the Kinki Region, Part 2). Located in Sōe District (present-day Hosshi-in-chō area, Yamatokōriyama City), the estate was originally established as the holding of Hosshi-in, a sub-temple (in-ke) of Kōfuku-ji, before being transferred to Daijō-in's control in the early Kamakura period. This source on shōen structure traces the process by which Hosshi-in Village was formed, covering the Kagen 4 (1306) land survey, the equal-shares (kintōmyō) name-field system, the existence of fusho (burden-bearing fields), and the village transformations of the Ōnin era.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Information Link
    Lectures on the History of Japanese Shōen, Vol. 7 (Shōen of the Kinki Region, Part 2) Publication date: March 1995　Call number: GB245-E5 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Historical Transformation of Yokota Shōen: Overview]

    Period Content
    Around the Kankō era (1004–1012) Chūan, the head priest (in'nushi) of Hosshi-in, became embroiled in a dispute with Tōdai-ji over delivery of the kōsai-yaku (a vegetable/produce levy). This is the earliest record confirming that Hosshi-in held lord-like (ryōshu) status over this area.
    Latter half of the 12th century Delivery of temple dues to Tōdai-ji began falling into arrears, reigniting conflict between the two temples. The dispute was provisionally settled through arbitration by the Fujiwara clan head (uji no chōja).
    Early Kamakura period The position of head priest of Hosshi-in passed to Jisson (a son of Matsudono Motofusa). After Jisson's death, his disciple Enjitsu (a son of Kujō Michiie) succeeded to the position, and Hosshi-in came under the concurrent authority (kentai) of Daijō-in. Yokota Shōen was thereafter organized as Daijō-in territory.
    Kagen 4 (1306) Daijō-in ordered the monks Insen and Raiin of Bodaisan Shōgan-in to conduct a land survey (kenchū). Registers including the torichō, tochō, nayosechō, and mokuroku were compiled, and an equal-shares name-field (kintōmyō) system was established, consisting of ten myō of roughly 2 chō 3 tan each. The primary aim was to facilitate the smooth levying of corvée labor (ninbu-yaku).
    Muromachi period The annual tribute (nengu) of just over 122 koku was divided into "fixed rice, 36 koku (for Hosshi-in's Buddhist services)" and "lord's rice, 84 koku (at the discretion of the monzeki)." Various levies — including uridai-sen, saimatsu-sen, kusa-yōto, and contributions of straw, matting, and brushwood — were assessed per tan of land.
    Ōnin–Bunmei era (latter half of the 15th century) Many residents of the shōen relocated to the neighboring Nakashō, a territory of Ichijō-in, where they jointly formed a moated settlement (kangō shūraku). New irrigation ponds were built and the irrigation system reorganized. The people of Yokota Shōen also built their own moated settlement, forming an independent village known as Hosshi-in Village.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Early confirmation of Hosshi-in's landholding rights and lord-like status The record of the dispute with Tōdai-ji during the Kankō era (early 11th century) shows that Hosshi-in held substantive lord-like status over the Yokota Shōen area from an early date. This reinforces the character of Hosshi-in not merely as a nominal in-ke but as a functioning administrative authority exercising local control.
    The process of the transfer of control from Hosshi-in to Daijō-in The process by which Hosshi-in came under Daijō-in's concurrent authority, triggered by the succession of head priests who were sons of regental (sekkanke) families — Jisson and Enjitsu — is a representative example showing that the mechanism of in-ke succession was directly linked to shifts in shōen control. This corresponds directly to the institutional background of in-ke lineage succession discussed in the Hashimoto family genealogical hypothesis (Blocks 59 and 60).
    Institutional consistency between the equal-shares name-field system and corvée labor The observation that the primary aim of the equal-shares name-field system established in the Kagen 4 land survey was "the smooth levying of corvée labor" corresponds directly to the record of corvée labor mobilization at Yokota Shōen in Bunshō 1, confirmed in Block 62. Together, these mutually complementary sources demonstrate that the corvée labor system at Yokota Shōen remained functional for more than 150 years.
    The significance of the 36-koku fixed rice allocation being specifically designated for Hosshi-in's Buddhist services The fact that during the Muromachi period a portion of the annual tribute (36 koku of fixed rice) was specifically designated for Hosshi-in's Buddhist services and rites shows that the institutional tie between Yokota Shōen and Hosshi-in persisted even after the estate came under Daijō-in's control. This is evidence that Hosshi-in continued its practical and financial involvement, rather than remaining merely a nominal former lord.
    Village transformation during the Ōnin era and the formation of Hosshi-in Village The autonomous formation of a moated settlement by the estate's residents, and its independence as "Hosshi-in Village," show that the name of the in-ke institution Hosshi-in remained rooted in the region even during the dissolution of the medieval shōen system. This can be understood as the background for how local lineages associated with Hosshi-in, such as the Hashimoto family, maintained regional continuity into the early modern period and beyond.
    64. Lectures on the History of Japanese Shōen, Vol. 2 (The Establishment and Possession of Shōen) — Religious Authority and the In-ke System in Temple-Held Shōen (The Privileged Status of Monzeki Temples and the Management of Branch Temples)
    A discussion of temple- and shrine-held shōen, included in Lectures on the History of Japanese Shōen, Vol. 2 (The Establishment and Possession of Shōen). This source on temple and shrine institutions examines the branch-temple (matsuji) and in-ke systems, the religious authority and economic foundations underlying monzeki-temple control, the principle prohibiting the diversion of the Three Treasures' property, and punitive measures such as rōmyō (name-confinement curses) and shrine-palanquin protests (mikoshi dōza), illustrating the institutional structure of monzeki privilege and in-ke succession.

    [The Institutional Structure of Temple-Held Shōen: Overview]

    Institution / Concept Content
    The head–branch temple relationship and the economic role of branch temples Branch temples (matsuji) were not only in a relationship of religious subordination but were also recognized as part of the "temple assets" (jizai) that supplied the annual tribute essential to the head temple's religious ceremonies and upkeep. Head temples did not hesitate to bring lawsuits before the imperial court to secure control over branch-temple territories.
    The in-ke system and shōen management A system developed in which in-ke institutions formed within a temple undertook the management of shōen estates on commission from the temple's administrative office (mandokoro). The economic strength of these in-ke played an important role in sustaining the finances of the temple as a whole.
    Rōmyō (Name Confinement) A punitive measure used against violations such as non-payment of annual tribute, in which the offender's name was confined within a temple hall and cursed. It functioned as a coercive force rooted in religious dread — a type of binding religious power that secular authority could not exercise.
    Mikoshi Dōza (Shrine Palanquin Protest) A demonstrative act in which a sacred palanquin (mikoshi) was carried to the imperial court. It was employed as a powerful political and religious means of recovering temple territory, and was one of the strongest forms of resistance temples could exercise against secular authority.
    The Prohibition on "Diversion" (Goyō) of the Three Treasures' Property Monastic precepts strictly forbade diverting temple property belonging to the Three Treasures — the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha — to other purposes. On this basis, temples developed a rationale criticizing even taxation by provincial governors (kokushi) as a form of prohibited "diversion," and used this logic to assert the inviolability of their shōen.
    The Privileged Status of Monzeki Temples Monzeki temples, headed by abbots drawn from the imperial family or regental (sekkanke) houses, established an economic foundation rivaling that of secular power-holders through their networks of branch temples and shōen management, backed by religious and political authority. Their kin and associates occupied positions on the periphery of this privileged status.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    General positioning of the economic and institutional background of the in-ke system This source presents, at the level of general academic scholarship, the institutional background by which in-ke such as Hosshi-in and Daijō-in were incorporated into shōen management. It serves as a foundational source for understanding, within their institutional context, the individual records of corvée labor mobilization and tribute collection at Yokota Shōen found in Blocks 62 and 63.
    The reality of religious coercive power as shown by rōmyō and mikoshi dōza The existence of religious punitive measures unique to temple-held shōen — such as rōmyō and mikoshi dōza, which secular estates could not employ — institutionally confirms the strength of the coercive authority that in-ke institutions such as Hosshi-in held over branch temples and estate control.
    The prohibition on diversion of the Three Treasures' property and the logic of temple-land inviolability The precept prohibiting the "diversion" of temple property functioned as an important legal and religious argument by which temple-held shōen protected themselves from arbitrary secular taxation and encroachment. It can be understood that this same logic underlay the dispute with Tōdai-ji over Hosshi-in's territory discussed in Blocks 55 and 56.
    Implications for the positioning of the Hashimoto family among lineages surrounding monzeki temples This source also notes the existence of kin and associates positioned on the "periphery" of a monzeki temple's privileged status, providing supporting grounds for the institutional and historical plausibility of the hypothesis that the Hashimoto family belongs to an in-ke lineage on the periphery of the monzeki institutions Hosshi-in and Daijō-in.
    65. Heian ibun, Vol. 10 (Supplement) — The Monk Kaichi's Land Sale Deed (Jōtoku 2) — Record of "Hosshi-in Hizen no Kimi's" Purchase and Resale of Land
    The monk Kaichi's land sale deed (Jōtoku 2, 1098), included in the supplement to Heian ibun, Vol. 10. It records that "Hosshi-in Hizen no Kimi" purchased, and later resold, a parcel of land within the seventh tsubo of the fourth bō, third jō, of the Left Capital (Sakyō). The deed carries a handwritten signature (kaō) and eight Tōdai-ji seals, along with a marginal note reading "within this tsubo, two tan were sold by Gentarō." It is presented alongside a group of related transactions involving Gentarō from Kanji 4 to Eichō 1 (including a tone's petition, a land transfer deed, and a disposition document), forming a body of Heian-period shōen and land-transaction records.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    "Hosshi-in Hizen no Kimi's" involvement in land transactions (late 11th century) As of Jōtoku 2 (1098), "Hosshi-in Hizen no Kimi" appears as an agent personally purchasing and reselling paddy land in the Left Capital. This primary source confirms that persons associated with Hosshi-in were directly involved in land transactions in the capital during the late Heian period, providing evidence that Hosshi-in was engaged in active property transactions as an in-ke institution from an early date.
    Position within the group of Gentarō-related documents Land within the same tsubo is repeatedly noted as having been "sold by Gentarō" (in marginal notes on both No. 4657 and Supplement No. 179), confirming that multiple parties and institutions were buying, selling, and transferring land within the same tsubo. Hosshi-in Hizen no Kimi also functioned as a participant within this late-Heian network of land circulation.
    Relationship to the Tōdai-ji seals and the reliability of the source Eight "Tōdai-ji" seals are stamped on the sheet of the sale deed, confirming that this is a primary source preserved and managed as part of the Tōdai-ji archive. It is an important source connecting to the background of the land-related relationship between Hosshi-in and Tōdai-ji (the dispute discussed in Blocks 55 and 56).
    The geographic extent of Hosshi-in's property activities The fact that persons associated with Hosshi-in — based at Yokota Shōen in Sōe District, Yamato Province — were also involved in land transactions in the Left Capital (Yamashiro Province) shows that Hosshi-in's property activities extended well beyond Yamato Province. This reveals a structure in which, as an in-ke institution, Hosshi-in maintained land and personal networks in both the capital and the provinces.

    [Supplementary Note] In the entry for the 28th day of the 2nd month of Kōshō 3 (1457) in Vol. 1 of the Daijō-in jisha zōjiki, concerning the dispute over Kazusa Shōen, "Mita" appears on Daijō-in's list of parties mobilized. This contemporary source confirms that Mita fell within Daijō-in's sphere of mobilization.

    66. Hashi-in Nobunaga's Kasuga Shrine Records, Vol. 2 (Bun'ei 12, Fifth Month) — The Order of the Sacred Relocation Ceremony and the Record of Hashi-in Nobunaga-bō Tokugō Geimon's Summons to Council
    A record of a Shinto ceremony from the fifth month of Bun'ei 12 (1275), included in item 248 (Diary, Vol. 2) of Hashi-in Nobunaga's Kasuga Shrine Records, Vol. 1, Part 2. This shrine-family (shake) record documents how "Hashi-in Nobunaga-bō Tokugō Geimon" was summoned to council as one of the two sōkan (general officiants) and undertook the practical duties of the sacred relocation ceremony (goxenza) and the presentation of the sacred treasures. It also records the roles of Nakatomi no Sukekata and the Shinto priest Yasumichi, showing the institutional connection between Hashi-in (Hashimoto-in) and the rites of Kasuga Shrine.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    [Excerpt] Quoted from the entry for the fifth month of Bun'ei 12 (the diary of Nakatomi no Sukekata) →

    Bun'ei 12, Fifth Month — Diary of Nakatomi no Sukekata

    5th day, 14th [day] — Shinto priest Yasumichi.
    (Omitted) This evening, at the Hour of the Rooster, an order came from the assembly of monks (shūto) stating that it had been determined the sacred relocation would definitely take place tonight, at the Hour of the Boar.

    Order of the sacred relocation ceremony. At the Hour of the Boar:
    The assembled monks (daishu) came to the shrine; the conch-horn signal was sounded and ceased. At the South Gate, as customary, this was repeated three times. From the third bay from the east of the Dance Hall (Maidono), the council (sengi) convened; Hashi-in Nobunaga-bō Tokugō Geimon, one of the two sōkan, was summoned in accordance with the order and urged forward into the courtyard. Sukekata attended in the vicinity of the Sumiyoshi Myōjin [sub-shrine]. (Omitted)

    The shrine officials came before the deity; entering the treasury through the side door, the presentation of the sacred treasures was overseen by the shōyo (chief officiant) Suketsugu, with the gonkan (deputy officiant) Sukeyoshi handling their conveyance. The treasures were carried around from the south side and brought before the deity. (Omitted) The Shinto priest Yasumichi, in formal attire, brought down the sacred image and the sacred sakaki branch; the shrine guardians stood holding them beneath the sacred bridge. (Omitted)

    When the treasures were brought down from the main shrine, they were held before the treasury of the Wakamiya's sacred treasures. Proceeding in order from the First Shrine, the sacred treasures each went ahead, exited through the two-story gate, and were brought into the temporary shrine (utsushidono). The sacred treasures proceeded in two files — the halberd on the left, the bow and arrows on the right — and entered the temporary shrine. (Omitted) After this, Sukekata went to the area of the sacred bridge, lowered a veil over his face, and brought down [the sacred object — a character is unclear in the source]; the shelf had already been withdrawn beforehand. Harutō brought [the item] forward to where the deity was, and it was affixed to the sacred image. After this, Sukekata received it and conveyed it to the temporary shrine.

    [Roles of Key Figures in the Ceremony]

    Person / Institution Role
    Hashi-in Nobunaga-bō Tokugō Geimon (one of the two sōkan) Summoned as one of the two sōkan to the council (sengi) that deliberated and determined the sacred relocation ceremony, and tasked with urging the assembly forward into the courtyard. This shows that Hashi-in was positioned as one of the two sōkan holding central authority over the management of the rite.
    Nakatomi no Sukekata The author of this record. He attended in the vicinity of the Sumiyoshi Myōjin sub-shrine and recorded in detail the practical proceedings of the relocation ceremony, including the conveyance of the sacred treasures and the delivery of the sacred image. He played a central role as a practical officiant within the shrine family.
    Shinto priest Yasumichi Having received permission following a petition to the temple authorities (jike), he served as the officiating Shinto priest for the palanquin relocation, responsible for bringing down the sacred image and the sacred sakaki branch. He also served as the officer who conveyed notice to the Wakamiya's Shinto priest.
    Chief Officiant (Shōyo) Suketsugu and Deputy Officiant (Gonkan) Sukeyoshi Shrine officials responsible for presenting and conveying the sacred treasures. They are recorded as the practical officiants responsible for managing the sacred treasures during the relocation ceremony.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Evidence that Hashi-in (Hashimoto-in) functioned as one of the two sōkan in Kasuga Shrine rites The record of the summons of "Hashi-in Nobunaga-bō Tokugō Geimon, one of the two sōkan" to the council on the sacred relocation confirms, through a primary shrine-family record, that Hashi-in (Hashimoto-in) held central institutional authority in the administration of Kasuga Shrine rites as of Bun'ei 12 (1275). This constitutes direct evidence of the institutional connection between the Hashimoto family and Kasuga Shrine / Kōfuku-ji.
    Source value as a detailed record of the order of the sacred relocation ceremony The record details the full order of the relocation ceremony, from the assembly of monks at the shrine at the Hour of the Boar through the presentation of the sacred treasures to their entry into the temporary shrine. It is a valuable shrine-family diary source that concretely illustrates the division of roles among the shrine family, the monk assembly, and the sōkan in the administration of medieval Kasuga Shrine rites.
    Clarifying the relationship between Kōfuku-ji, Kasuga Shrine, and Hashimoto (Hashi-in) The fact that Hashi-in participated as one of the two sōkan in the rites of Kasuga Shrine, which fell under the control of Kōfuku-ji, provides institutional supporting evidence for the hypothesis that the Hashimoto lineage was connected to the in-ke lineage of Kōfuku-ji (as discussed in Blocks 59 and 116, among others). The pattern of figures from in-ke lineages holding the sōkan office in Kasuga Shrine rites can also be confirmed in the case of Hashi-in.
    Confirmation of institutional legitimacy through reference to precedent References to precedent, such as "as customary" and phrasing noting that a matter had been reported as having no precedent, appear throughout the record, showing that each step of the relocation ceremony was carried out as an institutional practice grounded in precedent. This suggests that Hashi-in's participation in the council "in accordance with the summons" was likewise an institutional role positioned within such established practice.
    67. Yamato Shiryō, Vol. 1 – Record of Oda Nobunaga's Survey of Kōfuku-ji's Temple Lands (Tenshō 8 [1580]: The Sashidashi Land Survey by Koretō Hyūga-no-kami [Akechi Mitsuhide] and Takigawa Sakon-no-jō, and the Nishi-Hosshi-in Chronicle)
    A record of temple-and-shrine policy under the Nobunaga regime, found in Yamato Shiryō, Vol. 1 (pp. 23–25). It describes how, in the ninth and tenth months of Tenshō 8 (1580), Koretō Hyūga-no-kami (Akechi Mitsuhide) and Takigawa Sakon-no-jō (Kazumasu) visited Kōfuku-ji, Jōjin-in, and Kichijō-in and carried out a province-wide "sashidashi" (survey of temple landholdings). The text quotes the passage "Moreover, according to the Chronicle of Kōfuku-ji's Nishi-Hosshi-in, in the ninth month of Tenshō 8 the provincial survey took place," citing the Nishi-Hosshi-in Chronicle by name — evidence that Hosshi-in maintained its own chronicle, and a valuable source for temple-and-shrine policy under the Nobunaga regime.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Yamato Shiryō, Vol. 1 (pp. 23–25) Published: Taishō 3 (1914); Call number: 348-226 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Quotation: Core Passage on the Tenshō 8 Survey]

    The Old Records of Tōdai-ji's Yakushi-in state: "On the kanoe-tatsu day of the tenth month of Tenshō 8, Nobunaga's retainers Koretō Hyūga-no-kami and Takigawa Sakon-no-jō came together to this province and visited Kōfuku-ji, Jōjin-in, and Kichijō-in, where they carried out a province-wide sashidashi (declaration of holdings), reckoning how much annual tribute [nengu] was produced according to the submitted accounts. Neither temple's monzeki nor any of its in-ke [cloister households] was left out; high and low, all the people were subject to the survey without exception."
    Also, according to the Chronicle of Kōfuku-ji's Nishi-Hosshi-in: "In the ninth month of Tenshō 8, the provincial survey took place; the great warrior bands of Yamato Province at Takada and Kaijū Daibutsu-ku were put to death."

    How extremely strict this survey was is known from the report of temple landholdings that Hōryū-ji submitted to the two commanders at that time. Nobunaga had long resented the arrogance of the Buddhist clergy in concealing land and indulging their private greed, and intended to impose major reductions; to this end he first had the two commanders investigate their revenues. Unfortunately, he met betrayal and death [in the Honnō-ji Incident] before this could be accomplished. Later, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi surveyed the entire country and reduced the landholdings of temples and shrines, he was in fact carrying out Nobunaga's original intention.

    [Historical Context of Yamato Province: From Nobunaga's Entry into the Capital to the Land Survey]

    Period Event
    Eiroku 11 (1568) Oda Nobunaga enters the capital in support of Ashikaga Yoshiaki. Matsunaga Hisahide submits to him and is ordered to bring Yamato Province under military control.
    Tenshō 5 (1577), 10th month Oda Nobutada and the Hosokawa and Akechi generals, guided by Tsutsui Junkei, attack and capture Shigisan Castle. Matsunaga Hisahide takes his own life. Matsunaga's holdings within the province, together with the three districts of Uda and Yamabe, are granted to Junkei.
    Tenshō 8 (1580), 9th–10th months Koretō Hyūga-no-kami (Akechi Mitsuhide) and Takigawa Sakon-no-jō (Kazumasu) visit Kōfuku-ji, Jōjin-in, and Kichijō-in and carry out a province-wide sashidashi (survey of temple lands and annual tribute). The Nishi-Hosshi-in Chronicle likewise records that "the provincial survey took place."
    Tenshō 10 (1582) Akechi Mitsuhide kills Nobunaga (the Honnō-ji Incident). The survey is left unfinished. Toyotomi Hideyoshi later carries out a nationwide land survey, completing Nobunaga's original intention.
    Bunroku 4 (1595) By Hideyoshi's order, a nationwide land survey is conducted. In this province the yield is calculated at 448,950 koku. Major reductions are made to the landholdings of temples and shrines.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Confirmation that the "Nishi-Hosshi-in Chronicle" existed and kept independent records The fact that a "Chronicle of Kōfuku-ji's Nishi-Hosshi-in" existed as an independent chronicle recording the Tenshō 8 provincial survey, and that it is quoted in Yamato Shiryō, shows that Hosshi-in was not merely a subordinate cloister household but continued to exist as an organized institution that kept and managed its own historical records into the late sixteenth century.
    The meaning of "high and low, all the people were subject to the survey without exception" The phrasing in the Old Records of Tōdai-ji's Yakushi-in — "neither temple's monzeki nor any of its in-ke was left out... high and low, all the people were subject to the survey without exception" — shows that no one connected with the temples, including the monzeki and in-ke, could escape the sashidashi survey, underscoring how thoroughly the Nobunaga regime controlled temples and shrines. Hosshi-in was no exception.
    The historical significance of Akechi Mitsuhide's (Koretō Hyūga-no-kami's) survey of temple lands in Yamato Province That the Tenshō 8 sashidashi survey was carried out directly by Nobunaga's leading retainers Akechi Mitsuhide and Takigawa Kazumasu shows that the temple lands of Kōfuku-ji, Hosshi-in, and others were a matter of major political and economic concern to the Nobunaga regime. This source allows the sequence to be traced as a continuous whole: Nobunaga's policy of reducing temple landholdings was left unfinished by the Honnō-ji Incident, and was then carried forward through Hideyoshi's land survey.
    Evidence that Hosshi-in survived into the early-modern transition The fact that, as of Tenshō 8 (1580), the Nishi-Hosshi-in Chronicle was independently recording the provincial survey shows that the medieval in-ke (cloister household) system continued to function even during the transition into the early modern period. Read together with Block 61 (on Hashimoto Kiku'emon's role as an intermediary with the Nara magistrate's office in the early modern period), this helps clarify the continuity of the Hosshi-in lineage into the early modern era.
    68. Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 3 – Records of Buddhist Services and Funeral Rites at Nishi-Hashi-no-kin (Nishi-Hosshi-in) (Tenshō 3–8)
    Entries relating to Nishi-Hashi-no-kin (Nishi-Hosshi-in) found in Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 3 (fascicles 24–31), p. 3. They record the Shushō rite and mochi (rice cakes) of New Year Tenshō 6; the sekihan (red rice) sent as a reciprocal gift to the Daie-kata in the eleventh month of the same year; the death of Kōjin Senken-bō in the tenth month of Tenshō 8; the Hōon-kō service in the third month of Tenshō 7; and the Ninnō-kyō rite in the intercalary first month of Tenshō 3 — together forming a temple-diary source documenting the actual conduct of Buddhist services and funeral rites at Nishi-Hashi-no-kin (Nishi-Hosshi-in).

    Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 3 (fascicles 24–31), p. 3 Published: Shōwa 10–14 (1935–1939); Call number: 640-324 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Quotation] Excerpted from Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 3 →

    Tenshō 6, First Month
    18th day: The Shushō rite at the Great Hall (Ō-midō) was concluded; seven senior monks attended, down to Senkyō-bō. Thirty mochi were provided.
    Item: The Daihannya-kyō was read by rotation (tendoku) at Daijō-in and concluded; over sixty persons attended.
    Item: Later that day, [a representative] went up to the capital to pay respects to the mother, the Ōmandokoro; four bars of silver were presented.
    Item: The Shushō rite was conducted at Hashi-no-kin; eighty mochi were sent there, of which fifteen were distributed.
    It was the day of the Horse. The Great Officiant (daidōshi) conducted the rite; three hundred mon [in cash] and six to of fuse-dai (offering rice) were sent, with two to per attendant. A painted image of Kannon was borrowed from Hōzō-in; round mochi offerings (mochi-dama) were sent; a wooden image was borrowed from Nan'i-bō. Gyōran presented it.

    19th day: The Shinjukyō was read at Kanzen-in and concluded. Heavy rain fell from dawn.

    [List of Entries Related to Nishi-Hashi-no-kin (Nishi-Hosshi-in)]

    Date Content
    Tenshō 3 (1575), intercalary 1st month The Ninnō-kyō rite is performed at Nishi-Hashi-no-kin.
    Tenshō 6 (1578), 1st month, 18th day The Shushō rite is conducted at Hashi-no-kin. Eighty mochi are sent, of which fifteen are distributed. The Great Officiant's conduct of the rite, six to of fuse-dai, and two to per attendant are also recorded.
    Tenshō 6 (1578), 11th month Sekihan (red rice) is sent to Nishi-Hashi-no-kin, recorded as a reciprocal gift to the Daie-kata.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Direct record of Buddhist services at "Nishi-Hashi-no-kin = Nishi-Hosshi-in" The Tamon-in Diary, a primary diary source associated with Kōfuku-ji, records that Hashi-no-kin (Nishi-Hosshi-in) performed Buddhist services such as the Shushō-e, the Hōon-kō, and the Ninnō-kyō, confirming that even during the Tenshō era, Nishi-Hosshi-in continued to function as an in-ke (cloister household) with its own independent capacity to hold religious services.
    The mochi and sekihan exchanges reveal a gift network among cloister households The record that eighty mochi were sent from Nishi-Hosshi-in on the occasion of the Shushō rite, with sekihan later sent back as a reciprocal gift, shows that a system of reciprocal gift-giving among cloister households (an exchange of goods conducted through Buddhist services) was institutionally in operation. Such gift networks served as a means of maintaining personal and organizational ties between the in-ke.
    Consistency with Block 67 (the Tenshō 8 survey) in the same period During the same period (Tenshō 3–8) in which the Nishi-Hosshi-in Chronicle discussed in Block 67 records the Tenshō 8 provincial survey, the Tamon-in Diary continuously records the Buddhist services and funeral rites of Nishi-Hosshi-in. Taken together, the two sources give a fuller, multidimensional confirmation that Nishi-Hosshi-in continued to maintain its religious functions even amid the upheavals of the Nobunaga regime.
    Significance of the record of Kōjin Senken-bō's death The record of "the death of Kōjin Senken-bō" in the tenth month of Tenshō 8 shows that a monk with the specific bō-name "Senken-bō" resided at Nishi-Hosshi-in. That the existence of a specific individual attached to this in-ke can be confirmed through the third-party source of the Tamon-in Diary is important evidence supporting the substantive, continuing existence of Nishi-Hosshi-in.
    69. Nara Kenshi (History of Nara Prefecture), Vol. 6 (Temples) – Temple-Monk and Official Landholdings, and the Formation of Kanana-men-shō and Shinkan-shō (The Fumyō System, Tato Management, and the Spread of In-ke Control in Yamato Province)
    A discussion of the shōen (estate) system found in Nara Kenshi, Vol. 6 (Temples), p. 18. It examines the fumyō (name-holder) structure of temple monks and officials on the miso (offering fields) of Kōfuku-ji's Yuima-e endowment lands, the small-scale management carried out by tato (cultivating tenants), and the eleventh-to-twelfth-century shift from lay names (such as Nagatomi, Tsunetomi) to the names of temple monks as fumyō holders. It also quotes the passage from the Heihanki, in the entry for Hōgen 3, stating that "in Yamato Province, not a single tan of public land remained outside the fumyō-holdings of Kōfuku-ji and other temples" — a source on the shōen system showing that, by the mid-twelfth century, the public lands of Yamato Province had effectively been absorbed into the fumyō-holdings of Kōfuku-ji and its in-ke.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Nara Kenshi, Vol. 6 (Temples), p. 18 Published: June 1991; Call number: GC174-84 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Overview of the Institutional Structure: The Relationship Between In-ke Control and the Fumyō/Tato System]

    Concept / Institution Content
    Fumyō (負名, "name-holder") A person who bore responsibility for, and managed, a myō (a unit of paddy land) within a shōen. This source confirms a structure in which temple monks and mid-to-lower-ranking officials served as the "principal" (shujin) holding the fumyō, with tato (directly cultivating farmers) placed beneath them. The Yamamura family (holders of the Ōta Inumaru myō) is cited as a representative example of an official fumyō-holder in Yamato Province.
    Tato (田堵) A directly cultivating farmer who, under a landholder (fumyō), held individual charge of paddy plots by virtue of official documentation (kugen). Also referred to as yoriudo. In the Heiji 1 (1159) plot register (myōmyō tsubozuke) for Kotō-shō, figures such as Ban no Yoshihisa are listed under the heading "tato of the landholder of Tōdai-ji's Kotō-shō."
    Changes in the Fumyō Structure, 11th–12th Centuries In the eleventh century, fumyō holders bearing lay names (such as Nagatomi, Tsunetomi, and Kasame Kojirō) were common; but from the twelfth century onward, the sources show an increase in fumyō holders bearing the names of temple monks. In Yamato Province, monks affiliated with Kōfuku-ji and its in-ke gradually came to control shōen fumyō.
    What "Not a Single Tan of Public Land" Reveals About the Completion of In-ke Control The Heihanki entry for the seventeenth day of the seventh month of Hōgen 3 (1158) states that "in Yamato Province and at the Kasuga Shrine, [the land] belongs to the fumyō-holdings of Kōfuku-ji and other temples, and not a single tan of public land remains outside their individual control." This shows that, by the mid-twelfth century, the public lands of Yamato Province had effectively all been absorbed into the fumyō-holdings of Kōfuku-ji and its in-ke. Hosshi-in, too, was established as one component of this in-ke system of control.

    [Quotation: From the Text]

    (Inagaki Yasuhiko) states: "That the management of their landholdings was not direct management by the lord, but rather included the small-scale, independent management of farmers beneath him, is shown by recent scholarship beginning with that of Izutani ... their landholdings did not arise through land reclamation, and their management was, for the most part, not direct management" — and the "small-scale independent management by farmers" mentioned here would be that of the tato.

    The entry in the Heihanki for the seventeenth day of the seventh month of Hōgen 3 (1158) reads: "In Yamato Province and at the Kasuga Shrine, [the land] belongs to the fumyō-holdings of Kōfuku-ji and other temples, and not a single tan of public land remains outside their individual control [remainder omitted]."

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Proof that Hosshi-in was institutionally embedded in Yamato Province's system of in-ke control The Heihanki's statement that, by the mid-twelfth century, the public lands of Yamato Province had been absorbed into the "fumyō-holdings of Kōfuku-ji and other temples" corresponds directly to the contemporaneous dispute in which Hosshi-in contested landholder rights over Mita-shō with Tōdai-ji (Blocks 55–56) — a dispute resolved in Hosshi-in's favor when it was formally recognized as landholder by the chōja-sen decree of Kaō 1 (1169). This places Hosshi-in clearly, as a constituent member of Yamato Province's in-ke system of control, within the institutional framework documented by this scholarly source.
    The institutional reality of in-ke directly managing shōen as fumyō holders This source provides scholarly demonstration of the institutional reality that "in-ke bore management responsibility as fumyō holders of shōen," which is consistent with the fact, discussed in Block 63, that a fixed rice allotment (jōmai) of 36 koku at Yokota-shō was specifically designated for Hosshi-in's Buddhist-service expenses. The institutional argument of this source thus supports the conclusion that Hosshi-in functioned not merely as a nominal in-ke but as a practical, operating fumyō holder in shōen management.
    Grounds for understanding the Hashimoto family's continued local presence as "institutional succession within the in-ke lineage" rather than mere "localization" As this source shows, from the twelfth century onward the fumyō-holding of in-ke and temple monks became institutionally established in Yamato Province, and local figures attached to the in-ke were themselves deeply embedded in the management and operation of the shōen. The continued presence of the Hashimoto family in the vicinity of Hosshi-in should therefore be understood not as a matter of incidental "borrowing of a name," but as the continuation of a lineage institutionally rooted, as bōkan (cloister officials) and sata-nin (estate managers), within this system of in-ke control.
    The institutional background to the Kanana-men-shō / Mita-shō dispute and the confirmation of Hosshi-in's landholder rights The discussion of the formation of Kanana-men-shō and Shinkan-shō explains that the dispute with Tōdai-ji over "Mita-shō" (Kanana-men), which Hosshi-in contested (Blocks 55–56), arose as a structural rivalry within Yamato Province's system of in-ke control. The confirmation of Hosshi-in's landholder rights was, in institutional terms, the natural outcome of its status as an in-ke, and the Hashimoto family's involvement with Hosshi-in can likewise be understood as a consequence of that outcome.
    70. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (Meiō 6, Second Month) – Record of Unpaid Official Rice at Yokota-shō: The Rice Amounts Reported for Hashi-no-in (Hosshi-in) Emonkurō, Tayū, and Shichirō
    A record of unpaid official rice (mishin) at Yokota-shō, dated the second month of Meiō 6 (1497), found in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11, p. 122. Among the rice amounts for the previous tatsu year, as reported by the sata-nin and collected by the kyūshu, three names are listed under "Hashi-no-in (Hosshi-in): Emonkurō, Tayū, and Shichirō," together with each individual's rice amount (5 to 5 shō 4 gō; 9 koku 1 to 9 shō 5 gō; and 2 to 2 shō 6 gō) — a source documenting shōen economic administration.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Direct evidence confirming multiple local individuals recorded under the name "Hashi-no-in (Hosshi-in)" The Meiō 6 (1497) record of unpaid annual tribute at Yokota-shō lists three individuals — "Hashi-no-in Emonkurō, Tayū, and Shichirō" — under the name of Hosshi-in. That multiple local individuals connected to Hosshi-in were recorded as tribute-bearers of Yokota-shō in Daijōin's official ledgers allows this primary source to directly confirm that the local lineage affiliated with Hosshi-in was substantively active at the end of the fifteenth century.
    What the title "Tayū" reveals about the standing of this local lineage The title "Tayū" in the entry "Hashi-no-in Tayū" is an official-style designation, suggesting that the local individual connected to Hosshi-in was not a mere farmer but a person of a certain standing, belonging to the class of bōkan (cloister officials) or sata-nin (estate managers). This is consistent with the in-ke management arrangement described in Blocks 57–58 — "held by the Ko-bettō oku, Hosshi-in" — and reinforces the conclusion that the Hosshi-in lineage occupied a managerial position.
    The position of the Hosshi-in lineage within the list of Yokota-shō's tribute-bearers The same record lists other tribute-bearers such as Tankotono, Mitatono, Kōtono, Yoshioka, and Nakanshari, but the fact that three individuals are listed under the name "Hashi-no-in" indicates a notably prominent presence. This confirms that the Hosshi-in lineage was organizationally involved in bearing Yokota-shō's annual tribute through multiple named individuals sharing the burden among themselves.
    Continuity with Blocks 62 and 63: the long-term persistence of the Hosshi-in lineage at Yokota-shō Read together with Block 62 (the mobilization of laborers at Yokota-shō in Bunshō 1, 1466) and Block 63 (the conversion of Yokota-shō from Hosshi-in landholding to Daijōin landholding, and the equal-myō system), this Block 70 (the unpaid tribute of Meiō 6, 1497) shows that local individuals of the Hosshi-in lineage were continuously recorded at Yokota-shō throughout the fifteenth century. This forms a continuous body of evidence, confirmed across multiple sources spanning more than thirty years, for the local establishment of the Hosshi-in lineage.
    Additional information for No. 70: Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (Meiō 6, 1497)
    ✅ Confirmed fact: A record of "three individuals under Hashi-no-in." Among them, the name "Emonkurō" is confirmed.
    [Significance] Following the 1496 record of "Hashimoto," this shows the presence of a specific individual connected to Hashimoto-in (Hosshi-in). The common name "Kurō" corresponds to that of the shōya (village headman) "Kurōbei" in Shōhō 4 (1647), suggesting the possible continuation of a common personal name within the same lineage.
    71. Dai Nihon Komonjo, Iewake 18-1 (Tenji 2, Seventh Month) — Daijōkan Directive to Tōdai-ji: Edict Appointing Gon-Sōjō and Hōin-Daiwajō Shōkaku to the Office of Bettō
    A Daijōkan (Council of State) directive dated the twentieth day of the seventh month of Tenji 2 (1125), preserved in Dai Nihon Komonjo, Iewake 18-1 (p. 242). Acting on an Imperial edict, Minamoto no Ason Masasada, Provisional Middle Counselor (Gon-Chūnagon) of the Junior Third Rank, proclaims the appointment of Shōkaku — Gon-Sōjō (Provisional Senior Prelate) and Hōin-Daiwajō (highest clerical rank) — to the office of Bettō (Superintendent) of Tōdai-ji. The document is co-signed by Oduki no Sukune, Senior Secretary of the Left and Vice-Governor of Tango (with cipher mark), and Minamoto no Ason Morotoshi, Middle Controller of the Right and concurrently Vice-Governor of Bizen (autograph signature) — a personnel record for temple-shrine administration that documents the institutional system for appointing the office of Bettō.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link

    [Cited Text] Quoted from Dai Nihon Komonjo, Iewake 18-1 (p. 242) →

    Daijōkan Directive: To Tōdai-ji

    Regarding the Matter of Appointment to the Office of Bettō

    Gon-Sōjō, Hōin-Daiwajō, Shōkaku
    The above: Minamoto no Ason Masasada, Provisional Middle Counselor of the Junior Third Rank, proclaims, having received the Imperial edict:
    "Let this person be duly appointed Bettō of that temple." Let the temple take due notice. In accordance with this proclamation, let it be carried out. This directive, upon arrival, is to be treated as authoritative. Hence this directive.

    Twentieth day, seventh month, Tenji 2 [1125]
    Oduki no Sukune, Junior Fifth Rank Lower, Acting Senior Secretary of the Left, Doctor of Mathematics, Vice-Governor of Tango (cipher mark) — directive
    Minamoto "Ason" (Morotoshi), Junior Fourth Rank Lower, Acting Middle Controller of the Right, concurrently Vice-Governor of Bizen (autograph signature)

    [Structure of the Document and the Persons Involved]

    Role / Person Description
    Appointee: Shōkaku Gon-Sōjō and Hōin-Daiwajō — a high-ranking monk appointed to the office of Bettō of Tōdai-ji. Hōin was the highest of the clerical ranks, and the fact that a monk of this rank required an Imperial edict for his appointment demonstrates that appointment to the office of Bettō rested on Imperial authority.
    Proclaimant: Minamoto no Ason Masasada Gon-Chūnagon (Provisional Middle Counselor), Junior Third Rank — a senior court noble who proclaimed the appointment upon receiving the Imperial edict. This shows that the appointment to Bettō was issued as a formal decision of the Imperial court.
    Co-signatory: Oduki no Sukune (Senior Secretary of the Left) Junior Fifth Rank Lower, Senior Secretary of the Left, Doctor of Mathematics, Vice-Governor of Tango. Affixed his cipher mark as the administrative official responsible for the Daijōkan directive.
    Co-signatory: Minamoto no Ason Morotoshi Junior Fourth Rank Lower, Middle Controller of the Right, concurrently Vice-Governor of Bizen. His autograph signature guarantees the formal validity of the Daijōkan directive.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Description
    Institutional basis: appointment to Bettō carried out by Imperial edict and Daijōkan directive That the appointment to the office of Bettō of Tōdai-ji was issued through a Daijōkan directive — the highest administrative instrument of the Imperial court — shows that the appointment of a Bettō at a major temple was institutionalized as a joint decision of the court and the temple. It follows that the "monzeki's control over the right to appoint bettō at branch temples," discussed in Blocks 57 and 58, was itself built upon this court-level appointment system.
    Confirmation of the standing attached to appointing the highest-ranking monks — Hōin and Gon-Sōjō — to the office of Bettō That Shōkaku, the appointee, held the highest clerical rank of Gon-Sōjō and Hōin-Daiwajō shows that the office of Bettō was not merely an administrative post but one inseparably bound to the highest religious authority. This provides the context for understanding that the "ko-bettō" (sub-Bettō) of Hosshi-in functioned at the periphery of this same Bettō institutional system.
    Primary-source confirmation of the Bettō system in the late Heian period (early twelfth century) Tenji 2 (1125) falls just before the first half of the twelfth century (the Hōen–Kōji era, 1135–1144; see Block 56), when Hosshi-in began to contend with Tōdai-ji over proprietary rights to Mita-no-shō. That the Bettō appointment system was clearly functioning through Daijōkan directives during this period is significant as background evidence that Hosshi-in was active in the same era as an inge within this same institutional framework.
    Institutional correspondence between Imperial appointment and the "permission of the Sōjō of Tōrin-in" (Blocks 57 and 58) The formal appointment procedure shown in this document — Imperial edict, then Daijōkan directive, then acknowledgment by the temple — corresponds to the same institutional pattern of "appointment through the permission of a higher authority" confirmed in Blocks 57 and 58, where Yokobō Zenkyūbō's entry into the temple was authorized by the "permission of the Sōjō of Tōrin-in." The dispatch of Hosshi-in's ko-bettō can likewise be positioned as a logical extension of this same appointment system.
    72. Shinshū Kyōdan Kaitenshi (Unebi Shigaku Sōsho) — Monzeki and Ko-bettō: A General Account of the System of Holding Branch-Temple Bettō Offices and Dispatching Ko-bettō
    A scholarly discussion of the ko-bettō system contained in Kasahara Kazuo's Shinshū Kyōdan Kaitenshi (Unebi Shobō, 1942). It gives a detailed account of the system whereby a monzeki temple would itself hold the office of Bettō at a branch temple and dispatch a deputy known as a "ko-bettō" to manage it. It states that branch temples whose Bettō office was held directly by the monzeki were temples "of considerable income and established pedigree," and this general scholarly source on the inge management system includes the case of Hosshi-in (Oku-Hosshi-in; "ko-bettō, held by Oku-Hosshi-in").

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Shinshū Kyōdan Kaitenshi (Unebi Shigaku Sōsho) Author: Kasahara Kazuo　Publisher: Unebi Shobō　Year: 1942 (Shōwa 17) National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Overview of the Ko-bettō System]

    System / Concept Description
    Direct holding of branch-temple Bettō offices by the monzeki At monzeki temples such as Kōfuku-ji and Daijō-in, there were cases in which the monzeki itself directly held the office of Bettō at a branch temple. Under the formula "this temple's Bettō is the present monzeki," the monzeki retained the office in name while the actual administrative work was carried out by a deputy, the ko-bettō.
    Dispatch of the ko-bettō and its administrative function This scholarly work explicitly records the case of Hosshi-in being dispatched as ko-bettō, under the notation "ko-bettō: held by Oku-Hosshi-in." At branch temples the monzeki could not manage directly on site, the ko-bettō served as the monzeki's deputy, carrying out the function of maintaining and administering the temple.
    The standing of branch temples that required a ko-bettō Branch temples whose Bettō office the monzeki held directly are described as temples "of considerable income, and also of established pedigree," and the dispatch of a ko-bettō was a system applied only to branch temples of high standing and pedigree. Fuku-ji, the branch temple to which Hosshi-in was dispatched as ko-bettō, was likewise a temple of standing, with the pedigree of being "one of the three clan temples of the Fujiwara house."
    Institutional purpose: preventing encroachment by other lineages The purpose of the head temple retaining the right to appoint the Bettō was to prevent monks of other lineages from entering the position of abbot or Bettō at a branch temple, thereby avoiding the loss of the branch temple and its estates. The work also cites, as a cautionary counter-example, the case of Hase-dera losing a branch temple of Ninna-ji in Shōryaku 1, and on this basis it scholarly demonstrates the institutional necessity of Hosshi-in's dispatch as ko-bettō.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Description
    Positioning of "ko-bettō, held by Oku-Hosshi-in" as scholarly demonstration This source is a scholarly work that summarizes Hosshi-in's function as a ko-bettō not through an individual archival record, but as a general institutional theory. It confirms that the individual passages quoted from the same work in Blocks 57 and 58 belong within this broader theoretical context, and it substantiates that Hosshi-in's function as ko-bettō was not an incidental occurrence but an institutionally necessary role.
    Scholarly confirmation of Hosshi-in's standing as "the administrative body of a branch temple of established pedigree" The scholarly statement that "branch temples whose Bettō office the monzeki held directly were temples of considerable income and established pedigree" shows that the branch temple to which a ko-bettō was dispatched was itself a temple of standing, and this corroborates that Hosshi-in, entrusted with its administration, was likewise an inge of corresponding standing and reliability. This scholarly work thus indirectly attests to Hosshi-in's status as an inge.
    Integrated understanding together with Blocks 57–58 and 70 Read together with Blocks 57 and 58 (individual citations from the same work) and Block 70 (the Hashino-in record from Yokota-no-shō), this source completes a two-fold demonstration: that Hosshi-in was an "inge institutionally dispatched as ko-bettō" (Blocks 57, 58, and 72), and that it was also a "substantive organization that actually maintained local personnel at Yokota-no-shō" (Block 70).
    Independent institutional-theoretical corroboration by a third-party scholarly work This source is not a record produced by the Hashimoto family or by Hosshi-in itself, but a scholarly work on religious history published in Shōwa 17 (1942). That a researcher of medieval temple institutions demonstrates Hosshi-in's ko-bettō function as a matter of institutional theory gives it high evidentiary value as corroboration by an unbiased, independent scholarly authority.
    73. Museum (No. 326) — The Hashimoto Family and the Yoriki of the Nara Magistrate's Office: Records of Hashimoto Mataemon, Gonbei Masakata, Kikuemon Masataka, and Other Members of the Hashimoto Lineage
    A passage concerning the Hashimoto family contained in Museum, No. 326 (p. 24). It documents the Hashimoto family, who served for generations as yoriki (senior constables) of the Nara Magistrate's Office (Nara Bugyōsho), including Gonbei Masakata's (Tōtōsai) commission of a Takasago figurine in Kaei 2 (1849); the enrollment of Kikuemon Masataka, Heizō Masakazu, and Jōemon Masanari as disciples of Tomobayashi Mitsuhira; and the orders placed with the deer-carver Morikawa Toen between Ansei 4 (1857) and Bunkyū 3 (1863), of which roughly one-third were placed by members of the Hashimoto lineage as a whole. This genealogical source also records the branch designations "Kita-Hashimoto" (Northern Hashimoto), "Minami-Hashimoto" (Southern Hashimoto), and "Ike-Hashimoto" (Pond Hashimoto).

    [Bibliographic Information]

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Description
    Evidence of the Hashimoto family's continuous involvement with an official institution (yoriki of the Magistrate's Office) in early-modern Nara The statement that the family "served for generations as yoriki of the Nara Magistrate's Office" shows that a third-party publication (the journal Museum) records the Hashimoto family as formally incorporated into Nara's administrative institutions throughout the Edo period. Read together with Block 61 (Hashimoto Kikuemon's role as intermediary with the Nara Magistrate's Office), the family's sustained relationship with the Magistrate's Office is confirmed across multiple independent sources.
    Demonstration of the family's collective scale: the Hashimoto lineage accounted for roughly one-third of the orders The record that the Hashimoto lineage accounted for roughly one-third of all deer-carving orders placed with Morikawa Toen during the Ansei–Bunkyū period (1857–1863) shows that the Hashimoto family was engaged with Nara's culture and society not as a single individual or household, but on the scale of an extended clan comprising several branch lines, including Kita-Hashimoto, Minami-Hashimoto, and Ike-Hashimoto.
    The Hashimoto family's intellectual and political network, shown by the enrollment of multiple members as disciples of Tomobayashi Mitsuhira Three individuals — Kikuemon Masataka, Heizō Masakazu, and Jōemon Masanari — are recorded as disciples of Tomobayashi Mitsuhira, a figure associated with the sonnō jōi (revere-the-emperor, expel-the-barbarians) movement and the Tenchū-gumi. This shows that the Hashimoto family participated collectively, with multiple members, in the kokugaku (National Learning) and imperial-loyalist movements of the late Edo period. This is important background for Kikuemon's activities detailed in Block 75 (Noyama no Nageki).
    Confirmation of multiple branch lines: "Kita-Hashimoto," "Minami-Hashimoto," and "Ike-Hashimoto" The multiple designations found in the records show that the Hashimoto family had settled in Nara as several branch lines distinguished by direction or place name. This can be understood as evidence that the local Hashimoto lineage associated with the medieval Hosshi-in line branched into and settled as several distinct households within the region during the early-modern period.
    74. Ichijō-ke Ryō Kaseyama-yaki — Records of Hashimoto Gonbei Masakata (Tōtōō) and Hashimoto Kikuemon Masataka (Obikawa; of Nikaidō Lineage Origin)
    A passage concerning Hashimoto Gonbei Masakata (Tōtōō) and Hashimoto Kikuemon Masataka (Obikawa) contained in Ichijō-ke Ryō Kaseyama-yaki (p. 118). Masakata, a former yoriki of the Nara Magistrate's Office and a sukisha, is confirmed to have commissioned a Takasago figurine for his sixtieth-birthday celebration in Kaei 2 (1849), to have held the kaimyō "Chikyō Tōei Koji," and to be interred at the Kokkindō cemetery near Byakugō-ji. His adopted son, Kikuemon Masataka — of the Fujiwara clan name and Nikaidō honji, the eldest son of Chūjō Hiyuki adopted into the Hashimoto family — was a yoriki and a master of Hōzōin-ryū spearmanship recorded in Kawaji Toshiakira's diary Neifu Kiji.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Description
    Kikuemon Masataka's honji, the "Fujiwara-Nikaidō lineage," connects directly with the genealogical hypothesis This source explicitly states that he was "of the Fujiwara clan, Nikaidō honji, the eldest son of Chūjō Hiyuki, adopted into the Hashimoto family," which corresponds directly to Hypothesis 2 in Block 59 (the discussion positioning Hosshin-in's Zengyōbō/Ryōjō within the Suemochi branch of the Nikaidō lineage). That a Fujiwara-Nikaidō origin is recorded, via an adoption into the Hashimoto family, in the independent publication Ichijō-ke Ryō Kaseyama-yaki is significant as institutional and genealogical corroboration of the hypothesis.
    Confirmation in shogunal administrative records: the entry in Kawaji Toshiakira's Neifu Kiji That Hashimoto Kikuemon is recorded in Neifu Kiji, the official diary of Nara Magistrate Kawaji Toshiakira, means that a member of the Hashimoto family appears by name in shogunal administrative records at the magistrate level. This carries high evidentiary value as confirmation of the Hashimoto family's existence through an official administrative record.
    Continuity of the lineage confirmed through a present-day descendant and gravestone The confirmation of the gravestone at the Kokkindō cemetery near Byakugō-ji, together with information provided by the descendant Mr. Hashimoto Teruo (resident of Takatsuki City, Osaka Prefecture), shows that this source is not merely a transcription of a past record, but confirms a continuous lineage with an existing, substantive line of descendants.
    The standing of a master of Hōzōin-ryū spearmanship is consistent with Block 61 Whereas Block 61 (Kama Hōzōin Spearmanship) presents Hashimoto Kikuemon as an intermediary between the Nara Magistrate's Office and Hōzōin, this Block 74 records the same person as a "master" of Hōzōin-ryū spearmanship. The consistency between the two sources shows that the Hashimoto family's relationship with Hōzōin-ryū spearmanship was substantive rather than a mere coincidence in the records.
    75. Noyama no Nageki: Banbayashi Kōhei and the Meiji Restoration — Detailed Record of Hashimoto Masataka (Kikuemon / Tōichi, of Nikaidō-ryū Origin)
    A biographical record of Hashimoto Masataka (originally called Kikuemon, later renamed Tōichi) found in Noyama no Nageki: Banbayashi Kōhei and the Meiji Restoration (item 193). Born in Bunsei 5 (1822) and died in Meiji 19 (1886), he was born the eldest son of Nakajō Koreyuki of the Nikaidō lineage and was adopted into the Hashimoto family by Hashimoto Masakata, succeeding him as a yoriki (a mid-ranking administrative/law-enforcement officer) of the Nara Magistrate's Office. The record documents his mastery of the secret teachings of Hōzōin-ryū spearmanship, his role in arranging Banbayashi Kōhei's invitation to Nara, his discipleship at the Shinpūkan academy, his support of the imprisoned Kōhei in 1863, his own subsequent confinement and release at the time of the Restoration, and his later post as a Shinto priest (shishō) at Tamukeyama Hachimangū Shrine. It is a detailed personal biographical source showing his pursuit of kokugaku (National Learning) and waka poetry, his collection of old records, and his establishment of a private library.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Details Link
    Noyama no Nageki: Banbayashi Kōhei and the Meiji Restoration (item 193) Publication date: July 1977; Call number: HA28-17 View at National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Overview of Hashimoto Masataka's Basic Information, Career, and Activities]

    Item Details
    Name and Art-name Masataka; courtesy name (azana) Shiyū; art-name (gō) Taisen. Common name: Kikuemon, later renamed Tōichi.
    Birth/Death Years and Age at Death Born in Bunsei 5 (1822); died November 5, Meiji 19 (1886), at the age of 65. Grave: Byakugō-ji Temple.
    Origin and Lineage Birth father: Nakajō Koreyuki of the Nikaidō lineage (Masataka was born his eldest son). Adoptive father: Hashimoto Masakata (yoriki of the Nara Magistrate's Office). Residence: Gokenyashiki, in front of the Kuromon (Black Gate).
    Career Yoriki of the Nara Magistrate's Office (succeeding his adoptive father's post) → After the Restoration: summoned to serve the Chinbu Sōtokufu (Pacification Governor-General's Headquarters) → Junior Official (shōzoku) of Nara Prefecture → resigned in Meiji 4 (1871) → Shinto priest (shishō) at Tamukeyama Hachimangū Shrine.
    Martial Arts and Skills Mastery of the secret teachings of Hōzōin-ryū spearmanship, various martial arts including firearms, calligraphy and painting, and sarugaku (a precursor of Noh theater).
    Relationship with Banbayashi Kōhei Around the beginning of the Ansei era, he helped arrange for Kōhei's invitation to Nara. He became a disciple at the Shinpūkan, the academy of kokugaku (National Learning) and waka poetry that Kōhei had opened. In the autumn of Bunkyū 3 (1863), following the collapse of the Tenchūgumi uprising, he treated the imprisoned Kōhei with the respect due a master and was entrusted with a copy of the Nanzan Tōunroku and thirty-six poem-strips (tanzaku) of kokufū verse. He was subsequently confined for several years on suspicion by the Kyoto Shoshidai, and was released at the time of the Restoration.
    Scholarly and Cultural Activities He studied kokugaku (National Learning) and waka poetry, collected and transcribed old records, and established a library within his residence.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Explicit documentary record of adoption "from the Nikaidō lineage (as the eldest son of Nakajō Koreyuki) into the Hashimoto family" This source records the specific genealogical relationship "birth father: Nakajō Koreyuki of the Nikaidō lineage; adoptive father: Hashimoto Masakata" in a third-party publication, allowing the connection between the Hashimoto family and the Nikaidō lineage to be established as primary-source information. This is corroborated by two other independent sources — Block 59 (the genealogical hypothesis concerning Ryōjō and Zengyō-bō of the Suemochi branch of the Nikaidō lineage) and Block 74 (a record of the same lineage's surname) — which together converge to confirm the relationship between the Hashimoto family and the Nikaidō lineage.
    Continuation of public office after the Restoration — Chinbu Sōtokufu, Junior Official of Nara Prefecture, and Shinto priest at Tamukeyama Hachimangū Shrine Despite political confinement during the late Edo period, the record of his holding a succession of public posts after the Restoration — summons to the Chinbu Sōtokufu, Junior Official of Nara Prefecture, and Shinto priest at Tamukeyama Hachimangū Shrine — shows that the Hashimoto family maintained ties to Nara's public institutions and shrines even through the transition from the early modern to the modern era. This serves as evidence of continuity, showing that a family attached to a medieval in-ke (temple-affiliated aristocratic lineage) continued to hold public roles in the region into the modern period.
    Record of the Hashimoto family's scholarly interest, evidenced by the collection of old records and establishment of a library The account of his establishing a library within his residence and collecting and transcribing old records suggests that the Hashimoto family were not merely warriors and administrators, but possessed a scholarly consciousness aimed at preserving and passing on the records and documents of the in-ke lineage dating back to the medieval period. Such activity can be understood as the modern continuation of a family that had once served in a bōkan (temple-administrator) or scribal role attached to an in-ke.
    Multi-dimensional confirmation of the Hashimoto family from the early modern through modern periods via three sources — Blocks 73, 74, and 75 Three independent publications — the journal Museum (Block 73), Ichijō Family Domain Kaseyama Ware (Block 74), and Noyama no Nageki (Block 75) — record the Hashimoto family's activities from the late Edo through Meiji periods from different angles, together forming a body of evidence that mutually complements and confirms itself. The fact that multiple independent third-party sources confirm the modern existence of the Hashimoto family is an important factor strengthening the reliability of the evidence.
    76. Yamato Bunka Kenkyū Vol. 12, No. 6 — Record of the Meikōkan (Lecture Institute Attached to the Nara Magistrate's Office): Hashimoto Kikuemon Masakata and Hashimoto Naojirō Masataka Among Its Staff (Founded in Tenpō 3)
    A record of the Meikōkan found in Yamato Bunka Kenkyū, Vol. 12, No. 6 (Issue 110, May 1967). The Meikōkan was a lecture institute attached to the Nara Magistrate's Office, founded in Tenpō 3 (1832) by the Nara magistrate Kajino Tosa-no-kami Yoshiki. Among its eleven staff officials, two men from the Hashimoto family — Hashimoto Kikuemon Masakata and Hashimoto Naojirō Masataka — are recorded. This educational source documents that students were mainly the children of the Magistrate's Office's yoriki and dōshin (roughly twenty or more students), along with the textbooks used, the reward system, and staff composition.
