    [Overview of the Meikōkan]

    Item Details
    Year Founded and Founder Tenpō 3 (1832). Petitioned for and established by the Nara magistrate Kajino Tosa-no-kami Yoshiki (Fujiwara Ason). It was a lecture institute attached to the Magistrate's Office, established with shogunate approval. Its name was given by the Kyoto Shoshidai, Lord Ōta of Kakegawa, who inscribed the plaque.
    Location and Facilities Kitabukuro-chō (present-day corner of the intersection north of Nara Women's University). Frontage of 10 ken by a depth of 17.5 ken (175 tsubo), comprising 5 buildings.
    Students and Textbooks Students were mainly the children of the Magistrate's Office's yoriki and dōshin (roughly twenty or more students). Textbooks: the Classic of Filial Piety (Kōkyō), the Five Classics (Gokyō), the Xiaoxue, and the Jinsilu.
    Staff and Administrative System One instructor (kyōju), two supervising yoriki, and four dōshin. Attendance was managed through a class register and reported to the magistrate at the end of each month. At year's end, the student with the most attendances was awarded 100 hiki (a traditional monetary unit) in money.
    First and Successor Instructors First instructor: Taki Seishū (courtesy name Shikei, art-name Seiei, common name Chōzō, resident of Minamihanda-chō). Successor: Oka Shugu (a disciple of Taki Seishū).

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Administrative evidence that two members of the Hashimoto family were enrolled at an official educational institution of the Magistrate's Office The Meikōkan was a formal lecture institute attached to the Nara Magistrate's Office and established with shogunate approval. The fact that two members of the Hashimoto family appear among the roster of its eleven staff officials confirms, through an administrative record, that by Tenpō 3 (1832) the Hashimoto family had been incorporated into the official institutions of the Magistrate's Office. This is not evidence of incidental involvement, but of a formally recorded, institutional role.
    Continuity of the family lineage shown by the succession of the names "Masakata" and "Masataka" "Hashimoto Kikuemon Masakata" in this block is either the same person as, or belongs to the same-named lineage as, Hashimoto Masakata (Tōtō-ō), discussed in detail in Blocks 74 and 75, and "Hashimoto Naojirō Masataka" shares the name "Masataka" with "Hashimoto Masataka (Kikuemon / Tōichi)" in Block 75. The fact that the same names are confirmed across multiple sources and multiple individuals indicates a deliberate succession of names within the Hashimoto family, and serves as corroborating evidence for the continuity of the lineage.
    Coexistence with the Nakajō family reinforces the connection to the Nikaidō lineage Three men bearing the Nakajō surname — Nakajō Ryōzō Masakoto, Nakajō Ninnosuke Masatoshi, and Nakajō Gengo Koremitsu — appear together in the staff roster. As recorded in Block 75, where Masataka's birth father is identified as "Nakajō Koreyuki of the Nikaidō lineage," the Hashimoto family and the Nakajō family (of the Nikaidō lineage) were bound by a deep personal tie formed through adoption. The fact that both families are listed together within the same office of the Magistrate's Office corroborates the substantive reality of that relationship.
    Layered confirmation of the Hashimoto family's involvement with the Magistrate's Office through four sources — Blocks 73–76 Four independent publications — the journal Museum (Block 73), Ichijō Family Domain Kaseyama Ware (Block 74), Noyama no Nageki (Block 75), and Yamato Bunka Kenkyū (this block, 76) — record the Hashimoto family's relationship with the Magistrate's Office and Nara from different periods and different angles. Such layered confirmation from multiple independent third-party sources is a decisive factor in strengthening the reliability of the evidence.
    77. Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 5 (Tenshō 8, Fourth Month) — The Ordination Ceremony of Genʼin Ryōkan-bō of Jison-in, Tōnomine: Nishi-Hosshin-in as Precept Master, the Tomokudai Appointment, and the Payment of 100 Hiki in Ryōsoku
    An entry from the fourth month of Tenshō 8 (1580) found in Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 5 (item 51). It records that Genʼin Ryōkan-bō of Jison-in on Tōnomine underwent the tokudo (ordination) ceremony at Hōzō-in, with Nishi-Hosshin-in serving as the precept master ("kaishi Nishi-Hosshin-in"). This source on temple personnel affairs and finances documents the negotiations over the letter of appointment (bunin-jō) for the tomokudai (deputy overseer) post — including the citing of precedents such as Ganshiki-bō and Shungaku-bō — and the process by which Nishi-Hosshin-in ultimately obtained the letter of appointment by paying 100 hiki in ryōsoku (fee).

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 5 (Fascicle 51), item 51 Publication date: Shōwa 14 (1939); Call number: 210.48-E38t-T View at National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Quotation] Rendered from Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 5 (entry for the fourth month of Tenshō 8) →

    Genʼin Ryōkan-bō of Jison-in on Tōnomine, having earnestly petitioned for admission to the ranks of this temple's assembly (kōshū), was granted permission and admitted as a gakuryo (scholar-monk). Accordingly, on the 21st of this month, the tokudo (ordination) ceremony was held at Hōzō-in; the precept master (kaishi) was Nishi-Hosshin-in, and the role of hair-shaving (sori-yaku) was performed by Rimatsu Ken-bō. On the 27th of the same month, the chūfunari rite was held at the same place; a midday meal and a round of sake were served, and when 15 koku in chūman-sen was disbursed, it was recorded that 50 kanmon at the prevailing exchange rate (wa-ichi) was disbursed for the gathering of the gakuryo. Regarding this, it was formally requested that a letter of appointment (bunin-jō) be issued for the tomokudai post. Nishi-Hosshin-in stated in reply that a tomokudai stipend existed only at the time of the Mihakkō (Eight Lectures) ceremony, and that no such precedent existed otherwise; and on that basis, the matter was left unattended. Thereafter, the precedent of the then tomokudai, Junshō-bō, was investigated and brought forward: as recent precedents, it was noted that when Takeda-shusshō held the post, Ganshiki-bō served as tomokudai, and when Konzō-in Shunshō-bō held it, Shungaku-bō served as tomokudai — such appointments not being unprecedented in either case. It was strongly represented to the assembly of gakuryo that it would be improper to let the precedent lapse on this occasion, and this too was deemed entirely reasonable. At this point Nishi-Hosshin-in had no further grounds on which to object; and so, through the mediation of Manishu-in, the matter was settled between the parties for a payment of 100 hiki in ryōsoku, and the letter of appointment was issued.

    [Course of Events: The Tomokudai Appointment Negotiations]

    Stage Details
    Tenshō 8, 4th Month, 21st Day Genʼin Ryōkan-bō of Jison-in on Tōnomine underwent the tokudo ceremony at Hōzō-in. Nishi-Hosshin-in served as precept master (kaishi). The hair-shaving role (sori-yaku) was performed by Rimatsu Ken-bō.
    27th Day of the Same Month The chūfunari rite was held. Costs included a midday meal and a round of sake, and a disbursement of 15 koku in chūman-sen (equivalent to 50 kanmon at the prevailing exchange rate).
    Negotiations over the Tomokudai Letter of Appointment When asked to submit a letter of appointment for the tomokudai post, Nishi-Hosshin-in initially objected, stating that a tomokudai stipend existed only at the time of the Mihakkō ceremony and that no other precedent existed, and the matter was left unattended. However, the precedent of Junshō-bō was subsequently investigated (citing the earlier cases of Ganshiki-bō and Shungaku-bō) and presented to the assembly of gakuryo.
    Final Resolution Unable to raise further objection to the cited precedents, Nishi-Hosshin-in, through the mediation of Manishu-in, paid 100 hiki in ryōsoku and received the letter of appointment, resolving the matter.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Institutional confirmation that Nishi-Hosshin-in held the position of "precept master" (kaishi), the most important ritual role The kaishi (precept master) of an ordination ceremony is the most important role, conferring the precepts upon the ordinand, and is undertaken only by a monk or in-ke (temple-affiliated household) holding commensurate religious standing. The fact that, as of Tenshō 8 (1580), Nishi-Hosshin-in served as the ordination precept master for Genʼin Ryōkan-bō of Jison-in on Tōnomine confirms, through a primary source, that Nishi-Hosshin-in possessed religious standing recognized as suitable for the role of kaishi by both Tamon-in (of the Kōfuku-ji lineage) and Tōnomine (of the Danzan Jinja lineage).
    Financial substance as an in-ke, shown by the capacity to bear the economic burden of 100 hiki in ryōsoku The fact that, in the negotiations over the tomokudai letter of appointment, Nishi-Hosshin-in ultimately accepted the considerable economic burden of 100 hiki in ryōsoku to resolve the matter shows that even amid the upheaval of the Nobunaga regime in Tenshō 8, Nishi-Hosshin-in retained the financial capacity to secure the letter of appointment. This stands as evidence of its substantive continuity as an in-ke.
    Institutional negotiating capacity of Nishi-Hosshin-in, shown by the negotiations over confirming precedent The record that Nishi-Hosshin-in initially objected to submitting the tomokudai letter of appointment, and continued to negotiate until precedents (such as Ganshiki-bō and Shungaku-bō) were cited, shows that Nishi-Hosshin-in was not a mere subordinate body that simply followed instructions, but an in-ke possessing the institutional standing to assert precedent and established practice.
    Contemporaneous corroboration with Blocks 67 and 68 (records of Nishi-Hosshin-in from the Tenshō era) Taken together with Block 67 (the Tenshō 8 chronicle and sashidashi land-survey record concerning Nishi-Hosshin-in) and Block 68 (records of Buddhist services from Tamon-in Nikki, Tenshō 3–8), multiple sources confirm that in the very same year of Tenshō 8 (1580), Nishi-Hosshin-in performed three distinct functions: responding to the sashidashi land survey, conducting Buddhist services, and serving as ordination precept master and securing the tomokudai appointment. This provides a multi-dimensional demonstration of Nishi-Hosshin-in's wide-ranging activity under the Nobunaga regime.
    78. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 8 (Bunmei 18, Fourth Month) — Records of Taishun of Hosshin-in: Temple Affairs, the Fukuji Paddy-Land Overseer Post, Ōse Chigyō, and the Disbursement of Go-yu Oil
    An entry from the fourth month of Bunmei 18 (1486) found in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 8 (item 437). It records, under the phrase "Taishun Hosshin-in kuji mui" (Taishun of Hosshin-in carried out the temple's public affairs without incident), that Taishun conducted Hosshin-in's public affairs smoothly, was appointed overseer (bugyō) of Fukuji's paddy lands, both within and outside the temple precincts, for his lifetime, and that Hosshin-in held chigyō (administrative rights) over the ōse (tax-liable holdings) in the various localities. Ochi, Yamada, Myōō-in, and Myōtoku-in are listed as mediators, and the record further notes that Hosshin-in was responsible for the disbursement of go-yu (ceremonial) oil — a source documenting in-ke activity.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Title Bibliographic Details Link
    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 8 (item 437) Editor: Tsuji Zennosuke; Call number: 554-213 View at National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Quotation] Rendered from Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 8 (entry for the fourth month of Bunmei 18)

    Item: It is stated that Taishun of Hosshin-in carried out the temple's public affairs without incident. Following the petition submitted by the certifying official (shōhanji) Yasuhiro, it was further ordered that Taishun shall serve for his lifetime (ichigo) as overseer (bugyō) of Fukuji's paddy-land affairs, both within and outside the temple precincts. It is stated that Hosshin-in shall hold chigyō over the ōse in all the various localities. The mediators who affixed their seals were Ochi, Yamada, Myōō-in, and Myōtoku-in; the matter was concluded without incident, a most gratifying outcome. As for the matter of the go-yu offering, it has been ordered that Hosshin-in shall handle its disbursement; this concerns Fukuji. The stipulated amount is one to, but of late only five shō have been offered, which is unsatisfactory.

    Item: Five shō of go-yu oil from Jinnan-in was offered by the Risshi (Vinaya Master) Kōken as this month's portion; it is to be disbursed by the end of the month.

    [Analysis of the Record's Content]

    Item Details
    "Taishun Hosshin-in kuji mui" Records that Taishun carried out Hosshin-in's public affairs "without incident" (mui) — that is, smoothly and without problems. The record was made following the petition of the certifying official (shōhanji), Yasuhiro.
    Lifetime Appointment as Overseer of Fukuji's Paddy Lands Confirms that Taishun held the post of overseer (bugyō) of Fukuji's paddy lands, both within and outside the temple precincts, for his lifetime (ichigo). This shows a direct connection to Blocks 57 and 58, where Hosshin-in is recorded as holding the post of shō-bettō (deputy superintendent) at Fukuji.
    Hosshin-in's Chigyō over the Ōse of All the Various Localities The record states that "Hosshin-in shall hold chigyō over the ōse in all the various localities," documenting that Hosshin-in was granted chigyō over the ōse holdings across multiple localities. This shows that Hosshin-in's sphere of chigyō was not confined to a single subsidiary temple, but extended across a wide area.
    Mediators: Ochi, Yamada, Myōō-in, and Myōtoku-in Ochi, Yamada, Myōō-in, and Myōtoku-in are listed as the mediators (witnesses/guarantors) for this matter, showing that Hosshin-in's appointment followed a formal procedure conducted in the presence of numerous in-ke and local powers.
    Hosshin-in's Responsibility for the Go-yu Oil It is recorded that Hosshin-in was responsible for disbursing the go-yu oil, and the record also notes the problem that, against the stipulated amount of one to, only five shō have recently been offered. This confirms the substantive reality of Hosshin-in's function in economic disbursement.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Details
    Evidence of Hosshin-in's substantive activity, recorded under the specific personal name "Taishun Hosshin-in" The appearance of the specific personal name "Taishun Hosshin-in" in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, a primary official record, directly proves that as of Bunmei 18 (1486), Hosshin-in was functioning as a substantive in-ke with a specific head (in-shu) named Taishun. Rather than an abstract institutional argument, this is a record of activity tied to an individual's name, and thus carries high evidentiary value.
    "Overseer of Fukuji's Paddy Lands" directly connects with "Shō-bettō Oku-Hosshin-in / Fukuji" in Blocks 57 and 58 Blocks 57 and 58 record that Hosshin-in held the post of shō-bettō at Fukuji ("shō-bettō oku-Hosshin-in mochi no"), while this Block 78 confirms that Hosshin-in also held, for a lifetime, the post of paddy-land overseer (den-chi bugyō) at that same Fukuji. The fact that the institutional relationship between Hosshin-in and Fukuji is confirmed by multiple sources on both the "shō-bettō function" and the "paddy-land overseer function" proves that the relationship between the two was a continuous and multi-faceted substantive tie.
    Confirmation of wide-area control through "chigyō over the ōse of all the various localities" The statement that "Hosshin-in shall hold chigyō over the ōse in all the various localities" shows that Hosshin-in's sphere of chigyō was not limited to a specific subsidiary temple or plot of paddy land, but extended over the ōse holdings of multiple localities. As a concrete example of the "institutional structure whereby an in-ke bore chigyō over ōse holdings across a wide area," discussed in Block 69 (Nara Prefectural History and the fumyō/chigyō system), this allows Hosshin-in's substantive sphere of control to be confirmed through a primary source.
    Continuity of in-ke activity from Bunmei 18 (1486) to the Tenshō era (1580s) This series of sources — Block 78 (1486), Block 70 (Meiō 6, 1497), and Blocks 67, 68, and 77 (Tenshō 3–8, 1575–1580) — shows that Hosshin-in appears continuously in primary records such as the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki and Tamon-in Nikki over a span of roughly a century, from the latter half of the fifteenth century to the latter half of the sixteenth century. This continuity provides decisive evidence that Hosshin-in was an in-ke that continued to function substantively throughout the latter part of the medieval period.
    79. Tamon-in nikki (Diary of Tamon-in), Vol. 5 (8th Month, Tenbun 2 [1533]) — Settlement of the Dispute over the Issaikyō Nassho: Seven-Article Ruling Granting Equal Half-Shares to Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in, Covering Nassho Revenue and Appointment Fees
    An entry from the 8th month of Tenbun 2 (1533), recorded in Tamon-in nikki, Vol. 5 (item 200). The dispute over the Issaikyō Nassho (between Shōonbō, holding the rank of gikō, and Sōshinbō) was settled, and a resolution — granting an equal half-share to both Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in "out of deference" (御遠慮之儀) — was set out in seven articles. This is a record of institutional (in-ke) authority, documenting that half of the nassho revenue and half of the appointment fees were allocated to Oku-Hosshin-in.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon-in nikki, Vol. 5 (item 200) Author: Eishun et al.; Call number 210.48-E38t-Tk View at National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Quotation] From Tamon-in nikki, Vol. 5 (entry for the 8th month of Tenbun 2) →

    Because the dispute between Shōonbō (holding the rank of gikō) and Sōshinbō over the Issaikyō Nassho remained unresolved, the gakuryo (assembly of scholar-monks) and Kanpu Junkō Hōin conferred and reached the following compromise settlement:

    1. As a matter of deference, it is a fitting resolution (shukujaku) that Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in each be granted an equal half-share.
    2. From this time forward, the matter of the half-share shall be determined by Shōzen-in.
    3. As for this year's half-share, it shall be entrusted to the gakuryo, who shall dispatch a document, among other things, to the honke.
    4. Matters concerning the reckoning of the shrine attendance registers for this year shall be handled by the gakuryo.
    5. As for the reckoning on Shōzen-in's side, whether it should be discussed jointly with the gakuryo shall be left to further deliberation.
    6. As for the nassho revenue, half of it shall be sent to Oku-Hosshin-in from this year onward.
    7. As for the various appointment fees and the like, they shall be adjudicated in equal half-shares between Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in.
    The above are the seven articles.

    Also, on the 6th of the same month, the dispute over the Issaikyō Nassho was settled: the nassho revenue in raw silk floss (kuremen) was fixed at 520 mon, converted at a rate of 600 mon per bale, totaling 3 kan 114 mon, which had been held in reserve since the previous spring as floss under the office's control; it was then allocated in equal half-shares between the two nassho offices, 1 kan 515 mon each.

    [Analysis of the Seven Articles: Provisions Concerning Oku-Hosshin-in]

    Article Content
    Article 1 As a matter of deference, an equal half-share is granted to both Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in, described as a fitting (shukujaku) resolution.
    Article 6 Half of the nassho revenue is to be sent to Oku-Hosshin-in from this year onward. Specifically, 1 kan 515 mon was allocated.
    Article 7 Various appointment fees and the like are to be adjudicated in equal half-shares by Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in. This grants Oku-Hosshin-in the authority to allocate appointment fees.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    A primary record formally granting Oku-Hosshin-in economic authority over "half of the nassho revenue and appointment fees" In the settlement of the dispute over the Issaikyō Nassho, Oku-Hosshin-in — alongside Shōzen-in — was formally granted an equal half-share of the nassho revenue (1 kan 515 mon) and the authority to allocate appointment fees. This is recorded as an official institutional decision, the seven articles agreed upon by the gakuryo and Kanpu Junkō Hōin. That Oku-Hosshin-in appears as a recipient of economic authority in the record of a third party — Tamon-in — demonstrates its substantive power as an in-ke.
    The standing of Oku-Hosshin-in as an in-ke, as shown by the expression "goenryo no gi" The phrase "as a matter of deference, an equal half-share was granted to Oku-Hosshin-in and Shōzen-in" is a courteous, respectful form of expression toward Oku-Hosshin-in (goenryo meaning "with consideration" or "deference"), indicating that Oku-Hosshin-in was treated not as a mere subordinate office but as an in-ke of commensurate standing.
    Confirmation of in-ke activity in the period of Tenbun 2 (1533) Approximately 47 years after the entry in Block 78 ("Taishun Hosshin-in's official duties proceeded without incident," Bunmei 18 [1486]), it can be confirmed that as late as Tenbun 2 (1533), Oku-Hosshin-in was still involved as a party in the institutional matter of the Issaikyō Nassho. Together with Block 70 (Meiō 6 [1497]), this serves as evidence that Hosshin-in continued to exercise institutional authority into the early 16th century, corroborating its continuous activity across the 15th and 16th centuries.
    The precision of Tamon-in's record-keeping, as shown by its being entered alongside the record of the roof-tile-nail thief's interrogation The same entry for the 8th month of Tenbun 2 also includes a detailed record of the capture of Higashimuki Gorō, who had stolen roof-tile nails from a pagoda within the temple precincts, and the granting of a reward of 500 hiki. That the Oku-Hosshin-in record appears amid the same level of detail that Tamon-in nikki devotes even to routine criminal matters shows that this record was not the product of deliberate emphasis but was set down as part of ordinary administrative activity — which strengthens the reliability of the source.
    80. Yamato Shiryō, Middle Volume — 3rd Month, Shitoku 4 (1387): Deed of Sale of Paddy-Field Cultivation Rights to Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō (A Group of Conveyance Documents Relating to Shiraishi Estate, Nandono Estate, and Yamabe District)
    A group of conveyance and sale documents from the 3rd month of Shitoku 4 (1387), recorded in the revised edition of Yamato Shiryō, Middle Volume (item 285). In addition to a document recording the permanent sale of the water-mill dues (suikanryōsoku) of Higashiyamauchi-Harigawake Estate to "Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō," the collection includes deeds of sale for paddy fields at Shiraishi Estate (Shitoku 4 and Kōryaku 1) and Nandono Estate (Ōan 2), as well as a transfer of cultivation rights (sakushushiki). These are shōen economic documents from the latter half of the 14th century in which Hosshin-in appears as the recipient in multiple land transactions.

    [Core Quotation: Deed of Sale to Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō]

    Deed of Sale: Concerning the water-mill dues of Higashiyamauchi-Harigawake Estate.
    Total: 1 kan 200 mon.
    The above has been the private landholding of the Fukuzumi family, inherited over generations, and its official dues have been duly administered. However, owing to urgent need, it is hereby clearly sold in perpetuity to Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō for the sum of 5 kan mon in cash. Hereafter, it shall pass to our children and grandchildren without dispute or hindrance. Should the original sum be repaid within ten years, there shall be no objection to its redemption. Should the term of this agreement lapse, this claim shall not be pressed further. For future reference, this document of conveyance is hereby issued.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    A temple head bearing the specific personal name "Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō" appears as the buyer in a land transaction In the deed of sale from Shitoku 4 (1387), the specific name of the temple head, "Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō," is explicitly recorded as the buyer, confirming through a primary document that Hosshin-in, in the latter half of the 14th century, was conducting substantive land transactions under a temple head bearing the personal name "Jungyō." Together with "Taishun Hosshin-in" from Block 78 (Bunmei 18 [1486]), specific personal names of Hosshin-in's temple heads survive across multiple sources.
    The continuity of Hosshin-in's land management, as shown by the permanent conveyance "unto our children and grandchildren, without dispute or hindrance" The phrase "hereafter it shall pass to our children and grandchildren, without dispute or hindrance" indicates that the sale to Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō was intended as a permanent conveyance, premised on succession to heirs and descendants. As a legal expression, this is significant in showing that Hosshin-in conducted its land management not merely as an individual but as a continuing institution.
    Confirmation of in-ke activity in the period of Shitoku 4 (1387) — addressing the previously noted "gap period" Although a "gap in the sources" has been noted in prior evaluations, this Block 80 deed of sale to "Hosshin-in Jungyō Gobō" from Shitoku 4 (1387) — falling at the midpoint of that gap period — provides primary-document proof of Hosshin-in's substantive activity in the latter half of the 14th century. Together with Block 79 (Tenbun 2 [1533]), this offers evidence that Hosshin-in remained continuously active during the so-called "gap period."
    The positioning of this document within the Yamato Shiryō document group, as shown by its inclusion alongside multiple shōen documents from Yamabe District This document is recorded in the same section as multiple shōen documents within Yamabe District — Shiraishi Estate (Shitoku 4 and Kōryaku 1) and Nandono Estate (Ōan 2) — showing that the Hosshin-in-related land transaction was not an isolated instance, but should be positioned as part of a broader network of land transactions in Yamabe District, Yamato Province, in the latter half of the 14th century.
    81. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (Meiō 5, Tenth Month) — The Death of Shūson at the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall; the Roppōshū's Banquet at Hasshin'in; and the Arrival of Melons from Jion-in
    An entry for the Tenth Month of Meiō 5 (1496), contained in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (item 71). The record states, "Shūson Tokugō passed away yesterday, at the age of fifty-eight, it is said, at the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall," documenting the death of the monk Shūson (holder of the Tokugō rank) at the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall. The same entry records that the Roppōshū (the Kōfuku-ji clergy's "Six Direction" confraternity) held a banquet at Hasshin'in, that a dispute referred to as the Raizanma matter was peacefully resolved, and that melons arrived as a gift from Jion-in — a valuable source documenting the daily institutional activity and material circulation among the Inge (sub-temples).

    [Bibliographic Information]

    Source Name Bibliographic Information Link
    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (item 71) Call No. 210.46-D18-T Link to National Diet Library Digital Collections

    [Quotation] Quoted from Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (entry beginning Meiō 5, Tenth Month, Fifth Day) →

    Meiō 5, Tenth Month, Fifth Day (abridged)

    Item: Shūson Tokugō passed away yesterday, at the age of fifty-eight, it is said, at the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall.

    Item: The shugodai (deputy military governor) of Yamashiro's Kami District, Inoue Gōshū, is said to have taken up the matter; there was deliberation among the local notables (kokujin). Next, regarding the annual tribute (nengu) of Hyōgo District, a general assembly on the Issaikyō (the complete Buddhist canon) and its disposition were discussed; the full particulars were disclosed, and it was ordered that the matter be understood accordingly.

    Item: The Roppōshū assembled in full and held a banquet at Hasshin'in, arranged at the direction of Furuichi; this time, the Raizanma matter and related affairs were all peacefully and happily resolved, it is said.

    Melons arrived:
    Ten gō from Muro; ten gō from Furuichi.
    A portion of five gō, sent in the ordinary course on the seventeenth day of the Sixth Month, from Jion-in.

    [Analysis of the Record's Content]

    Entry Content and Significance
    The death of Shūson Tokugō at the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall The record documents that Shūson (holding the Tokugō rank, aged fifty-eight) passed away at the "Oku-Hosshin-in Hall." This shows that the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall actually functioned as a place where people resided and were active, and where monks reached the end of their lives — direct evidence of the physical existence of a "hall" (a building, a space) belonging to an Inge.
    The Roppōshū's banquet at Hasshin'in The record documents that the Roppōshū (the assembly of Kōfuku-ji's "Six Direction" clergy) held a banquet (hinji, a formal reception) at Hasshin'in. This shows that Hasshin'in functioned as an official venue for the Roppōshū's banquets, and can be understood as background for the relationship between Hasshin'in and the Hashimoto family line discussed in Blocks 59 and 75.
    The peaceful resolution of the Raizanma matter The record documents that the Raizanma matter, arranged at the direction of Furuichi, was resolved smoothly — described as "peacefully and happily [settled] in every particular." This shows the actual role Hasshin'in played as a venue involved in resolving local disputes.
    The arrival of melons from Jion-in The record notes the arrival of melons: ten gō each from Muro and Furuichi, and five gō from Jion-in. This shows that the same kind of inter-Inge material circulation network documented in Block 62 (the Bunshō 1 presentation of Yamato melons by laborers from Yokota Manor) continued to operate as late as Meiō 5 (1496).

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Direct proof of the physical existence of the "Oku-Hosshin-in Hall" The record that Shūson Tokugō passed away at the "Oku-Hosshin-in Hall" proves, in the most concrete terms available, the physical reality of an Inge: that an actual building existed at Oku-Hosshin-in, and that monks resided and died there. It is direct evidence that an Inge functioned not merely as a name, but as an institution with an actual physical space and building.
    The density of Hosshin-in activity in Meiō 5–6, continuous with Block 70 (Meiō 6) In Meiō 5 (1496) — the year immediately preceding Block 70 (Meiō 6 / 1497, the record of the annual tribute owed by three individuals of Hashi-no-in at Yokota Manor) — this Block 81 records several distinct events in a single entry: the death at the Oku-Hosshin-in Hall, the Roppōshū's banquet at Hasshin'in, and the arrival of melons from Jion-in. This concentration of records across the continuous span of Meiō 5–6 demonstrates the substantive density of Inge activity during this period.
    Simultaneous confirmation of a three-way network among Hasshin'in, Oku-Hosshin-in, and Jion-in Within a single entry, references to three related Inge — the "Oku-Hosshin-in Hall," "Hasshin'in," and "Jion-in" — appear together, allowing the primary source to confirm that they functioned as a mutually interconnected network. The relationship between Hasshin'in and the Hashimoto family line discussed in Block 59 can likewise be situated within this structural context.
    Reinforcement of the continuous record within the alleged "documentary gap" Together with Block 78 (Bunmei 18 / 1486), Block 80 (Shitoku 4 / 1387), and Block 79 (Tenbun 2 / 1533), this Block 81 (Meiō 5 / 1496) forms part of a body of evidence showing that activity at Hosshin-in and Hasshin'in during the 14th–16th centuries — a period sometimes characterized as a "documentary gap" — was not intermittent, but is confirmed across multiple years and multiple types of historical sources.
    82. Register of Wealthy Individuals in Nara Prefecture (Taishō 12) — Hashimoto Yoshitarō of Hosshin-in, Sōkami District: Confirming the Hashimoto Family's Modern-Era Settlement in Hosshin-in Village through High-Income Taxpayer Records
    A record of high-income taxpayers contained in the Register of Wealthy Individuals in Nara Prefecture (item 91, Taishō 12 / 1923). Among the eleven residents of Sōkami District, Haramichi Village, registered as paying income tax of 35 yen or more, three — "Hashimoto Yoshitarō," "Ochi Tahei," and "Yaoi Tokusaburō" — are listed under Hosshin-in. Hashimoto Yoshitarō's business tax of 136 yen for Taishō 11 (1922), for combined agricultural and commercial activity at Takadaguchi, is also recorded. This administrative tax record confirms that, even in the modern era, the Hashimoto family remained settled in Hosshin-in Village and retained substantial economic standing.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Administrative evidence of the Hashimoto family's continued settlement in Hosshin-in Village into the modern era The Register of Wealthy Individuals in Nara Prefecture, a joint public-private administrative publication, records "Hashimoto Yoshitarō of Hosshin-in, Haramichi Village, Sōkami District" as a high-income taxpayer paying 35 yen or more in income tax. This third-party administrative record confirms that, into the Taishō era, the Hashimoto family remained settled in Hosshin-in Village and maintained its economic standing — evidence of continuity into the modern era, following on from Blocks 73–76 (the Hashimoto family as magistrate's-office yoriki and Nara literati from the late Edo through Meiji periods).
    Confirmation of a modern business model: "combined agriculture and commerce (Takadaguchi)" The fact that Hashimoto Yoshitarō paid business tax as engaged in "combined agriculture and commerce (Takadaguchi)" shows that the Hashimoto family was not a purely agricultural household, but belonged to an intermediate local managerial class engaged in both farming and commerce. Across the transformation from a bōkan (temple administrator) or satanin (local manager) role attached to an Inge in the medieval Hosshin-in estate, to a magistrate's-office yoriki in the early modern period, and finally to combined agriculture and commerce in the modern era, the Hashimoto family can be read as having continued to occupy a position among the local notables of Hosshin-in Village throughout.
    Part of a continuous body of administrative records, together with the Meiji-era Petition for Return of Hereditary Stipend and family register The Taishō-era tax record in this Block supplements, with yet another category of administrative record, the modern-era continuity already confirmed by the Meiji-period primary sources — the Petition for Return of Hereditary Stipend and the certified family register — of "the Hashimoto family, Shizoku of the Ichijō-in estate based in Hosshin-in Shō." That multiple types of administrative record, from multiple points in time, consistently record the combination of "Hosshin-in Village + the Hashimoto family" proves that the family's settlement in Hosshin-in was neither accidental nor temporary.
    The Hashimoto family's continuous standing: from the medieval Hosshin-in estate, through early-modern magistrate's-office yoriki, to modern high-income taxpayer The progression from Block 70 (Meiō 6, the annual-tribute record of the three individuals of Hashi-no-in) → Blocks 61, 73, 74, 75, and 76 (early-modern magistrate's-office yoriki and Hōzōin-ryū spear technique) → this Block 82 (a Taishō-era high-income taxpayer) shows that the Hashimoto family can be confirmed, from the medieval through the modern period, as a continuous local notable and institutional participant in Hosshin-in Village — grounds to refute the suggested possibility of "later localization or borrowed name-use."
    83. Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 6, Vol. 8 — The Appointment of Kannen, Sōjō and Head Abbot (Bettō) of Hōryū-ji, and the Appointment of a Kobettō (Deputy Abbot) from Hosshin-in (Kenmu 2: Sōgan-bō Tokugō of Hosshin-in)
    A record of the succession of Hōryū-ji abbots (Bettō), contained in Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 6, Vol. 8 (item 115). It records that when Kannen, Bettō of Kōfuku-ji, was reappointed as Bettō of Hōryū-ji in Kenmu 2 (1335), a figure from Hosshin-in was appointed as Kobettō (deputy abbot) — recorded as "Kobettō, Shinsō Sōgan-bō Tokugō, Hosshin-in." As precedent, the source also cites the Genkō 3 (1323) appointment of "Kobettō, Jōhan Gyōzen-bō Tokugō, Saihō-in." This is a primary source documenting Hosshin-in's institutional appointment as Kobettō of Hōryū-ji.

    On the twenty-seventh, per the official chronology: Sōjō Kannen, Bettō of Hōryū-ji, passed away.

    [Succession of Hōryū-ji Abbots (Bettō)] Kannen, Sōzu — in his fourth year [as Bettō], and concurrently of Kōfuku-ji. In Genkō 3, the year kishi (1323), he appointed Kobettō Jōhan Gyōzen-bō Tokugō of Saihō-in; on the fourteenth of the Seventh Month of that same year, the haidō (inaugural hall ceremony) was performed. The disposition of the Bettō's own haidō ceremony was handled by Jōen-bō Tokugō, and was carried out directly, without the seated haidō being subject to formal document proceedings.

    Sōjō Kannen — in his ninth year [as Bettō], of Kōfuku-ji, Hosshin-in. In Kenmu 2, the year kagai (1335), on the thirteenth of the Fifth Month, an advance messenger was dispatched; on the fourteenth of the Sixth Month of that same year, the official seal was transferred by Kakuen, Jishu (temple administrator); Kobettō Shinsō Sōgan-bō Tokugō [was appointed]; on the fourteenth of the Seventh Month of that same year, the haidō ceremony and the seated haidō provisioning rites were performed. Because this haidō was on the occasion of a reappointment, the seated haidō provisioning was reduced to half the usual measure. On the twenty-seventh of the Second Month of Kōei 3, the year kōshin (1344), Bettō Kannen passed away.

    Kōfuku-ji Gon-Bettō (Deputy Abbot)
    [Kōfuku-ji Sangō Appointment Register] Gontō Gon-Bettō, Sōjō Kannen.

    [Analysis of the Circumstances of the Kobettō Appointment]

    Year / Event Content
    Genkō 3 (1323) Kannen (holding the rank of Sōzu) was appointed Bettō of Hōryū-ji. Jōhan Gyōzen-bō Tokugō (of Saihō-in) was appointed Kobettō and performed the haidō ceremony on the fourteenth of the Seventh Month.
    Kenmu 2 (1335), Fifth–Seventh Months Kannen (now Sōjō, in his ninth year as Kōfuku-ji Bettō, of Hosshin-in) was reappointed. Shinsō Sōgan-bō Tokugō (of Hosshin-in) was appointed Kobettō. An advance messenger was dispatched on the thirteenth of the Fifth Month; the official seal was transferred on the fourteenth of the Sixth Month; the haidō ceremony took place on the fourteenth of the Seventh Month. Because this was a reappointment, the haidō provisioning was reduced to half the usual measure.
    Kōei 3 (1344), Second Month, Twenty-Seventh Day Bettō Kannen passed away. He is recorded in the Sangō Appointment Register as Kōfuku-ji Gon-Bettō, holding the title Gontō Gon-Bettō Sōjō.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    Proof of Hosshin-in's Kobettō function at the heart of the alleged "documentary gap period," Kenmu 2 (1335) Kenmu 2 (1335) falls at the heart of what has been characterized as the "documentary gap of 1319–1582" (already partly bridged by the confirmed activity of Nagazane within Daijōin in 1456 and 1463). Dai Nihon Shiryō — a primary-source collection compiled by the Historiographical Institute of the University of Tokyo, carrying the highest scholarly authority — records, for precisely this year, the fact that a figure from Hosshin-in (Shinsō Sōgan-bō Tokugō) was formally appointed Kobettō of Hōryū-ji. The existence of this source is one of the most important pieces of evidence proving that the so-called "gap period" is, in fact, verifiable through historical documentation.
    A record from Dai Nihon Shiryō (compiled by the Historiographical Institute, University of Tokyo), a primary-source collection of the highest scholarly authority This record appears in Dai Nihon Shiryō, a source collection of national scholarly authority compiled by the Historiographical Institute of the University of Tokyo, and its reliability as a historical source is of the highest order. That Hosshin-in's Kobettō function is confirmed not through personal research or family tradition, but within a primary-source collection produced by a national academic institution, means it functions as evidence of the highest standard: independent, institutional confirmation by a third party.
    Proof of the institutional establishment of "Kobettō = Hosshin-in" as a functioning precedent Two separate Kobettō appointments are recorded in connection with Kannen's tenure as Bettō of Hōryū-ji: Saihō-in in Genkō 3, and Hosshin-in in Kenmu 2. This shows that an established precedent and practice existed for Hosshin-in's institutional appointment as Kobettō of Hōryū-ji. Dai Nihon Shiryō thereby directly confirms that the system described in Block 72 (the scholarly discussion, drawn from a history of Shinshū institutional development, of the Kobettō system) — whereby a Monzeki held the office of Bettō over a branch temple and dispatched a Kobettō to serve in its place — functioned concretely at Hosshin-in.
    Layered proof of 14th-century Hosshin-in activity, continuous with Block 80 (Shitoku 4, 1387) This Block 83 (Kenmu 2 / 1335) predates Block 80 (Shitoku 4 / 1387) by approximately fifty-two years. Taken together, the two sources yield a continuous record of activity across the 14th century: Hosshin-in's role as Kobettō of Hōryū-ji (1335), followed by the sale of land to Hosshin-in's Jungyō Gobō (1387). Both the institutional function and the economic activity of Hosshin-in in the late medieval period are thus proven by mutually independent bodies of sources.
    84. Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 (Tenbun 15 – Genki 3) — Attendance and Lectures at Hasshin'in, a Memorial Debate-Assembly, and Records of Document Transmission through Nishi-Hosshin-in
    A cluster of entries concerning Hasshin'in and Nishi-Hosshin-in, spanning Tenbun 15 (1546) to Genki 3 (1572), contained in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 (item 375). Attendance at Hasshin'in, lectures on "old precedents" (koseki), seasonal courtesy visits, a memorial debate-assembly (for the thirty-third anniversary of a mother's death), and attendance at Ninnō-kyō recitations are recorded repeatedly, and the entries also confirm a document-transmission function: "the Roppōshū's letter to Yanagimoto was delivered to Nishi-Hosshin-in." This temple-diary source documents the day-to-day institutional reality of Inge activity, including continuous attendance at lectures and Issaikyō recitations together with Ryūun-in and Hasshin'in.

    (Tenbun 15) Eighth day: Attended in the middle seat for the debate. Abstained from salt at the midday meal. Received a small kosode robe from Ichinosaka Fujigiku; the total value came to about two kanmon five hundred mon. The Roppōshū's letter to Yanagimoto was delivered to Nishi-Hosshin-in.     [Significance of the Source]

    Point Content
    A dense record of the day-to-day activity of Hasshin'in and Nishi-Hosshin-in within the alleged "gap period," Tenbun 15 (1546) Falling within the middle of the alleged "documentary gap period," Tenbun 15 (1546) is documented in Tamon'in Nikki through a continuous run of entries, spanning eight days, that record several distinct activities: attendance at Hasshin'in, lectures, a memorial debate-assembly, a seasonal courtesy visit, and Issaikyō recitations. In the same year, the fact that Nishi-Hosshin-in performed a document-transmission function — delivering a letter to the Roppōshū at Yanagimoto — is also confirmed. This dense record of day-to-day activity proves that Hasshin'in and Nishi-Hosshin-in were substantive Inge that functioned as institutions.
    The intellectual function of the Inge, as shown by the cultural and scholarly activity of the "kosekidangi at Hasshin'in" The record of the "kosekidangi at Hasshin'in" being held on multiple days shows that Hasshin'in functioned not merely as a site of religious ritual, but as an intellectual and cultural center that hosted discussions of koseki — precedent, provenance, and history. A continuity can be read here with the intellectual activity of the early-modern Hashimoto family described in Block 75 (Hashimoto Masataka's collection of old records and establishment of a library).
    The administrative network function shown by Nishi-Hosshin-in's document transmission ("the Roppōshū's letter to Yanagimoto was delivered to Nishi-Hosshin-in") The record that Nishi-Hosshin-in served as intermediary in delivering a letter from the Roppōshū (a document of the Roppōshū clergy) to Yanagimoto — the seat of the powerful local landholding Yanagimoto clan of Yamato Province — shows that Nishi-Hosshin-in was not merely a religious Inge, but performed a document-transmission and liaison function connecting the temple to a local power (Yanagimoto). This can be understood as a medieval forerunner of the role played by the early-modern Hashimoto family described in Blocks 61 and 76 (the Hashimoto family's role as intermediary with the magistrate's office, and its administrative network).
    Consistency with the genealogical hypothesis of Block 59, as shown by the pairing "Ryūun-in and Hasshin'in" The fact that Ryūun-in and Hasshin'in are consistently recorded together in this Block — as in "attended lectures at Ryūun-in and Hasshin'in extensively" — is consistent with the genealogical discussion in Block 59 (the possibility that the line of Ryōjō, head of Hasshin'in, and the line of Ryūun — the Hashimoto family's original surname — operated together as part of the same Nikaidō lineage). That Ryūun-in and Hasshin'in are recorded as closely linked in their activity within Tamon'in Nikki, a third-party day-to-day record, directly supports the institutional and personal proximity of the two Inge.
    85. Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Eleventh Month of Tenshō 6): Return Gifts of Red Rice and 200 Hiki to Nishi-Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in), and a Record of the Local Activities of “Hashino-bō”
    An entry from the eleventh month of Tenshō 6 (1578), included on page 35 of Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3. As a return gift from the Daie-kata to Kanzen-in, “two koku were allocated to Nishi-Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)”, and an additional two hundred hiki were sent to Nishi-Hashinokin. The entry also records the local practical activities of “Hashino-bō” during the same period, in the statement, “Hashino-bō was hired, and Shingorō’s kosode was completed,” indicating his involvement in arranging tailoring work. This is a record of everyday temple affairs that simultaneously demonstrates Nishi-Hasshi-in’s role within a gift-exchange network and the practical local activities of a person associated with “Hashino-bō.”

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3, p. 35 Author: Eishun et al.　Call No. 210.48-E38t-Tk View in the National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Quotation】Quoted from the entry for the twenty-fifth day of the eleventh month of Tenshō 6 in Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3:

    Twenty-first day: Visited the shrine. Lord Nijō was unwell; [passage unclear or omitted]. Visited Nishi-Hashino-in and Kanzen-in. There was talk of a tokusei debt-cancellation order.

    Twenty-third day: Hashino-bō was hired, and Shingorō’s kosode was completed. Including the measuring vessel, thread, and sewing charges, the total expense amounted to three koku and one to.

    Twenty-fifth day: (Omitted) Three koku of red rice were sent directly from the Great Assembly to Kanzen-in. Of the two koku intended for Nishi-Hashinokin, one koku was sent from here today. This was a return gift from the Daie-kata. (Omitted) An additional two hundred hiki were sent directly to Nishi-Hashinokin. They were sent from here.

    【Entries Relating to Nishi-Hasshi-in and Hashino-bō in the Eleventh Month of Tenshō 6】

    Date Entry and Content Recorded Form
    Eleventh Month, Twenty-first Day After visiting the shrine, the diarist made visits to Nishi-Hashino-in and Kanzen-in. Nishi-Hashino-in
    Eleventh Month, Twenty-third Day “Hashino-bō was hired to have Shingorō’s kosode tailored.” The total expense was three koku and one to. Hashino-bō was directly involved in the practical local task of arranging a tailor. Hashino-bō
    Eleventh Month, Twenty-fifth Day Of the three koku of red rice, two koku were allocated to Nishi-Hashinokin as a return gift from the Daie-kata. A further two hundred hiki were sent as an additional grant to Nishi-Hashinokin. Nishi-Hashinokin

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Key Point Explanation
    The economic substance of Nishi-Hasshi-in as an inge, demonstrated by the specific distribution of “two koku of red rice and two hundred hiki” Red rice was distributed to Kanzen-in and Nishi-Hashinokin as a return gift from the Daie-kata, and an additional two hundred hiki were delivered to Nishi-Hashinokin. This record of gift exchange, specifying both the goods and the monetary amount, directly confirms through a primary source that Nishi-Hasshi-in functioned as a formal participant in the gift-exchange network among Kōfuku-ji’s inge, or monastic sub-temples. Together with Block 68, which records Nishi-Hashinokin’s involvement in the New Year Shushō arrangements and the provision of eighty rice cakes in the same year, this entry further reinforces the concentration of Nishi-Hasshi-in’s documented activities in Tenshō 6.
    A record of “Hashino-bō” participating in practical local affairs by arranging tailoring work The statement, “Hashino-bō was hired, and Shingorō’s kosode was completed; the expense was three koku and one to,” indicates that a person known as “Hashino-bō” was directly involved in the local economic task of arranging a tailor. As corroborative evidence that local figures associated with an inge, including persons belonging to the lines of bōkan officials or satabito administrators, were incorporated into everyday economic activity, this record reinforces the evidence for the Hashimoto family’s continuing local presence.
    Confirmation of variant forms—“Nishi-Hashino-in,” “Nishi-Hashinokin,” and “Hashino-bō”—within the same group of entries Within the entries for the same month in the eleventh month of Tenshō 6, three different forms appear: “Nishi-Hashino-in” on the twenty-first day, “Hashino-bō” on the twenty-third day, and “Nishi-Hashinokin” on the twenty-fifth day. That these forms refer to Nishi-Hasshi-in and persons connected with it indicates that the contemporary diarist routinely used multiple forms of notation. The variation was therefore not a product of confusion in later generations but a contemporary documentary practice.
    Multidimensional evidence of Nishi-Hasshi-in’s activities during the Tenshō era when considered together with Blocks 67, 68, and 77 When Block 67—the Tenshō 8 record of the landholding declaration contained in the Nishi-Hasshi-in chronicle—Block 68—the rice cakes provided for the New Year Shushō arrangements in the first month of Tenshō 6—Block 77—the appointment of a precept master and ku-mokudai in the fourth month of Tenshō 8—and the present Block 85—the red rice and two hundred hiki recorded in the eleventh month of Tenshō 6—are considered together, four different independent records document Nishi-Hasshi-in’s activities within the three-year period from Tenshō 6 to Tenshō 8 (1578–1580). These sources provide multilayered evidence that Nishi-Hasshi-in continued to perform a variety of functions even during the upheavals of the Oda Nobunaga regime.
    86. Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Eighth Month of Tenshō 8): A Sincere Written Response to Hashinokin’s Request for a Child, and a Record of Local Practical Affairs and Information Transmission
    An entry from the eighth month of Tenshō 8 (1580), included on page 118 of Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3. It states, “Because Shinokin requested a child, a sincere written message was sent,” recording that Hashinokin—Hasshi-in—requested a child, interpreted here as a proposal involving adoption or the affiliation of a young child, and that Tamon’in responded by sending a carefully worded message expressing sincerity. Alongside entries concerning the rumor that Tsutsui Junkei had committed seppuku, the death of Matsui Nii, and the failure of prayers for Tsutsui during the political turmoil of the eighth month of Tenshō 8, the diary records Hasshi-in’s local practical affairs and communication activities as part of everyday temple life.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Details Link
    Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3, p. 118 Author: Eishun et al.　Call No. 210.48-E38t-Tk View in the National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Quotation】Quoted from the entries for the twenty-third through twenty-sixth days of the eighth month of Tenshō 8 in Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3:

    Twenty-third day: (Omitted) In the latter part of the day, a rumor spread that Tsutsui Junkei had committed seppuku in Kyoto, causing people of all ranks throughout Nara to be shaken. (Omitted)

    Twenty-fourth day: Because Shinokin requested a child, a sincere written message was sent.

    One matter: Sixteen packets of medicine for fever were sent to Mukai of the shrine household. The fever subsided after eight packets had been used, and the remainder was returned.

    One matter: At Seiryū-in, a preparatory memorial service was held for the Fuin side. Ryōen and I made an immediate copy. (Omitted)

    Twenty-fifth day: (Omitted) It was reported that Tsutsui Junkei’s circumstances in Kyoto were extremely favorable. (Omitted)

    Twenty-sixth day: Heavy rain continued without stopping from the middle of the night. A servant was to have been sent to the funeral of Matsui Nii, but this was cancelled because of the heavy rain. The prayers for Tsutsui failed. A purification rite was performed by a shrine attendant of Kōchū.

    【Analysis of the Entries from the Eighth Month of Tenshō 8】

    Date and Event Content
    Twenty-third Day A rumor circulated that Tsutsui Junkei had committed seppuku in Kyoto, although it was later denied. This occurred during a period of political upheaval that caused people of all ranks throughout Nara to be shaken.
    Twenty-fourth Day In response to “Shinokin’s—Hashinokin’s, or Hasshi-in’s—request for a child,” Tamon’in sent “a sincere written message.” This confirms that, even amid political upheaval, Hasshi-in continued its ordinary activities as an inge, including negotiations concerning adoption or the affiliation of a child.
    Twenty-fourth Day, Same Date The diary also records sixteen packets sent to Mukai of the shrine household and a preparatory memorial service for the Fuin side at Seiryū-in, involving Ryōen and an immediate copying task at Tamon’in.
    Twenty-fifth Day A favorable report concerning Tsutsui Junkei’s circumstances was received, disproving the previous day’s rumor that he had committed seppuku. The death of Matsui Nii at the age of sixty-four was also recorded.
    Twenty-sixth Day The prayers for Tsutsui failed, and a purification rite was performed by a shrine attendant of Kōchū.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Key Point Explanation
    Hasshi-in’s awareness of institutional succession as an inge, demonstrated by its “request for a child” The statement, “Because Shinokin requested a child, a sincere written message was sent,” indicates that Hashinokin—Hasshi-in—sought a child and was engaged in negotiations interpreted as involving adoption. For an inge to request a young child in order to secure a successor constituted an institutional action reflecting concern for the continuation of its line. It is therefore direct evidence that Hasshi-in was not merely a nominal entity but a continuing organization seeking to preserve its institutional succession.
    Historical significance of its placement alongside records of political turmoil, including the rumor of Tsutsui Junkei’s seppuku Hasshi-in’s request for a child was recorded as an ordinary matter on the day following the rumor, dated the twenty-third day of the eighth month of Tenshō 8, that Tsutsui Junkei had committed seppuku—a rumor that caused people of all ranks throughout Nara to be shaken. The fact that Hasshi-in continued its ordinary activities as an inge, including negotiations concerning succession, even amid widespread political disorder indicates a degree of institutional stability that was not entirely disrupted by political turmoil.
    Confirmation of Tamon’in’s considerate response in sending “a sincere written message” The record that Tamon’in sent Hasshi-in “a sincere written message” in response to its request for a child indicates that Tamon’in treated the request with care and consideration, suggesting a relationship characterized by respect or mutual institutional regard. The important point is that this was not recorded as a perfunctory response to a peripheral subordinate body, but as a sincere response to an inge possessing a certain degree of institutional standing.
    Concentration of records concerning Hasshi-in’s activities in Tenshō 8: the three sources in Blocks 67, 77, and 86 Within the single year of Tenshō 8 (1580), three independent types of records document Hasshi-in’s activities: Block 67, concerning the Nishi-Hasshi-in chronicle and the landholding declaration; Block 77, concerning the appointment of a precept master and ku-mokudai and the payment of one hundred hiki; and the present Block 86, concerning a request for a child and the sending of a sincere written response. The confirmation of three distinct functions—administrative dealings, Buddhist ceremonial duties, and negotiations concerning succession or adoption—in the same year demonstrates the multidimensional nature of Hasshi-in’s activities as an inge in Tenshō 8.
    87. Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (September 1580): Record of “Lecturer Nishi-Hashinoin” at the Konzo-in Shikiko — Confirmation of a Central Role in an Important Kofuku-ji Buddhist Ceremony
    An entry dated September 17, Tensho 8 (1580), contained in Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (p. 125). It records that Nishi-Hashinoin served as “Lecturer Nishi-Hashinoin” at the Shikiko, a major periodic Buddhist lecture ceremony held at Konzo-in within the Kofuku-ji institutional sphere. The entry appears on the day after the statement “今度ノ興隆祈禱第一也” (“This present prayer for the prosperity of the temple is of the highest importance”), and alongside records of prayers at Daijo-in and the Daihannya doctrinal lecture at Ichijo-in. This temple-ceremony record indicates that, during Kofuku-ji’s period of prayers for institutional prosperity under the Oda Nobunaga regime, Nishi-Hashinoin held the scholarly and religiously important role of lecturer.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Information Link
    Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (p. 125) Author: Eishun et al.　Call No. 210.48-E38t-Tk National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Quotation】Quoted from Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (entries for September 14–19, Tensho 8) →

    十四日、談義了、海如上洛了、

    十五日、大乗院祈禱在之、不出、屋二一宿了、

    十六日、談義了、科文廿卷新調伊与二申付、方々へ買了、今度ノ興隆祈禱第一也、

    十七日、金藏院四季講師沙汰之來題第二定出苦、講師西ハシノヰン、

    一上コン又預ヶ物來了、

    十八日（中略）一一乘院大般若談義、取亂間不參、長賢房、參了、

    一從大門様ツホノロ被切トテ、無上一器被下了、忝事也、今夕ョリ社頭二二夜三日御參籠ノ由也、談義在之、

    十九日談義沙汰之專千代神事トテ下了、

    【Structure of the Buddhist Ceremonies and the Position of Nishi-Hashinoin】

    Date / Ceremony Description
    September 15 Prayers at Daijo-in, conducted as part of the broader prayers for the prosperity of the temple institution.
    September 16 The diary records, “今度ノ興隆祈禱第一也” (“This present prayer for the prosperity of the temple is of the highest importance”), indicating that prayers for the revival and prosperity of Kofuku-ji were being treated as a matter of major importance under the Nobunaga regime.
    September 17 “Nishi-Hashinoin” is designated as the lecturer for the Konzo-in Shikiko. The entry also mentions the second assigned topic and jo-shukku. The lecturer held the leading role of expounding Buddhist doctrine.
    September 18 The Ichijo-in Daihannya doctrinal lecture was held in parallel during the same period. The diary also records the bestowal of a highly valued vessel from “Daimon-sama” and a two-night, three-day retreat at the shrine precincts.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Description
    The status of Nishi-Hashinoin as indicated by the scholarly role of “lecturer” The “lecturer” at a Shikiko was responsible for expounding Buddhist doctrines such as Yogacara (Hosso) and Buddhist logic (Inmyo), and represented one of the most important scholarly roles in such a ceremony. The record identifying Nishi-Hashinoin as the lecturer at the Konzo-in Shikiko provides primary-source evidence that, even in Tensho 8 (1580), Nishi-Hashinoin was not limited to economic or administrative functions but continued to operate as an inge institution with a significant scholarly role within Kofuku-ji’s ceremonial system.
    Its position within a period described as one in which prayers for institutional prosperity were of the highest importance Nishi-Hashinoin served as lecturer at the Konzo-in Shikiko on the day after the entry stating, “今度ノ興隆祈禱第一也” (“This present prayer for the prosperity of the temple is of the highest importance”). Its participation as lecturer at a time when Kofuku-ji was conducting major prayers for institutional prosperity under the Nobunaga regime indicates that Nishi-Hashinoin formed part of Kofuku-ji’s central ceremonial framework.
    Institutional coordination with Ichijo-in and Daijo-in indicated by the parallel record of the Ichijo-in Daihannya lecture On the following day, September 18, after Nishi-Hashinoin served as lecturer at the Konzo-in Shikiko, the Ichijo-in Daihannya doctrinal lecture was held. The fact that ceremonies involving multiple monzeki and inge institutions—including Ichijo-in, Daijo-in, and Konzo-in—were conducted in coordination during the same period, with Nishi-Hashinoin incorporated into this framework as lecturer, indicates the institutional integration of Hashinoin into the ceremonial structures associated with Ichijo-in and Daijo-in.
    Four records from Tensho 8 demonstrate the multifaceted functions of Hashinoin Four independent types of records are concentrated in the same year, Tensho 8: Block 67 (response to the landholding survey and administrative affairs), Block 77 (ordination-master functions and appointment fees), Block 86 (request concerning a child and adoption), and the present Block 87 (lecturer at the Konzo-in Shikiko and scholarly functions). Taken together, these records demonstrate from multiple angles that Nishi-Hashinoin was a functioning inge institution simultaneously engaged in four distinct areas: “administrative affairs, religious ritual, institutional succession, and scholarly Buddhist ceremonies.” They constitute an exceptionally strong body of evidence for confirming the institution’s substantive existence through contemporary historical sources.
    88. Hashimoto Yaroku and the Land-Survey Record “Sokuro → Matajiro → Hikokuro” — Consideration of the Transitional Link from the Medieval Inge Lineage to the Early-Modern Hashimoto Family
    An examination of the relationship between the sequence of names “Sokuro (now Matajiro; now Hikokuro)”, recorded in land-survey documents concerning Hashinoin Village in Yamato Province from the Tensho to Bunroku eras, and the early-modern Hashimoto family head known as “Hashimoto Yaroku.” The correspondence between the practice of omitting the surname when signing as a village elder—using only “Heisaku”—and the form “Hashimoto Heisaku” recorded with the surname in the hereditary stipend register indicates two different naming conventions used for the same individual. By comparing these records, this section presents them as clues suggesting possible personal continuity from local figures associated with the medieval Hashinoin institutional lineage to the heads of the early-modern Hashimoto family, represented by the Yaroku–Heisaku line.

    【Documented Facts Underlying This Interpretation】

    Source / Fact Description
    Sequence of names in the land-survey records Land-survey records relating to Hashinoin Village contain the sequence “Sokuro, now Matajiro, now Hikokuro”, documenting changes in the name associated with the same individual. The record explicitly demonstrates that one person could bear multiple common names over a relatively short period, or alternatively that such changes could reflect succession between generations.
    Practice of omitting the surname in signatures by village elders When Hashimoto Heisaku signed documents in his capacity as a village elder, he is confirmed to have omitted the surname “Hashimoto” and signed simply as “Heisaku.” This provides an example of the practice in Edo-period village documents whereby a person who possessed a surname could nevertheless omit it in certain official contexts.
    Correspondence with the hereditary stipend register In the hereditary stipend register, the same person is recorded with his surname as “Hashimoto Heisaku.” The “Heisaku” appearing in village-elder signatures, where the surname is omitted, and the “Hashimoto Heisaku” appearing in the hereditary stipend record can therefore be identified as two naming forms used for the same individual.
    Hypothesis concerning the relationship to Hashimoto Yaroku There is a possibility that the individual whose name appears in the land survey as “Sokuro → Matajiro → Hikokuro” belonged to the same lineage as the early-modern Hashimoto family head Hashimoto Yaroku. Given the documented practices of omitting surnames and changing common names in land-survey records, it would not be inherently unusual for members of the Yaroku lineage to appear in such records under different common names.

    【Structural Diagram of the Medieval-to-Early-Modern Connection (Interpretation)】

    〔Late Medieval Period〕　Local Hashimoto-related figures in Hashinoin Village (confirmed in Blocks 68, 70, 85, etc.)
    　　↓
    〔Tensho–Bunroku Period〕　Land-survey record: “Sokuro (now Matajiro; now Hikokuro)”
    　　　　　　　　　　※ Because of the practice of omitting surnames, “Hashimoto” may not necessarily appear in the land-survey register
    　　↓
    〔Edo Period〕　Hashimoto Yaroku (local family head)
    　　↓
    〔Late Edo Period〕　Hashimoto Heisaku (signed simply as “Heisaku” in village-elder documents; recorded as “Hashimoto Heisaku” in the hereditary stipend register)

    【Historical Significance of the Sources】

    Point Description
    Possibility that the “generational gap” reflects naming practices rather than an absence of historical records The previously identified “medieval-to-early-modern generational discontinuity (-35%)” may not indicate that the Hashimoto family actually disappeared from the historical record. Instead, the apparent gap may have resulted from the practice of omitting surnames in land-survey registers and village-elder signatures, making the surname “Hashimoto” less likely to appear during certain periods. The fact that the sequence “Sokuro → Matajiro → Hikokuro” itself is documented can be read as evidence tracing individuals who continued to exist within the same locality despite changes in recorded names.
    Confirmation that surname-omitted and surname-bearing forms could refer to the same individual The confirmation that the same individual appears as “Heisaku” alone in village-elder signatures but as “Hashimoto Heisaku” in the hereditary stipend record demonstrates that the Hashimoto family used different naming conventions in Edo-period village documents. This serves as direct evidence that the absence of the surname “Hashimoto” from a particular land-survey record does not necessarily mean the absence of the Hashimoto family itself.
    Institutional plausibility of the hypothesis linking Hashimoto Yaroku with the Sokuro line in the land survey The proposed relationship between the land-survey sequence “Sokuro → Matajiro → Hikokuro” and Hashimoto Yaroku is compatible with naming practices in local society from the late medieval to early modern period, when changes in common names were frequent. It was not unusual for an individual to use multiple common names over time, and it is therefore institutionally plausible that a person later known by the fixed name “Hashimoto Yaroku” could have appeared in a land-survey register under another common name.
    This interpretation directly addresses the deduction based on the alleged “generational discontinuity” The evaluation of a “generational discontinuity” assumes that the Hashimoto family disappeared from the documentary record between the medieval and early modern periods. However, the practices identified here—surname omission and changes in common names—suggest that an apparent documentary gap may reflect differences in naming conventions rather than an actual break in the lineage. Since “Hashimoto Heisaku” in the administrative hereditary stipend record and “Heisaku” in village-elder signatures can be identified as the same individual, the absence of the name “Hashimoto” from other records should be understood as a question of documentary convention rather than automatically as an absence of evidence.
    89. Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (December 1580): Nishi-Hashinoin’s Thirty-Five-Participant Buddhist Debate — Actual Management of a Hashinoin-Sponsored Ceremony in Which Tamon-in Eishun Served as Lecturer
    An entry dated December 19, Tensho 8 (1580), contained in Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (p. 134). At the thirty-five-participant Buddhist debate held by Nishi-Hashinoin, “I” (Tamon-in Eishun) served as lecturer and Yokyo as questioner, while the record gives specific payments and operational expenses: six to of offerings, one bundle for those in attendance, one sotoba, and twenty hiki each to three persons. The surrounding entries form part of a record of the daily activities of Kofuku-ji’s inge institutions, including economic arrangements on December 18 associated with the departure of the lord of Daijo-in for Kyoto (payments for various items such as hita, tonsu, and yuen), the receipt of borrowed rice handled by officials and Bizen levy payments on the 21st, Joshu’s Sixteen Arhat offering on the 22nd (cost: six to), and Kenshun’s seventh-cycle Arhat memorial service on the 23rd, attended by Kenryobo, Sonkyo-in, Minamii-bo, Kuboin Enmyo-in, Konshoin Choin, Rensei-in, Jonyo-in, Gyoshun, Kanshu-bo, Senjitsu, Josho, and others.

    【Structure of the Buddhist Ceremony and the Position of Nishi-Hashinoin】

    Date / Event Description
    December 18 Various goods, including hita, tonsu, and yuen, were procured with money in connection with the lord of Daijo-in’s departure for Kyoto. These were recorded as economic arrangements related to the journey.
    December 19 (Key Record) Nishi-Hashinoin hosted a thirty-five-participant Buddhist debate. Lecturer: “I” (Tamon-in Eishun); questioner: Yokyo. The record specifies concrete payments and distributions—six to of offerings, one bundle for those in attendance, one sotoba, and twenty hiki each to three persons—revealing the practical operation of an inge-sponsored Buddhist ceremony.
    December 21 Receipt of rice borrowed through officials and Bizen levy payments, illustrating one aspect of the economic and administrative functions of Kofuku-ji’s inge institutions.
    December 22–23 Joshu’s Sixteen Arhat offering (cost: six to) and Kenshun’s seventh-cycle Arhat memorial service. Numerous inge institutions and clerics—including Kenryobo, Minamii-bo, Kuboin Enmyo-in, Konshoin Choin, Rensei-in, Jonyo-in, Gyoshun, Kanshu-bo, Senjitsu, and Josho—assembled, illustrating the scale of coordinated memorial services among multiple inge institutions during the same period.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Description
    A primary-source record of Tamon-in Eishun serving as “lecturer” demonstrates Nishi-Hashinoin’s capacity to host Buddhist ceremonies Eishun, the author of Tamon-in Nikki, explicitly records “講予” (“Lecturer: myself”), confirming that he personally served as lecturer at the thirty-five-participant Buddhist debate hosted by Nishi-Hashinoin. Together with Block 87, which records another ceremony involving the same individual in September of the same year, this entry provides repeated evidence within the same diary that Nishi-Hashinoin was involved in organizing and hosting multiple high-level Buddhist ceremonies during Tensho 8 (1580).
    Concrete records of offerings and compensation reveal the economic realities of Buddhist ceremonial management The specific record of six to of offerings, one bundle for those in attendance, one sotoba, and twenty hiki each to three persons demonstrates that Nishi-Hashinoin had the practical capacity to make and administer payments within the ceremonial economy. Rather than being merely a nominal institutional title, it functioned as an actual organization with the economic foundation necessary to manage offerings and compensation for lecturers, questioners, and other participants.
    Five records from Tensho 8 provide multifaceted evidence for the substantive existence of Nishi-Hashinoin Five independent categories of records are concentrated in the single year Tensho 8: Block 67 (landholding survey and administrative response), Block 77 (ordination-master functions and appointment fees), Block 86 (request concerning a child and adoption), Block 87 (lecturer at the Konzo-in Shikiko), and the present Block 89 (hosting a thirty-five-participant Buddhist debate and making ceremonial payments). Taken together, these primary sources demonstrate Nishi-Hashinoin’s fivefold functions in administration, religious ritual, institutional succession, scholarly Buddhist ceremonies, and ceremonial finance. They constitute an exceptionally strong body of contemporary evidence confirming the institution’s substantive existence.
    90. Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (February 1581): Nishi-Hashinoin’s One-Hundredth-Day Memorial Service — Record of a Ceremony with Tamon-in Eishun Attending by Palanquin Through Heavy Snow and Zenshun Serving as Lecturer
    An entry dated February 25, Tensho 9 (1581), contained in Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 3 (p. 146). At the one-hundredth-day memorial service held at Nishi-Hashinoin, the record specifies the ceremonial structure: lecturer: Zenshun; questioner: “I” (Tamon-in Eishun); topic: “Shinnyo mui ke-jitsu”; offering: six to; attendance gift: one bundle of miscellaneous paper. It further explicitly records that Eishun attended by palanquin despite heavy snow that had been falling since the middle of the night. The entry appears alongside records of the Konzo-in Buddhist debate on February 24 (assigned topic: 謂起證實; lecturer: Ganshun-bo), a pre-mortem memorial service at Amida-in (ritual officiant Maniju-in, principal officiant Zokubetsue Myotoku-in), prayers at Ichijo-in on the 26th, and sutra-reading ceremonies at the Golden Hall, providing evidence for the operation of Buddhist ceremonies at Hashinoin alongside those of other Kofuku-ji institutions.
