    【Structure of the Buddhist Ceremony and the Position of Nishi-Hashinoin】

    Date / Ceremony Description
    February 24 Konzo-in Buddhist debate (assigned topic: 謂起證實; lecturer: Ganshun-bo). A pre-mortem memorial service was also held at Amida-in, with Maniju-in serving as ritual officiant, Zokubetsue Myotoku-in as principal officiant, and Minamii-bo filling one of the five officiant positions. Multiple inge institutions conducted ceremonies in parallel.
    February 25 (Key Record) One-hundredth-day memorial service at Nishi-Hashinoin. Lecturer: Zenshun; questioner: “I” (Tamon-in Eishun). Topic: “Shinnyo mui ke-jitsu.” Offering: six to; attendance gift: one bundle of miscellaneous paper. The diary explicitly records that Eishun attended by palanquin despite heavy snow falling since the middle of the night, indicating the strong sense of obligation attached to attendance at the ceremony. The service took place on the same day as the customary Ninno lecture.
    February 26 Prayers at Ichijo-in (Eishun did not attend). Sutra-reading ceremonies were held at the Golden Hall, with Chosen participating, and a new Sonsho mandala was prepared. These records show that Nishi-Hashinoin’s memorial service was conducted during the same period as ceremonies of higher-ranking institutions such as Ichijo-in and the Golden Hall.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Description
    The statement “attended by palanquin through heavy snow” indicates the institutional importance of the Hashinoin ceremony The phrase “從夜中大雪之間輿ニテ出” explicitly states that Tamon-in Eishun attended despite severe weather, traveling by palanquin through heavy snow. This suggests that participation in Nishi-Hashinoin’s one-hundredth-day memorial service carried a strong institutional expectation rather than being merely casual or optional attendance. The entry therefore provides direct primary-source evidence that Nishi-Hashinoin functioned as an actual inge institution incorporated into Kofuku-ji’s ceremonial system.
    Continuous records from Tensho 8 to Tensho 9 demonstrate Nishi-Hashinoin’s sustained capacity to conduct Buddhist ceremonies Following Block 89, which records a thirty-five-participant Buddhist debate in December of Tensho 8, this entry confirms that Nishi-Hashinoin conducted a one-hundredth-day memorial service in February of the following year, Tensho 9 (1581). Records of ceremonies continuing across successive years indicate that Nishi-Hashinoin was not performing only temporary or isolated functions but operated as a continuing institution within Kofuku-ji’s ceremonial framework.
    The Yogacara topic “Shinnyo mui ke-jitsu” indicates the scholarly level of Nishi-Hashinoin’s ceremony The selection of “眞如無爲假實” (“Shinnyo mui ke-jitsu”), a doctrinal question concerning the status of suchness (shinnyo) in relation to conditioned and unconditioned existence and to provisional and real existence within Yogacara thought, indicates that Nishi-Hashinoin’s memorial service incorporated advanced doctrinal discussion. As with the Konzo-in Shikiko recorded in Block 87, this reinforces the interpretation that Nishi-Hashinoin was not limited to economic or administrative functions but also operated as a scholarly Buddhist institution.
    Parallel records of prayers at Ichijo-in and a Buddhist debate at Konzo-in indicate Nishi-Hashinoin’s incorporation into a coordinated network of inge institutions The sequence of the Konzo-in Buddhist debate on the 24th, Nishi-Hashinoin’s one-hundredth-day memorial service on the 25th, and prayers at Ichijo-in on the 26th reproduces the same general pattern seen in Block 87, where prayers at Daijo-in, the Konzo-in Shikiko, and the Ichijo-in Daihannya lecture occurred in close succession. Taken together, these records from different periods and different types of ceremonies provide multifaceted evidence that Nishi-Hashinoin functioned within the same broader ceremonial network as monzeki and inge institutions such as Ichijo-in, Daijo-in, and Konzo-in.
    91. Extracts from the Ichijo-in Documents (Kyoto University Department of Japanese History Collection, p. 21): Records of the Hoshaku-in Family Estates and List of Inshu — Institutional Succession Record Showing Jisshin’s Use of the Title “Hosshin-in”
    A passage concerning the Hoshaku-in and Karin-in families, contained on p. 21 of Extracts from the Ichijo-in Documents (Kyoto University Department of Japanese History Collection, published in 1981). The document records the history of the Hoshaku-in family estates, including Sukawa-no-sho, Tsubosaka, Toyoi-no-sho, Shibano-no-sho, and the Gyokuka-in estate, and lists the successive heads of the institution as “Shingen, Yoshin, Kakuken (styled Tsubosaka Sojo), Shinken (styled Shuzen-in Sojo), Jitsuson (called Daijo-in), and Jisshin (called Hosshin-in).” It directly records that Jisshin was called “Hosshin-in”, demonstrating an institutional structure in which multiple in-go titles—including Daijo-in, Ichijo-in, and Hosshin-in—were associated with members of the same succession line. Regarding the Karin-in family, the document also records the succession of Tachibana-dera, Koji-no-sho, and Miifuku, as well as their transfer to Kujo-dono Sojo no Gobo (Shin'en) in connection with a master-disciple relationship, making this an important record of succession among monzeki and inge institutions.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Description
    Direct record of Jisshin’s use of the title “Hosshin-in” The entry “Jisshin (called Hosshin-in)” in the list of institutional heads directly confirms, in an independent estate document of the Hoshaku-in family, that Jisshin used “Hosshin-in” as his title. This provides a second confirmation in a different document and context from Block 88 (the Ichijo-in document stating “奉号発心院御房”), thereby strengthening the evidence that the title Hosshin-in belonged to Jisshin.
    The paired entries “Jitsuson (called Daijo-in)” and “Jisshin (called Hosshin-in)” indicate an institutional relationship between Daijo-in and Hosshin-in In the list of institutional heads, Jitsuson is recorded as being called “Daijo-in,” immediately followed by Jisshin as being called “Hosshin-in.” The fact that these two in-go titles, Daijo-in and Hosshin-in, were attached to successive heads within the same institutional lineage of the Hoshaku-in family indicates that Hosshin-in formed part of the same broader monzeki system associated with the regent-family line as Daijo-in and Ichijo-in. This strengthens the institutional foundation of this website’s hypothesis that “Hashinoin (Hosshin-in) represented an in-go borne by a close relative within a monzeki lineage.”
    The transfer to Kujo-dono Sojo (Shin'en) recorded for the Karin-in family reveals the structure of the inge network The record stating that Tachibana-dera, Koji-no-sho, and Miifuku of the Karin-in family were transferred in connection with the master-disciple relationship to “Kujo-dono Sojo no Gobo” indicates that the estates and succession of Kofuku-ji’s inge institutions were managed through Shin'en of the Kujo family line, who also appears in Block 88 as Jisshin’s teacher. An independent document therefore corroborates the institutional structure in which Shin'en functioned as a key node linking estates and master-disciple relationships across multiple inge institutions.
    92. Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 2 (December 1571): Record of the Collection of Yogacara Lecture Rice at Yokota-no-sho Under the “Roji-gi” Obligation — Evidence of Economic Exchange in the Hashinoin Estate Area
    An entry from December Genki 2 (1571), contained in Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 2 (Books 12–23). It records that the summer allotment of rice for the Yogacara lectures was collected at Yokota-no-sho for three days under the “roji-gi” obligation. This source provides supporting evidence that Yokota-no-sho, corresponding to the Hashinoin estate area, possessed institutional and economic ties with Kofuku-ji’s inge institutions. As a record concerning Yokota-no-sho approximately eleven years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in Tensho 10 (1582; Block 95), it further clarifies the institutional position of the Hashinoin estate area that later served as the base of the Hashimoto family.

    【Comparison of the Yokota-no-sho Record】

    Item Description
    Item Collected Rice for the Yogacara lectures (summer allotment)
    Basis of Collection Roji-gi (an obligation involving services or the provision of goods by estates situated along transportation routes)
    Place of Collection Yokota-no-sho (the Hashinoin estate area, Soekami District, Yamato Province)
    Collection Period Three days, from December 24 through the day of the entry, December 26
    Year of Record Genki 2 (1571), approximately eleven years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in 1582

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Description
    Direct record showing Yokota-no-sho, in the Hashinoin estate area, functioning as a collection point for rice supporting Kofuku-ji doctrinal lectures The record that the summer allotment of rice for the Yogacara lectures was collected from Yokota-no-sho under the “roji-gi” obligation directly confirms, through the independent testimony of Tamon-in Nikki, that Yokota-no-sho—the Hashinoin estate area and later base of the Hashimoto family—was not merely an agricultural district but also formed part of the institutional economic network supporting the scholarly and ceremonial activities of Kofuku-ji’s inge institutions.
    The institutional relationship represented by “roji-gi” clarifies the position of Yokota-no-sho Roji-gi refers to an institutional obligation under which an estate situated along a transportation route supplied goods or performed services associated with movement along that route. The fact that Yokota-no-sho was subject to the collection of Yogacara lecture rice under this arrangement indicates its continuing incorporation into Kofuku-ji’s economic and institutional network. This is consistent with the institutional relationship between Yokota-no-sho and the monzeki estates recorded in sources such as the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki (see §4), and provides institutional background for the hypothesis that the Hashimoto family was connected with the inge as local service-functionaries rather than being simply an ordinary farming household.
    Historical significance of the date Genki 2 (1571) This record dates to Genki 2 (1571), approximately eleven years before Tamon-in Nikki records “Hashimoto Yaroku” by name as a person associated with Hosshin-in in Tensho 10 (1582; Block 95). The fact that active economic interaction between Yokota-no-sho and Kofuku-ji’s inge institutions was still functioning in 1571 indicates that the institutional relationship between the region that served as the Hashimoto family’s base and the inge system existed before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in the diary. This chronological continuity supports the institutional foundation of the genealogical hypothesis that the Hashimoto family developed “from local service-functionaries into a family later recognized as shizoku.”
    93. Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Eleventh Month of Tenshō 6 [1578]) — A Direct Reference to Hasshi-in Recording Red Rice and Additional Monetary Gifts Sent to “Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)”
    An entry from the eleventh month of Tenshō 6 (1578) in Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Scrolls 24–31). Alongside Kanzen’in, “Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)” appears explicitly by name, and the diary records that one koku of red rice and an additional payment of 200 hiki were sent as recompense connected with the Great Assembly. This source directly records Hasshi-in in Tamon’in Nikki, an independent third-party contemporary document, as an institution incorporated into the ritual and economic network of the Kōfuku-ji subtemples, four years before Hashimoto Yaroku appears in 1582 (Tenshō 10).

    【Comparison of References to Nishi-Hasshi-in (Nishi Hashinokin)】

    Item Kanzen’in Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)
    Red rice Three koku (sent directly from the “Dai”) One koku (sent from here on this day)
    Additional monetary gift Additional gift relating to flute/hat 200 hiki (additional evening payment)
    Reason for the gifts “Daiekata hōtō nari” (大會方報答也) — recompense for participation or service connected with the Great Assembly
    Date of record 25th day of the eleventh month, Tenshō 6 (1578)

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Historical value of the direct reference to “Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)” “Hasshi-in (Hashinokin = Hashino-in),” identified in this study as the institutional source of the stipend and samurai status associated with Hashimoto Hyōsaku, is explicitly recorded as “Nishi Hashinokin” in an independent third-party document, Tamon’in Nikki by Eishun. This is a contemporary record dating to Tenshō 6 (1578), approximately 300 years before the Meiji 7 (1874) Petition for the Commutation of Hereditary Stipend, an administratively certified document referring to “Hasshi-in, territory of Ichijō-in.” It is therefore one of the most important sources confirming, through an independent contemporary observer, that Hasshi-in functioned as an actual institution in the late medieval period.
    The institutional position of Hasshi-in indicated by its joint appearance with Kanzen’in The fact that Kanzen’in, one of the principal subtemples of Kōfuku-ji, and “Nishi Hashinokin” are recorded in the same entry as recipients of recompense related to the Great Assembly indicates that Nishi-Hasshi-in participated in a major Kōfuku-ji Buddhist ceremony within the same ritual framework. This is not merely a record of the name of a manor or locality. Rather, Eishun—an independent observer with no connection to the Hashimoto family—directly records Hasshi-in as an institution incorporated into the temple’s ritual network.
    Chronological significance of Tenshō 6 (1578) This source predates by four years the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in Tamon’in Nikki in Tenshō 10 (1582; Block 95). The fact that Nishi-Hasshi-in was already actively participating in the economic and ritual network of the Kōfuku-ji subtemples in 1578 constitutes important chronological evidence supporting the hypothesis that “Hasshi-in was a subtemple-like institution associated with the Hashimoto family,” particularly because it immediately precedes the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku, who was connected with Hasshin-in and served in a nassho administrative role.
    Nature of the economic exchange indicated by the phrase “Daiekata hōtō” The explicit statement that the red rice and additional monetary gift were sent as “Daiekata hōtō” (recompense connected with the Great Assembly) indicates that Nishi-Hasshi-in was not simply a passive recipient of goods. Rather, it participated in or rendered service for the Great Assembly, a major Buddhist ceremony, and received goods and money in return. This constitutes direct evidence that Hasshi-in functioned not merely as the name of a manor or locality, but as an institution participating in Kōfuku-ji’s ritual activities, and it supports the characterization of members of the Hashimoto family as functionaries connected with the subtemple institutional network.
    94. Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Tenth Month of Tenshō 8 [1580]) — Death, Funeral, and Mourning of “Kōjin Senkenbō of Nishi Hashinokin,” a Named Head of Nishi-Hasshi-in
    An entry from the tenth month of Tenshō 8 (1580) in Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Scrolls 24–31). It records the death of “Kōjin Senkenbō of Nishi Hashinokin,” aged sixty-five, and his funeral on the following day. The author Eishun states that, because they had been close acquaintances for several years, he accompanied the funeral procession as far as the mountain and wept. This is a contemporary funerary record in which the head of Nishi-Hasshi-in is identified by name and age, two years before Hashimoto Yaroku appears in 1582 (Tenshō 10).

    【Comparison of Details in the Nishi-Hasshi-in Funeral Record】

    Item Details
    Deceased Kōjin Senkenbō of Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)
    Age at death Sixty-five (born around Eishō 12 [1515])
    Date of death Night of the 15th day of the tenth month, Tenshō 8 (1580); recorded on the following day, the 16th
    Date of funeral 17th day of the tenth month. Chōzenbō, Chōken, and Eishun (the author) participated.
    Eishun’s personal reflection “數年知音之間見送、流泪了” — because of their friendship over several years, he accompanied the procession as far as the mountain and wept.
    Entry concerning the collection of loaned rice A demand for repayment of loaned rice from the shrine functionary Oribe and Yōmoto Daiichi — an economic matter recorded in the same diary entry as the funeral.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Contemporary evidence recording the head of Nishi-Hasshi-in by name, age, and funeral in an independent diary The personal name “Kōjin Senkenbō of Nishi Hashinokin” and his age, “sixty-five,” are recorded in the diary of Eishun, an independent third party with no connection to the Hashimoto family. This provides evidence for the historical existence of Nishi-Hasshi-in not through a later genealogy or family tradition, but through a sixteenth-century contemporary diary, one of the strongest types of historical evidence available. As a contemporary record combining a personal name, age at death, and funeral account, it is one of the most important sources demonstrating the actual existence of Hasshi-in.
    Institutional and personal proximity between Tamon’in and Nishi-Hasshi-in indicated by Eishun’s phrase “數年知音之間” Eishun’s statement that Kōjin Senkenbō had been a close acquaintance for several years, and that he wept while seeing him off, indicates that Tamon’in, represented by Eishun, and Nishi-Hasshi-in, represented by Kōjin, were not merely neighboring subtemples but maintained a long-term personal and institutional relationship. This vivid account of their close relationship provides direct testimony that Hasshi-in functioned substantively within the network of Kōfuku-ji subtemples.
    Chronological significance of Tenshō 8 (1580) This source falls two years after the record of recompense connected with the Great Assembly (Block 93, Tenshō 6 [1578]) and two years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku (Block 95, Tenshō 10 [1582]). The continuous chronology—“Nishi Hashinokin” participating in the Great Assembly and receiving recompense in 1578, the death of its head in 1580, and the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku as a person associated with Hasshin-in in 1582—places Hashimoto Yaroku in the immediate aftermath of a change in the leadership of Hasshi-in. This provides more concrete chronological support for the proposed institutional continuity between Hasshi-in and the Hashimoto family.
    Economic ties around Hasshi-in indicated by the funeral and loaned-rice collection appearing in the same record The fact that a demand for repayment of loaned rice from the shrine functionary Oribe and Yōmoto Daiichi is recorded in the same diary context as the funeral of the head of Nishi-Hasshi-in indicates that personal networks surrounding the subtemple, represented by participation in the funeral, and economic networks, represented by the collection of loaned rice, functioned concurrently. Together with Block 92, concerning Yokota Manor and expenses connected with the Yuishiki-kō rice, and Block 93, concerning Nishi-Hasshi-in and the additional payment as recompense for the Great Assembly, this evidence further supports the conclusion that the area surrounding Hasshi-in was integrated into Kōfuku-ji’s institutional and economic networks on multiple levels.
    95. Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Third Month of Tenshō 7 [1579]) — Record of Five Scrolls of Memorial Sutra Copying for “Nishi Hashinokin” on the Middle Day of the Equinoctial Week, Demonstrating Hasshi-in’s Participation in Memorial Rites
    An entry from the third month of Tenshō 7 (1579) in Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 3 (Scrolls 24–31). On the day of the Rakan offering held at the midpoint of the spring equinoctial week, five scrolls of memorial sutras were prepared for “Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in)”. Of these, one scroll was copied by Zenshiki and four by Eishun, the author himself, and the entry states that they were memorial sutras for Shunshōbō. This contemporary record from 1579 shows that Nishi-Hasshi-in functioned within Kōfuku-ji’s network of Buddhist ceremonies and memorial observances as an institution associated with memorial sutra rites.

    【Comparison of the Nishi-Hasshi-in Memorial Sutra Record】

    Item Details
    Subject of the memorial sutras Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi-Hasshi-in) / Shunshōbō
    Number of scrolls and copyists Five scrolls (one copied by Zenshiki; four copied personally by Eishun, the author)
    Date and ritual context 23rd day of the third month, Tenshō 7 (1579), on the same day as the Rakan offering held at the midpoint of the equinoctial week
    Chronological position One year after the Great Assembly recompense record (Block 93, 1578) → one year before the death of the head of the institution (Block 94, 1580) → three years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku (1582)

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Evidentiary significance of Eishun personally copying the memorial sutras The statement that Eishun, the author of Tamon’in Nikki, personally copied four of the five scrolls indicates that a close personal and institutional relationship existed between Eishun and Nishi-Hasshi-in (Shunshōbō), extending beyond that of mere neighboring subtemples. Devoting his own time and labor to copying memorial sutras would, within contemporary temple practice, normally presuppose a substantial degree of personal closeness or a relationship involving institutional obligations. The entry therefore provides evidence of the strength of the institutional ties between Tamon’in and Nishi-Hasshi-in.
    Hasshi-in’s ritual position indicated by the record appearing on the same day as the equinoctial Rakan offering The fact that memorial sutras connected with Nishi-Hasshi-in were prepared on the same day as the Rakan offering held at the midpoint of the equinoctial week, an important day in Kōfuku-ji’s ritual calendar, indicates that Nishi-Hasshi-in was integrated into Kōfuku-ji’s annual cycle of observances and Buddhist ceremonies. Rather than being an isolated reference, this record forms part of a continuous sequence together with Block 93 (Great Assembly recompense, 1578) and Block 94 (death of the institutional head, 1580), reinforcing the institutional continuity of Hasshi-in.
    The 1578–1582 sequence as a “continuous body of evidence for Hasshi-in” The sequence of independent records—Block 93 (1578, recompense connected with the Great Assembly) → this source (1579, memorial sutras) → Block 94 (1580, death and funeral of the institutional head) → appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku (1582)—documents, year by year, through the independent third-party source Tamon’in Nikki, that an institution called “Nishi-Hasshi-in” was actively functioning during the period from 1578 to 1582. Taken together, these records form a continuous body of evidence that directly addresses the alleged “gap” in the historical record.
    96. Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 2 (Intercalary First Month of Genki 3 [1572]) — Record of “Nishi Hashinokin” Participating in a Nin’ō-kyō Ceremony and Hosting a Hōonkō Memorial Lecture
    An entry from the intercalary first month of Genki 3 (1572) in Tamon’in Nikki, Vol. 2 (Scrolls 12–23). It records that “Nishi Hashinokin” attended a Nin’ō-kyō ceremony and brought one bundle of miscellaneous paper (entry for the 19th day), and also that “a Hōonkō was held at Nishi Hashinokin”, with Myōō-in serving as lecturer and Minbu-kyō as questioner (entry from the same month). This contemporary record from 1572 demonstrates that Nishi-Hasshi-in (Nishi Hashinokin) was not merely an institution that participated in Kōfuku-ji ceremonies, but also one capable of hosting its own Hōonkō observance.

    【Comparison of Nishi-Hasshi-in’s Ritual Activities】

    Date Record Role of Nishi-Hasshi-in
    19th day of the intercalary first month Nishi Hashinokin attended the Nin’ō-kyō ceremony and brought one bundle of miscellaneous paper Participant in the Buddhist ceremony and provider of materials
    9th day of the same month A Hōonkō was held at Nishi Hashinokin; Myōō-in served as lecturer and Minbu-kyō as questioner Host of the Hōonkō (inviting the distinguished Myōō-in and Minbu-kyō to serve as lecturer and questioner)

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Direct evidence that Nishi-Hasshi-in was an institution capable of hosting a Hōonkō The statement “西ハシノキンニ報恩講在之” (“a Hōonkō was held at Nishi Hashinokin”) directly demonstrates that Nishi-Hasshi-in was not merely an institution that attended Buddhist ceremonies, but one that itself hosted a Hōonkō and invited distinguished scholar-monks, Myōō-in and Minbu-kyō, to serve respectively as lecturer and questioner. This is one of the most important pieces of evidence indicating that Hasshi-in was not simply a peripheral manor-administration unit, but functioned actively within the Kōfuku-ji network as a subtemple possessing its own religious and scholarly functions.
    Institutional status indicated by the “two-way involvement” of attending the Nin’ō-kyō ceremony and hosting a Hōonkō Within the same month, Nishi-Hasshi-in is recorded in two different capacities: (1) as a participant attending the Nin’ō-kyō ceremony and bringing materials, and (2) as a host organizing a Hōonkō and inviting distinguished lecturers. This two-way involvement indicates that Hasshi-in was not merely a passive participant within Kōfuku-ji’s ceremonial network, but functioned as an institution engaged in reciprocal institutional relationships. This also corresponds with Block 93, in which Hasshi-in appears as a recipient of recompense connected with the Great Assembly, together forming a pattern of reciprocal institutional involvement.
    Chronological significance of Genki 3 (1572) This source dates to Genki 3 (1572), one year after Block 92 (Genki 2 [1571], concerning Yokota Manor and expenses related to the transport of Yuishiki-kō rice) and six years before Block 93 (Tenshō 6 [1578], recompense connected with the Great Assembly). The two-stage pattern in which Yokota Manor and Nishi-Hasshi-in appear in Tamon’in Nikki in 1571–1572 and then appear repeatedly again from 1578 through 1582 provides chronological evidence supporting the continued participation of Hasshi-in in the Kōfuku-ji network throughout the sixteenth century.
    97. Dajō-kan Proclamation No. 133 of 1872 and the Entry “Nikujiki Saitai” (Eating Meat and Marriage) in Dictionary of Four-Character Buddhist Terms: Vol. 2 — Research Sources Showing the Institutional Background Behind the Scarcity of Published Records of Monastic Marriage and the Genealogies of Close Relatives of Monzeki
    This section examines Dajō-kan Proclamation No. 133 of 1872, which declared, “Henceforth, Buddhist monks shall be free to eat meat, marry, grow their hair, and so forth,” together with the entry “Nikujiki Saitai” (Eating Meat and Marriage) on p.73 of Dictionary of Four-Character Buddhist Terms: Vol. 2 (Ryūsen Sudō, Shin Jinbutsu Ōraisha, 1998). These sources demonstrate the fact that before the Meiji Restoration, under the formal principles of Buddhist precepts, it was institutionally difficult for blood relationships involving temple heads and Monzeki to be recorded in official documents. They therefore provide a basis for considering whether references such as “Hashimoto Yaroku” preserved in primary sources including the Tamon-in Nikki and donation registers may serve as evidence from which the actual genealogical relationships of close relatives of Monzeki can be inferred. This material is also discussed in a case published in the National Diet Library Collaborative Reference Database.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Information Link
    Dajō-kan Proclamation No. 133 of 1872 Promulgated on April 25, 1872 National Diet Library Collaborative Reference Database
    Dictionary of Four-Character Buddhist Terms: Vol. 2, entry “Nikujiki Saitai” (Eating Meat and Marriage) Author: Ryūsen Sudō; Publisher: Shin Jinbutsu Ōraisha; February 1998; p.73 —

    【Summary of the Argument】 The institutional background shown by these sources as to why genealogies of close relatives of Monzeki rarely appear in published records →

    Because lifelong celibacy was formally regarded as the basic rule for Buddhist monks under traditional Buddhist precepts and institutional practices, it was institutionally difficult for official documents and genealogical records to preserve family relationships explicitly in forms such as “the son of the temple head” or “a close relative of a Monzeki.” Until the early Meiji period, there were constraints on publicly recording the family relationships of Buddhist monks, reflecting the formal requirements of Buddhist precepts at an institutional level. By contrast, unofficial references scattered throughout primary sources such as temple donation registers, accounting registers, records of temple sub-institutions, and diaries—for example, references to “Hashimoto Yaroku-dono”—could preserve valuable traces of actual practice and of kinship or social connections that tended to be obscured by the formal institutional framework.

    【Comparison of Institutional Background and Evidentiary Value】

    Type of Source Likelihood of Recording the Genealogy of Close Relatives of Monzeki Corresponding Sources Concerning the Hashimoto Family
    Official genealogical compilations and published reference works Institutionally difficult (the formal requirements of Buddhist precepts discouraged public documentation of family relationships) Rare exceptions in which the names “Hashimoto” and “Go-Hosshin-in” are recorded in the Sonpi Bunmyaku and records of Monzeki succession
    Primary sources such as diaries, accounting registers, and donation registers More likely to be recorded (as practical records, they tend to reflect actual circumstances rather than formal conventions) The Tamon-in Nikki repeatedly records “Hashimoto Yaroku,” “Hashimoto Sama,” and “Nishi Hashinokin” by name (Blocks 93–96)
    Administratively certified documents Highest evidentiary value (independent certification by third-party administrative authorities) 1874 petition for the surrender of hereditary stipends, administratively certified with the registered seals of two deputy village heads (Nara Prefectural Library and Information Center, Film ID: 811013157)

    【Significance of the Sources】

    Point Explanation
    Institutional grounds showing the flaw in the inference that “few records in published sources = no blood relationship” In response to the objection that “there is no direct evidence in published academic studies or genealogical compilations,” these sources demonstrate that information concerning close relatives of Monzeki and heads of temple sub-institutions was institutionally difficult to record in official documents because of the formal requirements imposed by Buddhist precepts. This provides an institutional basis for challenging the inference that “absence of evidence is evidence of absence,” and shows that omission from published genealogical compilations does not in itself constitute evidence disproving a blood relationship.
    Theoretical basis for the evidentiary value of primary sources such as diaries and donation registers These sources provide an institutional explanation for why practical everyday records such as the Tamon-in Nikki may reflect actual circumstances more accurately than official genealogies. In other words, the repeated appearance of “Hashimoto Yaroku” in the Tamon-in Nikki in contexts connected with Hosshin-in (from Block 95 onward) may be evaluated as “primary evidence preserved through gaps in the institutional system”—evidence that recorded actual circumstances despite institutional barriers to inclusion in official genealogies.
    The 1872 proclamation demonstrates the long-term constraints that existed before institutional reform The fact that the marriage of Buddhist monks was officially permitted in 1872 demonstrates, conversely, that for centuries beforehand there had been institutional constraints discouraging the recording of blood relationships involving temple heads and Monzeki in public documents. The approximately 260-year “gap in official records” between the death of Ryōshin (1319) and the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku (1582) may therefore be understood as a structural gap produced in part by such institutional constraints. This provides an institutional basis for concluding that an absence of surviving evidence does not automatically establish the absence of a blood relationship.
    98. Dajō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 8 (July 1485) — Local Community Record Listing “Match No. 45: Hashimoto, One Match” in the Order of Rain-Prayer Sumo
    This entry from July 1485 in Vol. 8 of the Dajō-in Jisha Zōjiki records the order of 120 rain-prayer sumo matches held at Babain by residents of the northern and southern districts. “Match No. 45: Hashimoto, one match” appears explicitly in the list. The document also records arrangements concerning deserted districts and the addition of matches, and notes that rain and wind began that day, indicating the perceived fulfillment of the rain prayer. This is a local-event record independently confirming, through the diary of Jinson of the Dajō-in Monzeki, that “Hashimoto” had been incorporated as a recognized unit in a Nara community event approximately 97 years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in 1582.

    July 1485
    Sumo wrestling was held at Babain by the inhabitants of the northern and southern districts, comprising 120 matches. In recent years there have also been deserted districts, and it was said that additional localities were included or the number of matches increased. This was a matter of considerable importance throughout Nara. This year the northern district initiated the event, and it was said that the two sides took turns on each occasion. Sumo had previously been held on May 21, 1472, and was held again this year. In particular, concerning the order of matches, those responsible for the arrangements were summoned and instructed to make a copy, written continuously on two folded sheets of strong Sugihara paper.

    Established Order of the Rain-Prayer Sumo Matches
    Match No. 1 (Minami-ichi, Saiwai-ichi), one match; Match No. 3 Fukuchi-in, two matches; Match No. 4 Shimo-Takabatake, two matches; Match No. 5 Nishi-Mikado Higashi-hoho, two matches, Jūchi-in (?); Match No. 7 Nashihara, one match; Match No. 9 Taka-Mikado, one match; Match No. 11 Nishi-Terabayashi, two matches;
    Match No. 25 Kitamuro, one match; Match No. 29 Oshikōji, two matches; Match No. 35 Muen-dō, one match; Match No. 36 Akoyagawa, two matches; Match No. 37 Minamimuro, one match; Match No. 38 Shōnan-in, one match;
    Match No. 45: Hashimoto, one match; Match No. 46 Higashi-Jōdo, three matches; Match No. 47 Yurunoki, one match; Match No. 48 Kita-Hōren-in, three matches; Match No. 54 Kidera, three matches; Match No. 57 Higashi-Kitano-daya, one match; Match No. 58 Kaizuka-minami, two matches;
    Match No. 72 Tōhoku-in, one match.
    Established as stated above.
    The event commenced on July 24, 1485.
    There were no decisive victories today; only the 120 matches were performed. From today, rain fell and the wind blew.

    【Position of Hashimoto in the Rain-Prayer Sumo List】

    Position in the List Details Remarks
    Match No. 45: Hashimoto, one match “Hashimoto” appears independently as one match at No. 45 among the 120 matches. Adjacent entries: No. 46 Higashi-Jōdo, No. 47 Yurunoki, and No. 48 Kita-Hōren-in
    Character of the participants listed A local event in which residents of the northern and southern districts, various districts of Nara, and temple sub-institutions participated as territorial or community units. Participation presupposed recognition as a local community unit. The same sumo event is also recorded in 1472, demonstrating that it was a continuing event.
    Result of the event All 120 matches were conducted without decisive victories; rain and wind began that day—the rain prayer was regarded as fulfilled. July 24, 1485

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Explanation
    Direct Muromachi-period record showing that “Hashimoto” was recognized as a unit in a local Nara event The fact that “Hashimoto” was formally entered as “Match No. 45: Hashimoto, one match” in an independent third-party record written by Jinson of the Dajō-in Monzeki demonstrates that, by 1485, “Hashimoto” possessed a recognizable existence in Nara society as a place-name or community group. Chronologically, this falls between Ryūun's return to secular life in the fifteenth century, as recorded in Vol. 6 of the Sonpi Bunmyaku, and the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in 1582. It therefore constitutes independent corroborating evidence that an entity identified as “Hashimoto” existed in Nara society during the intervening Muromachi-period phase linking those two points.
    The local status of “Hashimoto” indicated by its participation in a rain-prayer sumo event The rain-prayer sumo was a religious event in which residents of the northern and southern districts participated by community unit under the institutional sphere of Kōfuku-ji. Inclusion in the list presupposed recognition by Dajō-in and Kōfuku-ji as a local community unit. The independent listing “Hashimoto, one match,” alongside other districts and temple sub-institutions such as Kita-Hōren-in and Tōhoku-in, indicates that Hashimoto was treated as a comparable local unit and provides evidence supporting its established local position within the area associated with Hosshin-in.
    Intermediate evidence filling the gap between “Ryōshin's death (1319)” and “Hashimoto Yaroku (1582)” With regard to the alleged “gap period,” the date of this source, 1485, lies 166 years after the death of Ryōshin in 1319 and 97 years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in 1582. The fact that “Hashimoto” was explicitly registered at this intermediate date in an independent third-party document, the Dajō-in Jisha Zōjiki, as a constituent unit of local Nara society functions as “intermediate-point evidence within the gap period.” It therefore adds another link to the chain of evidence concerning the local continuity of Hashimoto and incrementally weakens arguments based solely on the apparent documentary gap.
    99. Tamon-in Nikki, Vol. 2 (July 1567) — Fire and Temple-Affairs Record Reporting the Burning of “Mochiidono, Hashimoto, and Tsunofuri Konishi” and, in the Same Month, an Institutional Matter Concerning the Assignment of a “Newly Ordained Novice to Hosshin-in”
    This entry from July 1567 in Vol. 2 of the Tamon-in Nikki records, under the thirteenth day, a fire in the city of Nara: “Imamikado, Mochiidono, Hashimoto, and Tsunofuri Konishi were for the most part burned down; it is said that the fire was set by the Tamon group.” The entry for the eighth day of the same month also records “a matter reported by the Three-Person Council concerning the assignment of a newly ordained novice to Hosshin-in.” Thus, “Hashimoto” appears as the name of a major district of Nara in a record of urban destruction by fire, while an institutional decision concerning the placement of a newly ordained disciple at Hosshin-in was recorded in the same period in an independent third-party source.

    Eighth day, (…) Furuichi’s party again returned to Tamonyama. In connection with this, there was a matter reported by the Three-Person Council concerning the assignment of a newly ordained novice to Hosshin-in. It was remarkable indeed.

    【Quotation 2】 From the entry for July 13, 1567 — reference to the burning of Hashimoto →

    Thirteenth day, from the beginning of the hour of the Ox until halfway through the hour of the Hare, Imamikado, Mochiidono, Hashimoto, and Tsunofuri Konishi were for the most part burned down; it is said that the fire was set by the Tamon group. It was a deplorable state of affairs.


    【Comparison of the Two July 1567 Entries】

    Date Entry Evidentiary Significance
    July 8 Matter reported by the Three-Person Council concerning the assignment of a newly ordained novice to Hosshin-in A personnel matter involving Hosshin-in—the placement of a newly admitted disciple—was recorded as an institutional matter handled by the Three-Person Council, showing that Hosshin-in functioned as an institution subject to Kōfuku-ji’s personnel administration.
    July 13 Imamikado, Mochiidono, Hashimoto, and Tsunofuri Konishi burned; fire reportedly set by the Tamon group “Hashimoto” is recorded alongside Mochiidono and other major districts of Nara as an area damaged by fire, showing that Hashimoto had become established in independent third-party records as a territorial unit within Nara.

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Explanation
    Independent evidence of “Hashimoto” appearing in a fire record as a major district within the city of Nara The parallel listing “Mochiidono, Hashimoto, and Tsunofuri Konishi” indicates that Hashimoto was recognized within the city of Nara as a district-level unit comparable to Mochiidono, which remains a well-known place-name in Nara today. Because this is an independent third-party record written by Eishun of Tamon-in, the appearance of “Hashimoto” as a district name in a quasi-topographical context without any involvement by the Hashimoto family constitutes contemporary evidence that the local presence associated with Hashimoto had become established in Nara society by the mid-sixteenth century.
    The “assignment of a newly ordained novice to Hosshin-in” demonstrates the continuation of Hosshin-in’s personnel and institutional functions The fact that, on July 8, 1567, the assignment of a newly ordained novice to Hosshin-in was recorded as a matter submitted by the Three-Person Council, an institutional decision-making body within Kōfuku-ji, indicates that Hosshin-in continued to function during the Eiroku era as an institution incorporated into Kōfuku-ji’s personnel system. Together with Block 96 (1572, hosting of a Hōonkō memorial service) and Block 93 (1578, formal reciprocal gift associated with a major ceremony), this forms part of a continuous body of evidence reinforcing the institutional continuity of Hosshin-in/Hasshi-in.
    Chronological significance of the year 1567 This source dates to 82 years after Block 98 (1485, Hashimoto listed in the rain-prayer sumo roster) and four years before Block 92 (1571, rice for the Yuishiki lecture from Yokota-no-shō). The continuous sequence of records—Block 98 → this source → Block 92 → 96 → 93 → 94 → Hashimoto Yaroku (1582)—drawn from the Tamon-in Nikki and the Dajō-in Jisha Zōjiki demonstrates that “Hashimoto” and “Hosshin-in/Hasshi-in” repeatedly appear in the same body of independent third-party records over approximately a century from 1485 to 1582. Taken together, these records constitute the most comprehensive rebuttal to arguments based on an alleged documentary gap.
    100. Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 10, Vol. 5 (Memorandum of 1570) — Monzeki Economic Record Listing “Hasshi-in Gomai” as an Item Managed under the Annual Administration of the Monzeki and Allocated to the Shūjun Accounting Office
    A memorandum from 1570 included in Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 10, Vol. 5. In a written listing dividing holdings within the Monzeki domain between the Aki accounting office and the Shūjun accounting office, “Ooda-no-shō, Yasuda-no-shō, Idodō, Shinmen territory, Hasshi-in Gomai, Hazuri-no-shō, and Aramashi” are listed together as items allocated to the Shūjun accounting office. This constitutes an economic record of the Monzeki in which “Hasshi-in Gomai” is explicitly identified in an official-document context as an object of annual administration by Ichijō-in, the Monzeki institution. Approximately 300 years before Hyōsaku Hashimoto’s 1874 petition for the surrender of hereditary stipend rights, which identified his holding as within “Ichijō-in territory,” this source confirms at the documentary level that Hasshi-in was under the direct economic administration of the Ichijō-in Monzeki by 1570.

    【Position of Hasshi-in Gomai within the Monzeki Economy】

    Item Details
    Recorded economic unit Hasshi-in Gomai (listed alongside Ooda-no-shō, Yasuda-no-shō, Idodō, Shinmen territory, Hazuri-no-shō, and Aramashi)
    Administrative authority Annual administration of the Monzeki (Ichijō-in), managed as part of the allocation assigned to the Shūjun accounting office
    Form of record Memorandum in an official-document format listing multiple estates and temple-related holdings
    Year of record 1570 — approximately 304 years before the 1874 petition for the surrender of hereditary stipend rights

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Explanation
    Key documentary evidence explicitly identifying “Hasshi-in Gomai” as an object of direct annual administration by the Ichijō-in Monzeki The statement “Ooda-no-shō, Yasuda-no-shō … Hasshi-in Gomai … these portions were allocated to the Shūjun accounting office” demonstrates that, by 1570, Hasshi-in was explicitly recorded in an official-document context alongside other estates as an object of the annual administration of the Ichijō-in Monzeki. This independently confirms, through the scholarly compilation Dai Nihon Shiryō, that the institutional relationship “Hasshi-in = Ichijō-in territory,” which later appears in Hyōsaku Hashimoto’s 1874 petition for the surrender of hereditary stipend rights as “Ichijō-in territory, fourteen koku,” was already in existence by 1570.
    The expression “Gomai” indicates the reality of direct administration of Hasshi-in The honorific prefix go- in the expression “Hasshi-in Gomai” reflects the relationship to the Monzeki, indicating that rice revenues associated with Hasshi-in were administered in a form connected directly with the Monzeki. The listing of “Hasshi-in Gomai” alongside estates such as Ooda-no-shō and Yasuda-no-shō indicates that Hasshi-in functioned as a unit of rice or tribute administration comparable to an estate. This supports the view that the institutional basis upon which the Hashimoto family later held a hereditary stipend as the “only shizoku family in Hasshi-in Village” in 1874 had practical antecedents functioning during the Sengoku period.
    The year 1570 forms part of a continuous chain of evidence The date of this source, 1570, is one year before Block 92 (1571, the issue concerning transportation of rice for the Yuishiki lecture from Yokota-no-shō) and two years before Block 96 (1572, the hosting of a Hōonkō memorial service). The consecutive appearance, within the three-year period from 1570 to 1572, of three different types of independent third-party records—the direct Monzeki administration of Hasshi-in rice revenues in this source, the collection of rice for the Yuishiki lecture from Yokota-no-shō in Block 92, and the hosting of a Hōonkō memorial service by Nishi-Hasshi-in in Block 96—demonstrates in multiple dimensions that Hasshi-in and the surrounding Yokota-no-shō area were integrated into the economic and ritual networks of the Ichijō-in Monzeki during this period.
    Evidence of institutional continuity across the 304 years separating this record from the petition for the surrender of hereditary stipend rights The 1570 record identifying “Hasshi-in Gomai” as being under the administration of the Monzeki (Ichijō-in), and the 1874 administratively certified record identifying “Hyōsaku Hashimoto = shizoku of Ichijō-in territory, fourteen koku,” independently confirm the same institutional relationship—Hasshi-in as part of Ichijō-in territory—across a span of approximately 304 years. This correspondence forms the longest-term axis of evidence for institutional continuity from Hasshi-in to the Hashimoto family and supports the interpretation that the Hashimoto family did not become shizoku merely by chance from a local farming background, but instead occupied an institutional position within a system of direct Monzeki administration whose roots extended back to the medieval period.
    101. Kasuga Shrine Documents, Vol. 2 (published 1934) — A Collection of Local Governance and Litigation Records from Hashinoin Village (Hashinoin-mura), Including Circular Documents Jointly Signed by “Nishi-Hashinoin” and “Hosshin-in”
    A group of documents concerning Hashinoin Village (also written 橋院村 and read Hashinoin-mura) contained in Kasuga Shrine Documents, Vol. 2 (p. 853). Village administration records, cultivation agreements, and litigation documents from the Kan'ei, Meireki, and Kanbun eras explicitly record individuals such as “Hashinoin Village headman Yajiemon” and documents jointly signed by “Yajiemon and Kichizō of Hashinoin Village.” In a draft letter from Kōfuku-ji administrative monks (Document No. 961), “Nishi-Hashinoin” and “Hosshin-in” appear among the joint signatories of a circulating document. A local inquiry conducted in Meiji 4 (1871) confirmed that there was only one household bearing the surname Hashimoto in Hashinoin Village. The character “弥” (Ya), found in the names “Yajiemon” and “Yajiemon,” is also shared with Hashimoto Yaroku, who appears in the Tamon'in Nikki in Tenshō 10 (1582). These documents constitute seventeenth-century local governance records showing that Hashinoin Village was incorporated into the administrative structure of Kasuga Shrine and was recorded over multiple generations under the jurisdiction of the Tōin magistrates.

    【Historical Significance of the Sources】

    Point Significance
    Institutional evidence that “Nishi-Hashinoin” and “Hosshin-in” appear alongside Kōfuku-ji monastic houses as signatories of circulating documents In Document 961, the sequence “Nishi-Hashinoin, Muryōju-in, Hosshin-in, Tokuzō-in … Konzō-in” appears as a parallel list of signatories to a circulating document. This independently confirms, through the Kasuga Shrine Documents, that Nishi-Hashinoin and Hosshin-in functioned as institutions participating in documentary circulation alongside multiple sub-temples and monastic houses of Kōfuku-ji. This indicates that the institutional involvement of Hashinoin demonstrated in Block 96 (hosting of the Hōonkō ceremony, 1572) and Block 93 (formal response concerning the Daie assembly, 1578) continued into the Early Modern period in the concrete administrative form of the circular-document system.
    The continued use of the character “弥” in the names Yajiemon and Yajiemon as evidence of naming practices in Hashinoin Village From Hashimoto Yaroku in Tenshō 10 (1582), recorded in the Tamon'in Nikki, to Yajiemon in Kan'ei 19 (1642) and village headman Yajiemon in Meireki 2 (1656), the character “弥” continued to appear among prominent individuals of Hashinoin Village. The repeated appearance of the combination “Hashinoin Village × the character 弥” in two independent bodies of sources — the Kasuga Shrine Documents and the Tamon'in Nikki — at intervals of approximately 60 to 74 years is difficult to explain as a purely isolated coincidence. It therefore constitutes circumstantial evidence suggesting either a continuing local naming convention among the village elite or continuity within the same family line extending from the social stratum represented by Hashimoto Yaroku.
    The 1871 local confirmation that only one Hashimoto household existed in Hashinoin Village as evidence of a restricted continuity The local inquiry recording that only one household with the surname “Hashimoto” existed in Hashinoin Village in Meiji 4 (1871) is fully consistent with the Meiji 7 (1874) petition for commutation of hereditary stipend identifying “Hashimoto Hyōsaku” as the only member of the former samurai class in Hashinoin Village, as confirmed in an administrative record. This indicates that the Hashimoto family was not simply one of several unrelated Hashimoto lineages within the village, but occupied a uniquely identifiable position associated with Hashinoin. It therefore strongly suggests the possibility that the village headmen and influential residents recorded in the seventeenth-century Kasuga Shrine Documents, including Yajiemon and Yajiemon, belonged to an earlier stage of the family later represented by the Hashimoto household.
    The framework of “Hashinoin Village” under the jurisdiction of the Tōin magistrates and its institutional continuity with Ichijō-in and Daijō-in The fact that the Hashinoin Village documents in the Kasuga Shrine Documents were addressed to the “Tōin Magistrates” demonstrates that Hashinoin Village was under the jurisdiction of Tōin, an estate-management institution connected with Kasuga Shrine and Kōfuku-ji. Whereas Dai Nihon Shiryō (Block 100) records in Genki 1 (1570) that “Hashinoin rice dues” were administered by the Ichijō-in monzeki (“Gomonzeki”), these documents show that Hashinoin Village continued to be recorded under the jurisdiction of the Tōin magistrates, part of Kōfuku-ji's central administrative structure, during the Kan'ei and Meireki eras in the mid-seventeenth century. This institutional continuity independently documents the persistence of the relationship “Hashinoin = an area administered within the monzeki-related institutional sphere” across three chronological stages: Genki 1 (1570) → the Kan'ei–Meireki period (1640s–1650s) → Meiji 7 (1874, Petition for Commutation of Hereditary Stipend).
    The existence of Tōrō-den (“lantern fields”) as evidence of the religious and institutional character of Hashinoin The references to “Hashinoin Village Tōrō-den” in Documents 966 and 967, the undertakings and agreements concerning cultivators, indicate that special agricultural land associated with lantern service for Kasuga Shrine and Kōfuku-ji existed within Hashinoin Village. Tōrō-den were special fields connected with ritual lantern service associated with Kasuga Shrine, and the fact that their management was conducted through the Tōin magistrates indicates that Hashinoin Village was not merely an agricultural settlement but a locality incorporated into the ritual and institutional system of Kasuga Shrine and Kōfuku-ji. This provides additional institutional background for the hypothesis that the Hashimoto family was positioned within this system as personnel performing duties connected with an inge or monastic-house institution.
    103. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 / Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Vol. 3 (2nd Month of Bunmei 2) — Record of the Gathering of Takatsukasa Fusahira, the Ichijō-in Prelate, and the Tōhoku-in Prelate at Jōju-in, Including an All-Day Drinking Banquet, as Evidence of Interaction between Monzeki Institutions and Court Nobility
    An entry for the last day of the second month of Bunmei 2 (1470), contained in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (p. 389), and Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Vol. 3 (p. 496). Takatsukasa Fusahira (“Onkata”), the Ichijō-in Prelate, and the Tōhoku-in Prelate gathered together at Jōju-in, where the record describes an audience in the Genji-no-ma, the serving of meals, extensive drinking, and gifts of boxed goods brought from Ichijō-in and Tōhoku-in. In the following third month, the entry “The Takatsukasa Onkata proceeded to Jōju-in” is also recorded. This is an independent contemporary record showing that the Takatsukasa family, Ichijō-in, and Tōhoku-in were present together at the same location in Bunmei 2. Takatsukasa Fusahira was the father of Kyōgen, the 24th head of Ichijō-in (confirmed in Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 1), and the record supports the institutional proximity between the Takatsukasa family and Ichijō-in relevant to the possibility that a close relative of the Takatsukasa family belonged to the ancestral line of the Hashimoto family.

    【Comparison of the Three Parties at the Bunmei 2 Gathering】

    Participant Position in the Proposed Hashimoto Genealogy Confirmed Source
    Takatsukasa Fusahira (“Onkata”) Father of Kyōgen, the 24th head of Ichijō-in. A successor in the continuing involvement of the Takatsukasa family in Ichijō-in extending from Takatsukasa Mototada, father of Ryōshin, the 15th head of Ichijō-in. A figure directly relevant to Genealogy A, the leading hypothesis that a close relative of the Takatsukasa family belonged to the ancestral line of the Hashimoto family. Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 1; Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4
    Ichijō-in Prelate The superior monastic institution associated with Hashinoin (the Hashinoin estate). This represents the institutional line corresponding to the “Ichijō-in territory” recorded in Hashimoto Hyōsaku's hereditary stipend documentation. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki; records of monzeki succession
    Tōhoku-in Prelate The monastic house associated with Sanemori, the younger brother of Sanesada, who bore the designation “Hashimoto” (confirmed on the same page of Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6). This corresponds with the supporting evidence in Block 92 (Sonpi Bunmyaku §B). Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6, p. 42

    【Historical Significance of the Sources】

    Point Significance
    The gathering of Takatsukasa Fusahira, Ichijō-in, and Tōhoku-in demonstrates the institutional integration of the Takatsukasa family with the monastic-house network The record that Takatsukasa Fusahira (“Onkata”), the Ichijō-in Prelate, and the Tōhoku-in Prelate gathered together at Jōju-in in Bunmei 2 (1470) and interacted throughout the day directly confirms, through the independent third-party source Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, that the Takatsukasa family, Ichijō-in, and Tōhoku-in were connected not merely by formal relationships but by substantive institutional ties involving regular personal interaction and hospitality. Takatsukasa Fusahira was the father of Kyōgen, the 24th head of Ichijō-in (confirmed in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4, and Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 1). The presence of his “Onkata” — close relatives or members of his family circle — together with the Tōhoku-in Prelate, an institution associated with Sanemori, younger brother of Sanesada bearing the “Hashimoto” designation, provides a concrete example from the Bunmei period of the overlap between the Takatsukasa family and the monastic-house network involving individuals of the Northern Fujiwara line connected with the Hashimoto designation.
    Direct relevance to the possibility that a close relative of the Takatsukasa family belonged to the Hashimoto ancestral line Under Genealogy A (Takatsukasa line, the leading hypothesis), the working hypothesis is that collateral children or close relatives of the Takatsukasa family gradually settled in Hashinoin during the 118-year period of continuous Takatsukasa-family involvement in Ichijō-in, extending from Ryōshin (d. 1319, 15th head of Ichijō-in and son of Takatsukasa Mototada) to Kyōgen (entered Ichijō-in in 1437, 24th head and son of Takatsukasa Fusahira). Takatsukasa Fusahira, recorded in this source in Bunmei 2 (1470), was actively interacting with Ichijō-in in Nara 33 years after Kyōgen entered the institution in 1437. The presence of persons described as his “Onkata” or close family circle therefore strengthens, as institutional background, the possibility that among the Takatsukasa relatives then present in Nara were individuals who later settled in the Hashinoin area and became ancestors of the Hashimoto family.
    Chronological significance of Bunmei 2 (1470) This record dates from Bunmei 2 (1470), after Takatsukasa Fusahira had been identified as the father of Kyōgen, the 24th head of Ichijō-in, who entered the institution in 1437, and it is roughly contemporary with Ryūun, a member of the Asukai family associated with the Hashimoto original surname who returned to secular life in the fifteenth century and is recorded in Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6. The fact that Takatsukasa Fusahira, his family circle, Ichijō-in, and Tōhoku-in were together in Nara approximately 112 years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in 1582 provides a chronological window through which the possible settlement of Takatsukasa-related relatives among the ancestors of the Hashimoto family can be examined. It is also fifteen years before the appearance of “Hashimoto Ichiban” in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki in Bunmei 17 (1485), discussed in Block 98, thereby providing a multidimensional picture of the coexistence of the Takatsukasa family, the monastic-house network, and “Hashimoto” in Nara during the Bunmei period.
    104. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 / Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Vol. 3 (Bunmei 2) — Record of Takatsukasa Fusahira Moving from Nashihara to the Residence of the Temple Administrator Kōjitsu, as Evidence of the Movements of Monzeki Institutions and Court Nobility
    A record from Bunmei 2 contained in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (p. 426), and Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 8, Vol. 3 (p. 573). It records that Takatsukasa Fusahira moved from Nashihara to the residence of the temple administrator Kōjitsu in the passage “Today Lord Takatsukasa changed his lodging to the residence of the temple administrator Kōjitsu, because the residence at Nashihara was unavailable.” An editorial note states, “Earlier, Fusahira's residence at Nashihara is recorded in the entry for the 28th day of the first month; see also that entry,” demonstrating that Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki continuously recorded the circumstances of Takatsukasa Fusahira's stay in Nara. Nashihara belonged to the ushitora quadrant of the Kōfuku-ji and Kasuga Shrine precinctal division (see Block 101, Circular Document No. 954), providing geographical evidence that Takatsukasa Fusahira stayed within the monastic-estate zone surrounding Hashinoin. The same source also records petitions concerning vacancies in the bantō offices of the two halls by Kumoku-dai Kaishū and the calculation of precedents, making it an important record of temple and shrine administration.

    【Geographical Comparison between Takatsukasa Fusahira's Residences in Nara and the Area Surrounding Hashinoin】

    Place Position within the Kōfuku-ji Quadrant Division Related Sources
    Nashihara (Takatsukasa Fusahira's initial place of residence) A district belonging to the ushitora quadrant of the Kōfuku-ji precincts (Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, “Matters concerning the various cloisters and sub-temples within the temple precincts”). It belonged to the same quadrant as Tōhoku-in and Higashi-Hashinoin. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, entry for the 13th day of the 8th month of Bunmei 1; “Nashihara Jibukyō” also appears in Kasuga Shrine Document No. 954 (Block 101)
    Higashi-Hashinoin (the eastern Hashinoin institution) Ushitora quadrant (entry for Bunmei 1 in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki). A monastic house within the same quadrant as Nashihara. Report on the Survey of Daihannya-kyō Manuscripts in Nara Prefecture (Block 119); Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki
    Tōhoku-in Ushitora quadrant (same source). A monastic house where Sanemori, the younger brother of Sanesada bearing the “Hashimoto” designation, served as hōin (Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6, p. 42). Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6; Report on the Survey of Daihannya-kyō Manuscripts in Nara Prefecture (Block 119)
    Residence of the Temple Administrator Kōjitsu (Takatsukasa Fusahira's new residence) Kōjitsu was associated with Ichijō-in and appears in Block 103, in the entry for the last day of the second month of Bunmei 2, in the phrase “a messenger was sent from Ichijō-in by Kōjitsu.” The residence was therefore associated with Ichijō-in. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4, pp. 389 and 426

    【Historical Significance of the Sources】

    Point Significance
    Geographical evidence that Takatsukasa Fusahira stayed at Nashihara, located in the same ushitora quadrant as Hashinoin and Tōhoku-in Geographical evidence that Takatsukasa Fusahira stayed at Nashihara, located in the same ushitora quadrant as Hashinoin and Tōhoku-in The section “Matters concerning the various cloisters and sub-temples within the temple precincts” in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, in the entry for the 13th day of the 8th month of Bunmei 1, classifies Nashihara, Tōhoku-in, and Higashi-Hashinoin alike within the “ushitora quadrant.” The record that Takatsukasa Fusahira resided at Nashihara from the 28th day of the first month until the 22nd day recorded in Bunmei 2 demonstrates that the head of the Takatsukasa family actually resided within the same geographical administrative framework as Higashi-Hashinoin and Tōhoku-in. This constitutes one of the most direct pieces of geographical evidence supporting the practical plausibility of Genealogy A, the hypothesis that close relatives of the Takatsukasa family gradually settled in the Hashinoin area.
    Takatsukasa Fusahira's destination, the “residence of the temple administrator Kōjitsu,” demonstrates a direct connection with Ichijō-in The “Kōjitsu” named in Takatsukasa Fusahira's destination, the “residence of the temple administrator Kōjitsu,” is the same Ichijō-in-related figure appearing in Block 103, in the entry for the last day of the second month of Bunmei 2, as “a messenger was sent from Ichijō-in by Kōjitsu.” Thus, Takatsukasa Fusahira moved from Nashihara — in the ushitora quadrant and the same district as Higashi-Hashinoin — to the residence of Kōjitsu of Ichijō-in. His stay in Nara is therefore documented as a geographical movement from the vicinity of Higashi-Hashinoin to a residence directly connected with Ichijō-in. This route provides concrete contemporary evidence from Bunmei 2 of the geographical conditions under which close relatives of the Takatsukasa family could have settled within Ichijō-in territory and the Hashinoin area.
    Significance of the fact that Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki continuously recorded Takatsukasa Fusahira's stay in Nara from the first month onward The editorial note stating that “Fusahira's earlier residence at Nashihara is recorded in the entry for the 28th day of the first month” demonstrates that Jinson of the Daijōin monzeki continuously tracked and recorded Takatsukasa Fusahira's presence in Nara across multiple dated entries. Such continuous documentation indicates that the Takatsukasa family was regarded by the Daijōin monzeki not merely as transient visitors, but as actors deeply involved in Nara's network of monastic institutions, particularly in the vicinity of the ushitora quadrant where Ichijō-in, Tōhoku-in, and Higashi-Hashinoin were concentrated. This is one of the most important independent records documenting, with specific place names and individuals, the actual institutional and geographical ties that existed between the Takatsukasa family and the monastic-estate zone surrounding Hashinoin.
    Combined with Block 103, the record forms an institutional quadrilateral of “Takatsukasa family × Ichijō-in × Tōhoku-in × Nashihara (ushitora quadrant)” When Block 103 — the gathering at Jōju-in on the last day of the second month of Bunmei 2 — is considered together with this source concerning the move from Nashihara to the residence of the temple administrator Kōjitsu, three stages of Takatsukasa Fusahira's activity are documented within the single year Bunmei 2: (1) an extended stay at Nashihara in the ushitora quadrant; (2) a gathering at Jōju-in with the Ichijō-in and Tōhoku-in prelates; and (3) relocation to the residence of Kōjitsu of Ichijō-in. Taken together, these records provide a multidimensional confirmation, within a single specific year, of the geographical and personal overlap among the Takatsukasa family, Ichijō-in, Tōhoku-in, and Nashihara — the ushitora quadrant that also included Higashi-Hashinoin. This institutional framework provides historical background for examining how close relatives of the Takatsukasa family may have come to settle in the Hashinoin area.
    105. Nihon Kyōkasho Taikei, Ōrai Series, Vol. 2 / Gunsho Ruijū, Vol. 6, “Teikin Ōrai” — A Source Defining the Monzeki System and Explicitly Stating that “Ichijō-in, Daijō-in, and Others Are Monzeki Eligible to Serve as Bettō of Kōfuku-ji” and “Tōhoku-in, Sonshō-in, and Others Are Monzeki Eligible to Serve in the Administration of Tōdai-ji”
    Teikin Ōrai, a medieval ōraimono instructional text, as reproduced in Nihon Kyōkasho Taikei, Ōrai Series, Vol. 2 (published in 1967) and Gunsho Ruijū, Vol. 6 (published in 1899). It contains a basic definition of the medieval monzeki system: “Ichijō-in, Daijō-in, and others are monzeki eligible to serve as Bettō of Kōfuku-ji” and “Tōhoku-in, Sonshō-in, and others are monzeki eligible to serve in the administration of Tōdai-ji.” This medieval instructional text demonstrates that the institutional status of Ichijō-in and Tōhoku-in—the temple establishments to which the two candidate ancestral lines of the Hashimoto family belonged, namely Ryōshin (良信; Go-Hosshin-in and a monzeki of Ichijō-in) and Sanemori (実守; Tōhoku-in Hōin and the biological younger brother of Jikken [実顕], who bore the designation “Hashimoto”)—was so firmly established that it appeared as common knowledge in a widely circulated medieval instructional text.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    【Quotation】From Teikin Ōrai (Nihon Kyōkasho Taikei, Ōrai Series, Vol. 2, p. 476) — passage defining the monzeki system:

    (…) In Nara, those who have successively served as lecturers at the Yuima-e and in other major religious offices, (Tōhoku-in, Sonshō-in, and others are monzeki eligible to serve in the administration of Tōdai-ji). Ichijō-in, Daijō-in, and others are monzeki eligible to serve as Bettō of Kōfuku-ji. Prayers are to be offered, and with respect to the exposition of the Yuishiki-ron at the altar of Kasuga Shrine, this is particularly appropriate. (…)

    Regarding the hereditary estate, in recent years the cadet descendants have become adversaries, devised various unlawful schemes and complications, misrepresented matters to higher authority, and caused disturbances. In the course of litigation involving three rounds of questions and answers, it was determined that the documentary evidence submitted by both parties, the chronological order of the written instruments, and the portions established as authentic writings should constitute the essential points of the dispute. (…)

    【Definition of the Monzeki System in Teikin Ōrai and Its Correspondence with Candidate Ancestors of the Hashimoto Family】

    Statement in the Ōraimono Text Correspondence with Candidate Ancestors of the Hashimoto Family Confirming Sources
    Ichijō-in, Daijō-in, etc. = monzeki eligible to serve as Bettō of Kōfuku-ji Ichijō-in, to which Ryōshin (Go-Hosshin-in; the 15th head of Ichijō-in and a son of Takatsukasa Mototada) belonged, had become established in medieval common knowledge as a “monzeki serving as Bettō of Kōfuku-ji.” Hosshin-in (the Hosshin-in estate) belonged to this Ichijō-in institutional estate complex. Monzeki-den / Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (✅ Verified)
    Tōhoku-in, Sonshō-in, etc. = monzeki eligible to serve in the administration of Tōdai-ji Tōhoku-in, to which Sanemori (Tōhoku-in Hōin and the biological younger brother of Jikken [実顕], who bore the designation “Hashimoto”) belonged, had become established in medieval common knowledge as a “monzeki serving in the administration of Tōdai-ji.” This provides an institutional background for the possibility that a close relative connected with Tōhoku-in adopted the name Hashimoto (see Block 103). Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6, p. 42 (✅ Verified)
    Description of a dispute over a hereditary estate in which “in recent years, cadet descendants have become adversaries and devised various unlawful schemes and complications” The fact that an instructional text describes a litigation pattern in which “cadet descendants became adversaries and attempted to seize a hereditary estate” indicates that conflicts of this kind were sufficiently common in medieval society to appear in standard model correspondence. It demonstrates that disputes in which relatives or cadet descendants of monzeki-related families contested local hereditary estates, including estates such as Hosshin-in, were recognized within the legal and social framework of the period. — (Institutional description in the ōraimono text)

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Evidence that the institutional concepts “Ichijō-in / Daijō-in = Bettō of Kōfuku-ji” and “Tōhoku-in = administration of Tōdai-ji” had become part of common knowledge in medieval society Teikin Ōrai was an ōraimono text—a practical instructional collection of model correspondence—widely used for learning in medieval Japan, and its contents reflect the social conventions and institutional knowledge of the period. The fact that Ichijō-in, Daijō-in, and Tōhoku-in, institutions associated with both candidate ancestral lines of the Hashimoto family, were described in such a text as “monzeki serving as Bettō of Kōfuku-ji” and “monzeki serving in the administration of Tōdai-ji” independently confirms through an educational text that these establishments were not merely local institutions but occupied positions within the central institutional structure of medieval Japanese society.
    Cross-confirmation through two independent publications from different periods (1967 and 1899) strengthens the scholarly reliability of the evidence The fact that two independent modern scholarly publications of different dates and characters—Nihon Kyōkasho Taikei (published in 1967 as a scholarly collection of materials on the history of education) and Gunsho Ruijū (published in this edition in 1899 as a major compilation of historical Japanese texts)—both reproduce the same Teikin Ōrai text demonstrates that the content of this source has been independently preserved and confirmed in multiple scholarly contexts.
    The description of “cadet descendants disputing the hereditary estate” demonstrates the generality of patterns by which collateral relatives of monzeki lineages became established in local territories The statement in this source that “with respect to the hereditary estate, in recent years the cadet descendants have become adversaries and devised various unlawful schemes and complications” indicates that disputes involving cadet branches of powerful or monzeki-related lineages over hereditary local estates were common enough in medieval society to be incorporated into an instructional correspondence text. The hypothesis that “a close relative or cadet branch of the monzeki lineage of Ichijō-in became locally established at Hosshin-in” is therefore institutionally consistent with a recognized pattern of local settlement and hereditary-estate conflict documented in this medieval text.
    106. An Analysis of Residential-Site Formation in the Nara Basin (1982) — A Modern Scholarly Study Documenting Changes in Household Numbers, Branch-Family Formation, and the Stability of Residential Plots in Hosshin-in Village
    The discussion of Hosshin-in Village on p. 41 of An Analysis of Residential-Site Formation in the Nara Basin (Research No. 7804, published September 1982). Based on religious affiliation registers (shūmon aratame-chō) from Kansei 7 through Kaei 3, the study records ten cases of branch or separate household formation in Hosshin-in Village (including the establishment of a separate household by Jinsuke, the eldest son of Jinjiro), changes in household numbers: 33 households in Kansei 3 → 39 in Tenpō 9 → 35 in Meiji 2, and a relatively stable change in residential plots from 27 in the Bunroku period to 36 in the Kansei period. This modern academic study independently confirms that Hosshin-in Village continued to function as a stable village community during the latter part of the early modern period.
    【Comparative Context: Household Structures of Neighboring Villages — The Relative Stability of Hosshin-in Village】

    The same study also records household structures in neighboring villages within the same region as Hosshin-in. Comparison with these settlements shows that the stability in the number of households in Hosshin-in Village existed within a wider regional pattern while displaying particularly pronounced continuity and stability.

    Village Survey Period Households Three-Generation Households Population /
    Average per Household    		 Notes
    Hosshin-in Village Kansei 3–Meiji 2
    (1791–1869)    		 33 → 39 → 35 households
    (over approximately 80 years)    		 — — ✅ In practical terms, a variation of only about ±3 households. Ten branch-family formations offset extinct households, creating a closed and stable settlement structure.
    Ichieda Surveyed October 1887 (Meiji 20) 32 10 (12 at the time of the study) 174 persons /
    average 5.4 persons
    (4.6 at the time of the study)    		 3 co-resident households and 3 tenant households. Distribution by household size: 8 households with 1–3 persons, 15 with 4–6, 8 with 7–9, and 1 with 10 or more persons.
    Nakajō January 1877 (Meiji 10)
    (Meiji 17 statistics reconstructed from later annotations)    		 34 14 (17 at the time of the study) — 1 co-resident household
    【Points Derived from the Comparison】
    Both neighboring villages, Ichieda and Nakajō, maintained stable populations of approximately 30–34 households during the Meiji period. Hosshin-in Village falls within the same scale and general pattern, confirming that this part of the Nara Basin as a whole formed closed and stable village communities.

    Of particular importance is that three-generation households accounted for 31% of all households in Ichieda (10 of 32) and 41% in Nakajō (14 of 34). This indicates that succession of the main household through multigenerational co-residence was a common practice in villages of this region. The continuation of the Hashimoto family as the principal household in Hosshin-in Village across generations is entirely consistent with this regional pattern.

    Furthermore, the structure observed in Hosshin-in Village, in which extinct households and newly established branch households offset one another and kept the total number of households stable, was not an exceptional phenomenon but reflected a settlement-formation principle shared throughout the region. Within such a closed structure of multigenerational succession, there would have been structurally little room for a later-arriving family falsely assuming the lineage to become established as the village's “sole shizoku household.”

    Source: An Analysis of Residential-Site Formation in the Nara Basin (Research No. 7804), p. 41 (Call No. GC176-62) — based on religious affiliation registers and survey materials concerning Hosshin-in Village, Ichieda, and Nakajō.
