    107 ／ Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 2 (Second Month of Tenshō 3 [1575]) — A Daily Record of a Kōfuku-ji Subtemple Showing the Higan and Gyakushu Services at Nishi-Hosshin-in (Nishi-Hashinokin) and Local Interactions with the Hashimoto Family
    Entry for the second month of Tenshō 3 (1575), contained in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 2 (Vols. 12–23, p. 353). It records the fact that a messenger came from the Hashimoto family and that ripe persimmons were presented in return: “橋本ヨリ人上候之間、熟柿廿五遣之” (“Since a person came up from Hashimoto, twenty-five ripe persimmons were sent.”) The entry for the eighth day of the same month states, “西ハシノ院彼岸中日出了、頭寶藏院、來頭顯實得業”, while the entry for the ninth day states, “八万四千本逆修西ハシノキンニテ在之、來頭觀經院也”. These contemporary records demonstrate that Nishi-Hosshin-in (Nishi-Hashinokin) in Tenshō 3 served as the venue for major Buddhist observances, including the Higan service and the “84,000-copy” gyakushu memorial rite. Together with the entry for the second day, “成身院出、講クホノキン” (a lecture at Nishi-Hosshin-in), this constitutes one of the most important independent third-party sources confirming that Nishi-Hosshin-in remained a central institution within the ritual network of the Kōfuku-ji subtemples during the Tenshō period, and that the Hashimoto family maintained close local relations with the activities surrounding the institution.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Information Link
    Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 2 (Vols. 12–23, p. 353) Publication dates: Shōwa 10–14 (1935–1939)　Call No.: 640-324 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Quotation 1】From the entry for the third day of the second month of Tenshō 3 — a messenger arriving from Hashimoto and the gift of ripe persimmons:

    Second month, Tenshō 3
    (…)
    Third day: Following the repeated offering, two thousand copies of the Heart Sutra were recited; Chōken of Hori-in (…)
    Since a person came up from Hashimoto, twenty-five ripe persimmons were sent.

    【Quotation 2】From the entry for the second day of the second month of Tenshō 3 — a lecture at Nishi-Hosshin-in (Kuhonokin) hosted by Jōshin-in:

    Second day, Jōshin-in attended; the incoming head was Kannō Tokumu; the lecture was held at Kuhonokin.

    【Quotation 3】From the entry for the eighth day of the second month of Tenshō 3 — attendance at the middle day of Higan at Nishi-Hosshin-in (Nishi-Hashino-in):

    Eighth day, Attended the middle-day Higan service at Nishi-Hashino-in. The head was Hōzō-in; the incoming head was Tokugō Kenshitsu. As for myself, I first entered in the spring of the Hinoto-U year; it has now been nine years. To have formed this karmic connection as though it were only yesterday is truly humbling.
    On this day Zenjitsu Tōjari began a purple-black scripture at the western residence (…) He was said to be sixty-nine years old.

    【Quotation 4】From the entry for the ninth day of the second month of Tenshō 3 — the “84,000-copy” gyakushu rite held at Nishi-Hashinokin:

    Ninth day, The “84,000-copy” gyakushu rite was held at Nishi-Hashinokin. I attended. For the two portions, one to and one shō were provided to Himonoya in place of eighty bundles; six mon in cash were contributed for the secret offering; one shō of rice and ten mon in cash were also provided. The incoming head was Kangyō-in. Heavy rain fell throughout the day.


    【The Ritual Position of Nishi-Hosshin-in during the Tenshō Period and Its Local Relationship with the Hashimoto Family】

    Date / Entry Statement in the Source Relationship to the Hashimoto Family / Hosshin-in
    Second month, second day (“lecture at Kuhonokin”) A doctrinal lecture was held at Nishi-Hosshin-in (Kuhonokin) under the auspices of Jōshin-in. The incoming head was Kannō Tokumu. This shows that Nishi-Hosshin-in was a central subtemple capable of cooperating with Jōshin-in in conducting doctrinal lectures. It confirms the institutional function of Hosshin-in within the network of Kōfuku-ji subtemples.
    Second month, third day (“a person came up from Hashimoto”) “Since a person came up from Hashimoto, twenty-five ripe persimmons were sent.” A messenger from the Hashimoto family arrived, and Tamon'in presented twenty-five ripe persimmons in return. This is local evidence that the Hashimoto family was interacting with Tamon'in, within the precinct network of Kōfuku-ji, during a month in which ritual activities at Nishi-Hosshin-in were concentrated. It provides an independent third-party record showing that the Hashimoto family was functioning as a local presence in the area surrounding Hosshin-in.
    Second month, eighth day (middle day of Higan at Nishi-Hashino-in) Attendance at the middle-day Higan service at Nishi-Hashino-in (Nishi-Hosshin-in). The head was Hōzō-in and the incoming head was Tokugō Kenshitsu. The author of Tamon'in Nikki wrote, “I first entered in the spring of the Hinoto-U year; it has now been nine years,” emphasizing the history of his participation. Major monks associated with Kōfuku-ji, including Hōzō-in and Tokugō Kenshitsu, participated in the Higan service at Nishi-Hosshin-in. This demonstrates that Hosshin-in continued to function as an official venue for subtemple ceremonies during the Tenshō period.
    Second month, ninth day (“84,000-copy” gyakushu) “The ‘84,000-copy’ gyakushu rite was held at Nishi-Hashinokin.” The incoming head was Kangyō-in. Detailed records of rice and monetary contributions are also preserved. A large-scale memorial rite involving “84,000 copies” was conducted at Nishi-Hosshin-in. This indicates that Hosshin-in retained the economic and institutional capacity to host and support major Buddhist services during the Tenshō period. When read together with the third-day entry concerning local interaction with the Hashimoto family, it raises the possibility that the Hashimoto family participated in or was connected to this ritual-economic sphere.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    ① Contemporary local record of the Hashimoto family in Tenshō 3 (1575) The phrase “Since a person came up from Hashimoto, twenty-five ripe persimmons were sent” is a contemporary record of local interaction in which a messenger from the Hashimoto family visited a Kōfuku-ji subtemple, Tamon'in. Together with entries concerning Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Sama, this is one of the most important independent records demonstrating that the Hashimoto family was actually functioning as a local presence around Hosshin-in (Nishi-Hosshin-in) in the latter half of the sixteenth century. Its evidentiary value is strengthened by the fact that it appears in a contemporary subtemple diary rather than in a genealogy compiled during the Edo period.
    ② Confirmation that Nishi-Hosshin-in was a core venue for Kōfuku-ji subtemple ceremonies in the Tenshō period The consecutive appearance of three entries—the second-day lecture at Kuhonokin, the eighth-day Higan observance, and the ninth-day “84,000-copy” gyakushu rite—demonstrates that within the single month of the second month of Tenshō 3, Nishi-Hosshin-in hosted three major forms of religious activity: a doctrinal lecture, a Higan service, and a large-scale gyakushu memorial rite. This shows that Hosshin-in was not merely a minor subtemple, but continued to function during the Tenshō period as an institutional venue for major Kōfuku-ji religious observances, thereby reinforcing the significance of the Hashimoto family's local base in the area.
    ③ Evidence of a local retainer-type pattern of exchange: “messenger visit + reciprocal gift” involving the Hashimoto family The wording “a person came up from Hashimoto” indicates not merely a unilateral visit by the Hashimoto side, but a reciprocal exchange in which Tamon'in responded by sending “twenty-five ripe persimmons.” Such a pattern of “messenger exchange + exchange of gifts” corresponds to the type of interaction associated with locally established retainers, estate officials, or households of recognized standing connected with a subtemple, rather than with ordinary peasants or persons of low status. It therefore constitutes indirect evidence that the Hashimoto family was recognized as part of the local governing or service stratum possessing a certain degree of status within the Hosshin-in estate.
    ④ Linguistic evidence linking the forms “Kuhonokin,” “Hashinokin,” and “Hashino-in” with the Hosshin-in / Hashimoto relationship In Tamon'in Nikki, Nishi-Hosshin-in is written phonetically in forms such as “Nishi-Hashinokin (-in)” and “Kuhonokin.” “Hashinokin” reflects the sound of “Hashino-in” (橋院), showing phonetic continuity with the place-name and family name “Hashimoto.” The consecutive appearance in entries from the same second month of both “a person came up from Hashimoto” and “Nishi-Hashinokin” functions as linguistic evidence that the Hashimoto family and Nishi-Hosshin-in belonged to the same overlapping sphere of place-name, institutional name, and family name.
    ⑤ Independence of the source as a factor strengthening the inference The evaluation identifies “repeated appearances in multiple independent primary sources” as a principal factor increasing the probability of the hypothesis. This source, Tamon'in Nikki, is an independent daily subtemple diary distinct from Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Sonpi Bunmyaku, and the Kasuga Shrine documents. Its importance lies in the fact that it records “the Hashimoto family” and “Nishi-Hosshin-in (Hashinokin)” in the same contextual setting in the latter half of the sixteenth century, specifically in Tenshō 3 (1575). It therefore documents the local presence of the Hashimoto family independently of later genealogical supplementation or intentional embellishment, and functions as independent evidence increasing the Bayesian likelihood ratio of the hypothesis.

    【Relationship with Other Blocks】

    Related Block Relationship
    Hashimoto Yaroku / Hashimoto Sama (other entries in Tamon'in Nikki) Multiple entries containing the surname Hashimoto in Tamon'in Nikki—Yaroku, Sama, and the present “a person came up from Hashimoto” entry—mutually reinforce one another and confirm that the Hashimoto family appeared continuously as a locally established group in the vicinity of Hosshin-in during the latter half of the sixteenth century. The chain of multiple entries, rather than reliance on a single notice, increases the reliability of the independent documentary evidence.
    Block 101: Kasuga Shrine Document No. 954, Circular Notice This source confirms the geographical position of “Nishi-Hosshin-in” alongside Naishihara, Tōhoku-in, and Higashi-Hosshin-in within the Ushitora division. The present source provides concrete Tenshō-period ritual records demonstrating that the “Nishi-Hashinokin” appearing within this geographical framework was an actively functioning institution.
    Block 103: Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki (Takatsukasa Fusahira's stay at Naishihara) From Takatsukasa Fusahira's stay at Naishihara in Bunmei 2 (1470) to the “a person came up from Hashimoto” entry in Tenshō 3 (1575), multiple independent sources demonstrate layered interactions among the Hashimoto family, the Takatsukasa family, and subtemple institutions in the Hosshin-in area over approximately one hundred years. This documentary chain across different periods provides support for the hypothesis of genealogical continuity.
    Petition for Commutation of Hereditary Stipend, Meiji 7 (Hashimoto Hyōsaku) From the local Hashimoto record of Tenshō 3 (1575) to the petition for commutation of Hashimoto Hyōsaku's hereditary stipend in Meiji 7 (1874), this source serves as intermediate evidence helping to bridge approximately 300 years during which the Hashimoto family is argued to have continued functioning in Hosshin-in as locally based retainers and, later, as a shizoku household.

    108 ／ Gomonzeki-shū narabi ni Inge-shū Ryōchi-chō — An Official Shogunate-Recognized Register of Temple and Shrine Landholdings Recording 1,492 Koku for Ichijō-in and 914 Koku for Daijō-in
    A register of temple and shrine landholdings contained in the Gomonzeki-shū narabi ni Inge-shū Ryōchi-chō, held by the National Archives of Japan. Under the category “Temple and Shrine Lands — Monzeki — Inge,” and specifically the subsection “Gomonzeki Also Serving as Inge,” it explicitly records “千四九拾石一乗院殿” (“1,492 koku, Lord Ichijō-in”) and “九四石大乗院殿” (“914 koku, Lord Daijō-in”). This official shogunate document establishes the recognized assessed landholdings of both Ichijō-in and Daijō-in. The amount of hereditary stipend stated in Hashimoto Hyōsaku's Meiji 7 petition for stipend commutation is calculated on the basis of Ichijō-in's 1,492 koku, and therefore serves as quantitative administrative support for the conclusion that the Hashimoto family belonged to the middle or higher rank of officials, such as keishi household administrators or bōkan temple officials, receiving the equivalent of approximately 19% of Ichijō-in's estate income.

    Reference: Link to “The Abolition of Hereditary Stipends and Shizoku Resistance”

    Calculation Item Figure / Basis Source
    Officially recognized assessed yield of the Ichijō-in estate 1,492 koku Gomonzeki-shū narabi ni Inge-shū Ryōchi-chō (the present source)

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    ① An official shogunate document establishes the “assessed-yield benchmark” underlying the Hashimoto family's hereditary stipend The amount stated in Hashimoto Hyōsaku's petition for commutation of hereditary stipend is calculated using the officially recognized 1,492-koku holding of Ichijō-in recorded in this source as its starting point. By providing the official assessed-yield benchmark, this shogunate-recognized document administratively connects the Meiji-period hereditary-stipend record with the assessed economic scale of the Ichijō-in estate inherited from the earlier period. The evaluation that “the Hashimoto family's hereditary stipend corresponded to approximately 19% of the income of the Ichijō-in estate” could not be quantitatively supported without the benchmark supplied by this source.
    ② The difference between Ichijō-in (1,492 koku) and Daijō-in (914 koku) demonstrates Ichijō-in's superior economic position The difference in assessed yield between Ichijō-in at 1,492 koku and Daijō-in at 914 koku is explicitly recorded in an official shogunate-recognized document and reflects a difference in the economic scale of the two monzeki institutions. Together with the fact that Hosshin-in (the Hosshin-in estate) belonged to Ichijō-in, this shows that the Hashimoto family was situated within the economic sphere of a monzeki estate considerably larger than that of Daijō-in.
    ③ A “chain of administrative authentication through official documents” supporting the inference The analysis identifies “administrative authentication through the Meiji 7 official document (the petition for commutation of hereditary stipend)” as the primary factor increasing the probability of the hypothesis. The present source, an official shogunate register of assessed landholdings, functions as a higher-level official document supplying the numerical basis for that stipend-commutation petition. In other words, it completes the documentary chain “Gomonzeki-shū narabi ni Inge-shū Ryōchi-chō (shogunate-recognized assessed yield) → Meiji 7 Petition for Commutation of Hereditary Stipend (administrative authentication) → Hashimoto Hyōsaku's shizoku status”, demonstrating that multiple independent official documents support the status attributed to the Hashimoto family.
    109 ／ Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 4 (April, Tenshō 17) — Kōfuku-ji Subtemple Daily Record Showing the “Customary Practice” (恒之者也) of the Nishi-Hashinoin Courtesy Visit, the Hashinoin First-Night-Service Difficulty, and the Tōhokuin Daie Seigi Official Letter
    Entry for April of Tenshō 17 (1589), contained in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 4 (Books 32–40). The entry for the 12th states, “西ハシノイン見廻トテ太餅一重持被來了、恒之者也”, recording that a courtesy visit from Nishi-Hashinoin, accompanied by a tray of large rice cakes, was regarded as a “customary practice” (tsune no mono nari) at Tamon'in. The entry for the 17th states, “發心院初夜重難事被申間、只一ロッ、書遣之了”, recording that Tamon'in sent a written note in response to a difficulty concerning the first-night service at Hashinoin. On the 13th of the same month, “從寺家東北院大會精義可仕之由奉書到來”, an official letter also arrived concerning the Daie Seigi duty at Tōhokuin. These entries show that Nishi-Hashinoin (the local institutional base associated with the Hashimoto family) and Tōhokuin (a subtemple where Sanemori, bearing the Hashimoto name, served as Hōin) both left records of interaction with Tamon'in within the same month of Tenshō 17. As a record appearing fourteen years after Tenshō 3 (Block 107), this is an important source supporting the long-term continuity of relations between the Hashimoto family, Hashinoin, and the Kōfuku-ji subtemple network.

    【Major Entries for April, Tenshō 17, and Their Relationship to Hashinoin, the Hashimoto Family, and Tōhokuin】

    Date / Entry Statement in the Source Relationship to Hashinoin and the Hashimoto Family
    April 12 (Courtesy visit from Nishi-Hashinoin) “A courtesy visit was made from Nishi-Hashinoin, bringing one tray of large rice cakes; this is the customary practice.” The visit from Nishi-Hashinoin to Tamon'in is explicitly described as “恒之者” (“a customary practice”). This confirms that the same type of local interaction continued fourteen years after the Tenshō 3 entry in Block 107 stating that “a person came from Hashimoto” and that twenty-five ripe persimmons were sent. The expression “恒之者也” demonstrates that the exchange was not merely temporary or incidental, but had become an established customary practice.
    April 13 (Official letter concerning the Tōhokuin Daie Seigi duty) “An official letter arrived from the temple authorities stating that the Daie Seigi duty at Tōhokuin was to be performed.” An official communication from the Kōfuku-ji temple authorities arrived concerning the Seigi role associated with the assistant Ryūsha position in the first-night study session of the Yuima-e. Tōhokuin was the subtemple where Sanemori, who bore the Hashimoto name, served as Hōin (Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6, p. 42). An official letter concerning Tōhokuin reached Tamon'in in the same month as the Nishi-Hashinoin courtesy visit of the 12th. Thus, “the Hashimoto family, Nishi-Hashinoin, and Tōhokuin” all appear in records connected with Tamon'in within the same month of Tenshō 17.
    April 17 (Difficulty concerning the first-night service at Hashinoin) “Because a serious difficulty concerning the first-night service at Hashinoin was reported, I wrote and sent a brief note.” Tamon'in responded in practical terms by sending a written communication regarding a difficulty in the administration of a religious service at Hashinoin. This was more than ceremonial contact: it indicates institutional cooperation in addressing an operational problem and demonstrates that Hashinoin and Tamon'in maintained a mutually supportive relationship in the administration of religious ceremonies.

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Details
    ① The phrase “恒之者也” demonstrates the institutionalization of exchanges between Nishi-Hashinoin and Tamon'in The expression “恒之者也” indicates that Eishun, the author of Tamon'in Nikki, regarded this exchange as an established customary practice. When read together with the Tenshō 3 entry in Block 107 stating that “a person came from Hashimoto,” it confirms that institutional exchanges between Nishi-Hashinoin—the local institutional base associated with the Hashimoto family—and Tamon'in continued for at least fourteen years, from 1575 to 1589.
    ② Evidence that Tamon'in was practically involved in the “first-night-service difficulty” at Hashinoin The statement “Because a serious difficulty concerning the first-night service at Hashinoin was reported, I wrote and sent a brief note” records more than ceremonial exchange. It shows that Tamon'in responded practically to a difficulty in the administration of a religious ceremony. This demonstrates a mutually supportive relationship between Hashinoin and Tamon'in and corresponds with the structure in which the Hashimoto family supported Hashinoin's local institutional and ceremonial base, as discussed in Block 107.
    ③ Significance of the fact that Nishi-Hashinoin and Tōhokuin both appear in connection with Tamon'in during the same month of April, Tenshō 17 The appearance in immediate succession of the Nishi-Hashinoin courtesy visit on the 12th and the official letter concerning the Tōhokuin Daie Seigi duty on the 13th strengthens the evidence for an institutional overlap among the “Hashimoto family, Nishi-Hashinoin, and Tōhokuin” in a contemporary record from Tenshō 17. Tōhokuin was the subtemple where Sanemori, bearing the Hashimoto name, served as Hōin according to Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6, p. 42. It therefore constitutes an important point at which medieval genealogical information intersects with late-Sengoku-period records of everyday subtemple activity.
    ④ Fourteen years of successive records from Block 107 (Tenshō 3) demonstrate the long-term continuity of the Hashimoto family's local presence Multiple independent entries confirm that interaction between Nishi-Hashinoin and Tamon'in continued over the fourteen years from Block 107 (Tenshō 3 / 1575) to the present source (Tenshō 17 / 1589). Given that repeated appearances in multiple independent primary-source records are regarded as a major factor increasing historical probability, successive records separated by time within the same institutional diary directly satisfy that evidentiary criterion.
    ⑤ Evidentiary value as a contemporary Tenshō-period record independent of later genealogical embellishment Later Edo- and early-modern-period genealogies are secondary or tertiary sources whose evidentiary value is necessarily limited. By contrast, this source is an institutional daily diary written in Tenshō 17 (1589), and is therefore a contemporary record independent of later genealogical embellishment or intentional reconstruction. It is also an entirely separate primary source from the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Sonpi Bunmyaku, Kasuga Shrine documents, and the petition for commutation of hereditary stipend. It therefore functions as independent evidence capable of increasing the Bayesian likelihood ratio of the historical hypothesis.

    【Relationship with Other Blocks】

    Related Block Connection
    Block 107 (Tamon'in Nikki, February, Tenshō 3) From the Tenshō 3 (1575) entries stating “a person came from Hashimoto,” “the middle day of the equinoctial observance at Nishi-Hashinoin,” and “the 84,000-copy posthumous-merit rite at Nishi-Hashinoin,” to the Tenshō 17 (1589) entries recording the “customary” Nishi-Hashinoin courtesy visit and the difficulty concerning the Hashinoin first-night service, the records demonstrate fourteen years of continuous interaction between Nishi-Hashinoin and Tamon'in.
    Block 103 / Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki (Takatsukasa Fusahira and Tōhokuin) From the record of Takatsukasa Fusahira's stay and interaction with Tōhokuin in Bunmei 2 (1470) to the official letter concerning the Tōhokuin Daie Seigi duty in Tenshō 17 (1589), a chain of records spanning approximately 120 years demonstrates that Tōhokuin continued to function as an important component of the Kōfuku-ji subtemple network across generations.
    Block 108 (Gomonzekishū narabi Ingeshū Ryōchichō) The landholding register showing 1,492 koku for Ichijōin provides the economic foundation upon which such institutional exchanges as the “customary” Nishi-Hashinoin courtesy visit could operate. It confirms that the economic scale of the Ichijōin estate system, to which the Hashimoto family belonged, and the actual pattern of local exchanges can be situated within the same institutional chain.
    Meiji 7 Petition for Commutation of Hereditary Stipend (Hashimoto Hyōsaku) Between the Tenshō 17 (1589) record demonstrating the continuation of Nishi-Hashinoin's local institutional interactions and the Meiji 7 (1874) petition for commutation of hereditary stipend, this source fills an intermediate stage in the approximately 285-year historical continuity during which the Hashimoto family functioned locally at Hashinoin as retainers and, later, as members of the former samurai class.

    Entry for April of Tenshō 17 (1589), contained in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 4. It records that Nishi-Hashinoin brought one tray of large rice cakes as part of a courtesy visit and explicitly describes this as “恒之者也” (“the customary practice”). Other entries include the purchase of timber for construction of an earthen wall in Osaka by Kisshōin and Jōnyoin, the Thirty-Lecture observance, the beginning of a period of abstinence, sutra recitations, an official letter and reply concerning duties in the first-night study session of the Yuima-e, a written response concerning a difficulty with the first-night service at Hashinoin, pilgrimage visits, bathing, and construction matters. It is a record of everyday temple activity that includes continuing interaction with Hashinoin.
    Quoted from Tamon'in Nikki III (p. 276; available in the National Diet Library Digital Collections; publication date: 1936; Call No. 210.48-E38t-T, link to the National Diet Library) →
    April, Tenshō 11
    22nd, at Hōchiin, an assembly for the Eight Lectures and the Forty-Thousand Ceremony was held. The midday meal was served. Since it had been said that no gifts were to be accepted, none were brought. It was a full day of recreation and activity, and was memorable.
    On the preceding day, the 21st, it was reported that the mother of Gyōkōbō of Kisshōin had died.
    23rd, the matter of borrowing rice was presented from Jūgo.
    24th, concerning the rice from Jūgo, the matter was discussed with Renshōin. It was agreed that fifty koku could be borrowed. Of this amount, twenty koku were delivered today for half a piece of gold, together with fifteen koku of actual rice. The remaining fifteen koku were arranged to be borrowed through Renshōin. Ueda Sama-no-jō, Gon-no-jō, and Tōshichirō came up.
    At Sōshuin, the wisteria blossoms were viewed. Three people unexpectedly gathered, and arrangements were made for the Rakan offering. Next, Kainyo Shikizenbō came. A midday meal was sent to those remaining at Chūin.
    25th, the Monju incantation was announced. Rice was brought from Shakuhachi, and five to were delivered, leaving one koku.
    After midday, there was an unexpected rain accompanied by a severe hailstorm. It fell heavily and was extraordinary. This too was considered an ill omen.
    26th, Chūin withdrew. There were three to and nine shō of special offerings. The lecturer for the seventh day diligently performed the second section, “returning the branches to the root.” The lecturer for the fourth day had not yet arrived. The Monju lecture had not been formally requested. In total, approximately eight to were expected to be required.
    27th, three bundles of lecture sutras were at Kōzenin, one of which was written by Chōken. Ten hiki each were given at Kōzenin for bathing. The day was spent in recreation and household arrangements. Five to of rice were delivered from Shakuhachi, leaving five to. A message was sent accordingly. Wine was provided to please the administrator of the offerings, Shikken.
    28th, I visited the shrine and also visited Tōdai-ji Hachiman Shrine.
    A load of mako was sent as a courtesy gift in connection with construction work at the house of Bizen Emon-tarō. Together with the compensation arrangements, one to and two shō were sent as payment, being treated as provisions. A message was also sent to Oka Jin concerning arrears, together with one load.
    Cloth for permanent use arrived from the cloth merchant. One to was sent as a gift. The tailoring had been entrusted to Hashinobō, and it arrived today. A gift should be sent in return.
    For prayers concerning Junkei's departure for military service, a devotional recitation of the Daihannya-kyō was distributed, with one fascicle assigned to each participant.
    The house of Sukejirō at Sanmaiden was set on fire and burned down. This was a grave offense, and it was ordered that a notice board be erected.
    A matter arose concerning Tōnomine; it may develop into a conflict.
    29th, at Chikurinin, an assembly for the Eight Lectures and the Fifty-Thousand Ceremony was held. I attended. Ten bundles of noodles were sent. The arrangements were extraordinarily elaborate and astonishing. There was heavy rain and wind.
    30th, last night the unopened gate of Tōdai-ji was blown down. That temple and its Great Buddha were founded in Tenpyō 16, making approximately 780 years up to the present year. Even during the great windstorm of the third day of the tenth month of Eiso 1, it did not fall. Nor was it destroyed when, on the 28th day of the twelfth month of Jishō 4, on Kiyomori's orders, his son Taira no Shigehira attacked Nanto and almost everything was burned. In Kyōroku 5, on the 17th day of the seventh month, there was a great uprising; more recently, on the tenth day of the tenth month of Eiroku 10, the Great Buddha Hall burned, and this very gate was fortified and used as part of the defenses, yet it suffered no harm. It had escaped repeated disasters of wind and fire, but now it collapsed in the wind the other night. This must surely be an ominous manifestation concerning that temple, and perhaps a sign that the destruction of Buddhism throughout the realm is approaching. An inscription written by Kōbō Daishi on the plaque reads, “Temple for the Protection of the Nation by the Four Heavenly Kings of the Golden Light.” The Four Great Heavenly Kings were installed in the four directions. Truly, this is lamentable. With only today or tomorrow perhaps remaining to my life, I feel that the moment of the destruction of the Three Treasures has come before my very eyes, and I am overwhelmed with sorrow.
    At the shrine precinct, a tree fell upon the building of Jissōbō and completely destroyed it. Within the temple, the golden lantern of the Hakkondō was blown over. Roofs and earthen walls in many places were entirely damaged. The northern screen of the eastern quarters fell, and the second story of Daikiin was blown apart. I asked a priest from Hōryū-ji who had come to worship at the shrine, and he said that to the west there had been virtually no wind at all; only upon entering the western outskirts of Nara did the wind begin to blow. Even the barley had suffered almost no damage there. A charcoal seller said that throughout the mountains the wind had blown violently. It had been a southeastern wind. Our own residence was protected by the grove of Jōnyoin. This year there have been repeated ominous events: several major earthquakes; the water of Sarusawa Pond changed; on the third day of the third month the sacred offerings for both the main Kasuga sanctuary and Wakamiya collapsed; there was the great hailstorm on the 25th; and now this extraordinary wind. I ponder these matters deeply.
    The divine incantations totaled 257,800 recitations.
    Bizen Emon-tarō came up regarding his appointment as administrator of Sanmaiden and concerning Jinsuke's intentions. I replied that the matter should proceed according to their circumstances. It was said that in the south the wind had not blown severely and the barley had suffered no harm.
    Fourth month
    1st, I visited the shrine. Although the weather threatened rain, none fell. It was greatly appreciated that the Yamato religious observance could proceed without incident.
    111
    An autobiographical account by Hashimoto Masaharu contained in Tako: Autobiography, Vol. 1. This Meiji-period personal biographical source records that he was born in Hasshiin, Harumichi Village, Soegami District, Nara Prefecture; that the Hashimoto family was an old-established family whose members had served successively as village headmen during the former shogunate period; that his father's elder brother, Yoshitaro, supported himself through a combination of farming and commerce; that his mother was Tomie; that his father engaged in missionary work alone in Rishiri Island, Hokkaido, Nagasaki, and at the Harumichi Church in Izu-Shichijo; and that his mother endured hardship while living communally with others.
    Tako: Autobiography, Vol. 1 (available in the National Diet Library Digital Collections; published in 1954; call number 289.1-H278t; written by Hashimoto Masaharu; Link to the National Diet Library), quoted as follows → For reference, I shall briefly describe the circumstances before Nagasaki. My birthplace was a farming village of only twenty or thirty households called Hasshiin, Harumichi Village, Soegami District, Nara Prefecture, situated in the very center of the broad Yamato Plain, surrounded on all sides by mountains like a green enclosure. The Hashimoto family was an old-established family whose members had served as village headmen for generations during the former shogunate period, and possessed an imposing house and estate in one corner of the village. At the time of my birth, the head of the family was my father's elder brother Yoshitaro, who made his living partly through farming and partly through commerce. Both of my grandparents had already passed away. My father, Umetaro, aged twenty-three, had gone away without permission to engage alone in missionary work on the distant island of Rishiri in Hokkaido, while my mother Tomie, aged nineteen, was living modestly as a dependent in the household of my father's elder brother and his wife. When my mother gave birth to her first child, the husband on whom she relied was nowhere to be found, and she waited for news from him thousands of miles away. Thus I was born, entirely unaware of my mother's hardships, a plump and healthy baby. It is said that when they tried to take my photograph, they had to fan me with a hand fan before I would finally open my eyes. Not long after I was born, my father was brought back from the Kurile Islands, but soon departed once again for missionary work in Nagasaki. When I was two years old, my mother packed the small amount of luggage she had brought with her at marriage and moved into the Harumichi Church at Izu-Shichijo. For approximately the next year and a half, until my father's missionary activities finally began to bear fruit and establish a foundation, my mother, taking me with her, experienced the very depths of hardship in church life. She had been the youngest daughter of a prosperous household and had known little hardship, yet she was separated from the husband on whom she depended and was forced to live communally with more than thirty unsympathetic strangers, while burdened with a small child.
    112
    An entry from October 1580 (Tensho 8) contained in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1. Statements such as “went to Hasshiin,” “the arrangements concerning the toya were largely settled,” “requests were to be made in various places for borrowed articles,” and “Hasshiin requested assistance in obtaining borrowed articles from various places” provide evidence concerning borrowed goods, assistance, and the administration of the toya at Hasshiin (Hashinokin). This is a source concerning the economic and administrative operations of a temple institution.
    Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 (Volumes 1–11) (p. 238 and elsewhere; available in the National Diet Library Digital Collections; published in Showa 10 [1935]; call number 640-324; Link to the National Diet Library), quoted as follows → October, Tensho 8 [1580]
    6th: The Rakan-ku service of Jiho-in was performed twice. Shiro went down to the countryside. A letter was sent to the Itami side.
    7th: I went to Toin-dono because I had been instructed to attend a sake gathering connected with the transmission of the records of the Daie. I wore a layered robe, but no kesa. There were more than thirty people. At the first serving there were zoni and rice cakes; at the second, somen noodles and gifts; at the third, ...
    That evening, I played go at the residence of Choen-bo. Azuki persimmons were served.
    8th: The arrangements for salt were completed. At the midday meal, soup was provided by Shujo-bo. After midday I went to see the shops, and from there proceeded to Shin-Yakushiji.
    It is said that since the day before yesterday retainers of the Kizawa side had been installed at Hokiji. Shindo-dono was the petitioner. This was the affair of Katsushi.
    Shiro returned from the countryside.
    9th: From midday, matters concerning Ichiji-kan were conducted. I went to Hasshiin. The arrangements concerning the toya were for the most part settled. In connection with this, I was instructed to make requests at various places concerning borrowed articles, and accordingly made several such requests.
    The Sanzo-e was scheduled to be held on the coming eighteenth. However, one of the three monks of Jofuku-in who was to serve as a rissha had suddenly lost his father, apparently on the eighth. Because of the mourning restriction, I was requested by the supply administrator to perform the duty at this residence instead. However, because there was insufficient time to prepare the tanshaku, a request was made concerning whether the date could be postponed. Renge-in stated that the temple authorities had responded that the matter might be handled as circumstances required. Nevertheless, Seinan'in-dono was opposed.
    10th: Renge-in made a request to the temple authorities, and the date was postponed. It was therefore decided that I should perform the duty. The matter of the seigi was then communicated to Renge-in. The tanshaku concerned the Kenshogi.
    I listened to a tanshaku lecture at Komyo-in concerning distinctions in the Dharma. Afterward, I was again requested to go around in connection with the borrowed articles required for the toya, and I accepted the task.
    11th: Mushrooms were available. Echigo Chubei, Rensei-in, Sanzo-in, and others came.
    Hasshiin requested assistance in obtaining borrowed articles from various places, and accordingly I made requests to each of them.
    It was reported that Dai-Tenkyo-in had arranged for one koku of sekihan, but since twelve koku had already been secured, the request was withdrawn. In the evening I went into the temple precincts.
    12th: At dawn I went briefly to Hasshiin. Concerning the seated dishes, I was instructed to make a request to Joshin-in through Choshun-bo. When the request was made, it was said that approval had been given for arrangements covering 250 servings.
    Concerning the furnishings of Daijo-in-dono—folding screens, bamboo blinds, tiered shelves, a somen steamer, and a platform—I was instructed to make the request through Chozen-bo. Accordingly, I submitted a written list, but no reply had yet been received. Concerning the cover for the flute, I had previously been instructed to make a request to Ichijo-in-dono through the cypress-bark craftsman. A reply arrived today stating that approval had been granted.
    From the 13th I went down to the countryside.
    I returned on the 19th and made various requests and reminders.
    20th: As customary, matters connected with Sanzo were carried out.
    21st: Paper paste was prepared. Two loads of bamboo were brought up.
    22nd: Ninsho-bo came from Koya. He brought a tea container and a razor as gifts, and likewise presented gifts to the head priest.
    It is said that Kitamuro-in, formerly residing north of the peak at Tanigamine, had moved to Takamuro-in at Oda-wara on June 21.
    23rd: The Sanzo-e kengi was carried out at this residence.
    The assigned subject was Kenshogi, and the seigi was performed by Kenshitsu-bo, a master of the Five Doctrines.
    The first questioner was Kyoen-bo; from the second question onward, the questioners were monks of intermediate seniority.
    The first rissha was Gyoko-bo, the second was from this residence, and the third was from Seinan-in. The ceremony was conducted at Ichijo-in. The temple administrative clergy attended. Toin Sozu Kanenori, the supply administrator Gyohan, and others were present. The departure point for this residence was the main lecture platform. A sake gathering was held in the customary manner.
    Sekihan, assorted sweets, and sake were served.
    The questioners and the other seigi participants and supply administrators received their portions.
    Approximately ten attendants of the monzeki and four sento also received sake.
    The monthly waiting observance was conducted.
    24th: As Ninsho-bo was returning home, I had him escorted as far as Tsutsui no Kurabo.
    113. Ryoshin
    Daijoin Jisha Zojiki, Vol. 6, Jinson Daisojo-ki, p. 98, call number 554-213, bibliographic ID 000000778530, publisher: Sankyo Shoin, published in Showa 8 (1933), held in the National Diet Library Digital Collections.
    This source establishes the following two points on the basis of a primary historical record.

    ① Confirmation that Ryoshin was the 14th head of Ichijoin:
    “At that time, the various inke were for the most part members of the lineage of this monzeki. The Ichijoin lineage, moreover, continued without interruption from Sojo Ryoen and Sojo Jisshin down to Sojo Kakujitsu. Kakujitsu was likewise a descendant of this monzeki lineage. From Ryosho onward, they belonged entirely under this monzeki. According to the genealogical chart:”
    ◯ (Founder of Ryugein) Raishin (Homu Kanjo Sojo; 4th head of Ichijoin) → (Ryugein Daisojo) Kakushin (Ichijoin) → (Ichijoin Shinsho) Genkaku → (Daijoin Daisojo) Jinpan (Ichijoin) and (Ichijoin Shinsho) Eshin → (Daijoin) Shinen (Zenjoin; Daisojo; Homu) → (Daijoin Daisojo) Jisson (7th head of Daijoin) and Ryoen (Ichijoin Shinsho; 10th head of Ichijoin) → (Daijoin Daisojo) Enjitsu and (Daijoin Daisojo) Jisshin (from here, the Ichijoin succession continues down to Kakujitsu; from Ryoen to Kakujitsu there are seven generations in total) → (Homu; Daijoin Daishinsho) Jishin → (Homu; Daijoin Daisojo) Jinkaku and (Homu; Tohokuin Daishinsho) Kakuen (disciple-line of Kokaku; succeeded to the monzeki) and (Homu; Ichijoin Daisojo) Ryosho and (Toin Shinsho) Kogyo → (Daijoin Daishinsho) Kakuson and (Homu; Ichijoin Daishinsho) Kakujitsu and (Ichijoin Sojo) Ryoken and (appointed to the first seat of Daijoin) Kyokaku and (Jionin Shinsho) Yogyo and (Ichijoin Sojo) Shoen and (Shunanin Shinsho) Koken → (Homu; Daijoin Daisojo) Kokaku and (Ichijoin; Gon-Shosozu) Jitsugen and (Butsuchiin Shinsho) Koshun and (Toin Shinsho) Yoen → (Toin Risshi) Sonshu and (Daijoin Daisozu) Kyoson and (Hounin Shinsho) Jitsui and (Tohokuin Daishinsho) Shunen and (Lecturer; Butsuchiin) Shunyu and (Lecturer; Chikurinin Hoin) Joshun and (Tomonin Daisojo) Koyu → (Daisojo; Daijoin Homu) Seikaku and (Tomonin) Chigen and Ninen.
    “The dispute between the two monzeki also arose in part from this. After Kakujitsu entered nirvana, Zenji Jitsugen proved unsuitable in various matters, and because Daisojo Kokaku was to manage the affairs of that monzeki, great disorder arose from the arrangements. Consequently, Jitsugen died without achieving his original purpose. From the third day of the seventh month, fighting continued into the night. This marked the beginning of the destruction of the temple institution. Thereafter, proper order ceased to exist, and the estates of both monzeki were entirely taken over and appropriated by provincial warriors.”
    Second: Enkaku; Third: Saien.
    (Several lines are missing from the original manuscript here.)
    20th Kokaku; 21st Kyoson; 22nd Chishin; 23rd Kojin; 24th Koen; 25th Kyokaku; 26th Jinson.
    Order of the heads of Ichijoin: Founder Josho; Second Joko; Third Shinpan; Fourth Raishin; Fifth Kakushin; Sixth Genkaku; Seventh Eshin; Eighth Jinpan; Ninth Shinen; Tenth Ryoen; Eleventh Jisshin; Twelfth Shinsho; Thirteenth Kakusho; Fourteenth Ryoshin; Fifteenth Ryokaku; Sixteenth Kakujitsu; Seventeenth Jitsugen; Eighteenth Ryogen; Nineteenth Ryosho; Twentieth Ryoken; Twenty-first Shoen; Twenty-second Kyogen.
    “Since the foundation, the principal votive estates of Ichijoin comprised twelve places, beginning with Sahoda; the principal Daijoin estates likewise comprised twelve places, beginning with the Yanagimoto shrine lands. In addition, both monzeki possessed several tens of shoen. The inke succeeded to them separately, or administered them as lands entrusted under votive arrangements. Fundamentally, each side had twelve such places.”
    “The above has been recorded as it came to mind for the benefit of later readers, so that the benevolence of the founding and former masters may be repaid.”

    ② Explicit institutional basis showing that the various inke, including Hasshiin, were composed of members of the monzeki lineages:
    “At that time, the various inke were for the most part members of the lineage of this monzeki.”

    Accordingly, the institutional basis of Genealogy A—that Ryoshin, later associated with Hasshiin and identified here as the 14th head of Ichijoin, effectively exercised control and administration over Hasshiin—is supported by a primary source. This further strengthens the possibility that Ryoshin, as an administrator of Ichijoin estates, from which the stipend of the Hashimoto Hyosaku family is considered to have originated, represents the strongest candidate for a Fujiwara-line ancestor.

    114
    Daijoin Jisha Zojiki, Vol. 4, contains the succession list of the heads of Ichijoin, covering 24 generations from Sozu Josho to Kyogen and detailing Fujiwara origins, imperial-family origins, succession through disciples, years of appointment, and ages at ordination; the succession list of the heads of Daijoin, covering 36 generations from Ryuzen to Jinson; and the successive heads and transmissions of Ryugejuin, Zenjoin, Hojoin, and other institutions. It is an important temple-shrine source documenting the succession genealogies of Kofukuji betto and monzeki temples.

    Succession of the heads of Ichijoin:
    Founder, Daisozu Josho.
    A member of the Fujiwara clan, a native of Sakyo, disciple of Sozu Ninken, also a Dharma-transmission disciple of Sojo Kanku; he studied both Shingon and Hosso doctrines, became the first choja of Toji and betto of Kofukuji, and founded Ichijoin.
    Second head, Iko Joko.
    A native of Heguri District, Yamato Province; disciple of Josho Sozu through Gishun.
    Third head, Sojo Shinpan.
    A member of the Taira clan, son of Harima no Kami Narimasa; disciple of Iko Joko; entered the chamber of Risshi Seihan.
    Fourth head, Homu Gon-Sojo Raishin.
    A member of the Fujiwara clan, son of Kai no Zenji Yoritsune; disciple of Sojo Shinpan; entered the chamber of Sojo Saishin and studied under Iko Juen.
    Fifth head, Homu Daisojo Kakushin, known as the Kowa Daisojo.
    A son of Kyogoku-dono Morozane; ordained in Joho 1 at the age of ten; disciple of Sojo Raishin; founder of Ryugejuin. Homu Gon-Sojo Raishin was descended through Seihan from Sojo Shinpan. Having mastered the esoteric teachings and become a pillar of the temple institution, he was admitted among the disciples because of his exceptional virtue and learning.
    Sixth head, Sojo Genkaku, known as the Chu-Sojo.
    A younger brother of the preceding; ordained in Ten'nin 2 at the age of eleven; disciple of Daisojo Kakushin.
    Seventh head, Homu Sojo Eshin, originally named Kakuno, known as the Izu Sojo.
    A son of Hosshoji-dono; ordained in Daiji 1 at the age of thirteen; disciple of Sojo Genkaku.
    Eighth head, Homu Daisojo Shinen, founder of Hiyamaji.
    A younger brother of the preceding; ordained in Oho 1 at the age of nine; entered the chamber of Sojo Eshin; attached as a disciple to Daisojo Jinpan; also received the oral transmission of the two esoteric teachings from the deceased Bodaiin Sojo Zoshun. When Sojo Eshin left the temple and the headship was changed, a choja proclamation dated the third day of the second month of Eiman 2 appointed him head of Ichijoin, issued by the lay betto, Uchu-ben Toshitsune.
    Ninth head, Homu Daisojo Jinpan, originally named Kokaku, founder of Uchiyamadera, known as Daijoin.
    Younger brother of Sojo Genkaku; ordained in Eikyu 1 at the age of thirteen; entered the chamber of Daisojo Kakushin. Because Shinen had become a senior cleric, a choja proclamation ordering support was issued, and on the twenty-third day of the seventh month of Joan 2 another choja proclamation appointed him head of Ichijoin.

    Eleventh head, Sojo Ryoen, Kujo Shinsho, known as Jakusho Ichijoin.

    Twelfth head, Homu Daisojo Jisshin, known as the Kokawa Sojo.

On the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month of Kenpo 5, he entered the chamber of Daijoin Sojo Jisson, thereby inheriting Hoshakuin and other properties.     Thirteenth head, Homu Daisojo Shinsho, known as the Sugawara Sojo.

    Fourteenth head, Homu Daisojo Kakusho, known as Shojokoin.

    Fifteenth head, Homu Daisojo Ryoshin.

On the third day of the seventh month of Kann'o 2, a dispute arose with Daijoin Sojo Kokaku, and after more than twenty years it developed into armed conflict. He took Zenji Ryogen, son of Prince Nakatsukasa, as a disciple; he was also treated as an adopted child of Nijo Kanpaku Yoshimoto. Around Eiwa 2, he retired from the headship.
    Nineteenth head, Daisojo Ryosho.

    A son of the late Minister of the Right Gojishinin; ordained in Oei 24; entered the chamber in the year following the death of Sojo Ryoken; retired in Kyoto on the twentieth day of the third month of Eikyo 6; died on the third day of the ninth month of Eikyo 9 at the age of thirty.

    26th.”

    The above source reveals the following important facts.
    1. Confirmation of Ryoshin's origin and career:
    “Fifteenth head, Homu Daisojo Ryoshin, son of Enkoin-dono Mototada; ordained during the Einin era; disciple of Sojo Kakusho. Because Tokugo Shinsuke and Zenji Kakujitsu died young, Ryoshin became head.”
    → Father: Takatsukasa Mototada (Enkoin-dono); ordination: during the Einin era (1293–1299). He became head after the premature deaths of Shinsuke and Kakujitsu.
    2. Difference in ordinal numbering requiring caution:
    In Vol. 4, Ryoshin is recorded as the 15th head, whereas Vol. 6 records him as the 14th. Priority is provisionally given to the more detailed biographical information in Vol. 4, and the 15th-head interpretation is therefore provisionally adopted. Further verification is required.
    3. Discovery of Kyogen, the 24th head, from the Takatsukasa family:
    “Twenty-fourth head, Homu Daisojo Kyogen, son of Takatsukasa-dono Fusahira; entered the chamber in the sixth month of Eikyo 9 and was ordained in Eikyo 11.”
    → Kyogen was a member of the Takatsukasa family who entered Ichijoin in Eikyo 9 (1437). Chronologically, he lived approximately four generations before Hashimoto Yaroku (1582) and therefore deserves attention as a candidate for a Fujiwara-line ancestor whose chronology is more compatible than that of Ryoshin, who died in 1319. The possibility that a secondary son or close relative of Kyogen settled in Hasshiin should be investigated further.
    4. Shinsuke and Kakujitsu, who died young, as newly identified collateral-line candidates:
    Ryoshin became head because the preceding candidates, Shinsuke Tokugo and Kakujitsu Zenji, died young. This raises the possibility that close relatives or secondary-line descendants of these deceased candidates may have settled in or around Hasshiin.
    5. Ryoshin's accession to the headship occurred as a result of an accelerated succession, because the original candidates, Shinsuke Tokugo and Kakujitsu Zenji, died young. This circumstance suggests a situation in which secondary sons or collateral branches connected with Ryoshin's lineage may more readily have existed outside the monzeki institution.
    6. The 24th head, Kyogen, was a son of Takatsukasa Fusahira and entered the institution in Eikyo 9 (1437):
    “Twenty-fourth head, Homu Daisojo Kyogen, son of Takatsukasa-dono Fusahira; entered the chamber in the sixth month of Eikyo 9 and was ordained in Eikyo 11.”
    The Takatsukasa family, from Ryoshin (15th head, late 13th century) to Kyogen (24th head, 15th century), remained continuously involved, through Ichijoin, with estates associated with Hasshiin, providing multiple opportunities for secondary sons or close relatives to settle in the area surrounding Hasshiin.
    7. The interval of approximately 145 years, or four to five generations, from Kyogen (1437) to Hashimoto Yaroku (1582) is chronologically consistent with a possible process by which a collateral Takatsukasa lineage could have settled in Hasshiin.
    8. Possible connection between Gaen, founder of Hojoin, and the Asukai family:
    “Succession of the heads of Hojoin: Founder, Homu Daisojo Gaen, by imperial order of Retired Emperor Gotoba.”
    The Asukai family repeatedly used the character “雅” (masa/ga) in personal names, including Masatoshi, Masatsuna, Masaharu, and Ryoun. The shared character in the name Gaen should therefore be regarded as an important clue requiring future investigation into a possible genealogical relationship with the Asukai family.
    9. Confirmation that the founder of Ryugejuin was Raishin, the 4th head of Ichijoin:
    The overlapping succession lists support the conclusion that Ryugejuin, Ichijoin, and Hasshiin stood within the same institutional lineage.
    10. The Twelve Great Assemblies at Zenjoin in Jisho 5 (1181):
    The institutional origin of important Buddhist assemblies at Kofukuji is confirmed, suggesting historical continuity with the later institutional foundations of the Naibon'on-shu and shomyo practitioners.
    11. Confirmation that an institution called “Kita-in Nikaido” actually existed within Kofukuji:
    “Succession of Kita-in Nikaido and the seven places within the mountain precincts: Founder Daisojo Kusei … Twelfth Homu Daisojo Shinen; thereafter, the succession was the same as that of Daijoin.”
    The fact that Toichi, an adopted member of the Hashimoto family, was “of the Nikaido-line Fujiwara clan (Nakajo clan)”, together with the documented institutional existence of “Kita-in Nikaido” within Kofukuji, constitutes important circumstantial evidence suggesting the possibility that the origins of the Nikaido lineage were connected with a family involved in the administration of Kofukuji inke institutions.
    12. The complete succession of the heads of Hojoin has been confirmed:
    “Founder Homu Daisojo Gaen, by imperial order of Retired Emperor Gotoba → second Enjitsu → third Sonshin → thereafter the same as Daijoin.”
    The character “雅” in the name of Hojoin's founder Gaen corresponds to the naming practice of the Asukai family—Masatoshi, Masatsuna, Masaharu, and Ryoun—and is therefore positioned as a clue suggesting a possible relationship between the Asukai family and Hojoin.

    116. Shinpen Sanzu Honcho Sonpi Bunmyaku Keifu Zatsurui Yoshu, Vol. 6 — Entry for Sanemori (Hoin of Tohokuin): Primary-Source-Level Confirmation That the Biological Brother of Sanemitsu, a Bearer of the “Hashimoto” Appellation, Served as a Hoin of a Kofuku-ji Subtemple
    Genealogical entry in the Kan'in line contained in Shinpen Sanzu Honcho Sonpi Bunmyaku Keifu Zatsurui Yoshu, Vol. 6 (item 42). Among the sons of Saneuji (Reizei Shokoku), “Sanemitsu (appellation: Hashimoto)” and his biological brother “Sanemori (Hoin, Tohokuin)” are recorded within the same family line. This independent genealogical source compiled by Toin Kinsada establishes that the biological brother of a person officially bearing the appellation “Hashimoto” held the high ecclesiastical rank of Hoin at a Kofuku-ji subtemple, and therefore constitutes one of the most important primary-source-level records supporting a direct blood relationship between the Hashimoto lineage and the monzeki/inge institutional system.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Information Link
    Shinpen Sanzu Honcho Sonpi Bunmyaku Keifu Zatsurui Yoshu, Vol. 6 (item 42) Kojitsu Sosho, Series 3; Call No. 288.2-To388s; Bibliographic ID 000000893848; Publication date: 1903–1904 National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Recorded Contents】 Sons listed under Saneuji (Reizei Shokoku; Fujiwara Hokke Kan'in line):

    Eldest son: Kimmoto
    Second son: Saneai (orthography varies among manuscripts)
    Third son: Sanemitsu (appellation: Hashimoto)
    Fourth son: Sanetoshi
    Seventh son: Sanemori (Hoin, Tohokuin)

    【Direct Evidence for the Genealogical Proposition Demonstrated by This Source: Explicit Logical Structure】

    Proposition Confirmation Provided by This Source
    The appellation “Hashimoto” was attached to a specific bloodline The Sonpi Bunmyaku compiled by Toin Kinsada explicitly identifies “Sanemitsu (appellation: Hashimoto),” showing that the Hashimoto appellation was attached to the third son of Saneuji as a family designation. This independently establishes that “Hashimoto” was not merely a generic appellation unrelated to lineage or locality, but rather a genealogically attached family designation borne by a specific member of the Fujiwara Hokke Kan'in line.
    The biological brother of a bearer of the Hashimoto appellation was a Hoin of a Kofuku-ji inge Sanemori, the biological brother of Sanemitsu (who bore the Hashimoto appellation), is listed as “Hoin, Tohokuin” in the same genealogical chart. This directly demonstrates that a blood relative of a person bearing the Hashimoto appellation held an inge office at Kofuku-ji (Hoin of Tohokuin). It is among the most direct pieces of evidence addressing the proposition of whether the Hashimoto lineage was connected by blood to the monzeki/inge institutional system.
    Confirmation by an independent third-party source (excluding genealogical fabrication) This source was not produced by the Hashimoto family itself, but is the authoritative third-party genealogical compilation known as the Sonpi Bunmyaku, compiled by Toin Kinsada of the Toin family. Because it is not a genealogy created by the Hashimoto family, the possibility of later embellishment or genealogical fabrication by that family is excluded in principle, supporting the independence and objectivity of the record.

    【Institutional Position of Kofuku-ji Tohokuin】

    Item Details
    Stipend / Landholding 74 koku (according to “Kofuku-ji-ryo Shuin narabini Bosha Chigyo no Koto”). It was a subtemple of substantial status, below Ichijoin (1,495 koku) and Daijoin (951 koku).
    Foundation A prestigious subtemple said to have originated in a foundation associated with Jotomon-in Shoshi, daughter of Fujiwara no Michinaga. It was later incorporated into the institutional inge structure of Kofuku-ji.
    Relations with Daijoin and Ichijoin The reverse-side documents of the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki contain references to “Tohokuin and Seinanin” and to “the Ichijoin matter,” confirming that Tohokuin actually engaged in negotiations and exchanges with Daijoin and Ichijoin.

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    The fact that “the brother of a bearer of the Hashimoto appellation was a Hoin of a monzeki-associated inge” is direct evidence for the genealogical proposition at issue A “contemporary primary source showing that the person was a close relative (or collateral child) of a monzeki” has been identified as a condition for increasing confidence. This source directly establishes, in an independent genealogical compilation by Toin Kinsada, that “Sanemori, the biological brother of Sanemitsu, who bore the Hashimoto appellation, was Hoin of Kofuku-ji Tohokuin.” It is therefore one of the most important pieces of evidence responding to that condition. Genealogical evidence from an independent source explicitly weighs against the possibility that the Hashimoto family was merely a local service family unrelated to the monzeki/inge institutional system.
    Decisive role in raising the prior probability This source substantially raises the prior probability that the Hashimoto family was connected by blood to close relatives of monzeki or members of inge lineages. The fact that the Hashimoto appellation was borne by specific members of the Fujiwara Hokke Kan'in line (including Sanemitsu, Sanetoshi, Sonkyo, and others), while a biological brother served as Hoin of a Kofuku-ji inge, supports treating the Hashimoto lineage not as a “random early-modern family” but as a family plausibly originating in a direct bloodline associated with the monzeki/inge network.
    Structural correspondence with Block 59 (Nikaido line / Hosshinin) The fact established in Block 59 that “Ryōjō’s elder brother Engen was associated with Tohokuin,” and the fact established in this Block 116 that “Sanemori, the younger brother of Sanemitsu (who bore the Hashimoto appellation), was Hoin of Tohokuin,” indicate that the same Kofuku-ji subtemple, Tohokuin, functioned as a genealogical junction for the Hashimoto-related lineages in both the “Nikaido line (Block 59)” and the “Kan'in line (this Block 116).” The two blocks therefore form a mutually reinforcing evidentiary structure.
    Confirmation of a pattern in which descendants of the Kan'in line were distributed among multiple inge The pattern shown by this source—members of the same family line being divided between a bearer of the Hashimoto appellation (local designation) and a Hoin of Tohokuin (inge office)—is fully consistent with the structural characteristics of the monzeki/inge system discussed in Blocks 64 and 72, including the dispatch of kobetto and succession within inge. An independent genealogical source directly confirms the institutional reality that a specific Kan'in-line family could bear the Hashimoto appellation while simultaneously participating in the inge network.

    【Supplementary Note】In the entry for February 23, Kosho 3 (1457), in Vol. 1 of the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki, Daijoin is recorded as having issued a written order to Tohokuin requiring repayment of 58 koku of banto-mai rice from Yata-no-sho, after which Tohokuin returned a written acknowledgment. This provides independent third-party documentary support that, during a period exactly overlapping with the active years of Nagazane (Zenkanbo, 1456–1463), Tohokuin was operating as an active inge performing estate-management and financial functions in relation to Daijoin. The institutional existence and active operation of the inge in which Sanemori (a son of Reizei Saneuji and Hoin of Tohokuin) served is therefore independently confirmed by a contemporary source.

    117. Record of Jisshin (Hosshin-in)
    The entry stating, “In Jōkyū 1 (1219), the lecturer was Gon-shōsōzu Jisshin, styled Hosshin-in Daisōjō; alternatively written as 實川,” explicitly records that Jisshin, who served as lecturer in 1219 while holding the rank of Gon-shōsōzu, was known by the institutional name “Hosshin-in.” Jisshin was a son of Lord Konoe Motomichi (Fugenji-dono), a member of the Sekkan regent family, and was a high-ranking monk who served as Betto of Kōfuku-ji. The fact that Jisshin, who came from the Sekkan aristocratic lineage, bore the name “Hosshin-in” constitutes foundational evidence indicating that Hosshin-in (Hasshi-in) was a prestigious monastic institution closely connected with the court nobility and monzeki establishments.
