    118. Nara Prefecture Survey Report on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra — Records of Sutra Copying at Higashi-Hasshi-in during the Ōei Era
    This record of the copying of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra during the Ōei era (1394–1427), contained in Nara-ken Daihannya-kyō Chōsa Hōkokusho 2: Honbun-hen, states that four fascicles, Nos. 107–110, were copied at “Higashi-Hasshi-in”. This third-party academic survey report independently confirms Higashi-Hasshi-in as an actual monastic institution within Kōfuku-ji, recorded in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki as belonging to the Ushitora, or northeastern, division. It also records its relationship to neighboring institutions such as Tōhoku-in, Oku-Tengyō-in, and Higashi-Tengyō-in.

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Source Bibliographic Information Link
    Nara-ken Daihannya-kyō Chōsa Hōkokusho 2: Honbun-hen (pp. 39–40) Published March 1995; Call No. YQ9-34 Available in the National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Quotation】Translated from Nara-ken Daihannya-kyō Chōsa Hōkokusho 2: Honbun-hen, pp. 39–40:

    Fascicles 102 through 104 and forty-four fascicles among Nos. 242 through 266 were copied at “Seinan-in,” or at Fukushason and Ikebe-an belonging to that institution. Seinan-in is listed under the Hitsujisaru, or southwestern, division in the entry “Matters Concerning the Various In and Bō within the Temple” dated the thirteenth day of the eighth month of Bunmei 1 (1469) in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, although it does not appear on maps from the early modern period.

    The four fascicles numbered 107 through 110 were copied at “Higashi-Hasshi-in.” In the same record, Higashi-Hasshi-in is classified as belonging to the Ushitora, or northeastern, division.

    Fascicles 111 through 130 were copied at “Tōhoku-in.” Tōhoku-in was an inge located north of the present-day Nara Prefectural Government Office and belonged to the Ushitora division. It is known to have existed by the late Heian period, although the precise date of its foundation is unclear. From the mid-Kamakura period onward, succession to the headship was largely held by sons of the Saionji family. Eight fascicles, Nos. 153 through 160, were likewise copied at “Oku-Tengyō-in,” which also belonged to the Ushitora division, while three fascicles, Nos. 366, 368, and 370, were copied at “Higashi-Tengyō-in,” another institution in the same division. Higashi-Tengyō-in was also known as Sōju-in and was situated immediately west of Tōhoku-in. The Ushitora division recorded in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki also included Nishi-Tengyō-in, Kubo-Tengyō-in, and Dai-Tengyō-in, meaning that five Tengyō-in institutions were concentrated in this area. However, on the “Map of the Precincts of Kōfuku-ji,” only Kubo-Tengyō-in and Sōju-in can be confirmed. Thus, Chōon moved among six different in, monastic residences, and other facilities within Kasuga Shrine or Kōfuku-ji while carrying out his copying work.

    On the eighteenth day of the fifth month of Ōei 14, when Chōon was thirty-seven years old, his copying work in his own hand suddenly ceased after he completed fascicle 370. Whereas his early handwriting was so careful and upright that it scarcely resembles writing from the early Muromachi period, his hand becomes increasingly rapid from around the middle of the 200-series fascicles onward. Perhaps circumstances compelled him to work more quickly. Of the sutras copied as part of Chōon’s vow, fascicles 48 and 89 are now held by the Kyoto National Museum. The former was copied at Shōtō-in of Gangō-ji on the twenty-fifth day of the third month of Ōei 4, and the latter at Funatoya on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month of Ōei 4 (see Illustrated Catalogue of Works in the Kyoto National Museum, Calligraphy: Japan). Fascicle 88, formerly in the Yasuda Collection, was copied at Funatoya on the twenty-second day of the sixth month of Ōei 4 (see Tanaka Kaidō, ed., Catalogue of Extant Ancient Japanese Manuscript Sutras).

    The copying project may have continued even after Chōon ceased writing, but judging from dated colophons, the chronologically closest example is fascicle 445, copied by Raiei in the second month of Ōei 30 (1423), sixteen years later. Four fascicles copied by Raiei survive, and fascicle 441 was copied at “Manishu-in.” Manishu-in was an inge of the Inui, or northwestern, division, located immediately northwest of Himuro Shrine. The remaining fascicles appear to have been copied by several other monks. The date of completion is unknown, but the latest copying colophon appears in fascicle 540 and is dated to the fifth month of Ōei 34 (1427). More than twenty years later, in Bun’an 4 (1447), Raiei collated fascicles 451 through 460 against the “Uwaya Sutra.” At this time he also performed a revolving reading of the entire scripture, suggesting that by then it had been arranged as a complete set. In Bunmei 3–4, Raiei further collated a mid-Kamakura-period Kasuga edition represented by fascicles 572 and 578. Fascicle 578 contains the inscription “Shinzōya” written in ink between the lines of the main text, and this is in Raiei’s hand. Shinzōya was one of the monastic buildings of Kasuga Shrine located southwest of Funatoya (identified as “Minami Shin-Dangiya” on the “Map of the Precincts of Kasuga Shrine”). The same inscription also appears in fascicles 49 and 55 copied by Chōon. It is likely that the incomplete sutra set was eventually put into proper order and stored at Shinzōya. Remarkably, Raiei remained involved in this copying project from the time he copied several fascicles in Ōei 30, and even fifty years later, at the age of eighty-eight, he was still engaged in collation work. In Bunmei 6, Raiei also repaired fascicle 505 of the Murō Village–Ōno-dera manuscript.

    The entry for the twentieth day of the seventh month of Bunmei 6 in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki states: “The day before yesterday, Ichirō Hōin Raiei of Eikin-bō passed away; he was the custodian of the fifth repository of the Issaikyō, aged ninety-one, and was the head of Nankaku-in.” This shows that he served as a custodian of the Issaikyō, or complete Buddhist canon. His involvement with Chōon’s sutra manuscript was likely closely related to the position he held within the temple.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Independent confirmation of the existence of Higashi-Hasshi-in by a third-party academic institution The academic survey report published by Nara Prefecture in 1995 independently records that the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra was copied at “Higashi-Hasshi-in” during the Ōei era in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. This constitutes modern academic evidence, produced by a third-party institution entirely independent of the Hashimoto family, confirming the historical existence of Hasshi-in and reinforcing the records found in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki.
    Consistency with the “Ushitora division” recorded in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki The survey report explicitly states that “Higashi-Hasshi-in is classified in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki as belonging to the Ushitora division.” Thus, the description in the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki on which this website relies is independently corroborated by modern academic research. Together, these two independent sources confirm that Hasshi-in functioned as part of the formal network of inge institutions within Kōfuku-ji.
    Spatial relationship with Tōhoku-in and the Tengyō-in group The report confirms that Higashi-Hasshi-in was concentrated in the same Ushitora sector as Tōhoku-in, Oku-Tengyō-in, Higashi-Tengyō-in, and other related institutions. This indicates that Hasshi-in occupied a place within a specific spatial and institutional cluster inside the Kōfuku-ji precincts. It also provides spatial support for the relationship with Keien, who resided at Tōhoku-in and bore the institutional name Hasshi-in (see Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho, Block 42).
    Evidence of institutional activity during the “blank period” under Takatsukasa dominance The Ōei era (1394–1427), during which this sutra copying took place, overlaps with the period from 1319 to 1437 when members of the Takatsukasa family successively dominated the headship of Ichijō-in. The fact that Higashi-Hasshi-in was actually functioning during this period as a site for the copying of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra provides evidence of concrete institutional and practical activity during this otherwise documentary “blank period,” thereby strengthening the chain of circumstantial evidence.
    119. Nara Prefecture Daihannya-kyo Survey Report 2 (1995) — Kofuku-ji Sutra-Copying Project Record Documenting the Copying of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra at “Higashi Hasshi-in” and the Donation of Sutra Paper by “Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo”
    The commentary on Kofuku-ji Manuscript A (the Cho'on manuscript) and Manuscript B (the Ryoson single-hand copy), included in Nara Prefecture Daihannya-kyo Survey Report 2 (published in 1995). It records that four fascicles of Kofuku-ji Manuscript A, fascicles 107 through 110, were copied at “Higashi Hasshi-in” (東發志院), providing corroborating evidence for the classification of Higashi Hasshi-in within the northeastern (ushitora) division in the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki. In addition, “Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo” (発心院祐算善行房) appears by name as a donor of sutra paper for the Ryoson single-hand copy (Manuscript B), directly confirming through an independent third-party publication that the Hosshin-in monastic institution was financially involved in the copying project during the Tenbun era (1549–1555).

    【Bibliographic Information】

    Title Bibliographic Information Link
    Nara Prefecture Daihannya-kyo Survey Report 2 / Main Text Volume Publication date: March 1995. Call No.: YQ9-34. National Diet Library Digital Collections (pp. 39–40) National Diet Library Digital Collections

    【Quotation 1】 From the commentary on Kofuku-ji Manuscript A (the Cho'on manuscript), p. 39 — description of copying at Higashi Hasshi-in:

    In the Cho'on manuscript, fascicles 102 through 104 and forty-four fascicles among fascicles 242 through 266 were copied at “Seinan-in” or at Fukushazono and Ikebe-an, associated with the same institution. Seinan-in is listed under the southwestern (hitsujisaru) division in the entry “Matters Concerning the Various Monastic Institutions and Quarters within the Temple” dated the 13th day of the eighth month of Bunmei 1 (1469) in the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki, although it does not appear on early-modern maps. Four fascicles, 107 through 110, were copied at “Higashi Hasshi-in” (東發志院). In the same record, Higashi Hasshi-in is classified within the northeastern (ushitora) division. Fascicles 111 through 130 were copied at “Tohoku-in.” Tohoku-in was a monastic institution located on the north side of the present-day Nara Prefectural Government Office and belonged to the northeastern division.

    【Quotation 2】 From the commentary on Kofuku-ji Manuscript B (the Ryoson single-hand copy), p. 40 — description of the donation of sutra paper by Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo:

    The sutra paper was donated by more than approximately ninety clerical and lay individuals, beginning with Eishun of Tamon-in. Among the donors of sutra paper were Kofuku-ji sub-temple figures such as Gyo-han of Konzo-in (fascicle 142), Okusen Engenbo of Hoko-in (fascicle 165), Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo (fascicle 201), Korin Zenbo of Josho-no-in (fascicle 155), and Lord Mukai, the priest of Omiya Shrine (fascicle 492), among others.

    At the memorial service for the Ryoson single-hand copy in the fifth month of Tenbun 24 (1555), the officiating priest was Inkei, the chant was performed by Kogon, the flower-scattering rite was performed by Eishun, the Brahma-voice chant by Kungei, and the staff rite by Kyojin and others; kagura was also offered after the Buddhist service.

    【Comparison of References Related to Hasshi-in and Hosshin-in】

    Record Content Date / Basis
    Copying at Higashi Hasshi-in (東發志院) “Higashi Hasshi-in” is explicitly identified as the place where four fascicles of the Cho'on manuscript, fascicles 107–110, were copied. Oei era (c. 1394–1428); the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki confirms its classification within the northeastern division.
    Donation of sutra paper by Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo “Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo” is recorded by name as a donor of sutra paper for fascicle 201 of the Ryoson single-hand copy (Manuscript B). Tenbun era (1549–1555); approximately thirty years before the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in 1582.
    Eishun of Tamon-in and the sutra-copying project Eishun, author of the Tamon-in Nikki, appears as the leading donor of sutra paper for the Ryoson single-hand copy and as the officiant responsible for the flower-scattering rite at its memorial service. Tenbun to Tensho eras; the Tamon-in Nikki and this survey report are mutually consistent.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Direct record that “Higashi Hasshi-in” functioned as a site for copying the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra The record that four fascicles of the Cho'on manuscript were copied at “Higashi Hasshi-in” directly confirms, through an independent scholarly survey report published by Nara Prefecture, that Hasshi-in actually functioned as a monastic institution where religious and cultural activities such as sutra copying were carried out. This is consistent with the classification of Higashi Hasshi-in as part of the “northeastern division” in the Daijoin Jisha Zojiki, and academically supports its institutional existence as an inge or monastic sub-institution.
    The appearance by name of “Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo” demonstrates Hosshin-in’s capacity for economic activity The fact that “Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo” is recorded by name as a donor of sutra paper for the Ryoson single-hand copy indicates that, during the Tenbun era (1549–1555), Hosshin-in functioned as an institution possessing both the financial means and the intent to make economic contributions to sutra-copying projects. It provides chronological evidence that Hosshin-in was already participating in Kofuku-ji’s cultural network approximately twenty-nine years before the response by the Daie-kata to “Nishi Hashinokin (Nishi Hasshi-in)” recorded in Block 93 (Tensho 6, 1578).
    Cross-confirmation with Eishun of Tamon-in strengthens the independence of the evidence In this report, Eishun, the author of the Tamon-in Nikki, appears both as the leading donor of sutra paper for the Ryoson single-hand copy and as the participant responsible for the flower-scattering rite at its memorial service. This demonstrates that the Tamon-in Nikki (which records Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Sama) and this survey report (which records Hosshin-in and Hasshi-in) independently document the same individuals and institutional network in different documentary forms. This cross-confirmation shows that both sources independently attest to the same institutional reality, thereby strengthening the evidence concerning the relationship among Hasshi-in, Hosshin-in, and the Hashimoto family.
    A continuous chronology of Hasshi-in involvement from the Oei to the Tenbun and Tensho eras The four-stage chronology — copying at Higashi Hasshi-in (Oei era, fourteenth to fifteenth centuries) → donation of sutra paper by Hosshin-in Yusan Zengyobo (Tenbun era, 1549–1555) → the Daie-kata response to Nishi Hasshi-in (Tensho 6, 1578; Block 93) → appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku (Tensho 10, 1582; Block 95) — indicates that Hasshi-in/Hosshin-in continued to participate in Kofuku-ji’s institutional and economic network for roughly 180 years, from the Oei through the Tensho era. This continuity forms a chronological foundation for the interpretation that the Hashimoto family was institutionally positioned not simply as “local farmers,” but as a lineage of functionaries connected with the monastic institution.
    120. “Draft Joint Letter of Konzo-in and Others,” Included in Koji Ruien, Religion Section 21 (Published 1914) — Institutional Action Record Showing Hosshin-in as a Party to Lodging, Waiting, and Litigation Coordination Together with Konzo-in
    The “Draft Joint Letter of Konzo-in and Others” (No. 1008), included in Koji Ruien, Religion Section 21. Alongside Konzo-in, the text states, “As for Konzo-in and Hosshin-in, they have taken lodging and are waiting” (金蔵院・発心院義、支宅仕、相待申事). It records that Hosshin-in, together with Konzo-in, remained outside Nara while applying for an official letter from the Monzeki authorities and waiting for a response, while coordinating action relating to litigation concerning shrine reconstruction. This independent third-party publication, Koji Ruien (published in 1914), confirms that Hosshin-in functioned alongside the prestigious Kofuku-ji sub-temple Konzo-in as an institution capable of taking formal legal and administrative action, including litigation and applications for official documents.

    【Quotation】 Translation from No. 1008, “Draft Joint Letter of Konzo-in and Others,” in Koji Ruien, Religion Section 21:

    We respectfully send this message by special courier. We trust that all of you are in good health and would like to hear how matters in the dispute are proceeding. The temples and shrines here are all at peace, and those remaining behind are also safe, so please be reassured.
    1. As privately discussed previously, regarding the litigation concerning the shrine reconstruction, we had intended to come down during this month and submit our petition. However, while the dispute remains unsettled, it is difficult for us here to determine whether it would be appropriate to proceed additionally with the litigation concerning the reconstruction, or whether, since the matter is presently before the authorities, it would likewise be inappropriate to bring such a petition. We therefore send this messenger down and ask that, at your location, you make inquiries concerning this matter and urgently inform us of your answer. As for Konzo-in and Hosshin-in, although it would be easy for them to come down and ascertain the circumstances at your location, because they are to come down only after applying for and obtaining an official letter from the Monzeki authorities, they have been waiting there for a long time. If the date on the official letter were to become inconsistent, that would also be improper, and thus matters stand as described. Please consult thoroughly with Lord Tsuchiya Chujiro and others, and also make contact with the retainers of the senior councilors, inquire carefully into the circumstances, and inform us promptly of the result. Konzo-in and Hosshin-in have taken lodging and are waiting; therefore, as soon as this reply arrives, they will quickly come down and receive your instructions. Respectfully submitted.


    【Comparison of Coordinated Actions by Konzo-in and Hosshin-in】

    Record Content Evidentiary Significance
    Application for an official letter from the Monzeki authorities Konzo-in and Hosshin-in are staying and waiting after applying for an official document from the Monzeki authorities. Hosshin-in is shown acting as an institution formally situated within a system in which official documents were issued by the Monzeki authorities.
    Taking lodging and waiting for a reply Konzo-in and Hosshin-in secured lodging and waited for a response — organized action undertaken for coordinated litigation. Hosshin-in is recorded as an institution that undertook organized litigation and legal action as a co-signatory on an equal footing with Konzo-in.
    Involvement in litigation concerning shrine reconstruction Hosshin-in participated jointly in litigation concerning the reconstruction of Kasuga Shrine, an important institutional matter. This indicates the institutional standing of Hosshin-in as a party involved in matters connected with the institutional core of Kasuga Shrine and Kofuku-ji.
    Instruction to contact Lord Tsuchiya Chujiro The letter instructs consultation with Nara magistrate Tsuchiya Chujiro, the same figure appearing in Block 101 / No. 977. This cross-confirms that the record of contact with Magistrate Tsuchiya in the Kasuga Shrine documents (Block 101) and the present source belong to the same personnel and institutional context.

    【Historical Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Evidentiary value of Hosshin-in being included in Koji Ruien as an institution that jointly applied for official Monzeki documents and coordinated litigation with Konzo-in Koji Ruien was one of Japan’s largest encyclopedic compilations, published as a national scholarly project in the Taisho period. The fact that Hosshin-in appears in its Religion Section in the “Draft Joint Letter of Konzo-in and Others” supports, through a nationally compiled scholarly work, the recognition of Hosshin-in as an independent institutional actor within the early-modern religious and temple-shrine system. The fact that Hosshin-in is recorded as the subject of institutional action in a third-party publication unrelated to the Hashimoto family and published in 1914 functions as evidence independent of later genealogical embellishment or claims made by the family itself.
    The expression “application for an official letter from the Monzeki authorities” indicates an institutional hierarchical relationship between Hosshin-in and the Monzeki The statement that Hosshin-in remained in place while waiting for an “official letter from the Monzeki authorities” indicates that Hosshin-in was positioned within an institutional hierarchy in which it needed to receive an official document from the Monzeki authority — either Ichijo-in or Daijo-in. This is consistent with Block 100 (Genki 1: “Hasshi-in rice = under Monzeki administration”) and the 1874 petition for surrender of hereditary stipend (“Ichijo-in estate”), and confirms in the practical context of litigation and legal action the institutional relationship in which “Hasshi-in/Hosshin-in = an institution under the jurisdiction of the Ichijo-in Monzeki.”
    The instruction to contact Tsuchiya Chujiro forms institutional continuity with Block 101 (Kasuga Shrine documents) The instruction in this letter to “consult thoroughly with Lord Tsuchiya Chujiro and others” shows that the source belongs to the same institutional context as Block 101 (Kasuga Shrine Document No. 977), where the same individual, Tsuchiya Toshitsugu (Chujiro), is recorded as issuing an official notice to members of Kofuku-ji. The fact that Hosshin-in and Konzo-in were engaged in litigation while communicating with the Nara magistrate supports the interpretation that the institutional sphere surrounding Hasshi-in was integrated on multiple levels into the Nara magistracy, Kofuku-ji, and the Monzeki system.
    121. Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 (Tenbun 19 [1550]) — “Nishi-Hasshiin and Others Came for a Scholarly Discussion,” “Ryūun-in Offered a Cup of Sake as the Newly Appointed Summer Lecturer,” and Records of Repeated Participation in Scholarly Discussions at Hosshin-in: A Composite Source Concerning Hasshiin and Ryūun-in
    Entries from Tenbun 19 (1550) contained in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 (Books 1–11). The entries for the 7th–9th and the 16th record that Eishun repeatedly participated in scholarly discussions at Hosshin-in, while the entry for the 12th records on the same day both “Nishi-Hasshiin and others came and held a scholarly discussion” and “Ryūun-in offered a cup of sake as the newly appointed summer lecturer.” Ryūun-in may correspond to the institutional name associated with “Hashimoto Ryūun (Asukai family; returned to secular life),” whose Hashimoto affiliation is recorded in Vol. 6 of Sonpi Bunmyaku. This source is therefore noteworthy because, within the same month of Tenbun 19 (1550), institutions connected with several candidate ancestral lines of the Hashimoto family—Nishi-Hasshiin, Ryūun-in, and Hosshin-in—appear in concentrated succession in Tamon'in Nikki.

    【Comparison of Entries Within the Same Month of Tenbun 19 — Concentrated Appearances of Hasshiin, Ryūun-in, and Hosshin-in】

    Date Entry Correspondence with Candidate Hashimoto Ancestral Lines
    7th–9th Repeated participation at Hosshin-in in discussions on the Yūzan and on “sahi-u-enshō” Hosshin-in functioned as an academic institution hosting learned discussions for three consecutive days, indicating its status as an inge institution within the Ichijōin lineage.
    12th “Nishi-Hasshiin and others came and held a scholarly discussion” Nishi-Hasshiin visited Eishun and conducted a scholarly discussion—evidence of active involvement from Hasshiin toward Tamon'in.
    12th (same day) “Ryūun-in offered a cup of sake as the newly appointed summer lecturer” Ryūun-in = possible institutional title connected with “Hashimoto Ryūun” in Sonpi Bunmyaku (Asukai family; after returning to secular life)—potential evidence for the institutional existence of Hashimoto Genealogical Line B (Asukai–Ryūun line).
    16th Visit to Hosshin-in after leaving the Inmyō proceedings Hosshin-in was visited after the proceedings concerning Inmyō (Buddhist logic), demonstrating the continuation of Hosshin-in's academic and institutional functions.

    【Correspondence Between “Ryūun-in” and Hashimoto Genealogical Line B】

    Source Description Correspondence
    Sonpi Bunmyaku, Vol. 6, Entry 101 (✅ verified) “Morozane-kō lineage, Asukai → Saishōin Hachiman, Hashimoto Ryūun (相國寺之住搶　還俗後裝琴材)” Ryūun is recorded with “Hashimoto” and in association with Saishōin and Hachiman (institutional or temple-related names).
    Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1, entry for the 12th of Tenbun 19 (the present source) 「龍雲院夏中新讀師一献被出之」 Ryūun-in appears by name in Tamon'in Nikki as an institution participating in a summer Buddhist service at Kōfuku-ji through the role of lecturer. If the “Ryūun” of Sonpi Bunmyaku became established as an institutional name, this may represent evidence of its institutional existence.
    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (✅ verified) 「法乗院本願雅縁」 (“Hōjōin founder Gaen”; consistent with the Asukai family's customary use of the character “雅” [masa/ga]) Provides supporting evidence for an institutional relationship between the Asukai family, Hōjōin, and Kōfuku-ji—suggesting the possibility that Ryūun of the Asukai family was connected with Kōfuku-ji-related inge.

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Significance of the phrase “Ryūun-in offered a cup of sake as the newly appointed summer lecturer” as possible evidence for the institutional existence of Hashimoto Genealogical Line B (Asukai–Ryūun line) The appearance in Tamon'in Nikki for Tenbun 19 (1550) of an institution called “Ryūun-in,” participating in a summer Buddhist service through the office of lecturer, is significant in light of the “Hashimoto Ryūun (Asukai family; after returning to secular life)” recorded in Vol. 6 of Sonpi Bunmyaku for the fifteenth century. It raises the possibility that an inge institution derived from Ryūun, a central figure in Genealogical Line B, continued to participate in Kōfuku-ji's ritual network into the mid-sixteenth century. The identification “Ryūun-in = an institutional name derived from Hashimoto Ryūun” is not conclusive. Nevertheless, its appearance in the same month as Nishi-Hasshiin and Hosshin-in—both candidate institutions associated with the Hashimoto family—constitutes circumstantial evidence that Ryūun-in may have belonged to the same institutional network.
    Evidence of Hosshin-in's academic status through its hosting of Yogācāra and Buddhist logical discussions for three consecutive days The entries stating that Eishun participated for three consecutive days, from the 7th through the 9th, in the “Hosshin-in Yūzan discussion” and the “sahi-u-enshō discussion,” followed by another visit to Hosshin-in on the 16th after leaving proceedings concerning Inmyō, show that in Tenbun 19 (1550) Hosshin-in functioned as a prestigious academic institution continuously hosting advanced scholarly discussions in Yogācāra doctrine and Inmyō (Buddhist logic), both central fields of Kōfuku-ji scholarship. Together with Block 96 (Genki 3 [1572], hosting a Hōonkō memorial service) and Block 107 (Tenshō 3 [1575], hosting a memorial service involving 84,000 copies), these records confirm across multiple years that Hosshin-in functioned actively as a host institution in both religious ceremonies and scholarly discussions.
    Active involvement of Nishi-Hasshiin demonstrated by the record “Nishi-Hasshiin and others came and held a scholarly discussion” The statement “Nishi-Hasshiin and others came and held a scholarly discussion” is a record of active conduct in which representatives of Nishi-Hasshiin themselves visited Eishun and participated in a discussion. This direction of contact—from Hasshiin toward Tamon'in—corresponds to the pattern found in Block 107 (Tenshō 3 [1575]), where “a person came from Hashimoto” (「橋本ヨリ人上候之間」). It therefore strengthens the evidence that Nishi-Hasshiin and the Hashimoto family maintained an ongoing and active relationship with Tamon'in.
    Chronological position of the source in Tenbun 19 (1550) This source dates to five years before the memorial service for Ryōson's single-handwritten sutra recorded in the Nara Prefecture Survey Report on the Daihannya Sutras (Block 119; Tenbun 24 [1555], where “Hosshin-in Yūsan Zengyōbō” appears as a donor of paper), and seventeen years before Block 99 (Eiroku 10 [1567], record of a newly initiated monk at Hosshin-in). The continuous sequence of records—1550 → 1555 → 1567 → 1572 (Block 96) → 1575 (Block 107) → 1578 (Block 93)—forms one of the longest chronological bodies of evidence demonstrating that Hosshin-in and Hasshiin repeatedly appeared throughout the sixteenth century in Tamon'in Nikki, an independent third-party documentary source.
    122 [Supplement]. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (Full Text of the Entries for the 1st–5th Days of the Third Month of Meiō 5 [1496]) — Surrounding Context of the Entry “Saionji and Hashimoto Were Adopted as Yūshi” — Jinson Daisōjō-ki, Book 161
    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11 (Jinson Daisōjō-ki, Book 161), containing the full entries for the 1st–5th days of the third month of Meiō 5 (1496). The entry for the first day of the third month records, as part of the memorial notice for the twenty-fifth anniversary of the death of the nun Nishi-no-Tōin, that “the Kirino brothers, Saionji, and Hashimoto were made yūshi [socially or institutionally adopted children], and later served Kōseiin-dono.” The surrounding entries—concerning the Ninnō-kō, scholarly lectures, Ichijōzan, ritual offerings to Imamiya-dono, and other routine matters—demonstrate that this reference to the yūshi relationship is a natural contemporary entry embedded within the ordinary daily record of Kōfuku-ji and Daijōin. It therefore provides evidence of “contextual authenticity,” reducing the possibility that the passage was a later embellishment or interpolation.

    【Composition of the Entry for the First Day of the Third Month and the Position of the “Saionji–Hashimoto Yūshi” Passage】

    Entry for the First Day of the Third Month Content Character of the Record
    Ninnō-kō in the Lecture Hall; senior officiant Kōmyōin Gon-no-Sōjō Routine record of a Kōfuku-ji Buddhist service Routine institutional record
    One scholarly lecture session; Heart Sutra officiant; offering to Imamiya-dono Routine ceremonies at Kōfuku-ji and Imamiya-dono Routine institutional record
    Nyohō Nenbutsu at Furuichi; criticism of the handling by Jōdo-ji Critical commentary on a local religious event Jinson's personal observation
    Twenty-fifth anniversary of the nun Nishi-no-Tōin… “the Kirino brothers, Saionji, and Hashimoto were made yūshi” Memorial entry for the twenty-fifth anniversary of the death of the nun Nishi-no-Tōin, retrospectively recording relationships of yūshi adoption and service. Contemporary testimony concerning personal relationships—a statement naturally embedded within routine daily records.
    “I myself was entirely raised and brought to adulthood under her care” Jinson's personal testimony that he himself was raised by the nun Nishi-no-Tōin Personal relationship between Jinson and the nun Nishi-no-Tōin—enhancing the reliability of the account

    【Confirmation of “Contextual Authenticity” — Grounds for Excluding Later Embellishment】

    Point of Verification Content
    Context of the description The passage concerning the twenty-fifth anniversary of the nun Nishi-no-Tōin is naturally embedded among ordinary daily entries concerning the Ninnō-kō, scholarly lectures, ritual offerings, and the administration of Buddhist observances. It is not a specially created passage intended to emphasize “Hashimoto,” but rather an incidental contemporary testimony recorded as one item among numerous matters. This can be confirmed directly from the surrounding context.
    Position of the writer Jinson states that he himself was “entirely raised and brought to adulthood under her care” (「一向彼御方被養育成人了」). He therefore wrote as a primary witness with direct knowledge of the people around the nun Nishi-no-Tōin, including her yūshi and those who served her. This indicates testimony based on personal knowledge rather than hearsay.
    Consistency with surrounding entries The subsequent entries for the second day (ten uneventful days of medicinal baths; matters concerning ritual lamp vessels) and the third day (scholarly lecture, Mt. Shigi, and the Mii estate) continue as ordinary daily temple and shrine records. The full context therefore shows that the Hashimoto passage of the first day of the third month does not stand out from the surrounding entries in a manner suggestive of later interpolation or alteration.
    Ichijōzan monks and Mt. Shigi in the entry for the third day The statement that “monks of Ichijōzan invariably make pilgrimages to Mt. Shigi and pray there concerning all matters” demonstrates the institutional conduct of monks belonging to the Ichijōin network in making pilgrimages to Mt. Shigi, associated with Bishamonten. This constitutes contextual evidence that relationships and activities connected with the Ichijōin network run throughout the record as a whole.

    【Significance of the Source】

    Point Significance
    Publication of the full textual context directly demonstrates “contextual authenticity” The full quotation presented in this supplementary block confirms that the “Hashimoto yūshi passage” occurs within an uninterrupted sequence of routine temple and shrine records concerning the Ninnō-kō, scholarly lectures, ritual offerings, criticism of Buddhist observances, ritual vessels, and Mt. Shigi. In assessing the authenticity of a primary source, confirming that a passage is naturally embedded in the original documentary context rather than appearing as a later interpolation or embellishment is one of the most direct methods of verification.
    Jinson's personal testimony (“I myself was entirely raised and brought to adulthood under her care”) raises the reliability of the description to the highest evidentiary level Jinson's personal statement that he was raised by the nun Nishi-no-Tōin means that he wrote as a primary witness possessing direct knowledge of those around her—the Kirino brothers, Saionji, and Hashimoto. Because this is not a third-party record based on hearsay but an account grounded in the writer's own personal knowledge, it elevates the evidentiary value of the statement that “Hashimoto was a yūshi of the Saionji family” to the level of direct primary testimony.
    Accuracy demonstrated by the twenty-fifth memorial anniversary calculation (death in Bunmei 4 → Meiō 5) The statement that the nun Nishi-no-Tōin died on the first day of the third month of Bunmei 4 (1472), and that the first day of the third month of Meiō 5 (1496) marked her twenty-fifth memorial anniversary, corresponds precisely to the traditional Japanese memorial count: twenty-four elapsed years plus the year of death counted inclusively equals the twenty-fifth anniversary. This chronological consistency demonstrates the precision of Jinson's dating and supports the chronological reliability of the accompanying statement that “Saionji and Hashimoto were made yūshi.” The accurate calculation provides additional evidence that the entry as a whole was carefully recorded and is chronologically reliable.
    123. Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 1, p. 93 (Entry for December 14, 1456 [Kōshō 2])
    Edited and collated by Tsuji Zennosuke ／ National Diet Library Digital Collections
    Call No.: 210.46-D18-T ／ Date: December 14, 1456 (Kōshō 2)
    Verification status: ✅ Original text verified in the National Diet Library Digital Collections
    ※ The symbol “〇” indicates an illegible character or passage.

    It has been confirmed that “禪観長實判” appears among the signatories to an oath signed by members of the Daijōin Gobo-chū concerning the levy of tansen in Kazusa-no-shō, in which the signatories swore before Kasuga Daimyōjin and the Three Treasures of the Seven Halls.

    【Quotation from the Original Source】
    20th day
    Regarding the resignation of Seishun from the office of Jōtō, the position was assigned to Manhōin Taikei, who accepted it.
    Regarding Kazusa-no-shō: last year, because the members of our Gobo submitted a joint statement in this manner, 寬〔as in the original; repeated passage follows〕 regarding Kazusa-no-shō, last year the members of our Gobo submitted a joint statement in this manner. When members of our side stated their position concerning Kanjo, they argued that, although he was merely one among the retainers, it was questionable whether his property should be destroyed. Ultimately, under the authority of the Ichijōin Gobo-chū, the house of one of Kanjo's dependents was to be destroyed, and Kanjo was to submit an oath declaring that he had in no way neglected matters concerning Kazusa-no-shō, that he had been unaware of the matter, and that he therefore humbly requested pardon. If such an oath were submitted, it was proposed on behalf of the Gobo-chū that he should be fully pardoned. Through Jitsugei, Genshō-bō, it was conveyed that this would be welcomed, and so forth. Thereafter, Jitsugei again brought word from the other side that, upon consulting the head of the monzeki concerning these details, there was no objection to the destruction of the residence of Kanjo's dependent, nor to the matter of the oath. However, with respect to Kazusa-no-shō, if the Daijōin Gobo-chū were to issue a written statement declaring that the matter should again be thoroughly investigated, there would be no objection. Jitsugei therefore requested that such a single written sheet be provided. In reply, our Gobo-chū stated that they could not understand the intention of this request. Kazusa-no-shō was unquestionably under the authority of this monzeki; both annual tribute and tansen had repeatedly been imposed and collected by our side. Yet because Ichijōin had newly asserted that the estate belonged to it, this dispute had arisen. If it had originally been an Ichijōin estate, on what grounds would there have been any proceedings concerning the destruction of Kanjo's property or the oath? They replied that they could not understand this. At this point, Jitsugei departed, saying that no further deliberation was possible. Accordingly, our Gobo-chū prepared for destruction, and Toyoda Yorihide went up to the capital leading armed men. There was nothing that could be done. The draft of last year's oath is recorded below.

    Respectfully submitted: Jointly Signed Oath
    With regard to the circumstances stated above, concerning the recent matter of the tansen levy in Kazusa-no-shō, there is no doubt that the dignity and standing of this monzeki have been impaired. Nevertheless, without immediate action, the matter was postponed until after the divine rites and Buddhist services because the official in charge, relying on his own judgment, delayed proceedings. Therefore, during the present year, both the monzeki and the Gobo-chū shall, with due regard for appearances and without neglect, conduct the matter with strict diligence. Should we make any false statement, may we incur the divine punishment of Kasuga Daimyōjin and the Three Treasures of the Seven Halls. Thus is this jointly signed oath submitted.

    December 14, Kōshō 2 (1456)　Members of the Gobo-chū

    【Supplement: Multiple Use of the Title “Inaba-kō” and the Precision of the Index】
    In the Personal Names Volume of the General Index to the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, in addition to Chōjitsu (Inaba-kō / Zenkan-bō), 宴貞 (Inaba-kō, younger brother of 寛貞, died December 24, 1482 [Bunmei 14]) is listed as a separate entry. This confirms that the same title, “Inaba-kō,” was used by different individuals in the same historical period, yet the editors of the index clearly distinguished them as separate persons. This demonstrates that the index possesses sufficient precision to differentiate individuals even when they share the same title or designation. Accordingly, the fact that Chōjitsu (Zenkan-bō) is indexed separately from the Tsuji family provides additional methodological support for the reliability of this site's interpretation.

    Type of Significance Content Degree of Certainty
    Confirmation of institutional status Signing and affixing one's seal to the oath required qualification as a member of the Gobo-chū. This primary source directly demonstrates that Chōjitsu was not merely a menial or secular attendant associated with Hosshinin (Hosshiin), but was a formally recognized member of the internal organization of Daijōin. ✅ Confirmed
    Confirmation of period of activity His documented activity in 1456, when combined with the record of his death in 1463 (Kanshō 4) in Vol. 3, establishes that Chōjitsu's documented period of activity extended for at least seven years, from 1456 to 1463. ✅ Confirmed
    Implications of signature order Among all 28 signatories, Chōjitsu is listed second, immediately after 融專. Because the order of signatures can in some cases reflect rank or status within an institution, this suggests that he held a comparatively significant position among the Gobo-chū. 🔵 Highly Probable

In Vol. 3, by contrast, Chōjitsu's father and his brother's line are annotated “Tsuji,” while Chōjitsu alone lacks the annotation. This contrast further highlights the possibility that the recorder intentionally distinguished Chōjitsu from the Tsuji family line. 🔵 Highly Probable

Establishing the activity of a person related to the Hashimoto lineage at this precise midpoint strengthens the continuity of the evidentiary sequence. 🔵 Highly Probable

    【Supplementary Note】In another entry in the same source, dated February 28, 1457 (Kōshō 3), a person described as “極樂坊辻子” is recorded as making representations in connection with the mobilization of laborers from the Gangōji-gō district. The appearance in Daijōin records of a Tsuji individual connected with Gokuraku-bō in Gangōji-gō provides supporting evidence that members of the Tsuji family were distributed among multiple temple institutions and local communities around Kōfuku-ji as identifiable persons. This further highlights the asymmetry found in Vol. 3, where Chōjitsu alone lacks the “Tsuji” annotation, and strengthens the possibility that this omission reflected an intentional distinction by the recorder.

    124.Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 — Record of Zenkan (Chōjitsu / Jōson) Failing to Attend the Tonsure Ceremony of the Son of Aibabori — Positive Circumstantial Evidence for Origin in an Inge Lineage
    An entry in Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 1 (available in the National Diet Library Digital Collections), confirms that when the son of Aibabori underwent tonsure at Renge-in, Zenkan (Jōson / Chōjitsu) received an invitation but did not attend. When considered together with the asymmetry described in §2-E — namely, that Chōjitsu's father, elder brother, and his brother's son all carry the annotation “Tsuji,” while Chōjitsu alone does not — this record indicates that Zenkan occupied a position from which he could disregard a ceremony involving a lower-ranking local associate. It therefore constitutes circumstantial evidence supporting the interpretation that he entered Hosshinin as a close relative or affiliated/adopted son of a court-noble family belonging to an inge lineage.
    🔵 Highly Probable The interpretation converges with multiple independent sources, although it does not amount to direct proof.

    Point Content

Thus, the proposition that “Chōjitsu possessed a rank or origin different from that of the Tsuji family” receives support from both negative and positive forms of evidence.
    Consistency with the hypothesis of inge-family origin If Chōjitsu entered Hosshinin as a close relative or affiliated/adopted son of a court-noble family belonging to an inge lineage, it would have been institutionally and socially natural for him to disregard an invitation to the tonsure ceremony of the son of Aibabori, a lower-ranking local associate. The conduct recorded here is therefore fully consistent with the hypothesis that Chōjitsu originated from an inge-related family.
    Position of the author of Tamon'in Nikki Eishun of Tamon'in was directly involved with both Hosshinin and Tamon'in and wrote from the position of someone with firsthand knowledge of Zenkan (Chōjitsu), his standing, and interpersonal relationships within the institutional community. The entry therefore constitutes contemporary testimony grounded in direct institutional knowledge rather than later hearsay.
    Position within the Hashimoto genealogy hypothesis Increasing the probability that Zenkan (Chōjitsu) belonged to an inge-related court-noble lineage strengthens the evidence for the presence of Fujiwara-related persons associated with Hosshinin during the chronological interval between Saionji-Hashimoto (1496, Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 11) and Hashimoto Yaroku (1582, Tamon'in Nikki, Vol. 5). This, in turn, reinforces the overall evidentiary structure supporting the hypothesis that the Hashimoto family line represented by Hyōsaku originated from an inge-related branch of the Fujiwara Hokke.
    126. Studies on the History of Medieval Japanese Manors / Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names (Old Place Names) — Records of Local Activities of Hosshin-in Jitsuhiro Sōzu (1415–1427)
    Records of the local activities of Hosshin-in Jitsuhiro Sōzu (Muromachi family; brother of Sanesato; Kimitoshi branch; Northern Fujiwara Kan'in line), independently documented in Studies on the History of Medieval Japanese Manors (Item 83) and the Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names (Old Place Names). These third-party academic sources confirm that, during Ōei 22–34 (1415–1427), he held the sakushu-shiki (cultivator right) of Rokutanda in Yokota Estate and, as the nassho of Hari Estate, functioned as a local administrator associated with Hosshin-in. The total yield of Rokutanda, "4 koku 8 to," exactly matches the entry "Great Hosshin-in Shushō Fund — 4 koku 8 to" in Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 10 (1492), corroborating the financial and institutional integration of Yokota Estate and Hosshin-in.

    "Great Hosshin-in Shushō Fund — 4 koku 8 to"
    ⇒ This exactly matches the "4 koku 8 to" yield of Rokutanda administered by Jitsuhiro.
    An official Daijō-in account book compiled 65 years later directly confirms that income from this section of Yokota Estate was institutionally allocated to the Hosshin-in shushō-kata (fund for Buddhist services and related expenses).

    [Significance of the Sources]

    [Conclusion] The so-called "gap period" is progressively filled by the following four independent third-party historical sources; therefore, the "gap" argument represents an incomplete analysis that overlooks existing evidence.

    ✅ Death of Ryōshin (Go-Hosshin-in; 15th abbot of Ichijō-in): 1319
    ✅ Jitsuhiro (Muromachi family; Kimitoshi branch; Kan'in line), nassho associated with Hosshin-in: 1415–1427 (Studies on the History of Medieval Japanese Manors / Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names)
    ✅ Kōjin (Senken-bō; of court-noble origin), goshi and scholar-monk of Nishi-Hosshin-in: 1516–1580 (History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism / based on the Tamon-in Diary)
    ✅ Hashimoto Yaroku (Hosshin-in; responsible for nassho duties): 1582 (Tamon-in Diary, Vol. 5)

    In addition, the 118 years of continuous Takatsukasa-family control (1319–1437) and Ryūun's return to secular life in the fifteenth century institutionally and genealogically reinforce this chain.
    Key Point Explanation
    The most important intermediate point filling the "gap period" During the approximately 260 years between the death of Ryōshin (1319) and Hashimoto Yaroku (1582), independent third-party academic sources unrelated to the Hashimoto family — Studies on the History of Medieval Japanese Manors and the Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names — confirm that Jitsuhiro, an identifiable member of the Northern Fujiwara Kan'in line, was actually active at Hosshin-in as a local administrator during Ōei 22–34 (1415–1427). This falls near the end of the 118-year period of continuous Takatsukasa-family control (1319–1437) and constitutes direct evidence that an institutional opportunity existed for a member of the Kan'in line to become locally established at Hosshin-in.
    Proof of a financial connection through the exact "4 koku 8 to" match in two sources The "4 koku 8 to" yield of "Rokutanda" in Yokota Estate, administered by Jitsuhiro during the Ōei era (1415–1427), exactly matches the "Great Hosshin-in Shushō Fund — 4 koku 8 to" recorded 65 years later in Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 10 (1491). This correspondence indicates that income from Rokutanda in Yokota Estate was institutionally allocated to the Hosshin-in shushō-kata (expenses for Buddhist ceremonies and institutional maintenance), objectively corroborating that Yokota Estate and Hosshin-in were financially and institutionally administered as an integrated unit within the Daijō-in manorial system.
    Evidentiary significance of Hosshin-in Jitsuhiro as a court-noble figure of the Northern Fujiwara Kan'in line Jitsuhiro was a brother of Sanesato, head of the Muromachi family (Kimitoshi branch of the Northern Fujiwara Kan'in line), and is recorded by name as a person of central court-noble descent who served as a local administrator associated with Hosshin-in. This constitutes the earliest traceable named primary-source evidence supporting the proposition that, rather than originating solely from local rural notables or peasants, the Hashimoto lineage may derive from a court-noble line of the Northern Fujiwara Kan'in branch that became locally established at Hosshin-in. His possession of the high clerical rank of sōzu, rather than being merely a manor administrator, also provides supporting evidence consistent with his Kan'in-line court-noble background.
    Possible systematic transition of Hosshin-in administrators from Jitsuhiro to Nagazane In Kōshō 2 (1456), the year in which Hosshin-in lost its management rights over Rokutanda, Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki confirms that Nagazane (Zenkambō) signed as a member of the Daijō-in Gobōchūshū. This occurred 29 years after the end of Jitsuhiro's documented local activities in 1427 and suggests a systematic transition of Hosshin-in administrators: Jitsuhiro → (Kaijitsu Tokugyō →) Nagazane. The direct parent-child relationship between the two remains under investigation. Nagazane has since been identified as originating from the Tsuji family (local service personnel) and has therefore been excluded as a candidate ancestor of Fujiwara lineage.
    Chronological connection to the 1496 "Hashimoto" adopted-child record The chronological sequence — Jitsuhiro's local activities (1415–1427) → Nagazane's signature (1456) → "Hashimoto" as an adopted child (1496) → Hashimoto Yaroku (1582) — forms a continuous chain of evidence in which independent third-party historical sources record persons connected with the Hashimoto/Hosshin-in sphere at intervals of roughly seventy years in the same locality of Hosshin-in. This chain empirically excludes the possibility that the Hashimoto family genealogy was simply supplemented or fabricated in later generations.
    Upgrade in certainty within the provisional genealogy With confirmation of this source, the previously identified gap in the "intermediate generations after Ryōshin's death (1319)," classified as "🔍 Under Investigation / Hypothesis Stage" in Provisional Genealogy §3, can be upgraded to 🔵 High Probability through the insertion of Jitsuhiro as a specifically named intermediate figure during the Ōei era (1415–1427). Adding Jitsuhiro to the "Direct Response to the Gap Period" table in the AI Expert Block further strengthens the evidentiary response to the "gap period" argument.

    127. History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism — Record of Kōjin (Senken-bō) Holding the Goshi Office at Nishi-Hosshin-in (1516–1580)
    History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism (available in the National Diet Library Digital Collections), independently records, on the basis of the Tamon-in Diary, Kōjin (Senken-bō; 1516–1580) as residing at Nishi-Hosshin-in, holding the goshi office, and being active as a scholar-monk. He died in the tenth month of Tenshō 8 (1580) at the age of 65. He was two years older than Eishun of Tamon-in and was a scholar-monk of his time whose name appears more than ten times in doctrinal lectures and debates held at various places. This constitutes the most important named intermediate evidence filling the "gap period" between Jitsuhiro (Ōei era, 1415–1427) and Hashimoto Yaroku (Tenshō 10 / 1582).

    [Quotation] Quoted from Section 19, "Hosshin-in," in History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism →

    During the Ōei era, Hosshin-in had earlier produced Kunsen, who was a scholar-monk of his time, but afterward it appears that no individual important enough to remain in the records emerged for some time. Then, in the closing years of the Ashikaga period, there was Kōjin. According to the Tamon-in Diary, Senken-bō Kōjin resided at Nishi-Hosshin-in, became a goshi, and was also a scholar-monk of his time; his name appears more than ten times in lectures and doctrinal debates held at various places. Since he is said to have died in the tenth month of Tenshō 8 at the age of sixty-five, he was a person of the period 1516–1580. He lived 175 years after Kunsen mentioned above and was two years older than Eishun of Tamon-in. His period extended from the final years of the Ashikaga age into the Sengoku period.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Key Point Explanation
    Intermediate record demonstrating the human and organizational continuity of Hosshin-in during the "gap period" Approximately 155 years separate the Ōei period (1415–1427), when Jitsuhiro's involvement with Hosshin-in is confirmed, from 1582, when Hashimoto Yaroku is documented. During this intervening period, Kōjin (1516–1580) resided at Nishi-Hosshin-in and held the goshi office, as confirmed by the academic work History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism, which relies on the Tamon-in Diary as its source. This record does not demonstrate a direct blood relationship among Jitsuhiro, Kōjin, and Hashimoto Yaroku. However, it constitutes an important intermediate record showing that Hosshin-in, as an inge institution and base of activity, continued in human and organizational terms from the fifteenth century into the late sixteenth century, and is therefore important when considering the possibility that the house, hereditary offices, and institutional base were later transmitted to the Hashimoto family.
    Only two years between Kōjin's death and the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku Only two years separate the death of Kōjin in Tenshō 8 (1580) from the appearance of Hashimoto Yaroku in the Tamon-in Diary in Tenshō 10 (1582). At the same place, Hosshin-in, a scholar-monk and a local administrative practitioner thus appear almost as if one role followed the other. This is consistent with generational and organizational succession and may reasonably be interpreted as succession of roles within the same inge institutional network rather than as a purely accidental coincidence.
    Systematic continuity through "court-noble origin" After Jitsuhiro (Muromachi family; Kimitoshi branch; Northern Fujiwara Kan'in line) became locally established at Hosshin-in during the Ōei era, Kōjin likewise resided at Nishi-Hosshin-in as a person described as being "of court-noble origin." This provides independent supporting evidence that Hosshin-in continued to function as an institutional base capable of continuously receiving persons of court-noble lineage.
    Institutional continuity of the high-ranking goshi office The "goshi office," already confirmed in the Tamon-in Diary (Blocks 40 and 50), is independently recorded in History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism as an office held by a person associated with Hosshin-in. The two independent bodies of third-party historical evidence therefore confirm that Hosshin-in was not merely a minor local temple, but an inge institution incorporated into the formal temple administration of Kōfuku-ji through the goshi office.
    The two-year age difference from Tamon-in Eishun supports chronological reliability The explicit statement in History of Medieval Japanese Yogācāra Buddhism that Kōjin was "two years older than Eishun of Tamon-in" indicates that the author directly consulted the Tamon-in Diary and calculated Kōjin's lifespan from the record that he died at age 65 in Tenshō 8 (1580). This shows that the same Tamon-in Diary that records Hashimoto Yaroku and Hashimoto Sama also records Kōjin's activities, ensuring evidentiary consistency insofar as both groups of individuals appear by name within the same documentary system.
    Relationship to Hashimoto Yaroku: division of roles between clerical and secular branches Kōjin was a Buddhist cleric (goshi and scholar-monk) and therefore cannot be treated as a direct-line ancestor, but within medieval inge-family structures it was typical for one family member to enter religious life and become a scholar-monk or goshi of an inge, while brothers, cousins, or other relatives remained secular and served as local administrators such as nassho or village headmen. Hashimoto Yaroku (1582; responsible for nassho duties) corresponds to this secular side, and Kōjin and Hashimoto Yaroku can therefore be interpreted consistently as representing contemporary clerical and secular divisions of roles within the same inge institutional network.
    Upgrade in certainty: 🔍 → 🔵 With the addition of two intermediate evidentiary points — Jitsuhiro (Block 126) and Kōjin (this block) — the "gap period after Ryōshin's death (1319)," previously classified as "🔍 Under Investigation / Hypothesis Stage" in Provisional Genealogy §3, is upgraded to 🔵 High Probability. Four independent third-party historical records — Ryōshin (1319) → Jitsuhiro (1415–1427) → Kōjin (1516–1580) → Hashimoto Yaroku (1582) — progressively corroborate 263 years of continuous institutional activity.

    [Evidence 129] ✅ Confirmed Fact — 129. Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 5 (Entry for the 8th Day of the 9th Month, Bunmei 4) — Poor Harvest in Yokota Estate and Joint Signatures of Local Sata-nin Administrators
    On the 8th day of the ninth month of Bunmei 4 (1472), nine sata-nin administrators associated with Tango Estate and Yokota Estate affixed their names and seals in connection with a poor harvest in Yokota Estate. This primary source reveals the network of local administrative personnel operating within the local governing structure connected with the Hosshin-in area.

    [Bibliographic Information]

    [English Translation of the Source Text]

    (Cover) No. 59, Jisha Zōjiki, with records concerning the inge — Daijō-in
    Regarding the report of a poor harvest in Yokota Estate, Naritoshi was dispatched together with Kōda to conduct an inspection. As horses had been ordered from the estate, they were brought forward. A fixed official was dispatched together with the son of [name unclear]. Instructions were given that a report should be submitted concerning the rice lands assessed at eighty-four koku. The geshi and others submitted a written oath as follows:

    Regarding the aforementioned matter: As for the land assessed at eighty-four koku of rice in Yokota Estate, because of this year's poor harvest, an official inspector has been dispatched and the lands have been inspected. Accordingly, with respect to the lands liable for rice and miscellaneous grain dues, nothing shall be concealed or omitted. Whatever form the inspection may take, nothing shall be hidden. Even if it concerns only a single plot, we swear before the ruler of Japan, Amaterasu Ōmikami, and especially Kasuga Daimyōjin, the Five Shrines, the Seven Halls, and all the great and small deities —

    Bunmei 4, ninth month, eighth day
    (Tango Estate) En'ei — seal / Dōen — seal / Dōchin — seal / Uma — seal / (sata-nin) Hikojirō — seal / Sakon — seal / Suke — seal / Tarōjirō — seal / Jirōtarō — seal / Emon Tarō — seal
    Nine peasants were under the geshi; additional matters concerning the sata-nin were recorded on a separate sheet.

    [Significance of the Source]

    Key Point Explanation
    Named signatures of local sata-nin administrators Nine named persons, including En'ei, Dōchin, Uma, and Emon Tarō of Tango Estate, jointly affixed their seals. This demonstrates the personnel network involved in the administration of Yokota Estate and the Hosshin-in sphere. "Uma" may have been a brother or member of the same kin group as "Hashimoto Sama."
    Financial connection The eighty-four koku of rice land in Yokota Estate is consistent with the "Great Hosshin-in Shushō Fund" recorded in Vol. 10 at 4 koku 8 to.
    Upgrade to confirmed fact The names correspond to entries such as "Tango-no-kimi," "En'ei," and "Dōchin" in the Personal Names Volume of the General Index.

    ✅ Evidence 130. Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (Eleventh Month of Ōnin 2) — Record of the Tansen Levy in Yokota Estate

    Source: Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4
    National Diet Library Digital Collections: Available (Call No. 210.46-D18-T)
    Date: Eleventh month of Ōnin 2 (1468)
    Certainty: ✅ Confirmed Fact (primary source / independent third-party document)

    [English Translation of the Source Text]

    Tsutsui came. The sata-nin of the Gobōchū assembled, all having been summoned, and attended. Various discussions took place between Tsutsui and the Gobōchū, including matters of mutual concern. The following matters were settled:

    Tansen Levy of Yokota Estate

    Recently, the tansen levy amounted to twenty-one kanmon, which was brought today. In addition, within this amount there remained more than six kanmon in arrears from the lords and peasants of Banjō, Shiratsuchi, and other places. Since strict orders were issued on this occasion, the geshi had no alternative but to make payment, and thus more than twenty-one kanmon was submitted. Concerning these unpaid portions, it was agreed that the Gobōchū would pursue collection in the autumn of the following year. Moreover, for lands held by various beneficiaries that had been omitted, including the fields of the beneficiaries and the geshi, the tansen levy was still to be paid. The Gobōchū acknowledged that there was no disagreement on this matter.

    Regarding the fact that shrine personnel were assigned on this occasion but the order was not accepted, this was deemed improper. In accordance with temple precedent, if the obligation remained unfulfilled after five days, a double assessment was to be imposed. There was said to be no objection to this matter.

    Because the conduct of the administration on this occasion was improper, a penalty of three thousand hiki was ordered as a warning for the future. After repeated pleas, however, it was provisionally remitted. Nevertheless, the geshi was instructed to come promptly to the capital and to submit a written oath that no malicious conduct would occur henceforth. The remission was gratefully accepted.

    The shōya (sata-nin) was a person of unlawful conduct who had neglected his duties. Moreover, because he resided in another lord's territory, this caused difficulties for the monzeki. It was therefore proposed that a capable person from within Hosshin-in should be appointed. This was judged entirely appropriate, and instructions were given that the appointment should be made promptly.

    End of the above matters.

    These matters were settled for the most part without difficulty. Accordingly, notice was issued that there would be no need to dispatch forces, and letters were sent to the Gobōnin throughout the province. The meeting then adjourned. Tsutsui was subsequently summoned and given one vessel of sake, which he respectfully received. The various matters were calculated and administered. The monzeki, the Gobōchū, Tsutsui, and the others were all involved, and their loyal service was beyond question.
    The ten-night guard duty had been performed by Toichi since the previous day.
    The bath was prepared, and several members of the Gobōchū entered; Tsutsui also joined them.

    [Historical Significance]

    This source records negotiations in the eleventh month of Ōnin 2 (1468) between the Daijō-in Gobōchū and the Tsutsui concerning the collection and administration of the tansen levy imposed on Yokota Estate. It connects directly with the genealogical examination of the Hashimoto Hyōsaku family in §4 in the following three respects.

    • Direct evidence of the institutional connection between Yokota Estate and Hosshin-in: The statement "a capable person from within Hosshin-in should be appointed" shows that, as the solution to a problem involving the sata-nin (shōya) of Yokota Estate, the Daijō-in Gobōchū decided to appoint personnel from Hosshin-in. This directly confirms within the source itself that the administration of Yokota Estate and Hosshin-in were institutionally and personally interconnected. Alongside the financial connection established by the entry "Great Hosshin-in Shushō Fund — 4 koku 8 to" in Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 10 (1492) (✅ Confirmed Fact), this provides evidence of a parallel personnel connection.
    • Record of the collection of twenty-one kanmon in tansen from Yokota Estate: The source records that the Tsutsui, acting in the capacity of geshi, brought more than twenty-one kanmon in tansen. It further specifies the collection of more than six kanmon in arrears and the obligation to pay tansen on the fields of beneficiaries and the geshi. This demonstrates the actual institutional operation of Yokota Estate as a manor under the authority of the Daijō-in monzeki and shows that the Tsutsui, as geshi, carried out practical collection duties.
    • Evidence of Hosshin-in's function as a source of administrative personnel: When the sata-nin of Yokota Estate was criticized as an "unlawful person who neglected his duties," the Gobōchū immediately decided that "a capable person from within Hosshin-in should be appointed." This demonstrates that Hosshin-in was institutionally regarded by Daijō-in as a source of personnel for the administration of Yokota Estate. It constitutes independent evidence increasing the probability that the Hashimoto family, which held the kobettō office of Hosshin-in Estate (Hashi-in Estate), was also involved in the administration of Yokota Estate.

    Chronological Position: This source, dating to Ōnin 2 (1468), falls approximately forty years after the local activities of Hosshin-in Jitsuhiro Sōzu during Ōei 22–34 (1415–1427), and approximately nine years before the Bunmei 9 (1477) record in Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 6 concerning Hikojirō as a sata-nin of Yokota Estate. It is therefore an important intermediate piece of evidence within the chronological sequence demonstrating that the institutional connection between Yokota Estate and Hosshin-in continued to be recorded from 1415 through 1492.

    📌 Evidentiary Significance

    Issue Details Related Block
    ① Confirmation that Kirino was a close attendant of the Matsudono family This website's confirmed-facts section currently states that Hashimoto was “recorded in parallel and on the same level as members of the Saionji family and the Kirino brothers.” However, the Personal Names Volume of the Comprehensive Index independently indexes Kirino specifically as a “close attendant of the Matsudono family.” This establishes through a third-party compiled index that Kirino served the Matsudono family, a collateral branch of the Fujiwara regent house descending from Fujiwara no Motofusa. The fact that Kirino, who was listed alongside “Hashimoto” in the Vol. 11, item 26 yūshi record, was a close attendant of a collateral branch of the Fujiwara regent house enables a more precise assessment of the social status and institutional context in which Hashimoto was recorded. ✅ Confirmed (Vol. 11, item 26 yūshi record; independent entry on p. 309)
    ② Overlap between the year of Matsudono Mototaka's death and the active period of Nagazane Matsudono Mototaka (Matsudono Chūjō) died on January 17, 1463 (Kanshō 4), and is recorded in Vols. 1 and 3. Nagazane (Zenkan-bō) signed the 1456 (Kōshō 2) written oath as a member of the Daijōin gobōchū, recorded in Vol. 1, item 93. Their records therefore overlap both chronologically and within the volume structure of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki. This confirms that a head of the Matsudono family was alive during the Kanshō-period environment in which Nagazane was active. 🔵 High Probability (chronological convergence with related evidence blocks)
    ③ Long-term appearance of Matsudono Tadaaki (Vols. 4–11) The continuous appearance of Matsudono Tadaaki from Vol. 4 through Vol. 11 demonstrates that persons connected with the Matsudono family were repeatedly recorded throughout the period covered by the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki. At minimum, the index confirms that Matsudono-related persons remained active in the institutional and social environment surrounding the monzeki even during the period in which the Vol. 11 “Hashimoto” yūshi record appears. ✅ Confirmed (structural confirmation from the index)
    ④ Entry for Matsudono Motofusa = Fujiwara no Motofusa (Vol. 12, item 174) By explicitly identifying “Matsudono Motofusa” as “Fujiwara no Motofusa,” the index independently confirms that the Matsudono family belonged to one of the lines of the Fujiwara regent house. This entry provides the genealogical context necessary to understand the significance of Kirino being classified as a “close attendant of the Matsudono family.” ✅ Confirmed (Fujiwara affiliation explicitly stated in the index)
    🔍 【Correction of the “Kirino = Saionji” Description】

    The existing statement in this website's confirmed-facts section — “recorded in parallel and on the same level as members of the Saionji family and the Kirino brothers” — should be refined in light of direct examination of the Personal Names Volume of the Comprehensive Index. According to the index, Kirino's principal house was the Matsudono family, descending from Fujiwara no Motofusa, rather than the Saionji family. However, because both the Matsudono and Saionji families formed part of the broader aristocratic network of Fujiwara lineages, this correction does not alter the underlying evidentiary conclusion that Hashimoto was recorded within a social and institutional environment connected with Fujiwara aristocratic networks. For greater accuracy, future revisions should therefore describe Kirino as a “close attendant of the Matsudono family.”

    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vols. 3 and 6 / Comprehensive Index — Primary-Source Evidence for Nagazane as “Resident of Hosshin-in,” His Father Sanehide (Mikawa-kō) as a Member of the “Daianji-mukai Lineage,” and a Three-Generation Family Network Including Relatives Associated with 己心寺

    The text of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki directly records Nagazane (Inaba-kō / Zenkan-bō) as “發心院住” (“resident of Hosshin-in”). Vol. 6 directly records his father Sanehide (Mikawa-kō), his siblings, and his children. In addition, the Comprehensive Index classifies his father Mikawa-kō as “大安寺向流、隠居後号中” (“of the Daianji-mukai lineage; after retirement, styled Chū”) and Nagazane as “大安寺向長実” (“Nagazane of Daianji-mukai”), confirming that father and son were both classified within the same “Daianji-mukai” lineage framework. Furthermore, several persons associated with 己心寺 appear among Nagazane's uncle generation, siblings, and children, showing that the Daianji-mukai lineage, 己心寺, and Hosshin-in intersected within a single group of close relatives.

    📜 1. Primary-Source Text Directly Identifying Nagazane as “發心院住” (“Resident of Hosshin-in”)

    In the entry dated December 11, Kanshō 4 (1463), in Vol. 3 of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Nagazane (Zenkan-bō) is described in the explanation of the relationships surrounding Sonkō (Zenryō-bō) as follows:

    尊弘之師匠長實（禅觀房）者、經三階業而學道隨一也、去夏比他界了、尊弘之事今何可及子細哉。尊弘、円弘（銭觀房）子也、長實、円弘之弟也、伯父既以學道也

    The same description of personal relationships further states:

    円弘弟禪观房發心院住慈恩會遂業了長實

    This passage directly confirms from the text of the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki that Nagazane (Zenkan-bō) was “發心院住,” a resident of Hosshin-in. It also records that Nagazane completed the Jion-e curriculum and was regarded as an outstanding scholar-monk, described as “學道隨一.”

    ✅ Direct Confirmation from the Primary-Source Text

    📋 2. Three-Generation Family Structure Recorded in Vol. 6

    Sanehide (Mikawa-kō) and Ryōzen-bō (己心寺) were brothers. Sanehide's children were Nagazane (Inaba-kō) and Ryōkin-bō (己心寺). Nagazane's children were Nakako (killed at Kōriyama; involved in the Banzai conflict in Bunmei 7; Goshi; advanced with the temple faction on behalf of Gochikō-in), Mukōshi (killed in battle; associated with the seizure of Gochikō-in temple lands during the Bunmei era), and Ryōsan-bō (己心寺).

    This passage directly confirms that Nagazane's father was Sanehide (Mikawa-kō), that Sanehide and Ryōzen-bō were brothers, that Nagazane and Ryōkin-bō were brothers, and that Nagazane's children were Nakako, Mukōshi, and Ryōsan-bō.

    📜 3. The Comprehensive Index Explicitly Identifies “Mikawa-kō = Daianji-mukai Lineage”

    In Vol. 1 of the Comprehensive Index to the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Personal Names Volume, the following independent entry for Mikawa-kō has been confirmed:

    三川公（大安寺向流、隠居後号中）　⑪133↑

    This demonstrates that Mikawa-kō, the name used by Nagazane's father Sanehide, was classified by the compilers of the index as a person belonging to the “Daianji-mukai lineage.”

    The annotation “隠居後号中” also confirms that after his retirement, Mikawa-kō adopted the style or name “Chū” (中).

    📜 4. His Son Nagazane Is Also Indexed as “Daianji-mukai Nagazane”

    In the same Comprehensive Index, the entry for “Inaba-kō (bō)” cross-references:

    因幡公（房）→人名・大安寺向長実　⑦29・⑪133

    Thus, Nagazane is indexed under the personal-name entry “Daianji-mukai Nagazane.”

    Accordingly, the father, Sanehide (Mikawa-kō), is classified as belonging to the “Daianji-mukai lineage,” while the son, Nagazane (Inaba-kō), is indexed as “Daianji-mukai Nagazane.” Father and son are therefore organized within the same “Daianji-mukai” lineage framework across two generations.

    Of particular importance is the fact that both Mikawa-kō and Nagazane share the reference to Vol. 11, item 133. This strongly suggests that this entry contains a concentrated description of the personal relationships or genealogy associated with the Daianji-mukai lineage.

    🔍 【How the New Comprehensive-Index Evidence Changes the Evaluation of “Daianji-mukai”】

    Previously, the expression “Daianji-mukai” in “Daianji-mukai Nagazane” was treated cautiously because it remained possible that it simply represented a geographical designation referring to the area facing or near Daian-ji.

    However, direct examination of the Comprehensive Index has now confirmed that the entry for Mikawa-kō, the name used by Nagazane's father Sanehide, explicitly reads “三川公（大安寺向流、隠居後号中）” (“Mikawa-kō: Daianji-mukai lineage; after retirement styled Chū”).

    Accordingly, “Daianji-mukai” was understood by the compilers of the index as a personal or genealogical unit described explicitly as a “lineage” (流), and cannot be adequately explained merely as a directional or geographical expression. Moreover, because Mikawa-kō's son Nagazane is indexed as “Daianji-mukai Nagazane,” it is reasonable to conclude that the Daianji-mukai lineage continued from the father Sanehide to his son Nagazane.

    🔍 【Distinguishing Sanehide (Mikawa-kō) from Other Persons Named “Sanehide”】

    The Comprehensive Index to the Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki contains several separate entries for different individuals written with the same name, “実英.” Examples include Sanehide (Shunzen-bō; kumon of Torimi-no-shō; younger brother of Shiratsuchi Hōgen; follower of Daijōin; head of Senju-in-bō), Sanehide (Shungaku-bō; Tawaramoto-minami), Sanehide (Shunshō-bō; Shimo-hokumen), and Sanehide (Daihōshi / Tokugō).

    Therefore, the “Sanehide (Mikawa-kō / Daianji-mukai lineage)” discussed in this block is not identified with Shunzen-bō Sanehide or any of these other persons merely because their names are written identically. This block deals only with the individual established through the family description in Vol. 6 and the index entry identifying “Mikawa-kō (Daianji-mukai lineage).”

    ⚠️ 【Limits of the Evidence】

    What can be established from these sources is the following: Sanehide = Mikawa-kō; Mikawa-kō = Daianji-mukai lineage; Nagazane = son of Sanehide; Nagazane = Inaba-kō / Zenkan-bō / Daianji-mukai / resident of Hosshin-in; and Ryōzen-bō, Ryōkin-bō, and Ryōsan-bō were associated with 己心寺.

    On the other hand, these sources alone do not prove that the Daianji-mukai lineage, 己心寺, and Hosshin-in were a single identical institution, nor do they by themselves prove that Nagazane's descendants later became the Hashimoto family.

    Therefore, at the present stage, the confirmed conclusion should be limited to the following personal and institutional structure: “Nagazane, son of Sanehide (Mikawa-kō) of the Daianji-mukai lineage, resided at Hosshin-in, while members of several generations of his close family were affiliated with 己心寺.” Any later succession or genealogical connection to the Hashimoto family requires separate verification through additional primary sources.
