    ✅ [Verification of the Original Text in History of Medieval Japanese Shōen] Accurate Description of the Relationship of Jikkō and Jōsei with Hasshiin

    📌 [Important: Confirmation Extending the Period of Jikkō’s Activity]
    In addition to this website’s previously cited record that “Sōzu Jikkō moved to Hasshiin and managed agricultural land there from 1415 to 1427,” this document confirms that Sōzu Jikkō held the sakunushi rights (cultivation-holder rights) to “Rokutanda” within Shinmen-no-shō, an estate belonging to Daijōin.
    Arrears in annual tribute are recorded for Kōshō 2 (1456) and Chōroku 1 (1457), independently supporting the conclusion that the institutional activities associated with Jikkō at Hasshiin — or those of his successors — continued from 1415–1427 until at least 1456–1457, approximately thirty to forty years after the record of his residence at Hasshiin.

    ⚠️ [Important: Refinement of Jōsei’s Institutional Position]
    This website currently states that “three independent sources confirm that Jōsei (Hasshiin / Kuzuha Nyūdō) was involved in the administrative affairs of Hasshiin.” However, the original text on p. 83 of History of Medieval Japanese Shōen records that the Daijōin monzeki explicitly stated concerning Jōsei: “於定清者且借住分云々,” meaning that Jōsei was regarded merely as a person temporarily residing there.
    Although Jōsei’s residence at Hasshiin is certain, he was not officially recognized as the holder of the Hasshiin administrative office. For academic accuracy, the expression “a person involved in the administrative affairs of Hasshiin” should therefore be refined to “a person who resided at Hasshiin.”

    📌 [Supplementary Record: Fourth Independent Source] On pp. 322–323 of History of Medieval Japanese Hossō/Yogācāra Buddhism (National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. HM121-110), the chapter heading explicitly identifies him as “Jōsei (Kennyabō) (Hasshiin).” The text further states that “Jōsei was my [Jinson’s] fellow student and was a scholar of the time.” His lifespan is established as 1399–1477, with a record stating that in the twelfth month of Bunmei 9 he died at the age of seventy-nine as “the bōshu of Hasshiin, Gon-Daisōzu, Jōsei Goshi.” This constitutes a fourth independent academic source supporting the connection between Jōsei and Hasshiin, in addition to Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, History of Medieval Japanese Shōen, and the General Index of Personal Names. Accordingly, the previous description of “three independent sources” can be upgraded to “four independent sources.”

    The monzeki rejected the request and explicitly characterized Jōsei’s position as “karizumi-bun”, meaning a temporary resident.
    The petition was also connected with the presence of the official shuto Furuichi Tanehide.
    This confirms that Tanehide was already connected with Hasshiin six years before the previously cited 1475 record in Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 6, concerning the yūshi relationship involving Kakuin.     		「発志院事ハ、当門跡自専地、坊務ニ初任平宛出之処、称無坊務之間不及問答、於定清者且借住分云々」

    「① 雖為作主、地主方年貢無沙汰上者、不可及子細事也」     		✅ Confirmed
    (Institutional Structure) A three-tiered structure can be identified in Shinmen-no-shō: landlord (Daijōin) — sakunushi (Hasshiin) — cultivating peasants.
    The condition in which the sakunushi was removed was called “jikimu” or direct administration. Land for which Daijōin controlled both the landlord rights and sakunushi rights was called “jisaku-ippuchi”.
    Hasshiin, as sakunushi, was also responsible for collecting the landlord’s share of annual tribute.     		“The three layers of landlord (Daijōin), sakunushi (Hasshiin), and cultivating peasants overlapped.” ✅ Confirmed

    📌 [Updated Timeline of Jikkō’s Activities]

    1415–1427 Sōzu Jikkō resided at Hasshiin and was active in the management of agricultural land (previously cited on this website; Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names, etc.)
    Early 15th century Sōzu Jikkō acquired the sakunushi rights to “Rokutanda” within Shinmen-no-shō, an estate of Daijōin (History of Medieval Japanese Shōen, p. 83; present document)
    1456–1457 Hasshiin, or Jikkō’s successors, failed to pay the annual tribute for Rokutanda (History of Medieval Japanese Shōen, p. 83; present document)
    1458 Daijōin placed Rokutanda under direct administration (History of Medieval Japanese Shōen, p. 83; present document)
    1469 Jōsei Goshi, classified as a temporary resident, petitioned for restoration of Rokutanda → petition rejected (History of Medieval Japanese Shōen, p. 83; present document)
    1475 “Sōzu Jōsei ... resided at Hasshiin” (Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 6; previously cited on this website)

    📚 Source: History of Medieval Japanese Shōen, pp. 83–84 (1966)
    National Diet Library Digital Collections, Call No. 210.4-A164t

    Evidence Item 134 🔵 Highly Probable

    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vols. 4 and 5, and Related Indexes — Combined Analysis of the 1468 Appointment of a “Capable Person from within Hasshiin” and the Local Population of Yokota-no-shō

    A record from Ōnin 2 (1468), stating that a sata-nin of Yokota-no-shō was to be appointed “from within Hasshiin,” shows an institutional connection with the later village-headman and village-elder offices held by the Hashimoto family in the early modern period.

    Principal Source ① Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (entry for the 11th month of Ōnin 2)　NDL Call No.: 210.46-D18-T
    Principal Source ② Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 5 (entry for September 8, Bunmei 4; Vol. 5, p. 300)　Same as above
    Principal Source ③ History of Yamatokōriyama City, Main Volume (account of the origins of the Hasshiin settlement)
    Principal Source ④ Documents of Wakatsuki-no-shō, Yamato Province, Vol. 1 (“Register of Tansen Levies on Daijōin Estates, Kyōtoku 2”)
    Principal Source ⑤ General Index to Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki: Personal Names (entries for Emonkurō, Tango-no-shō, Keisan, etc.)

    📋 Analysis of the Appointment of the Yokota-no-shō Sata-nin in Ōnin 2 (1468)

    Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4 (11th month of Ōnin 2): 「庄屋（沙汰人）、事不法無沙汰仁躰也、剩他領中ニ止住爲門跡難義也發志院之內ニ器用躰可被仰付之事、此条尤也、早々可申付云々」
    “The village headman (sata-nin) is a lawless and negligent person, and moreover resides in another estate, causing difficulty for the monzeki. A capable person from within Hasshiin should be appointed to the position. This is entirely appropriate, and the appointment should be made without delay.”

    History of Yamatokōriyama City explains this passage as follows: “This problem was resolved through the intervention of Tsutsui Jun’ei by selecting ‘a capable person from within Hasshiin’ and appointing him to the office, with Sen’ami ordered to carry out the arrangement. This sata-nin represented an institutional predecessor of the village headman (shōya) of the early modern period.”

    📊 Records of Yokota-no-shō in the Kyōtoku 2 (1453) Tansen Register

    The “Register of Tansen Levies on Daijōin Estates, Kyōtoku 2,” contained in Vol. 1 of Documents of Wakatsuki-no-shō, Yamato Province, records Yokota-no-shō as comprising 23 chō and 1 tan, with assessments of 21 kan and 70 mon in Eikyō 3 and 19 kan in Eikyō 10, together with records of Geshi Tango-no-shō and Tsukai Keitoku. This demonstrates that the institutional administration of Yokota-no-shō had already been documented fifteen years before the sata-nin dispute of 1468.

    [Institutional Continuity with Ōnin 2 (1468)]
    Furthermore, according to the analysis in Atsuta Kō’s “Tsutsui Jun’ei and His Age,” included in The Basic Structure of Medieval Society, Geshi Tango-no-shō again appears in connection with the Yokota-no-shō tansen dispute of Ōnin 2 (1468). Acting as geshi, he advanced payment for more than six kan of unpaid dues owed by the tono-bara and peasants of Banjō, Shiratsuchi, and other areas. Accordingly, the administrative structure of Yokota-no-shō recorded in Kyōtoku 2 (1453), involving “Geshi Tango-no-shō and Tsukai Keitoku,” is reinforced by evidence that Tango-no-shō was still functioning in practice as geshi at least fifteen years later, in Ōnin 2. The identification of Tango-no-shō as a member of the Tsutsui lineage, however, is an academic inference drawn by Atsuta Kō from political and personal relationships. (→ Evidence Item 148)

    📊 Signatories to the Yokota-no-shō Written Oath of Bunmei 4 (1472) (Vol. 5, p. 300)

    📌 Evidentiary Significance

    Issue Findings Confidence
    ① Institutional Origins of the Hashimoto Family’s Village-Headman Office In Ōnin 2 (1468), the monzeki decided that “a capable person from within Hasshiin” should be appointed as sata-nin of Yokota-no-shō. History of Yamatokōriyama City explicitly describes this sata-nin institution as a predecessor of the early modern village-headman system. The confirmed fact that Hashimoto Heisaku held the status associated with village-headman and village-elder functions in Meiji 7 raises the possibility that the institutional background of the Hashimoto family’s local administrative role extended back to this 1468 arrangement. The interpretation that the family’s later village-headman office belonged to a tradition of institutionally appointed, locally based administrative positions that could become hereditary is reinforced by the combination of the primary source (Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki, Vol. 4) and the modern municipal history (History of Yamatokōriyama City). 🔵 Highly Probable
    ② Confirmation of Western Hasshiin as an Identifiable Institution through an Independent Index Entry The independent index entry “Western Hasshiin” (Vol. 8, p. 409) confirms that Western Hasshiin, where Senkenbō Kōjin was active, existed as an identifiable institution or locality within the documentary world of Daijōin Jisha Zōjiki. This provides additional index-based support for the historical foundation of Block 127, concerning Kōjin, Western Hasshiin, and the office of Goshi. ✅ Confirmed
    ③ Extension of Documentary Evidence for Yokota-no-shō Administration Back to the Kyōtoku 2 Tansen Register The tansen register of Kyōtoku 2 (1453), preserved in Vol. 1 of Documents of Wakatsuki-no-shō, Yamato Province, demonstrates that Yokota-no-shō was already under systematic administration as a Daijōin estate fifteen years before the sata-nin dispute of Ōnin 2 (1468). The offices of Geshi Tango-no-shō and Tsukai Keitoku are documented, reinforcing the existence of a systematically recorded administrative structure in Yokota-no-shō that extended from the Ōei-period sata-nin system represented by Hikojirō into the later fifteenth century. ✅ Confirmed

    Legal Notes / Applicable Laws and Regulations

    The following is an organized summary of legal points relevant to the representation of genealogical claims, compiled for clarity and professional reference. The following is a summary of legal frameworks potentially relevant to genealogical misrepresentation, compiled for informational purposes only. This does not constitute legal advice and should not be relied upon as such. Applicable law varies by jurisdiction; readers are advised to consult qualified legal counsel in their respective countries.

    Primary Potential Legal Conflicts Under Japanese Law

    1. Public Offices Election Act, Article 235
      Crime of Publication of False Matters: Prohibits the distribution of false information regarding a candidate's career or qualifications to influence an election.
    2. Act against Unjustifiable Premiums and Misleading Representations (Premiums and Representations Act).This Act is broadly comparable to false advertising statutes in other jurisdictions, including the FTC Act in the United States and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive in the EU.
      Article 5 (Prohibition of Misleading Representations): Restricts "superiority misrepresentation" where the quality or content of a service is portrayed as significantly better than it actually is.This Act is broadly comparable to false advertising statutes in other jurisdictions, including the FTC Act in the United States and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive in the EU.
    3. Unfair Competition Prevention Act
      Article 2, Paragraph 1 (Definition of Unfair Competition): Covers acts that cause confusion with another person's goods or business, or misleading indications regarding the quality or content of services.
    4. Other Related Laws
      • Penal Code (Forgery and False Accusation):
        • Article 246 (Fraud): Applicable if financial gain is obtained through a falsified background.
        • Article 172 (False Accusation): Applicable if a formal complaint or accusation is made based on facts known to be false.

    Relevant International Regulations (Potential Issues in Multilingual Expansion)

    United States
    • Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Act, Section 5: Prohibits unfair methods of competition and deceptive acts or practices in commerce.
    • State-level False Advertising Laws: Individual states regulate deceptive representations by businesses.
    • California Civil Code: Background falsification can be subject to civil liability as a fraudulent act.
    • Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008:Prohibits misleading representations about a trader's identity, qualifications, or affiliations. Unverified claims of noble lineage used in commerce may fall within this scope.
    • Defamation Act 2013:Statements must be substantially true, honest opinion, or in the public interest to be defensible. The analysis presented on this site is intended to qualify under the "public interest" defense (Section 4).
    • Fraud Act 2006, Section 2 (Fraud by False Representation): If financial gain is obtained through knowingly false genealogical claims, criminal liability may arise.
    European Union (Including French, Spanish, and Portuguese-speaking regions)
    • Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (2005/29/EC): Prohibits misleading actions and omissions that deceive consumers.
    • GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): Regulations regarding the handling of inaccurate personal data and the "right to rectification."
    • Note on Defamation Risk (EU/UK): Operators of websites making claims about identifiable individuals should be aware that in several EU member states and the United Kingdom (Defamation Act 2013), published statements may carry legal risk if they are found to lower the reputation of a living person. The statements on this site are framed as good-faith historical analysis and public interest commentary, not assertions of personal wrongdoing.
    China (Simplified Chinese)
    • Advertising Law: Prohibits false advertising (notably Articles 4 and 28).
    • Anti-Unfair Competition Law: Prohibits misleading representations that deceive or mislead the public.
    South Korea
    • Act on Fair Labeling and Advertising: Prohibits false or exaggerated advertisements.
    • Unfair Competition Prevention and Trade Secret Protection Act: Prohibits acts that unfairly take advantage of another person’s credit or reputation.
    ⚠️ Important Note for Multilingual Sites: The regulations summarized above are particularly relevant for websites offering content in multiple languages targeting specific jurisdictions. Representations made in different languages may be subject to the laws of the countries where those languages are predominantly used. It is recommended to consult with legal professionals familiar with each specific region when expanding content internationally.This site does not name or accuse specific individuals. All references to "unsubstantiated claims" are directed at categories of conduct, not at identified persons. This approach is consistent with the "public interest" defenses available under Japanese, U.S., EU, and UK law, and is intended to minimize legal risk while preserving the family's right to publish historical analysis.
